en: In the year of Bingshen, Yuzi received the precepts from Master Chengjiang;
thereafter, he studied Chan under Master Daisui. This is the "Preface to the Virtues of Shunzhu" as spoken by the Buddha in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
However, as for the Vinaya section, I had not had the leisure to investigate its reality, and it remained nothing more than a hollow reputation.

It was only after receiving the Dharma from my late master Shuanggui that I traveled south and arrived at the Vinaya Hall of Mount Hua. Upon seeing the majestic deportment [of the masters there], my mind was struck with awe and I felt an unending sense of shame.
Desiring to rely upon their teachings to redeem my prior transgressions, I lamented that I had been adrift on the waves of ignorance and constrained by two or three friends. When I reached—
Having completed his travels, he returned to Yuzhou and first offered incense to his former masters, Fajie and Shishi.

Although the newly established *Huayan* monastic regulations were not yet fully refined, they had been briefly set forth; thus, while Chan and Vinaya were practiced together, there was still a tendency toward the empty and the unreal.

Consequently, he confined himself in retreat for three years, during which time he daily recited the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Ten Thousand Buddhas Sutra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Brahmajāla*, and other scriptures. Only...

Even seeking the punctuation and reading of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (Fàn wǎng) in its upper scroll is difficult; how much more so is it to grasp its meaning and flavor, and to practice according to the Dharma?
It has long been the case that in Shu there have been no Vinaya masters, nor the substance or study of the Vinaya.

Consequently, I have spent over a year closely investigating Master Sanmei’s *Direct Commentary*, yet I have made but slight progress. However, its literary principles are vast and its citations are extensive. My superficial...

It is truly difficult for scholars to enter [this path]. Unless one has awakened to the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*), extensively studied and heard much, and applied a meticulous mind to the sūtras, śāstras, and vinaya, they will not understand the profound intention of the Samādhi Upādhyāya.
Although this present work follows the *zhuzi* (marginal notes) based on the main text, even these *zhuzi* and the filled-in characters have been extracted from the direct exegesis;
occasionally, my own views have been set forth separately, yet these too— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
I dare not fabricate the Dharma-eye of Master Waisan. How could I borrow this to peddle my own reputation?

My true intent is to cleanse my mind and wash my body to atone for the faults of my neglected precepts, and to enable even superficial students to gain some understanding of the essence of the precepts.
The application of the fundamental precepts of the thirty minds and ten stages consists of the ten grave and forty-eight light offenses.

Herein, the master of precepts has a basis; the application of the precepts has substance; and the study of the precepts has its root. By diligently practicing them in person, one realizes the self-nature, which is the originally inherent Vajra Jewel Precept.
This draft is completed and entrusted to the Elder Ciyun Xian to transcribe. At that time...
The twentieth year of the Kangxi era, the *xinyou* year, the twenty-fifth day of the ninth lunar month. Recorded by Huya Deyu.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-brahmajāla-sūtra*, scroll one, according to the vermilion annotations.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, by imperial decree.
Shu Yu Huarock Ji, Guan Shengke Deyu, Shun Zhu Ciyun Temple, Jia Nanhuixian. Transcribed:
The Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Chapter, Part One.
First, regarding the title of the sutra:

"Buddha" is the Sanskrit term *buddha*, which in the language of China means "Awakened. This awakening has three meanings: self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of awakening. What is meant by self-awakening?
Ordinary beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of affliction, thus being unable to awaken themselves; only the Tathāgata...

Coming from the state of an ordinary person, one resolves the mind to uphold the pure precepts of the Buddha. One transcends the involvement of mind, intellect, and consciousness; one departs from the paths of both ordinary beings and sages to study.
By awakening to the true emptiness of one's own nature and realizing that afflictions and karma are illusory, it is called "self-awakening. What is meant by "awakening others"?

Because those of the two vehicles weary of birth and death and seek nirvana, they are unable to awaken others. Only the Tathāgata realizes the wisdom of equality and attains the emptiness of the dharma-nature;

by exercising unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*), he enters the realms of both Māras and Buddhas to extensively transform sentient beings so that they may leave suffering and attain happiness.
Therefore, this is called "awakening others. What is meant by "fulfillment of awakening"? It refers to the Bodhisattva’s arousal of great compassion to deliver sentient beings.
Awakening and practice have not yet been perfected; only when the Tathāgata’s mind is free from both form and matter does fundamental wisdom manifest.

When the five stages of dwelling are exhausted and the two types of death are extinguished, the three types of awakening are perfected and all virtues are complete; therefore, it is called "fulfillment of awakening. The Tathāgata is endowed with the ten titles.
Now, by citing a single title, all ten titles are simultaneously revealed. This Buddha is the sovereign who can preach the Dharma within this Sahā world.
"Preaching" refers to the meaning of the Dharma that is preached. That which is called "the Buddha's preaching" is what was personally proclaimed by the Awakened Sovereign himself;
it is not something that can be preached by Bodhisattvas or Śrāvakas. As for the *Brahmajāla*, the World-Honored One...

Without departing from the Bodhi tree, he ascended to the fourth dhyāna heaven. There, observing the cause of the net-lattice banners of the Great Brahma Kings, he preached that immeasurable worlds are like the holes in a net; each and every world is distinct and different, and they are immeasurable in number.
The gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so. This is the metaphor of the Brahma Net, used here as an illustration to represent [the truth].

This is the Dharma. The metaphor of the infinite mesh-holes of the net represents the infinite worlds, the infinite minds of sentient beings, the infinite gateways of the Buddha's teachings, the infinite distinct stages of the Bodhisattvas, and the infinite realms of enjoyment of all Buddhas.
Since this single metaphor encompasses many meanings, the title is established based on this analogy. As for "Sūtra," it is the Sanskrit term *sūtra*.
*Āgama* (羅): in the language of China, this means *sūtra*. Above, it accords with the principle of all Buddhas, speaking in harmony with the Way;

below, it accords with the capacities of sentient beings, teaching according to their faculties. Hence it is called *sūtra* (契經). Furthermore, *sūtra* (經) means thread, path, spring, and carpenter’s line.
These are all names established according to their respective meanings, yet they do not, in total, go beyond the four characters: "pervasive," "encompassing," "constant," and "dharma."
"Penetrating" (貫) means to thread together the essential purports of all Buddhas; "gathering" (攝) means to encompass the capacities and circumstances of those to be transformed;
"constant" (常) means unchanging through antiquity and the present; and "Dharma" (法) means that both ordinary beings and sages follow the same track.

The four characters "Buddha-spoken Brahma-net" (*Buddhabhāṣita-brahmajāla*) constitute the meaning to be explained (*vācya*), while the character "sūtra" (*sūtra*) constitutes the text that explains it (*vācaka*). The title is formed by combining these two—the expressed and the expresser. Therefore...
Titled: *The Scripture on the Brahma’s Net Spoken by the Buddha*.
2. Explanation of the Translator:
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
As for the Yao Qin: the ruler of the state of Qin was surnamed Yao and named Xing; this refers to the Later Qin and not the Former Qin. As for the "Three Baskets" (Tripiṭaka):
these are the Sūtra-piṭaka, the Vinaya-piṭaka, and the Abhidharma-piṭaka. A "Dharma Master" (Dharmācārya) is one whose learning is comprehensive across these Three Baskets.

Using the sūtras as the eternally abiding and unchanging One Mind, the vinaya as the inherently pure and unconditioned three karmas, and the śāstras as the definitive analysis of right and wrong, heterodoxy and orthodoxy—taking these as one's own teachers and using them to teach others, and manifesting one's name through virtue, they are thus called "Tripiṭaka.
As for the Dharma Master Kumārajīva, his name in the language of China is "Child Longevity" (Tóngshòu); this means that although the master was a child...
Because he possessed venerable virtue, he was called "Child-Lifespan" (Tóngshòu). "Shi" refers to his mastery of the written characters and knowledge of this land.
He was originally a native of Kucha and entered Chang’an in the third year of the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.

He translated ninety-eight sections of sutras and treatises; the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is foremost among them. Regarding the master’s attainment of the stages of sagehood and saintliness, the *Nanshan Ganying Zhuan* states: "Seven..."

The Buddha has already come; he is the master who has translated the scriptures. "One who received the imperial decree" refers to one who, by the command of the King of Qin, translated this scripture.
"Translation" (yi) means to change; it is to change the language of the Brahma kingdom into the speech of the Middle Kingdom (Huaxia).
To present both the Chinese and the Indic together and combine them into a title, it is therefore said: "Translated by Kumārajīva by Imperial Decree."
III. Explanation of the Title of the Chapter:
"The Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind," Part One.

Regarding "Bodhisattva": in the Sanskrit language it is *bodhisattva*; in the Chinese language it means "enlightened sentient being. The Western Regions prefer extensive terminology, whereas here [in China]...

Briefly explaining the joy [of this teaching]: it preserves only the Bodhisattva, whose meaning encompasses *tathāgata*. This refers to one who propagates the Dharma above and transforms beings below.
"The ground of the mind" refers to the thirty minds and ten stages (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, speaking in terms of the Dharma, it refers to the original ground of the mind of sentient beings.
Those who are deluded regarding it revolve through the six realms of ordinary beings; those who awaken to it enter directly into the four noble ranks. Thus do all Buddhas [teach].

The Tathāgata realizes this; the Bodhisattvas cultivate this; and sentient beings are deluded regarding this. Out of compassionate mindfulness, the Tathāgata gives rise to kindness and exercises pity, coming and going through the three realms eight thousand times solely to illuminate the original ground of the mind inherent in all sentient beings.
He desires only that sentient beings rely upon this ground of the mind to receive the Vajra Radiant Jewel Precepts as the fundamental cause for their cultivation.
Seek by reflecting upon yourself; do not seek elsewhere. Therefore, it is called the "Mind-Ground" (*cittabhūmi*). "Chapter" (*pin*) signifies a category;
it carries the meaning of various categories following one another. This great scripture consists of one hundred and twelve fascicles and sixty-one chapters.
The "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Chapter" is precisely the tenth. The text of this single chapter is divided into two fascicles, the upper and the lower.
The upper section clarifies the stages of cultivation, realization, and practice regarding the Bodhisattva’s wisdom and principle—the thirty minds and ten grounds.

The lower section clarifies the Bodhisattva’s mind-ground precepts, including their gravity, allowances, prohibitions, abstentions, observances, transgressions, and violations—namely, the fifty-eight precepts.
As the scroll is divided into upper and lower parts, and this scroll occupies the upper position, it is titled "Part One of the Chapter."
○ Fourth, the correct interpretation of the sutra text:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha was in the fourth dhyāna stage, within the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara,
together with immeasurable Great Brahmā Kings and an assembly of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas, preaching the Lotus Throne.
The Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground as Taught by Vairocana Buddha in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
"At that time" refers to the occasion when immeasurable devas, humans, and bodhisattvas had assembled.
"Śākyamuni Buddha" identifies the principal teacher who performs the transformation; in the Sanskrit language he is called Śākyamuni, which translates in meaning as "The Capable Benevolent One."
"Silent stillness. It expresses the virtue of the lineage of the Able One (Śākyamuni) through silent stillness, and it manifests the ultimate principle through silent stillness.

Furthermore, while the Able One does not abide in nirvāṇa, silent stillness does not abide in saṃsāra. Moreover, "benevolent" (ren) means patience (*kṣānti*); hearing good, one does not immediately rejoice, and hearing evil, one does not immediately become angry—it is the ability to endure both good and evil.
Furthermore, it refers to the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Therefore, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). Regarding the phrase "in the stage of the fourth dhyāna," this indicates the place where one dwells. "In" (*zhai*) means to dwell. "Fourth" (*di*) refers to the sequence;
that is, there are nine stages in total across the three realms. The desire realm constitutes one stage, called the "Stage of Mixed Dwelling of the Five Destinies. The form realm has four stages:
the first dhyāna is called the "Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Seclusion," and the second dhyāna... [and so forth].
The first is called the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration (*samādhi*). The third dhyāna is called the stage of sublime bliss free from joy.
The fourth dhyāna is called the stage of purity through equanimity and mindfulness. The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has four stages: first, the stage of the infinity of space;

second, the stage of the infinity of consciousness; third, the stage of nothingness; and fourth, the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This corresponds to the [upper] levels of the form realm.
The fourth dhyāna is the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness. Among the nine stages, it is the dwelling place of the Heavenly King Maheśvara;
it is also called the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*akaniṣṭha*).

Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmamegha-bhūmi*) frequently reside there to preach the Dharma. *Maheśvara* translates into Chinese as "Great Sovereign" (*Dà Zìzài*). Furthermore, it is also said:
He is majestic and powerful; some call him the Three-Eyed One. This deity is the ultimate pinnacle of honor within the three realms.
The *Fuxing ji* states: "The Heavenly King of the Form Realm has three eyes and eight arms; he rides a white ox and holds a white fly-whisk.

Possessing great majesty and power, he dwells in the abode of the Bodhisattvas and can know the number of raindrops in the three realms; he governs and controls the great trichiliocosm. Regarding this:
Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), this deity alone is honored; he is the sovereign who presides over all the Great Brahmā Kings (*Mahābrahmā-devaputra*).

Because the Buddha wished to manifest that the path of the mind, its ethical discipline (*śīla*), and its secrets are exceedingly profound, most honorable, and most noble, he preached therein within the inner courtyard of the palace of the Great Brahmā King. The phrase "with immeasurable [others]" indicates those who were listening to the Dharma.

As for "the multitude": the immeasurable Great Brahmā Heavenly Kings manifest as one Śākyamuni corresponding to a thousand, a hundred, or ten billion Śākyamunis, thereby marking a thousand, a hundred, or ten billion worlds;
thus, the Brahmā Kings within those thousand, a hundred, or ten billion worlds assemble simultaneously.
As for "unspeakably unspeakable multitudes of bodhisattvas," this refers to the assembly of listeners at the Dharma gathering, not [to the Buddhas].
These are all beings of great capacity who can be known through calculation. When it speaks of the "Lotus-womb World" (*Padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), it refers to the place where the Dharma is received.
When it says "spoken by Vairocana Buddha," it clarifies the person who transmits the Dharma.
Thus, the teaching of the Dharma has its lineage, and the transmission of the Dharma has its source. In the Sanskrit language, *Vairocana* means...

"Purity and Fulfillment" means that all evils are purified and exhausted, while all virtues are fully perfected; this is the Sambhogakāya Buddha. Its meaning is explained extensively in the lower fascicle.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground": the term "Mind-Ground Chapter" is explained in the preceding text.

"Dharma" (dharma) carries the meaning of "guiding and maintaining," while "Gate" (mukha) carries the meaning of "penetration. This refers to practicing according to the Dharma until one reaches Buddhahood.
The Ground. This refers to what are called the "Single Path to Nirvana" of the Bhagavāns of the ten directions, the Great Dharani Gate, and the Non-dual Dharma Gate.
As the Master said: "Having entered this gate, do not harbor conceptual understanding," and so forth. Therefore, it is called a "Dharma Gate.
This section describes the teaching of the Transformation Buddha, specifically the "Chapter on the Exposition of the Mind-Ground Dharma Gate."
This was how it came about.
At that time, the body of Śākyamuni emitted rays of wisdom-light, which illuminated everything from this Palace of the Heavenly King up to the Lotus-womb World-system (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*).

"At this time" refers to the occasion when Śākyamuni Buddha was expounding to the assembly the chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground as taught by Vairocana Buddha and its underlying causes and conditions.
Regarding "Śākyamuni’s realization and vision": "body" refers to the entire body; "emitting" means manifesting;
"wisdom" (hui) refers to the wisdom of suchness (tathatā); and "light" (guang) refers to the radiance of the fruit-virtue.
This universal radiance is not possessed by the Buddhas alone; it is inherent in all sentient beings.

Yet, because they are obstructed by ignorance, which veils their wisdom, they fail to realize it. Therefore, the World-Honored One, through great skillful means, has graciously revealed this light, none other than to illuminate the light of the precepts within the original ground of the mind that each person possesses, so that they may cultivate and maintain it for themselves.
This is the realization and verification. "That which is illuminated" refers to the statement that follows from what precedes; it indicates the locus where the entire light shines.
From the Palace of the Heavenly King up to the Lotus-womb World (*padmagarbha-loka-dhātu*), these demonstrate the extent of the locus illuminated by the entire light.
Sentient and insentient beings alike are entirely encompassed by this all-pervading wisdom-light; they are gathered within this single radiance.
This adornment constitutes the manifestation of auspicious signs through the emission of light, describing the causal conditions for its inception.
Within all those worlds, all sentient beings looked at one another with joy and happiness, yet they were unable to understand this light;
they all gave rise to doubts as to what its cause and conditions were. Immeasurable devas and humans likewise gave rise to such doubts.

Regarding the phrase "all therein" (*tatra sarve*), this collectively refers to both the primary and secondary retributions—that is, the celestial palaces and the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha*).

In every place illuminated by the light, all sentient beings throughout all worlds gaze upon that light one toward another, experiencing joy and happiness. Because their types and numbers are immeasurable, they are termed "all."
Because the various phenomena arise together, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). This light did not exist previously, yet now it has suddenly appeared.

Since each has beheld this light, they all protect and benefit one another; therefore, it is said that they are joyful and happy. However, they are not yet able to know the nature of this light and so forth.
Although the jewel-light is emitted, the marks of defilement have not yet been emptied. Ordinary people with their physical eyes are merely bathed by this light;
thus, they are unable to know for what causes and conditions this light was realized, nor are they able to know for what causes and conditions it is emitted.
Not only do ordinary beings of the broad earth give rise to such doubts, but even those who possess the radiance of their own bodies...

The minds and wisdom of the immeasurable devas and humans were obscured and dull; they did not know from where the light emanating from the Buddha’s body originated, and they likewise gave rise to doubts.
This refers to what is called: "Without leaving its original place, it is eternally profound and still; seek it and you will find it, yet it cannot be seen.
This section describes the third occasion of beholding the light and giving rise to doubt, setting forth the introduction to the inquiry. The above is a general account of the people.
The devas did not fully comprehend the ultimate causes and conditions of the Buddha’s radiance.
At that time, from within the assembly, the Bodhisattva Master of Profound Penetration and Flower Radiance arose from the Great Adornment Flower Radiance Samādhi.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he emitted rays of light the color of white clouds of vajra; this light illuminated all worlds.
"At that time" refers to the moment when humans and devas conceived doubts and reflections. "Among the assembly" indicates that this gathering constitutes the primary audience for the teaching.
This Bodhisattva is a great Bodhisattva, the leader of the primary audience within the unspeakably unspeakable assembly of the *Avataṃsaka* oceanic gathering.
The Buddha emitted this light, which is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom; it is not...

Those who possess great wisdom cannot fully comprehend it. Only this Bodhisattva, who possesses the flower of great practice and whose wisdom is brilliant and subtle, can penetrate this light and act as the leader and guide among the assembly.
Because his name is manifested through his virtue, he is called the Bodhisattva Chief of Profound Penetration and Flower-Light.
As for "arising from the Great Adornment Flower-Light Samādhi": [it means that he has emerged from this state].
It arises from itself. Regarding the meaning of "Great, Vast, and Complete," there are three aspects to the ocean of the fruition of the adorned *dharmakāya*:
first, the six perfections and myriad practices; second, all-encompassing wisdom; and third, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Among these, the "flowers" are the flowers of practice.
Virtue and merit constitute adornment; radiance is wisdom, which constitutes the adornment of wisdom;
samādhi is right concentration, which constitutes the adornment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Because these three are fully perfected, it is called "Great Adornment.
This Bodhisattva, dwelling within this concentration, arises from that very concentration; therefore, it is said he comes "from the Flower-Light of Great Adornment."

This clarifies the arising of samādhi. Regarding the phrase "by the Buddha’s spiritual power" and so forth, it means that when this bodhisattva inquires about the Great Dharma, they must rely upon the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power to be able to give rise to wisdom. Thus, it is asked: "By virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power."
Only then can one emit the radiant light of the vajra-like, firm, noble, white-cloud-pure wisdom that is like an illusion.
As for "the light illuminating all worlds," this reveals that the traces of this light are pervasive, perfectly interfused, and without obstruction.

This section comprises the assembly of the four patriarchs of the Mysterious [Teachings]. Within the inquiry, there are two parts. First, the arising of meditative concentration and the emission of light that illuminates all beings in order to gather the assembly.
Among them, all the bodhisattvas come together in a great assembly; with one mind and different voices, they inquire about this light. The light...
Regarding what these characteristics are:
"within this" refers to within all worlds. "All bodhisattvas" refers to the great bodhisattvas within all worlds.
"They all come to assemble" means that they do so because of the illumination of the light.
They gathered together at this place in unison. Those who shared the same intention were moved with awe by the light and, expressing a common doubt, questioned him.
As for their speaking with different voices, it was because each person had their own body and mouth, which varied according to the individual.
When they asked, "What kind of appearance does this light have? they were inquiring about the wisdom emanating from the entire body of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

It is light. This light is precisely the realm within the fruit [of Buddhahood]. Previously, when sentient beings had not yet resolved their minds on Bodhisattvahood, they merely doubted the causes and conditions;
thus it was asked, "By what cause and by what condition? These various Bodhisattvas, however, are persons within the state of the cause, yet they inquire about matters pertaining to the fruit;
therefore it is asked, "What are the characteristics of this light? By what cause and by what condition? This is followed by Śākyamuni’s request for an explanation.
Questioning Śāntamati regarding the passage on what causes and conditions allow all sentient beings to attain the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva and so forth;
this concerns the nature of "light. Furthermore, it concerns the subsequent inquiry into what the marks of the fruit of Buddhahood will be upon its attainment.
This section constitutes the second assembly’s presentation of questions. From the beginning up to this point is the introduction.
The section on divisions is concluded. Below, the Main Body (Zhengzongfen) is elucidated.
At that time, Śākyamuni immediately lifted up and received the great assembly of this world, returning to the Lotus-womb Treasury World (Padmagarbhalokadhātu).
Within a palace of hundreds of billions of purple-gold adamantines and radiant light, he beheld Vairocana Buddha seated upon a majestic throne of hundreds of billions of lotus flowers,
amidst a blaze of brilliant radiance.
"At this time" refers to the moment when this great assembly of humans, devas, and bodhisattvas requested instruction.
Śākyamuni is the manifested trace-Buddha who uplifts and receives the great assembly of this world; these beings are those who are transformed by him.
"Uplift" (*qíng*) refers to being held above, while "receive" (*jiē*) refers to being supported below. Thus, he uplifts and receives this light, and that which is illuminated by it is one [realm].
This refers to the great assembly of those with the root-nature who have gathered from throughout all worlds, having resolved their doubts.

As for the phrase "returning," it means that this Śākyamuni, along with all the bodhisattvas and all sentient beings, originally flowed forth from a single ray of light within the fundamental and manifested traces of the Mind-Ground Precepts of Vairocana in the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu); now they once again return to their original essence. Thus, [it is called] the Lotus [Assembly].

Regarding "the lotus pedestal" and so forth: this refers to the locus of the fundamental and manifested forms of Vairocana, namely the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*), which will be explained in detail in the subsequent text.
"A hundred million" includes four hundred million, ten billion, one hundred billion, ten trillion, and one hundred trillion;
this [number] is specifically the three hundredth ten-trillionth within those four hundred million. The radiance of purple-golden diamond (*vajra*) symbolizes the realm of bodhi-wisdom.
The palace represents the realm and principle of *nirvāṇa*. This means that the principle arises from the clarity of wisdom, while wisdom is produced by the principle.
Through the principle, wisdom is made profound; through wisdom, the principle is realized. Thus, principle and wisdom are perfectly interfused; the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are unimpeded;

and the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are perfectly interfused, such that the trace and the source are non-dual. One who beholds Vairocana Buddha sees Śākyamuni returning to his original realm, beholding him face-to-face.
One directly perceives the realm of the Dharmakāya and Jñānakāya of the Original Teacher; this is what is meant by "today, for the first time, seeing one’s own mother’s face.
Those who sit upon the majestic, radiant thrones of hundreds of millions of billions of lotuses are none other than those seated upon the throne of Vairocana.
As for the use of lotus flowers as seats, the blossoming of the lotus symbolizes the simultaneous manifestation of both the provisional and the ultimate. Majestic...
"Flame" refers to the appearance of blazing intensity. "Radiance" refers to the characteristic of the illuminating function of wisdom.

Because this Tathāgata, while on the stage of causal practice (*hetu-bhūmi*), destroyed delusions and realized the truth through great wisdom, he attained, within the state of fruition, the merit of retribution that abides upon this lotus throne of brilliant radiance;
it is both for his own peace and for the peace of others. That they are all called "one hundred million *koṭis*" [refers to their number].
That is to say, the light of the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundred billion Śākyamunis forms a lotus-flower seat that surrounds the palace and throne of Vairocana;
hence it is called the "seat of a hundred trillion brilliant, radiant lotus-flowers. This clarifies the aspect of the perfect convergence of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
While the *Avataṃsaka* explains this extensively as a hundred trillion, here, at the beginning of the main body of the teaching (*śāstrakāya*), the path of the mind-ground is clarified.

There are four [sections]. First, the Emanation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) acts as the petitioner on behalf [of the assembly]; this also has two parts. First, "Gathering Beings and Returning to the Source," which describes the principle that the function of gathering beings returns to the essence, such that the Buddha of Birth and the Buddha of Essence are without difference.
At that time, Śākyamuni and the great assembly simultaneously paid homage at the feet of Vairocana Buddha. Śākyamuni Buddha then said:
"In this world, by what causes and conditions do all sentient beings, both those on earth and those in space, attain the ten stages of the Bodhisattva path and achieve the fruit of Buddhahood?
What are their characteristics? As described in the 'Chapter on the Source of the Buddha-nature'..."
He extensively inquired about all the seeds of the bodhisattvas.
At that time, Śākyamuni arrived and, as the Buddha Śākyamuni spoke, he described the ritual for requesting the Dharma; this signifies the devotion of the three karmas.
"At one time" refers to the moment a single thought of reverence arises, which signifies the devotion of the mental karma. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, which is the body.
"Karma" refers to sincerity. Śākyamuni Buddha said that verbal karma is sincerity. Even when the Buddhas request the Dharma, they still maintain this ritual;
it may be known that the same applies to other petitioners of the Dharma.
"In this world" refers to within this Sahā world. "The earth and space": the earth is the human realm, and space is the celestial realm. One.

"All sentient beings" refers to those among all beings in the worlds of humans and devas whom Śākyamuni Tathāgata uplifts and receives, whose doubts are resolved upon seeing the light, and whose spiritual faculties have matured. As for the causes and conditions by which they attain the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva:
"causes and conditions" refers to causal practice, while "stages" refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. The meaning is that all sentient beings [attain this through such means].
Having resolved to attain Bodhicitta and returned from delusion to the truth, one desires to cultivate the Buddha-way;

ultimately, by what causes and practices does one reach the fruit of Buddhahood? This is the first question, which corresponds to the previous inquiry regarding the causes and conditions for becoming a deva or human.
As for the phrase "what will be the appearance when the fruit of Buddhahood is attained," the meaning is that at the time of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood—

"In the end, what kind of realm is this? This is the second question. It refers to the meaning of the previous passage where the Lord Flower-Light emits light to assemble the multitude, who, with one heart but different voices, ask what the characteristics of these lights are.
This is a brief inquiry, whereas in the "Chapter on the Source of Buddha-Nature," there is a detailed inquiry into the Buddha-nature that is the seed of all bodhisattvas.

The "Chapter on the Original Source" (*Mūlaprakaraṇa*) is one of the sixty-one chapters of the Great Treatise (*Mahāśāstra*). Within that chapter, it extensively clarifies the true causal seed for attaining Buddhahood.
Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is identical to bodhicitta; it is the meaning of original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*). When situated within the state of sentient beings, it is termed "Buddha-nature";
when not situated within the state of sentient beings, it is termed "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*). Here, because we are discussing its presence within the causal state, [it is called Buddha-nature].
This is called Buddha-nature; the seed of the bodhisattva is precisely the mind of the causal stage. This is the second section, the formal request for the resolution of doubts.
Thus concludes the化身佛 (nirmāṇakāya buddha) acting as the questioner.

At that time, Vairocana Buddha was filled with great joy; he manifested the essential nature of the light of space and entered the samādhi of the eternally abiding Dharma-body of the original source of Buddhahood, demonstrating it to the great assembly.

"At that time" refers to the moment when Śākyamuni requested instruction. "Greatly rejoicing" means that this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground enables sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness; as this is precisely the Buddha's fundamental intention, he rejoices greatly.
"Manifesting the essence-nature of the light of space": here, "light" is the wisdom within the portion of the fundamental essence-nature.
This light pervades the ten directions without coming or going; it circulates through the three periods of time without undergoing change or transition.
Throughout all worlds—far and near, ancient and modern—all material phenomena appear in response to conditions.
Yet, within this, not even a single mark of light as small as a mustard seed can be found; it is just like empty space. Therefore...
It is said that the nature of the essence is the radiance of empty space. Regarding the "Samādhi of the Original Source, the Buddha-attainment, and the Ever-abiding Dharmakāya":

"Original" (ben) refers to the root; "source" (yuan) refers to the deep wellspring. This means that this essential nature is the fundamental root and deep source from which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain the Way of Buddhahood.
It is eternal and unchanging; it abides without moving. It is a dharma of non-action and non-conditioning.

This is the samādhi of the body in right concentration and right reception. "To show it to the great assembly" means to use this very source of right concentration to demonstrate it to the great assembly, causing them to awaken to and enter the luminosity of wisdom that is inherently possessed by themselves.
The adamantine jewel-precept, once attained, is attained forever; it shall never again be lost or regressed. This is Śākyamuni’s response. Response.

There are three parts: first, a general response concerning the *cittabhūmi* (the ground of the mind); second, an extensive response explaining the names; and third, a concluding response to the meaning of the questions.

The first, the general response, has four sections: first, revealing the characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); second, admonishing the audience to listen, reflect, and practice; third, personally recounting the causal practices; and fourth, citing the characteristics of one's own fruition.
This [first section] reveals the characteristics of meditative concentration.
"Listen attentively, O sons of the Buddha; contemplate well and practice accordingly.
Regarding "sons of the Buddha," the Buddhas are their compassionate fathers, and they are called "sons" because they succeed to the Buddhas' legacy.

"Listen attentively" and so forth refers to the thorough examination through the three types of wisdom: hearing, contemplation, and cultivation. "Listening" means receiving; that is to say, if the assembly of sons of the Buddha...

If one listens with careful discernment and sincere faith, yet the Dharma heard does not correspond with the mind, then since the mind and the Dharma do not correspond, from what source could mental wisdom and sublime conduct arise?
Therefore, one is first cautioned to listen. Regarding "skillfully reflecting and practicing":
if one reflects differently from how one listened, then listening is of no benefit; if one practices differently from how one reflected, then reflection is likewise in vain.
It is said: "It is like a person who counts another's treasures while not possessing even half a coin of his own;
though one has much learning, if one does not practice the Dharma, it is likewise so. Therefore, he again exhorts them to contemplate and practice.
This is Śāntarakṣita Tathāgata’s proclamation to the assembly present before him, which serves as the general response containing the two exhortations to listen, contemplate, and practice.
I have practiced the Mind-Ground for a hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; taking this as the cause, I first abandoned the state of an ordinary person and attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
Regarding the phrase "I [have practiced] for a hundred *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpas]": "I" refers to myself, Śākyamuni; "have" (*yi*) means that the karmic process has already been completed and experienced.
This means: *asaṃkhyeya* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "incalculable. *Kalpa* is a Sanskrit term;

here it is translated as "discrimination of time periods. It says that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni has already passed through the time periods of a hundred incalculable *kalpas*, taking the cultivation of these thirty minds and ten stages as the causal conditions. From the initial generation of the mind, he first renounced...
Ordinary beings who, throughout the duration of these kalpas, have not removed even a hair’s breadth of ignorance,

afflictions, greed, anger, or pride, yet claim to have suddenly transcended the Buddha-way through a single morning or evening of minor causes and conditions, slight merit and practice, or half-understood knowledge— though this may be so at first...

One who abandons the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and immediately attains equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is one by whom sentient beings have received the Buddha-precepts;
such a person enters the rank of all Buddhas. It is only after enduring long-term diligent suffering that one can achieve this. As the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* states:
"It is impossible for any Buddha to attain unsurpassed bodhi without passing through three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Thus, there is no such case.
Therefore, it is for this reason that one first awakens to the nature-sea of Vairocana and subsequently practices the gateway of Samantabhadra’s conduct;
there is indeed a profound significance to this. This constitutes the general response in which he three times sets forth his own causal practice.
It answers the question of what causes and conditions allow transformed Buddhas and all sentient beings to achieve the ten stages of the Bodhisattva path.
He is titled *Rocana Buddha*. He dwells in the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury World-Ocean.
"Titled" refers to his name. *Rocana*—the interpretation of which was seen above—is the name of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) Buddha. "Dwells" means to reside.
Regarding the Lotus-Womb Treasury World-Ocean, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that there are twenty layers of Flower-Treasury World-Oceans,
all situated within the Fragrant Water Ocean of Boundless Sublime Flower Radiance. This world is where,
in the past, Vairocana Tathāgata cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva for as many eons as there are atoms in this world.
During his practice, he was purified by the proximity of Buddhas as numerous as atoms; now, having realized that fruit, he dwells here.

This Sahā Flower Treasury World (Puṣpasaṃcayakṣetra) is situated precisely at the thirteenth layer, surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in thirteen Buddha-fields—this being the place where Vairocana Tathāgata appeared. [In] the Sanskrit language...
Vairocana—whose Chinese translation means "pervading all places"—is the name of the Dharmakāya Buddha. The Sanskrit term *Rocana* (or *Lośana*) translates as "various lights shining everywhere";
it refers to that which shines universally throughout all things. Although the names of these two sūtras differ, their essence is the same:
the Dharma is the Reward-body (*Saṃbhogakāya*), and the Reward-body is the Dharma-body. The Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha dwells within a lotus flower.
The "Treasury Adorned World-Ocean" is the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) Vairocana Buddha abiding within the Lotus-Pedestal Treasury World-Ocean.
"Ocean" carries the meaning of inclusion, profundity, vastness, and the encompassing reflection of all things;

it is the environment and the person (the *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* and *sabhāga-vipāka*) of the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis, none of whom do not arise from this Flower Treasury World of Vairocana.
It flows forth from the ocean of the mind of Śākyamuni Buddha. Because this ocean possesses the two gates of True Suchness (tathatā) and arising-and-ceasing, it is called an "ocean.
Within this general response, four points are raised to illustrate the characteristics of its own fruit. Regarding these characteristics of the fruit, there are two meanings:

a general clarification of the characteristics of the fruit and a specific clarification of the characteristics of the fruit. This is the first, the general clarification of the characteristics of the fruit. Question: What are the causes? That is to say—
First, awakening to this luminous Vajra Jewel Precept within the Mind-Ground is the cause. Question: What is the condition? Answer:
Practicing the Dharma-gate of the thirty minds and ten stages according to the teaching is the condition.

Question: What is the fruit? Answer: Attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment is the fruit. Question: What is its characteristic? Answer: It is designated as the Buddha Vairocana dwelling upon a lotus.

The Flower-Pedestal Treasury World-Ocean has the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—as its characteristic. This concludes the general answer to the two questions regarding cause and effect.
Its pedestal is all-pervasive with a thousand petals; each petal is one world, thus constituting a thousand worlds. I manifest as a thousand [Buddhas].

Śākyamuni presides over a thousand worlds. Subsequently, regarding a single leaf-world, there are further ten billion Sumeru mountains, ten billion suns and moons, ten billion sets of four continents, ten billion Jambudvīpas, and ten billion Śākyamuni Bodhisattvas.
Seated beneath ten billion bodhi trees, each spoke upon the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground as you have asked.
Each of the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine Śākyamunis likewise manifested a thousand times ten million Śākyamunis, and it was just the same for them all.
That terrace is one great lotus flower within the Great Fragrant Water Sea. Within the flower is a lotus pedestal; upon the pedestal is a Buddha.
This Buddha is the Śākyamuni who is both the original and the manifested (honji-suijaku); he is the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) among the primary retributions (*po-jō*).
The pedestal is the flower-pedestal where Śākyamuni resides; it is the environmental retribution (*e-jō*) upon which the bodies of the original and manifested Buddhas rely.

This is the land [of that Buddha]. Regarding the phrase "its terraces are all-encompassing and equal," this means that the original lotus pedestal is surrounded on all sides by a thousand petals, and each petal constitutes a world;
thus, they form a thousand worlds. This reveals both the primary and secondary rewards (*niśraya-vipāka*) of the fundamental and the manifested [bodies].
Furthermore, it manifests as the world that serves as the secondary reward for the manifested Buddha. I have transformed myself into a thousand Śākyamunis.
The term "etc. refers to my own self-designation as Vairocana; this is not the "self" of ordinary beings or outsiders.
This reveals both the fundamental and the manifested bodies of the Buddha, as well as the manifested body of the Buddha that appears as the Teacher within the world-realm of the traces.
Since the Buddhas in each and every one of these worlds are all bodies manifested by Vairocana, it is said: "I manifest myself as the thousand Śākyamunis."
Kāśyapa occupies a thousand-world system. Subsequently, he manifests his traces by relying on a single world-system;

furthermore, he transforms this trace-body into a land that serves as the *niṣyanda* (retributive) environment for the Buddha-body. Regarding the phrase "subsequently relying on one petal" and so forth:
this refers to taking up the very last petal from among the thousand petals as an illustrative example. This single trace-flower further manifests as ten billion flowers.
Each individual flower constitutes a world; thus, there are ten billion worlds. Within each individual world, there is a single Mount Sumeru;
thus, there are ten billion Sumeru mountains. In the Sanskrit language, "Sumeru" means "Wondrously High" (Miaogao).
Because it is composed of various jewels and rises above all other mountains, each individual Mount Sumeru possesses...
Each sun and moon revolves around Mount Sumeru; therefore, there are ten billion suns and moons.
Each sun and moon travels through the four continents (cāturdvīpa) in one day and night; therefore, there are ten billion sets of four continents.
Within each set of four continents, there is one Jambudvīpa in the south; therefore, there are ten billion Jambudvīpas. [In the original] Sanskrit: *jambudvīpa*.
Jambudvīpa is translated here as "Supreme Gold" (*śreṣṭha-suvarṇa*), because the trees there flow with liquid gold and the rivers produce golden sand.
Regarding the "one hundred billion Śākyamuni Bodhisattvas," this further reveals the body of the Buddha who manifests his traces, and moreover, it reveals the Buddha-body that manifests those traces.
That is to say, each of the thousand Śākyamunis manifests ten billion Śākyamunis as appropriate for those to be converted;

hence it is said that "ten billion Bodhisattvas and Śākyamunis sit upon ten billion [thrones]," and so forth. This summary reveals the meaning of the Tathāgata’s compassionate intent (*vatsalya*) in manifesting birth, renunciation, the attainment of enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the deliverance of sentient beings. Each of these Śākyamunis manifests [these deeds].

Regarding the realization of the Way through the eight phases: from the very beginning, they were all simultaneously present without departing from the Bodhi tree to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and even up to the Brahma Heaven.
In all these places, they preached the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground transmitted by Vairocana, and all emitted bodily radiance to stir the hearts of humans and devas.
Therefore, it is said that beneath each of the ten billion Bodhi trees, [the Buddha] sat and spoke on the Bodhisattva path as you have asked.

The *tuo* (mound) is the ground of the mind. Regarding the "remaining nine hundred" and so forth: from among the thousand flowers mentioned above, one flower is singled out to manifest one Buddha among the thousand Buddhas;
the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine Śākyamunis are likewise manifested. Furthermore, how does this work?
Since one leaf and one Buddha are manifested in this manner, so too are the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine Śākyamunis.

The environment and inhabitants of Kāśyapa’s world were likewise each manifested individually; even the inquiry into the Dharma-gate of the Ground of the Mind was similarly so—without duality or distinction.
These two [sections] specifically clarify the characteristics of the fruition (*phala*). Within the characteristics of the fruition, there are two parts:
first, arising from the essence to manifest function; second, withdrawing function back into the essence. This [section] is the first: arising from the essence to manifest function.

The preceding section generally indicated the characteristics of the fruit to clarify the essence of the environment and its inhabitants; this section specifically clarifies the characteristics of the fruit to clarify the functions of the environment and its inhabitants.
The Buddha upon the thousand-petaled lotus is my transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis are the transformation bodies of those thousand Śākyamunis.
I am their source, and am named Vairocana Buddha.
This Śāntamati understands that ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle cannot penetrate the function that is identical to the essence;

yet they claim there is a real distinction between the fundamental and the manifested, or between the original and the responsive manifestations. Therefore, he states that the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are the transformation bodies of the thousand Śākyamunis.
The thousand Śākyamunis are the emanations (nirmāṇakāya) of Vairocana. Ascending the platform and so forth represent the arising of function from essence;
that is, the function of the very essence. This clarifies the reversion of function to essence—that is, the essence of the very function.

It correctly demonstrates that essence is not separate from function and function is not separate from essence; essence and function are non-dual. Therefore, it is said: "I take this as the name of the source."
He is Vairocana Buddha. These two [aspects] subsume function within essence.

At that time, upon the seat of the Lotus-womb Treasury, Vairocana Buddha extensively answers the questions posed by the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis concerning the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground Dharma" (these two extensively explain the names).
"At that time" refers to the moment when the fundamental and the phenomenal were revealed, and all manifestations were brought back into the essence.

"Extensive answer" is said in contrast to the brief answer above; the brief answer merely stated, "I have cultivated the mind-ground for a hundred kalpas," yet it was feared that the assembly might not know what kind of mind-ground this was. Therefore, the words of the request are cited here, and the detailed answer follows below.

Thus it is. All Buddhas should know that within the stage of firm faith and patience (*kṣānti*), there are ten minds directed toward the fruit of the ten stages of departure (*daśa-prasthāna-citta*): first, the mind of relinquishment; second, the mind of precept; third, the mind of patience;
fourth, the mind of diligence; fifth, the mind of concentration; sixth, the mind of wisdom; seventh, the mind of aspiration; eighth, the mind of protection; ninth, the mind of joy...
The "mind" refers to the ten summit-minds (*daśa-śīrṣa-citta*).
The "various Buddhas" are the thousand Buddhas, the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, and the Buddhas of the various traces.

"One should know" means that the Original Buddha calls out to these Buddhas of the various traces, saying: "You should know the names and stages of these ten minds within the ten stages of setting forth (*daśa-prasthāna*)."

Regarding the ten minds of progression toward the fruit within the stage of firm conviction and patience (*kṣānti*): "firm" (*dṛḍha*) means solid; "conviction" (*śraddhā*) means faith; and "patience" (*kṣānti*) means endurance.
These are distinguished as the three levels of worthiness (*tri-pudgala*) and the ten stages of the noble ones (*daśa-ārya*). The Sūtra divides this into six stages, each possessing five factors:

intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), wisdom (*prajñā*), firmness (*dṛḍha*), and patience (*kṣānti*). Each of these five factors is further divided into six types according to the six stages. These constitute the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*).
"Stage" refers to the stage of the lineage of cultivation (*śikṣāgotra*). "Contemplation" refers to abiding in contemplation. "Wisdom" refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Firmness" refers to firm faith. "Patience" refers to patient acceptance through faith. When these two factors are combined, it is termed "firm patience of faith" (*adhimukti-kṣānti*).

Regarding the term "middle," it signifies that within this firm patience of faith there are ten types of persons who simultaneously give rise to the vast aspiration for upward propagation and downward transformation, and who proceed toward [enlightenment].

The Buddha-ocean is such that none can cause one to regress; therefore, it is said that within the stage of "firm faith and patience" (*kṣānti*), one directs the ten minds of advancement toward the fruit.
What are these ten minds? First, the mind of relinquishment (*tyāga*); "relinquishment" means giving away, carrying the sense of having no stinginess or regret. Second, the mind of precept (*śīla*);

"precept" refers to the monastic rules, carrying the sense of extinguishing evil and generating good. Third, the mind of patience (*kṣānti*); "patience" means acceptance, [carrying the sense of] being at peace...
1. The meaning of patience as being unshakable. 2. The mind of exertion; "exertion" refers to diligence (*vīrya*), which carries the meaning of advancing toward [the goal] without retreat.

3. The mind of concentration; "concentration" refers to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), which carries the meaning of being neither dull nor distracted. 4. The mind of wisdom; "wisdom" refers to insight (*prajñā*).

1. The mind of illumination (*āloka-citta*): the meaning of unimpeded clarity and realization. 2. The mind of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta*): "aspiration" means yearning; the meaning of seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below.
3. The mind of protection (*ārakṣā-citta*): "protection" means guarding and maintaining; the meaning of being able to skillfully act as a protective embankment.

4. The mind of joy (*pramudita-citta*): "joy" means rejoicing; the meaning of being free from suffering and attaining happiness. 5. The mind of the crown (*mūrdhan-citta*): "crown" refers to the crown of the head; the meaning of being most honored and unsurpassed.
The Meaning of "Venerable. ○ These two explain the characteristics of the *cittabhūmi* (mind-ground), the first clarifying the characteristics of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten minds of aspiration (*daśa-prasthānacitta*), one enters into the patience of the firm dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). The ten minds of cultivation (*daśa-paripuṣṭacitta*) are directed toward the fruit:

1. the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), 2. the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), 3. the mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), 4. the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), 5. the mind of giving (*dāna*), 6. the mind of kind speech (*priyavāditā*).
Seventh is the beneficial mind; eighth is the harmonious mind; ninth is the concentrated mind; tenth is the wisdom mind.
From this phrase, one follows the preceding [section] to enter the "firm" (kṣānti) stage. Regarding the subsequent mention of "firm dharma-patience" (*dharmakṣānti*) and so forth:

"Dharma" refers to knowing that all dharmas are empty and provisional, yet establishing all dharmas to transform sentient beings—this is precisely the provisional dharma. Within these ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*),...

"Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the nature-lineage (*gotra*). "Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the contemplation of practice. "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

"Firmness" (*dṛḍha*) refers to firmness in the Dharma. "Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to patience in the Dharma. Because these two factors are combined in speech, it is called "firm Dharma-patience" (*dṛḍhadharma-kṣānti*).

In this stage, one has previously entered deeply into the profound and subtle truth of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*). The sublime practices for enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*) arise based upon this truth, mobilizing the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
The mind practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to benefit sentient beings, nurture the holy embryo, and perfect holy virtue, thereby heading toward the ocean of the Buddha-fruit.
Therefore, it is said: "The ten ways of nurturing the mind directed toward the fruit of Bodhi. What are these ten ways of nurturing the mind?

1. The mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*): the sense of cherishing and caring for sentient beings. 2. The mind of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*): the sense of pitying and taking pity on sentient beings. 3. The mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā-citta*):

the sense of rejoicing when others obtain happiness. 4. The mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*): the sense of providing for all without stinginess. 5. The mind of giving (*dāna-citta*): the sense of universal wisdom and lack of attachment.
6. The mind of kind speech (*priyavāda-citta*): the sense that all that is spoken is virtuous. 7. The mind of beneficial [action] (*arthacaryā-citta*)...

1. The mind of benefit (*upakāra-citta*): the meaning of transforming and giving birth through superior practice. 2. The mind of equality (*samatā-citta*): the meaning of secretly harmonizing and gathering beings for their transformation. 3. The mind of determination (*niyata-citta*): the meaning of maintaining certainty without confusion. 4. The mind of non-retrogression (*avinivartana-citta*): the meaning of being irreversible from the path of enlightenment.

5. The mind of protection (*paritrāṇa-citta*): the meaning of safeguarding others from suffering. 6. The mind of joy (*pramudita-citta*): the meaning of rejoicing in the Dharma. 7. The mind of benefit (*hitacitta*): the meaning of providing assistance. 8. The mind of equality (*samacitta*): the meaning of concealing one's own superiority while gathering and transforming others. 9. The mind of concentration (*samādhi-citta*): the meaning of maintaining stability without distraction. 10. The mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*): the meaning of penetrating illumination without obstruction. These two clarify the ten aspects of the bodhisattva practices (*daśa-pratipatti*).

O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten developmental minds (*cittāny āpyāyakāni*), one enters into the ten adamantine minds (*vajracittāni*) of firm cultivation and patience that lead toward the fruit:
first, the mind of faith; second, the mind of mindfulness; third, the mind of dedication; fourth, the mind of penetration; fifth, the upright mind;
sixth, the non-retrogressive mind; seventh, the Mahāyāna mind; eighth, the signless mind; ninth, the wisdom mind; and tenth, the indestructible mind.

From this phrase, the preceding entry into the "firm" (kṣānti) stage is concluded, and the subsequent cultivation of firm patience and so forth is initiated. "Cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to increased cultivation.

Within these ten adamantine stages (*vajrapada*), "nature" (*prakṛti*) is the lineage of the path of application (*prayogamārga-gotra*); "contemplation" (*darśana*) is the contemplation of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-prajñā*).

"Perseverance" (*kṣānti*) refers to the cultivation of perseverance; "patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the cultivation of patience. When these two meanings are combined, it is called "the cultivation of perseverance and patience.

These ten stages of *pariṇāmanā* (dedication) constitute the "mind of resolve through practice" (*adhimukti-caryā-prasthāna-citta*). The preceding ten stages of *vihāra* (abidings) were entered by means of the fulfillment of faith;
these ten stages of *pariṇāmanā* are entered by means of the fulfillment of practice. Thus, at the conclusion of the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, the Bodhisattva...
Because of the desire for fulfillment, one immediately, within the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness), deeply realizes that the practice currently being cultivated is free from marks.
Thus, in every thought-moment, the true mark of the mind is present; in every instant, there is *tathatā*; in every action, there is perfect interfusion.

One cultivates the samādhi of the vajra, gathers all dharmas of practice, and enters deeply into contemplation of principle, becoming increasingly luminous until entering the ocean of the Buddha-fruit. Therefore, it is said:
From these ten stages of nurturing the mind (*cittotpāda*), one enters the firm cultivation of patience (*kṣānti*) and proceeds toward the fruit through the ten adamantine minds (*vajracitta*).

What are called the ten minds of dedication (*pariṇāmanācitta*)? First is the mind of faith (*śraddhācitta*): it is the conviction that one’s own mind will certainly attain Buddhahood, being forever free from doubt or attachment.

Second is the mind of mindfulness (*smṛticitta*): it is the state of never losing the true wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) of all Buddhas in every moment of thought. Third is the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanācitta*)...
1. A mind that turns back but does not remain; it inclines toward non-retrogression because it neither dwells upon nor retreats from unsurpassed bodhi.
2. A fourfold-reaching mind; "reaching" means thorough penetration, illuminating everything without obstruction, for it is pure both internally and externally. 3. A direct mind.
1. The Mind of Rectitude: It is upright because it illuminates equality and enters the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). 2. The Mind of Non-retrogression:
It does not regress to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), for its progress toward the Path is unceasing. 3. The Mind of the Mahāyāna:

By means of the vehicle of wisdom (*jñāna-yāna*) and the vehicle of practice (*caryā-yāna*), it carries and employs [beings] to extensively deliver sentient beings into the ocean of Buddhahood. 4. The Mind of Signlessness (*animitta-citta*): By means of Prajñā-pāramitā...

The *pāramitā* illuminates clearly; because delusive thoughts and liberation are non-dual, this is the ninth, the mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*). Wisdom is precisely the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-prajñā*).
By observing and illuminating with wisdom, one realizes the immeasurable dharma-realms and enters into all dharmas, for there is neither accumulation nor reception.

The ten indestructible minds are not destroyed by the eight māras. Because one enters the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and attains mastery over appearing and disappearing, these ten minds are perfected.

The principle of the two emptinesses becomes manifest, invoking the empowerment of all Buddhas; one attains the *mōding* (crown-moistening) samādhi and realizes the *dhāraṇī* gate of the equality of space.
This is precisely the entry into the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). These three clarify the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).

Above, the names and characteristics of the three grades of worthy ones (*śaikṣa*) regarding contemplative practice have been concluded. Below, the characteristics of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are clarified.
O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten adamantine minds, one enters the stage of the firm noble patience (*kṣānti*), which consists of the ten stages leading to the fruit:
(1) the Stage of Essential Nature Equality; (2) the Stage of Essential Nature Good Wisdom; (3) the Stage of Essential Nature Radiance; (4) the Stage of Essential Nature... [text ends].

The second is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom; the third is the Ground of the Radiance of the Nature of Body; the fourth is the Ground of the Flower-Light of the Nature of Body; the fifth is the Ground of Fulfillment of the Nature of Body;

the sixth is the Ground of the Buddha’s Roar of the Nature of Body; the seventh is the Ground of the Flower Adornment of the Nature of Body; and the eighth is the Ground of Entry into the Buddha-realm of the Nature of Body.
This single phrase concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent stage of "Entering the Firm and Holy" (*kṣānti*).

This means that when the merits of practicing the holy conduct during the three preceding stages of worthiness are fully perfected, one attains entry into the *dhāraṇī* gateway of the Ground of Equality (*samatā-bhūmi*). From this point onward, one is designated as "Holy.
Therefore, it is said: "From these ten adamantine minds, one enters into the firm and holy patience (*kṣānti*), [proceeding through] the ten grounds toward the fruition. These ten...

Within the stages (*bhūmi*), "nature" (*prakṛti*) is the nature of perfect enlightenment; "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is the contemplation of the stages; "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is signless wisdom; and "firmness" (*dṛḍha*) is the firmness of virtue.
"Patience" (*kṣānti*) is correct patience. When these two meanings are combined, it is called "the firm, noble patience.

This is the realization-awakening of the mind, because it realizes the *tathatā* dharma. Why are they called the ten stages? First is the stage of the equality of essential nature (*dharmatā-samatā-bhūmi*). That is to say:
This bodhisattva enters the true dharma-gate of the great wisdom of equality regarding the dharma-body of all Buddhas, thereby gathering in sentient beings;
because that wisdom is impartial, it is the second stage, the Stage of Wholesome Wisdom of Essential Nature.

This means that this bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the great wisdom of equality regarding the dharma-body and clearly penetrates all roots of goodness. The third is the Stage of Radiance of Essential Nature.
The Ground of Clarity (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*): This refers to the bodhisattva’s realization of the radiance of boundless, sublime wisdom.

Through the knowledge that understands via meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they are able to know the dharma-gates of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, because they have entered the radiance of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

The Fourth Ground, the Ground of Blazing Nature (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*): This refers to the bodhisattva who, by means of the flames of wisdom, burns the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and enters into goodness.

Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they transform and teach all sentient beings, enabling them to perceive the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the Buddha. Fifth is the Stage of Wisdom Illuminating Essential Nature (*Dharmatā-prakṛti-prabhāsvara-bhūmi*).
This refers to the Bodhisattva who, by means of the wisdom of the ten powers (*daśabala-jñāna*), illuminates and knows the two natures of good and evil, existence and non-existence.
It gives rise to all meritorious practices by turning the ineffably ineffable Dharma-gates. Sixth is the Ground of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature (*Tattva-prabhāsa-puṣpa*).
This means that the Bodhisattva here, through the flowers of great wisdom-practice, causes them to bloom all at once.

Regarding the category of the ten supernormal powers and clear wisdom, they manifest their bodies to the assembly in various transformations; for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, they cannot be fully described.
7. The Stage of Fulfillment of Essential Nature (*svabhāva-paripūrṇa-bhūmi*): This refers to the bodhisattva who is fully endowed with the eighteen categories of noble knowledge (*ārya-jñāna*).
Throughout all buddha-fields, in accordance with the mental activities of sentient beings, he manifests as a Buddha, attains enlightenment, and turns the wheel of Dharma.
8. The Stage of the Buddha’s Roar (*buddha-ghoṣa-svabhāva-bhūmi*): This refers to the bodhisattva who enters the rank of the Dharma King (*dharmarāja*).
Samādhi. His wisdom is like that of a Buddha, and he bestows the joy of the Dharma upon all sentient beings.
As a great Dharma Master, he destroys the four māras; his Dharma-body is fully perfected, and he teaches the Dharma with fearlessness, like the roar of a great lion.

Ninth is the Ground of the Flower Ornament of Essential Nature (*Tattva-vairocana-bhūmi*): this means that this Bodhisattva attains the Flower Ornament of the Buddha and is well able to protect the Dharma-body.

By means of the Buddha’s majestic deportment and the Tathāgata-samādhi, they enter and emerge from ten billion four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpaka*) simultaneously, attaining Buddhahood and turning the wheel of Dharma all at once.
Because they manifest such deeds in a single thought-moment, these ten essential natures enter the stage of the Buddha-realm;
that is to say, this bodhisattva, by protecting the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), attains entry into the Vajra-samādhi and becomes fully endowed [with its qualities].
This concludes the Chapter on the Ten Merits. It is fully endowed with the gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī of the dharma-gate of ineffable speech;
it is not within the reach of lower stages, for only the Buddhas—the Buddhas—can exhaust its source through their immeasurable body, mind, and speech.

These four clarify the characteristics of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* states that the six wheels of copper, silver, gold, lapis lazuli, *maṇi*, and crystal correspond to the six positions—the stages of practice, dwelling, direction, ground, equality, and wondrousness. These have all been explained in detail in the *Zhijie* (Direct Explanation), so they will not be cited here at length.
Regarding the contemplative practices, abandonments, and realizations of these ten holy stages: on the first stage, one abandons the superior-grade delusions.
One realizes the lower grade of wisdom. From the second stage through the seventh stage, one abandons the middle-grade afflictions and realizes the middle-grade wisdom.
From the eighth stage through the tenth stage, one abandons the lower-grade afflictions and realizes the superior-grade wisdom.

This constitutes the transformation of the mental states associated with the five sensory consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), and the transformation of the mental states associated with the sixth consciousness into the [Wisdom of Wondrous Observation].
The wisdom of observation transforms the mental states associated with the seventh consciousness into the Wisdom of Equality;
the mental states associated with the eighth consciousness transform into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

When these four wisdoms are perfectly luminous, the three bodies manifest in their entirety—namely, the Great Perfect Stainless Wisdom appearing simultaneously, universally illuminating the lands within the dust-motes of the ten directions. This concludes the answer and explanation.
The section on the names and characteristics of the mind-ground is concluded. Below, the conclusion of the answer serves as an exhortation to practice.
This is the Chapter on the Forty Dharma-Gates; when I was formerly a bodhisattva, it was the root source through which I cultivated entry into the fruit of Buddhahood.
This "Chapter on the Forty Dharma-Gates" generally sets forth the rules for the ground of the mind.
"I was previously a bodhisattva" here cites the fruit to clarify the cause. "The source for cultivating entry into the Buddha-fruit" here cites the cause to clarify the fruit.
If there were not a supreme cause, one could not obtain a supreme fruit; if there were not a supreme fruit, how could a supreme cause be revealed?
This refers back to the very source itself, serving as a model for sentient beings to practice and enter [the path]. These three points constitute the intent of the response to the question.

Within this intent, there are two parts: first, citing the Dharma and stating the causes; second, providing exhortations for practice and realization. This is the first part: citing the Dharma and stating the causes.
In this way, all sentient beings enter the ten stages of the adamantine path of development and advancement;

they realize the fruit to be attained—the unconditioned, signless, great fulfillment, and eternal abiding—wherein the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, and the fulfillment of the dharma-body and wisdom-body are perfected.
These two characters thus inherit from above that the source of one’s own attainment of Buddhahood lies herein; and all sentient beings should likewise do so.

That is to say, just as I in the past practiced the Bodhisattva path—cultivating, entering, setting out upon, and nurturing the practices of the ten *bhūmis* and the forty stages of the noble ones as the mind of the causal ground—I have now attained realization and shall continue to do so in the future.
The fruition consists of the marks and signs of the fulfillment of the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* and *jñānakāya*, which are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and signless (*animitta*).
"Unconditioned and signless" reveals the *dharmakāya*. "Greatly fulfilled and eternally abiding" reveals the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The ten powers and eighteen unique qualities reveal the *dharmakāya*. Regarding the phrase "the *dharmakāya* and so forth," it means that one realizes this unconditioned [state].

This constitutes the fruit of the fulfillment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Realizing this great perfection and permanence constitutes the fruit of the fulfillment of the Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).

Realizing these ten powers (*daśabala*) and eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) constitutes the fruit of the fulfillment of the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), and the manifestation of hundreds of thousands of millions of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Therefore, it is said that the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body are fully perfected.
This intent contains two parts: an exhortation and the realization of cultivation. Regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*): first, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible;
second, the power of knowing the karmic retribution of the past, present, and future; third, the power of knowing all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis;
fourth, the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya*) of various characteristics; fifth, the power of knowing the various inclinations (*nānādhimukti*).
It is also called the power of desire (*chanda-bala*). The sixth is the power of knowing the various elements (*nānā-dhātu-jñāna-bala*), which is also called the power of nature (*gotra-bala*).

The seventh is the power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*). The eighth is the power of knowing past lives with outflow-free knowledge (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti-āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-bala*). The ninth is the power of knowing the unimpeded divine eye (*divya-cakṣur-vaiśāradya-jñāna-bala*).

The tenth is the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows through the permanent severance of all habitual tendencies (*āśrava-kṣaya-jñāna-bala*). These are the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
1. No failure in physical conduct. 2. No failure in verbal conduct. 3. No failure in mental conduct. 4. No lack of concentration. 5. No lack of mindfulness.
6. No lack of equanimity. 7. No decline in aspiration. 8. No decline in mindfulness. 9. No decline in diligence.
10. No decline in wisdom. 11. No decline in liberation. 12. No decline in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
13. No diminution in vision; 14. bodily action follows wisdom; 15.
verbal action follows wisdom; 16. mental action follows wisdom; 17. unimpeded knowledge of the past; 18.
unimpeded knowledge of the present; 19. unimpeded knowledge of the future. These eighteen modes of conduct are called "unshared" because—
This is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening of all Buddhas; it is not shared with provisional or lesser bodhisattvas, nor can it be known as the realm of ordinary beings.
Therefore, it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).
At that time, on the seat of magnificent great radiance in the Lotus-Womb World, were Vairocana Buddha, the Buddhas upon the thousand petals,
the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, and the Buddhas of all worlds.
"At that time" refers to the moment when Śākyamuni Tathāgata raised the cause to illustrate the fruit in order to encourage practice.
"The lotus pedestal," and so forth, as well as the "thousand billion Buddhas," are explained as before.
As for the phrase "the Buddhas of all worlds," these are the immeasurable and inexhaustible wisdom-Buddhas produced through the successive transformations of the thousand billion Śākyamuni Buddhas.

Dwelling within all worlds, they preach the Dharma to benefit sentient beings; this represents the Buddha who arises from the immeasurable and inexhaustible wisdom born of the precepts of the mind-ground.
As the text of the lower fascicle states: "It is by this that the multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust, attain perfect enlightenment.
This is the explanation requested by the third, Flower-Light (Huaguang). There are two parts to this request for explanation; first:
