Not following the teachings of non-Buddhists or malevolent spirits, one is able to depart from all suffering by oneself;
this is the meaning of compassion based on dharmas (*dharmālambanā maitrī*). Furthermore, it can cause all beings to be equalized;

this means that it not only enables them to give rise to right faith so as not to be destroyed by the sufferings of Māra, but also enables all sentient beings to personally realize unsurpassed *bodhi*.

Awakening the mind, one realizes the principle and realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and attains the true fruit of bliss—the samādhi of compassion that benefits sentient beings through the realization of emptiness.
This is precisely the meaning of "unconditioned great compassion" (*anālambana-mahāmaitrī*).

As for the phrase "not the real," it means that this compassionate fruit of bliss is neither the provisional "real dharma" of the Lesser Vehicle nor its minor fruits; nor is it the tainted cause and effect of good and evil belonging to humans or devas.
What kind of fruit is this? This fruit of the bliss of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the wisdom and understanding that accords with a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-jñāna*).
It is suchness (*tathatā*) without duality, the equality of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the self-bliss of the samādhi whose essential nature is right reception (*samyaksamādhi*).
This is the first explanation of the stage of the mind of loving-kindness.
The second is the stage of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*).

Compassion here refers to the immeasurable mind of compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*). In other sūtras, it is called the "practice of benefiting others" (*anugrahacaryā*), because it means constantly transforming sentient beings so that they may obtain the benefits of the Dharma.

If, O Sons of the Buddha, one practices the path by means of compassion that is empty, empty, and signless, one personally extinguishes all suffering and gives rise to wisdom regarding the immeasurable sufferings of all sentient beings.

Taking non-killing as the condition, taking the dharma of non-killing as the condition, and taking non-attachment to self as the condition, one constantly practices non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexual misconduct; thus, all sentient beings are not troubled, and one awakens the bodhicitta.
As for the mind: within emptiness, one perceives all phenomena as they truly are. Within the practices of the spiritual lineage, one gives rise to the mind of the wisdom of the Path.

Toward the six types of kin and the six types of enemies—among these three categories of kin and enemies—one bestows the supreme happiness of wisdom. Amidst the conditions of supreme enemies, one attains the fruit of happiness in nine grades.
When emptiness manifests, one’s own self and all other sentient beings are equal in a single happiness, and great compassion arises.
"If a Buddha-son acts out of compassion": the character "with" (yi) carries significant force.

It means that although a Bodhisattva with a compassionate mind can extract others from suffering, this cannot be achieved without possessing great and firm power; therefore, it says "with compassion. Regarding "emptiness of emptiness" and so forth:

It is said that this compassion is not the compassion of worldly affection for sentient beings; rather, it is the Bodhisattva’s spontaneous coming and going through great compassion that is empty, signless, and non-conceptual.

By virtue of the conditions of this great compassion, one practices the Bodhisattva path and manifests the appearance of extinguishing all personal suffering and affliction, yet within the conditions of the immeasurable suffering and affliction of all sentient beings, one gives rise to [great compassion].
This refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*). Regarding "not killing" and so forth, this is the meaning of personally extinguishing all suffering.
The factors of birth, phenomena, and self—these three conditions (*pratyaya*)—must converge for the karma of killing to be established; if even one is lacking, it is certainly not established.

One who maintains the precept against killing merely empties one condition, whereby all three conditions become empty. Thus, by constantly practicing non-killing, one extinguishes suffering, and yet...
Not stealing and not committing sexual misconduct are likewise the extinction of suffering. As for the phrase "all beings are equal," this refers to the meaning of generating wisdom amidst suffering.
It means that this Bodhisattva, thus extinguishing suffering, leads by example and follows in practice, personally moving all sentient beings;
they likewise refrain from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, extinguish all afflictions, and give rise to the bodhicitta. Thus it is born.
This is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This concludes the section on uprooting suffering. Regarding the phrase "in the view of emptiness" and so forth:

it means that a Bodhisattva is able to penetrate and illuminate all phenomena within the principle of the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā-tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), such that they are all exactly as the true mark is.

Whether sentient or insentient, there is not a single phenomenon that does not possess this true mark of ultimate emptiness. Because of delusion and a lack of awakening, [beings remain obscured] regarding...
Within the category of the seed-nature of sentient beings, one gives rise to a mind of immeasurable skillful means and wisdom that practices the path through the conditions of compassion.
Toward parents, brothers, sisters, and the six classes of kin, as well as the six classes of enemies— whether they be relatives or foes—
one bestows the wisdom of superior happiness upon those in the three lower grades of enmity, and bestows the nine grades of inferior happiness upon those in the three upper grades of enmity.
This chapter shows that one obtains the fruit of happiness. Although the old woman to the east of the city vowed not to see the Buddha, she harbored no ill will toward him;
this is the condition for the arising of enmity. When she saw the Buddha, she retreated into her room, where all four walls were filled with Buddhas; she then covered her eyes with both hands.

The ten fingers are all Buddhas; this corresponds to the aforementioned "giving joy through wisdom. When Devadatta pushed the mountain to crush the Buddha, it was an instance of the aforementioned "enmity as a condition.
Although [the Buddha] was in hell, he experienced a bliss like that of the third dhyāna heaven; this refers to the attainment of the fruit of bliss in the nine grades.

As for the middle grade giving joy, it need not be stated explicitly, as it can be understood. This concludes the section on "giving joy. Regarding the phrase "when emptiness appears," this refers to compassion.
When the true mark of reality—the emptiness of the path and its wisdom—is manifested, one’s own body is freed from suffering and attains happiness;
likewise, the bodies of all other sentient beings are simultaneously freed from suffering and attain happiness.

By bestowing upon them the fruit of compassion and joy of a single equal flavor, one causes every person to give rise to the great compassionate mind that uproots suffering and bestows happiness. This is the second explanation.
This is the stage of compassion (*karuṇā*).
○ Third is the stage of sympathetic joy (*muditā*);

"joy" here refers to the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā-citta*). In another sutra, it is called the "practice of non-opposition," meaning that one constantly cultivates wholesome dharmas.
This is because of humility and reverence.

O Disciples of the Buddha, when the mind of joy in non-arising arises, the essence and characteristics of the lineage, the path, and wisdom—the mind of joy in the emptiness of emptiness—do not cling to "mine.

Appearing and disappearing within the causes and effects of the three periods of time, there is no accumulation; all that exists enters the practice of the contemplation of emptiness, and it is thus perfected.
He rejoices in all sentient beings. He causes them to give rise to emptiness and enter the Way; he causes them to abandon evil associates and seek out virtuous friends;
he shows them the good path and leads all sentient beings into the family and Dharma of the Buddhas. He constantly gives rise to joy as they enter the rank of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, he rejoices because these sentient beings enter into right faith, abandon false views, and turn their backs on the suffering of the six realms of existence.
Regarding the phrase "if a Buddha-son rejoices" and so forth: "rejoicing" (悅) refers to one's own internal satisfaction; "joy" (喜) refers to feeling delight upon seeing others.
The "mind of non-arising" is the mind of signlessness (*animitta*). Signlessness is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
It means that at this moment of joy, the seed-nature, its divisions, the fundamental essence, and its characteristics are all like the true mark: empty, possessing nothing, and perfectly integrated.
This is the principle of great emptiness; it is also a mind of joy that is empty and yet further empty. Regarding "non-attachment" and so forth:
it means that since even the self is empty, who is there to whom one belongs such that attachment would arise? Therefore, it is called "non-attachment to what belongs to the self."

At this time, the Bodhisattva may emerge or dissolve. Within the three periods of past, present, and future, and throughout the ten directions, there is no experiencing whatsoever of either good causes and good fruits or evil causes and evil fruits; how then could there be any accumulation?

The entire realm of consciousness, the realm of form, and the realm of desire—all states of existence—are without exception empty. Sentient beings within the three realms, because of their grasping and attachment...
Therefore, one does not attain this state of joyful mind through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Because this Bodhisattva is free from attachment, wherever they enter among all things, this practice of the contemplation of emptiness is spontaneously accomplished without the need for deliberate mental effort.
Regarding the phrase "equal joy": it means that once the contemplation of emptiness is perfected, one universally delivers both enemies and kin with equanimity, extensively transforming all beings.
All sentient beings do not understand how to give rise to the contemplation of emptiness; yet this Bodhisattva manifests the arising of emptiness for them.
Sentient beings do not understand how to enter the Path; yet this Bodhisattva manifests the entry into the Path for them.
Sentient beings do not understand how to abandon wrong views and evil associates; yet this Bodhisattva manifests the abandonment of evil associates for them. Sentient beings do not understand...
He seeks a true and virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to reveal to him the wondrous and excellent right path.
Why does this Bodhisattva manifest the seeking of a spiritual friend to show him the wondrous path?

It is because he desires, in general, to cause all sentient beings to enter the family of those born into the Buddha-dharma, rather than the family of heterodox outsiders; to enter the Dharma of those born into the Buddha-dharma, rather than the provisional [teachings].
This is the middle way of the Lesser Vehicle. Regarding the phrase "constantly arising," it means that it does not stop at this alone.

The immeasurable compassionate mind of a Bodhisattva has no point of rest; therefore, in every thought and every moment, they constantly give rise to self-rejoicing and the joy of others, entering into the state of all Buddhas.
Above, they harmonize with all Buddhas through the same power of compassion, and then return.
He still maintains the same physical appearance as all sentient beings, appearing below in a manner identical to them so that they may gaze upon him with unified devotion.
He remains just like those sentient beings who take refuge in the Triple Gem and enter into right faith;

he breaks free from the cage of worldly existence and abandons false views, turning away from the various sufferings of the six realms and proceeding toward the true bliss of the Four Noble Truths. For this reason:
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva’s mind and intentions are fulfilled, joy arises. These three [explanations] clarify the stage of the joyful mind (muditā).
Fourth is the stage of the equanimous mind (upekṣā).
"Equanimity" here refers to relinquishing immeasurable practices. In another sutra, it is called "the practice of non-deflection," meaning the practice of great diligence (mahāvīrya).
Practice. This is because it enables all beings to reach ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

O Disciples of the Buddha, you should constantly give rise to a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*). Within the unconditioned, signless, and empty Dharma, which is like space, one should equally illuminate both good and evil, existence and non-existence, and the two states of sin and merit. Free from the notions of "person" and "mine," one should [cultivate] oneself...

He regards the unattainability of the intrinsic nature of others as great equanimity (*upekṣā*). Furthermore, regarding his own body, flesh, hands, feet, men, women, kingdoms, and cities—as being like illusions, like transformations, like flowing water, or like the flame of a lamp—he relinquishes everything without generating a mind of grasping, constantly cultivating that equanimity.

Regarding the phrase "If a Buddha’s disciple constantly gives rise to [this mind]," it means that this Bodhisattva, from beginningless kalpas, has resolved their mind and practiced the conduct of relinquishment (*tyāga*) to benefit others;
therefore, it is said they "constantly give rise to the mind of relinquishment. "Non-creation" (*akṛta*) means there is no person who creates the act of relinquishing.
"Signlessness" (*animitta*) means there is neither the dharma that is relinquished nor the recipient of the relinquishment. Such is the essence of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).
Within the dharma of emptiness, it is ultimately like space—empty and devoid of anything whatsoever.

Since one is able to relinquish that which is to be relinquished, all being like space, then the two causes of good and evil, the two views of existence and non-existence, and the two retributions of sin and merit [are likewise relinquished].
Within these two dharmas, one observes them with equanimous wisdom as a single path of illumination.

This is ultimately like space—empty and devoid of anything whatsoever. Within this, one seeks the essential nature of the marks of persons, the marks of self, the mind of self, and the mind of "mine," as well as the marks of sentient beings—self and other—and does not find even so much as the tip of a needle.
It can be attained; it is also ultimately like space, empty and non-existent.

Only by generating the mind in this way and contemplating in this manner can it be called "great equanimity" (*mahopekṣā*). This is the meaning of self-emptiness (*ātmaśūnyatā*). Regarding "oneself and so forth":
it extends to one's own internal treasures—the body, flesh, hands, and feet—as well as external treasures—the kingdom, cities, men, and women.
Contemplate them with equanimity: they are all like illusions and transformations, lacking any substantial nature. Internal and external wealth cannot be apprehended;

they are like flowing water or the flickering flame of a lamp, devoid of substantial nature. Wealth belonging to self or others likewise cannot be apprehended; therefore, one should relinquish everything.
This is the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). As for the "unborn mind," it is unborn.
The mind is precisely the mind of the true reality (*dharmatā*) in which there is no agent, no object, and no action—the three spheres being empty of intrinsic nature.
"Constantly cultivating equanimity" means that this Bodhisattva’s mind of equanimity is vast and expansive, enduring forever without weariness or cessation.
This explains the stage of the four types of equanimity.
The fifth stage, the stage of the mind of giving (*dānacitta*),

is the practice of giving that subsumes all dharmas. In another sutra, it is called "the practice free from delusion and confusion," meaning that one is not lost or distracted by ignorance (*avidyā*).
If, O sons of the Buddha, you can employ a mind of giving toward all sentient beings—giving with body, speech, and mind; giving wealth and giving the Dharma—to guide and instruct all sentient beings;

and if you regard your inner body, outer body, kingdoms, cities, men, women, fields, and houses as all being the mark of Suchness (tathatā), even to the point that there is no thought of material objects, nor of recipient or giver, whether internal or external, neither uniting nor dispersing.
Acting through transformation without a [discursive] mind, one penetrates both principle and practice. All marks manifest in present action.
If a disciple of the Buddha can employ giving and so forth—meaning that by means of the mind of giving, one can immediately don the armor of the mind of teaching;
donning it for all sentient beings is the application of the mind of the recipient; and bodily giving means personally taking up the burden and enduring toil.
The giving of labor: even to the point of relinquishing one’s head, eyes, marrow, brain, body, flesh, hands, and feet.
The giving of speech: that is, having no harshness in one’s mouth; speaking words that are well-refined, up to the point of speaking with joy and praise, and uttering truthful speech.
The giving of mind: that is, having no anger, hatred, greed, delusion, or envy in one’s heart; up to the point of always maintaining reverence and manifesting a gentle demeanor. The giving of wealth.
These include kingdoms, cities, wives, children, precious treasures, fields, houses, and the means of livelihood.

The gift of Dharma consists of the provisional and ultimate teachings, the skillful means of the various vehicles—both Great and Small—and the use of causes, conditions, and parables to teach, transform, and guide all stingy sentient beings.

Enable them to penetrate the Dharma and penetrate giving. Know that the five aggregates of the internal body and the external body—the four elements, the seven treasures, kingdoms, cities, men, women, fields, houses, and other such things—are in their very essence entirely empty, all being the mark of *tathatā* (suchness). There is no dharma to be given;
there is not even any material wealth to be contemplated. There is no recipient of the gift, no giver of wealth, and no self who gives. The three spheres are empty.

The marks are likewise all suchness. Both the six internal sense faculties and the six external sense objects have no causes or conditions by which they can arise or combine, and no causes or conditions by which they can cease or disperse.
There is no mental activity to be performed, and there are no sentient beings to be transformed.
To have no mind to be exercised is called "attaining the principle"; to have no birth to be transformed is called "attaining generosity. Being thus able—

Having attained understanding of principles, one is further able to master the practice of giving. What hindrance could there be to the constant presence of all internal and external giving before one, such that it would never encounter obstruction?
This explains the mental state regarding the five kinds of giving.
The sixth is the stage of the mind of agreeable speech (*priyavāda-citta*).

Agreeable speech is subsumed under the dharma of loving speech (*priyavāda*). In another sutra, it is called "the practice of goodness" (*kuśala-pratipatti*), meaning that one is constantly born within Buddha-fields throughout all lifetimes.
If a Buddha’s disciple enters the Samādhi of Essential Loving Speech, they shall accord all words of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and all speech that is truly real with this single word.
They shall harmonize the minds of all sentient beings, remaining free from anger and contention.

Possessing the wisdom of the emptiness of all phenomena, which is without objective conditions, they shall constantly give rise to a heart of love. Their conduct shall accord with the intent of the Buddhas and likewise accord with all others, by means of the Holy...
The Dharma-speech instructs all sentient beings; one should always act in accordance with the mind to give rise to roots of goodness.

As for the phrase "if a disciple of the Buddha enters into the nature of reality," etc., "loving speech" (priyavāditā) is the ultimate compassion and kindness, most intimate and earnest, a gentle and harmonious instruction.
It is said that these soft and excellent words are not the concern of ordinary or inferior beings.
Seeing these words of biased attachment, one should know that they arise from the samādhi of the Tathāgata’s essential nature of loving speech (*priyavāditā*).
The Tathāgata possesses five kinds of speech: first, truthful speech; second, real speech; third, suchness-speech; fourth, non-deceptive speech;
and fifth, non-contradictory speech. Although this text contains only three [terms], the middle one encompasses all five meanings. This is the Dharma-speech of the Truth.
This is true speech; all words of reality are subsumed under non-deceptive speech. They all accord with the single word, which is to say, speech that is suchness and not otherwise.

It is said that since this Son of the Buddha has produced his language from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), every word he utters to reveal the Dharma is without exception real, and is necessarily neither deceptive nor false, but accords with the single word, never...
Two phrases. If a person can constantly cultivate these five phrases as causes, they shall experience the fruit of the Tathāgata’s broad and long tongue.
Regarding "harmonizing" and so forth: "harmonizing" means that the aforementioned phrases act as the harmonizers, while the minds of all sentient beings are the objects to be harmonized.
"Freedom from anger" is harmony of the mind; "freedom from contention" is harmony of speech. Sentient beings are of many kinds; [this applies to] their minds and mouths...
There are many distinctions. This Bodhisattva is able to tame those who are difficult to tame, causing all mental discursive expressions to become peaceful, free from anger and contention.
Regarding the phrase "all dharmas are empty," it means that this Bodhisattva constantly uses the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to illuminate and realize that all phenomena are empty.
This wisdom of emptiness pervades all dharmas, both sentient and insentient.
Yet it does not require inducement or encouragement. Great compassion without an object likewise pervades all phenomena.

Although this wisdom of emptiness is without an object, the Bodhisattva constantly accords with sentient beings; his heart of nurturing, protecting, and cherishing sentient beings never rests for even a moment.
Whatever he practices accords above with the mind of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, sharing in their identical power of compassion.
Furthermore, this also accords with the minds of all sentient beings below, sharing in the same compassionate longing.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the noble Dharma," it means that this Bodhisattva instructs sentient beings without employing any other methods;

he solely uses the noble truth of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-satya*) and the five modes of speech to admonish, instruct, and harmonize all sentient beings, always acting according to their hearts so that they may be free from [affliction].
It dispels anger and contention, giving rise to and developing all roots of goodness, serving forever as the seeds for the path to Bodhi.
These six explain the mind of well-spoken words.
○ Seventh, the stage of the beneficial mind.

"Benefit" (*yi*) is precisely what is subsumed under "beneficial conduct" (*artha-caryā*). A separate sutra names this "the practice of non-attachment," meaning that both self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) are entirely empty.
O Son of the Buddha, when the mind of benefit arises, one should extensively practice the path of wisdom through the essence of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), gathering all illumination.
The Flame Dharma Gate. Having gathered the seven riches of contemplative practice, because the people before him obtain benefit, he accepts body and life and enters the Samādhi of Benefit.
He manifests all bodies, all speech, and all minds, shaking the great world.
Whatever he does or undertakes, others enter into the seeds of the Dharma, the seeds of emptiness, and the seeds of the Path, thereby obtaining benefit and joy. Thus he manifests.

Manifesting in the six realms of existence, one does not regard the immeasurable matters of suffering and affliction as a source of distress, but rather acts solely for the benefit and advantage of others.

If a disciple of the Buddha is equal in benefiting others, their "true wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*) is the self-realization of the *tathatā-jñāna* (wisdom of suchness) that is inherently present; their "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) is the fundamental essence of this very wisdom;
and their "path of wisdom" (*jñāna-mārga*) is the skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) for benefiting sentient beings. Thus it is said: "If a disciple of the Buddha..."

When you practice this gathering through beneficial conduct (*hitakārya-saṃgraha*), you must rely upon the essential nature of the originally existing, true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) in order to be able to extensively practice the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) of the path of wisdom. "Gathering all" refers to the meaning of extensively practicing the path of wisdom.

The "Flame-Blaze Dharma Gate" (*jvālā-dharmaparyāya*) is a metaphor for the immeasurable gates of skillful means (*ananta-upāya*) that serve as the causes and conditions for various kinds of wisdom. Regarding what is... [text ends]...:
This refers to "opening the gate of expedient means and revealing the true reality. The "contemplative practices" refer to the three contemplations of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
The "seven riches" refer to the seven riches of faith, precepts, learning, renunciation, wisdom, shame, and remorse.
All such paths to omniscience are to be extensively practiced and accumulated. Regarding the phrase "the former person attains benefit," it says:
When those who currently act for the benefit of others attain this path of omniscience, they are then able to harmonize with the light and blend with the dust,
manifesting the reception of a body and life composed of the four great elements and five aggregates just like that of ordinary sentient beings,

thereby entering into this work of benefit. Within the samādhi of right concentration, they manifest all wheels of the body through various supernatural powers, and all wheels of speech through various instructions.

The wheels: the wheel of the mind that records all things, which benefits all sentient beings by causing those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment to resolve upon it, and causing those who have already resolved to increase in their progress.
Because of the divine power of these three wheels, the trichiliocosm shakes in six ways. These six kinds of shaking consist of: trembling, rising, surging, and quaking.

"Roaring and striking" refers to this. Regarding "all that is done," etc., it means that whatever actions are performed and whatever activities are engaged in, they all cause others to enter this contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Within the Dharma-seed of the Seven Riches, it is the Dharma-gate of radiant brilliance;
within the seed of emptiness, it is the extensive practice of the path of wisdom; and within the seed of the path, it is the attainment of great benefit and great peace.
It is joy. Regarding "manifesting forms" and so forth: it refers to the aforementioned manifestations of body, speech, and mind;
it is not known what kind of physical form they are, nor in what location they manifest.
That is to say, they manifest such forms individually within the realms of gods, humans, asuras, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, and animals. Within the realm of gods...
There are the afflictions of the five signs of decline; the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death among humans;
the afflictions of anger and strife among asuras; the afflictions of cold and agonizing pain in the hells;
the afflictions of deep gloom and lamentation among ghosts and spirits; and the afflictions of anxious wandering and sorrow among birds and beasts.
Therefore, it is said that they do not regard immeasurable matters of suffering and affliction as calamities.
This means that these bodhisattvas conceal their holiness and manifest as ordinary beings, humbling their dignity to conform to the lowly;

they must act in this way, giving good things to others so that others may obtain benefit and happiness, while taking suffering upon themselves without regarding it as a calamity, but solely intent on benefiting others.
This is considered to be for the sake of benefit. This explains the seventh stage, the Stage of the Beneficial Mind (*hitacitta*).

The eighth is the Stage of the Identical Mind (*samānacitta*), where "identical" refers to the inclusion of *samānārthatā* (common purpose). In another sutra, it is called the "Difficult-to-Attain Practice" (*durlabha-caryā*), meaning the accomplishment of roots of goodness that are difficult to attain.

Therefore, O Son of the Buddha: by means of the wisdom of the nature of the Way, one is identical with the dharma of emptiness and non-arising; by means of the wisdom of non-self, one is identical with the non-duality of birth.

Emptiness and the source are one in the realm of objects; the suchness-characteristic of all dharmas is eternally arising, eternally abiding, and eternally ceasing as worldly phenomena continue in succession.
Transforming immeasurably, they are able to manifest immeasurable activities of form, body, color, and mind, entering all six realms of existence.

In all matters they are identical; in emptiness they are identical to the unarisen; in the self they are identical to non-substantiality. Because they divide their bodies and disperse their forms, they enter the Samādhi of Identical Dharma.
"If a Buddha-son [uses] the Way as equal" means "to employ. The Way is awakening; it is the Buddha. The nature of the Way, the nature of awakening, and the nature of the Buddha are one.
This wisdom has a name but no form; therefore, it can equally enter into the principle of emptiness and non-arising.
It is said that Bodhisattvas skillfully employ this wisdom to accord with this principle. Wisdom and principle are perfectly interfused, possessing purity.
It is the purification of the body. Regarding the phrase "by means of non-self and so forth": the wisdom of non-self is itself the wisdom of cessation (*śānti-jñāna*).
Sentient beings grasp at the four great elements and the five aggregates as a real self, thereby transmigrating through the various realms of existence.

This Bodhisattva, by means of the wisdom of cessation, illuminates this body subject to birth; he realizes that the four great elements do not exist and that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty—neither arising nor ceasing.
Birth and birth-extinction are non-dual; this is precisely the possession of the perfect body. Regarding "emptiness is equal":

it refers to the emptiness of the nature of the Way, the emptiness of non-arising, the emptiness of non-self, and the emptiness of birth. Thus, ten thousand streams share one source, and a thousand differences share one realm.
What dharma could possibly not be thus? Since all dharmas of this world and the world-transcending realms possess the aspect of suchness (tathatā), then...
He possesses a thousand billion transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Regarding the phrase "always arising, etc.":

since the four formless realms have been clarified and the three bodies (*trikāya*) are fully manifest, what prevents arising from being identical with arising, abiding with abiding, and cessation with cessation? Regarding the phrase "the continuity of worldly phenomena, etc.":
although within the laws of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is a continuous succession of births and lifetimes, wandering and revolving in saṃsāra without end...
They are inexhaustible; and within this, these Bodhisattvas are also able to manifest infinite and inexhaustible forms, bodies, physical appearances, mental activities, and karmic deeds.
They enter the six realms of existence: among the devas they are the same as devas; among humans they are the same as humans;
and even among animals they are the same as animals. To those who should be delivered by such a body, they immediately manifest that very body.
I shall preach the Dharma for you. What is it that all things have in common? It is that they are identical to emptiness and non-arising, and thus their principle is suchness.
It is that the self is identical to non-substantiality, and thus the phenomena are suchness. Because the principle is suchness, although the body is divided, it has never been divided.
Because the phenomena are suchness, although the form is dispersed, it has never been dispersed. By what cause and condition is it able to manifest suchness?

Is it through these supernormal powers that one performs the great work of a Buddha? It is because one has entered the samādhi of "entering into the same dharma" that one is able to perform this great work of a Buddha.
This explains the stage of "concordant mind."
The ninth stage, the state of concentrated mind,

is precisely the practice of supreme concentration (*samādhi*). In another sutra, it is called the "practice of wholesome dharmas" (*kuśaladharma-carita*), because it refers to the method for teaching the Dharma to others and attaining Buddhahood.

O Sons of the Buddha, furthermore, from a state of meditative concentration, one observes with wisdom and realizes emptiness. Though each moment of mind contends with conditions regarding the phenomena of "mine," it remains unmoved within the realms of consciousness and form.
Whether moving against or with the flow, emerging or submerging, one constantly enters the hundred samādhis and the ten factors of dhyāna.
With the wisdom of a single thought, one forms this vision: that all notions of self and person, whether internal or external, are but the seeds of sentient beings.
All are without conjunction or dispersion; they are integrated, accumulated, arisen, and active, yet are ultimately ungraspable.

"If the Buddha’s disciple, furthermore... and so forth means that this Buddha’s disciple, furthermore, from within his own mind of great quiescent concentration (*mahā-śānti-samādhi*), observes for himself the wondrous wisdom inherently present, and realizes for himself the true emptiness inherently present. Mind-moment following mind-moment in succession, it is solely stillness.

This is the condition. Regarding the phenomena belonging to the self (*ātmiya-dharma*), one perceives only the mark of emptiness. As for the "consciousness realm" (*vijñāna-dhātu*) and the "form realm" (*rūpa-dhātu*):

the consciousness realm refers to the four heavens of empty space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), and the form realm refers to the four dhyāna heavens. Why does this passage first mention the consciousness realm and the form realm without mentioning the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
It is because the Bodhisattva at this stage has long cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and realized the body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-kāya*); from that Dharma-realm...

Come! Since the entire body and the entire realm are all characterized by emptiness, one enters the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) and the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) without wavering or transformation.
Regarding "reversal and conformity" and so forth: the Bodhisattva passes away from beyond the three realms.
Emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and passing away from it; emerging from the sphere of nothingness and passing away from it;
continuing thus down to emerging from the first dhyāna—this is "conformity. This refers to emerging from outside the three realms and entering within the three realms.

Passing away from the first dhyāna and emerging from the second dhyāna; passing away from the second dhyāna, and so on up to emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—this constitutes [the reverse order].
This is "contrary" (*ni*). This refers to the movement from within outward. From the perspective of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body, moving from above downward is "conforming" (*anuloma*);
from the perspective of the segmented bodies (*bheda-kāya*) of sentient beings in the desire realm, moving from below upward is likewise conforming.

These words describe the benefit of the Bodhisattva’s mind and mind-objects being tranquil and conditioned: appearing and disappearing with mastery, practicing both contrary and conforming ways, such that even the heavens cannot fathom them.
For this reason, his mind constantly enters the hundred and eight samādhis of great quiescence; though within the realm of consciousness, it remains unshaken.
His mind constantly enters the ten factors of dhyāna; though within the realm of form, it does not undergo transformation.
Regarding "with a single thought," it means that by means of wisdom corresponding to a single thought, he gives rise to insight that penetrates and illuminates desire.

Throughout all realms, regarding all selves and persons—whether internal faculties or external objects—the nature of sentient beings' consciousness and the seeds of ignorance are neither obscure nor clearly manifest;
they are all without arising or conjunction, without cessation. They disperse without accumulation and gather without formation;
they are harbored without origination and stilled without creation. All that is made is empty, like an illusion or a transformation, ungraspable and non-existent. Furthermore...

"Unwavering" means it does not shift or transform. The ten factors of dhyāna are initial application (vitarka), sustained application (vicāra), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), concentration (samādhi), tranquility (praśrabdhi), equanimity (upekṣā), mindfulness (smṛti), wisdom (prajñā), and neither-pain-nor-pleasure (aduḥkhāsukha). This explains the stage of the concentrated mind.
○ The tenth stage is the stage of the mind of wisdom (*prajñācitta*);

"wisdom" here refers to the practice of supreme wisdom (*viśeṣa-prajñā*). In another sutra, it is called the "practice of reality" (*tattva-caryā*), because the two truths are neither as they appear nor are they without characteristics.
If, O sons of the Buddha, you cultivate the mind of wise vision, you shall observe that the fetters of various false views and afflictions have no determinate essence or nature.

Because they accord with the patience of emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṣānti*), they are not the aggregates (*skandha*), not the elements (*dhātu*), and not the sense-bases (*āyatana*). They are not sentient beings, not a single self (*ātman*), and not cause or effect.
It is not a dharma of the three periods of time. It arises from the nature of wisdom; light upon light forms a single flame, and clarity upon clarity brings vision. It is empty and receives nothing.
This wisdom and its skillful means nourish and cultivate the mind. This mind enters the path of the emptiness of emptiness and gives rise to the mind of non-arising.
It ascends to the Chapter on the King of the Ocean Eye, wherein the Hundred Dharmas Gate of Illumination of the Mind has already been explained.

"If a Buddha’s disciple produces wisdom," etc., means "to produce" or "to give rise to. It says that the Buddha’s disciple gives rise to this wisdom-vision (*prajñā-darśana*), which is able to illuminate and contemplate through knowledge (*jñāna*).
By contemplating the various fetters of false views and afflictions, one breaks through what they are deluded by.

This Bodhisattva, regarding all demonic and externalist attachments—namely, the constant clinging to the sixty-two types of false views, the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*)—[overcomes them].
All afflictions and fetters are individually illuminated and shattered like flowers in the sky or the moon reflected in water; they possess no determinate essence or nature. Why is this?
Because when one observes them with the wisdom of compliant patience (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*), they are of the same substance as empty space.

Since they are identical to emptiness, the five aggregates (*skandha*) are empty and are not aggregates; the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses (*indriya-viṣaya-vijñāna*) are empty and are not realms (*dhātu*); the six faculties and six objects [are likewise empty].
Emptiness is not an entrance; sentient beings are empty, yet they are not non-existent beings. The single self is empty, yet it is not a lack of a single self.
Sin and merit are empty, yet they are not without cause and effect. Past, present, and future are empty, yet they are not the absence of the three periods of time.

In every phenomenon and at every point, there is the continuity of the empty nature of the singular wisdom of Dharma. Thus, the light of the aggregates, the light of the realms, and the light of the nature of Dharma-wisdom arise as a single flame.
It penetrates thoroughly. When the realm of darkness is illuminated, the nature of the Dharma-wisdom is luminous and clear, and one sees it without doubt.
When the realm of darkness is empty, the nature of the Dharma-wisdom is empty, such that there is neither a subject that receives nor an object received.

Regarding "that wisdom is equal," this refers to the various skillful means within the contemplation of that wisdom, which nurture and develop the mind and bring about the accomplishment of the body of wisdom, because it is not realized through another.
Furthermore, regarding "this mind": "mind" refers to the nurturing mind; "entry" refers to realization-entry; and "arising" refers to the initiation [of wisdom].

"Emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) is the truth of the two kinds of emptiness—the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena—which is that which is realized. "Path" refers to the Middle Way.

The statement means that within the realization, entry, and initiation of the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness, one perceives the meaning of the Middle Way; therein, one gives rise solely to this non-... (the remainder of the text).
One gives rise to the mind [of awakening] and freely steers the compassionate vessel to universally transport all sentient beings so that they may all ascend to the other shore of Prajñā.
In the preceding "Chapter on the King of the Ocean-Eye," these ten minds—the gateway to the illumination of the hundred dharmas—were already explained, with each one’s meaning elucidated in detail.
This concludes the commentary on the stage of the ten wisdom-minds.
Vairocana Buddha said: "O thousand Buddhas, listen attentively! You previously stated that there are ten minds within the diamond-seed (vajra-bīja).

This Primordial Source Buddha addresses the thousand emanation Śākyamuni Buddhas who are present as the appropriate recipients, admonishing them to listen with careful scrutiny so that he may explain in detail the meaning of the diamond (vajra).
Your previous statement was a restatement of the question regarding the diamond-seed.
Regarding the "ten minds" of the son, their meaning is permitted to be analyzed in detail. Where there is such a question, there must be such an answer.
A separate sutra is titled the *Daśapariṇāmanā* (Ten Dedications). "Pariṇāmanā" (*hui*) means to turn back; "pariṇāmanā" (*xiang*) means to direct toward.

This refers to giving rise to the mind of great compassion to deliver all sentient beings, turning back the wholesome dharmas of the ten abodes and ten practices to direct them toward three places: first, the True [Dharma].

First, the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is that which is realized; second, the two unsurpassed bodhisattva-enlightenments are that which is sought; third, all sentient beings are those who are to be delivered.

By means of the mind capable of dedication and the virtuous deeds dedicated, one directs them toward those myriad classes of beings to fulfill the brahma-conduct and enter equally into the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
These three clarify the meaning of the ten dedications. Part two: first, the general heading and the restatement of the question.
Second, the detailed explanation of its meaning. This [section] is the general heading that introduces the inquiry. Below follows the detailed explanation of its meaning, which consists of ten parts.
First is the stage of the position of faith (*śraddhā-adhimukti*).

"Faith" here refers to the dedication of the mind of faith. In another sutra, it is named "the dedication of rescuing and protecting sentient beings while remaining free from the mark of sentient beings."
"Turning toward" means that by means of the ten practices and supernatural powers previously cultivated and realized, one transforms and delivers sentient beings;
yet there is no mark of one who delivers nor of the beings delivered, for it is delivering while being without deliverance.

If, O disciples of the Buddha, there are those with faith, for them all practices take faith as their foremost priority. It is the root of all virtues. They do not give rise to the minds of heterodox paths or wrong views.

Free from the attachment to names and designations of various views, they will certainly not undergo the existence produced by the karma of fetters. They enter into the realm of emptiness and unconditioned dharmas.

The three marks are neither non-existent nor existent. There is no arising of arising; there is no abiding of abiding; there is no cessation of cessation. There is not a single dharma that exists as empty.

The wisdom of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is exhausted. It is the extinction of difference, the emptiness of form, and the emptiness of the subtle mind and mind-states.

Because the subtle mind and mind-states are themselves empty, faith and faith are quiescent and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Even their conjunction has no basis. Yet, the master—the self and the person—[remains].
This refers to the function of names. The "provisional self" of the three realms cannot be apprehended as having the characteristics of an accumulation [of dharmas];

therefore, it is called the "markless faith. If the Buddha-disciples designate the person, then "faith" designates the Dharma. "All practices" refers to the myriad practices from the Ten Abodes up to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment.
Regarding the phrase "taking faith as the foremost," faith is precisely right faith; this means that this right faith does not... [text truncated].
Among the ten special vajras, this is the foremost of the first. Beginning from the stage of the Ten Faiths, it has already attained precedence over the myriad practices as the primary one.
Thus it is said: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness.
All the flowers and fruits of the bodhisattvas' wisdom arise from this right faith. Therefore, it is said:
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) take faith as their foremost; it is the root of all virtues. From non-arising to non-attainment, this correctly represents the true locus of faith.

How could the false ever overcome the true? All the various minds of the ninety-six types of external paths (*tīrthika*), the sixty-two false views, and so forth—along with all their perspectives, names, attachments, existences, and fabrications [are surpassed by it].
All karmas are likewise ultimately not received, just like dust blown by the wind. Regarding "entering emptiness and so forth":
because there is no arising and no receiving, all dharmas are empty; because all dharmas are empty, one is finally able to realize and enter this.
Within this unconditioned dharma of emptiness, this emptiness is precisely true emptiness, and the unconditioned dharma is the principle of emptiness. To enter [it]...

This refers to the realization and entry into the principle of true emptiness and unconditioned emptiness. The three characteristics culminating in the emptiness of all phenomena correctly represent and express faith in the principle of emptiness.

These three characteristics—namely, the characteristic of arising, the characteristic of abiding, and the characteristic of cessation—are themselves empty and non-existent once one enters the unconditioned dharma of emptiness through firm and authentic faith. Thus, these three characteristics also become empty and do not exist.
Since there is neither existence nor non-existence, it is called "non-non-existence" (*wu-wu*). The "non-existence" below gives rise to the ultimate expression of the principle of non-non-existence.
The "non-existence" above refers to emptiness; it speaks of the principle of emptiness wherein all phenomena—sentient and insentient—within the world are exhausted and unborn.
The "non-existence" below refers to the contemplative wisdom that is able to enter this principle of emptiness and non-arising; this wisdom, too, should likewise [be understood as non-existent].

Because there is no arising, it is said that "non-arising is non-arising. The same applies to the correct faith, contemplative wisdom, and insight regarding non-abiding abiding and non-extinction extinction.
Since the phenomena of arising, abiding, and extinction are already non-existent, then whether one considers a hundred, a thousand, or all things, what phenomenon would not be non-existent?
There is not a single phenomenon that is not empty; this is what is meant by "all."
The emptiness of dharmas is likewise non-existent; this is the meaning of being utterly exhausted without remainder. Regarding "the conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and so forth:
the conventional truth is the worldly truth, which refers to mundane phenomena. The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the true truth, which refers to supramundane phenomena.
The conventional truth, the ultimate truth, and the mundane and supramundane wisdoms of contemplation—all reach their final exhaustion here without remainder.
"The emptiness that extinguishes differentiation" refers to the emptiness that extinguishes the coarse delusions of various views and karmas within the desire realm.
"The emptiness of form" refers to the emptiness that extinguishes the subtle delusions of the form realm—the non-arising of arising, the non-abiding of abiding, and the non-extinction of extinction.
Furthermore, regarding the emptiness of each and every subtle thought: this refers to the cessation of the realm of consciousness such that not a single dharma remains;

it is the emptiness of the subtle delusions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, wherein conventional wisdom is exhausted, ultimate wisdom is exhausted, the obstruction to principle is exhausted, and the obstruction to knowledge is exhausted.
Because these subtle delusions are extinguished by the emptiness of each and every thought, and because the mind itself is likewise empty, this very cognitive faculty of faith is [emptied].
Furthermore, the principles and objects of faith are naturally quiescent without requiring their elimination;

even their fundamental essence and constituent parts are quiescent and non-existent. Because they lack an essential nature, who is there to believe, what is there to be believed, and who could be joined with whom through mutual dependence?
Nevertheless, within the three realms, those who establish themselves as sovereign lords—there are...
The "self" and the "person" that exist have names and functions; these are all merely provisional selves and persons within the three realms, provisional names and provisional functions.
If one seeks, accumulates, or seeks out characteristics within this self, they are utterly unobtainable.
Within the person—within its name and its function—is there any obtainable accumulation or characteristic to be found? If this is so, then it is precisely called "without essence or characteristics."
This is the stage of right faith. This explains the initial stage of the position of faith.
○ Second is the stage of the mind of mindfulness;
"mindfulness" refers to the dedication of the mind of mindfulness. Other scriptures name this the "Indestructible Dedication," meaning that one is free from the marks of sentient beings.
This is that which can be destroyed; destroying that which can be destroyed and remaining far removed from all forms of detachment is called the "indestructible dedication.

If, O Son of the Buddha, you maintain the six recollections—constantly mindful up to constantly practicing giving—the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is empty, without attachment and without liberation.

Regarding the marks of arising, abiding, and ceasing, they are unmoving, unattainable, and neither coming nor going; yet, within all karmic actions and their recipients, they are of one unified whole.

Mutually dedicating signs, entering the wisdom of the Dharma-realm; wisdom and wisdom mounting one another, vehicle upon vehicle entering quiescence. Flame upon flame is impermanent; light upon light is non-existent.

Birth after birth does not arise; shifting and changing through the path of emptiness. Transforming the former and turning toward the latter; transformation within transformation, transformation within transformation.
Simultaneously dwelling together; flame upon flame is a single mark. Arising and ceasing at one time—already transformed, not yet transformed, transforming.
Transformation and manifestation also each attain one [result].
Feeling is likewise so. "If a Buddha-son forms a thought," and so forth: "thought" means clear recollection and not forgetting.

When a Buddha-son in his proper station forms a thought, what kind of thought does he form? It refers to forming six kinds of thoughts. What are the six thoughts? First, the thought of... [the first thought].

The Buddha is constant awakening, which is precisely mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti). Second is mindfulness of the Dharma; third, mindfulness of the Saṅgha; fourth, mindfulness of the precepts;

fifth, mindfulness of the heavens; sixth, mindfulness of giving. Even when abbreviated to the four foundations of mindfulness, these are merely two ends that are constantly practiced, which is precisely mindfulness of giving.

Constantly contemplate the Middle Way and the principle of emptiness within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since one does not perceive any mundane phenomena that can bind, there is no attachment;

since one does not perceive any noble realization that can be attained, there is no liberation. Being without both attachment and liberation, although there is arising, there is no characteristic of arising;
although there is abiding, there is no characteristic of abiding; although there is cessation, there is no characteristic of cessation. Since these three...
Regarding "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*): who could move toward or arrive at coming and going? Since there is neither movement nor arrival, there is no coming and no going.

Yet, regarding all karmas, the recipient gathers and merges them, fusing them into a single unified mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*), and dedicates this toward the realization and entry into the principle of the wisdom of emptiness within the *dharmadhātu*.
As for "wisdom upon wisdom mounting one another": the superior wisdom is that which constantly contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) to shatter [delusions].
The true wisdom of the mundane world; the inferior wisdom that immediately arises as the wisdom of realization through emptiness and entry into the principle of the *dharmadhātu*.

"Vehicle" (*yāna*) carries the meaning of a wheel-vehicle. This signifies that this true wisdom and the wisdom of principle deliver sentient beings in every thought-moment into the *dharmadhātu*, like a wheel-vehicle that never ceases.
Regarding "the vehicle of the vehicle’s quiescence": the superior vehicle consists of constantly contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to deliver [beings].
The True Vehicle of the mundane world; the Inferior Vehicle is the principle-vehicle that arises from emptiness to deliver sentient beings and realizes entry into the Dharma-realm.
"Quiescent extinction" (nirvāṇa) signifies the meaning of being unmoving, non-attaining, and neither departing nor arriving.

It is said that this True Vehicle, the Principle Vehicle, is fundamentally empty and quiescent: it revolves without revolving, and revolves while not revolving. As for "flaming and impermanent," "flaming" refers to—
This is the flame of wisdom (*prajñā-jvālā*). Each flame is itself wisdom; it is without permanence and has no fixed location.

It is said that this flame of wisdom does not enter the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), nor does it depart from the Dharma-realm. It comes and goes to deliver sentient beings, never remaining fixed in a single place.
Regarding "each light is non-existent": light is the light of wisdom within the vehicle of wisdom (*jñāna-yāna*); each light is itself wisdom.
Furthermore, there is no sense of destroying delusions through non-existence or realizing the truth through non-existence.

It is said that this light of wisdom—the light of wisdom—shines upon and destroys the coarse and subtle delusions of sentient beings within the triple world; yet these are fundamentally empty and there is nothing to be removed.

It shines through the entire dharma-realm; it is empty and possesses nothing, yet there is nowhere it enters. It is detached yet not detached; not detached yet detached. It enters yet does not enter; does not enter.
Thus one enters. Therefore it is said: "Light upon light, non-being upon non-being. Regarding "birth after birth without arising":
since it is light upon light and non-being upon non-being, then birth after birth does not arise; though arising, there is no arising.

Without movement, one reaches the coming and going, and through transformation and change, one turns toward the Way of Emptiness and enters the Dharma-realm. "Turning" (zhuǎn) means returning; "changing" (yì) means directing. One turns birth toward the non-existent.

Birth. It is the turning from the mundane toward the sacred, and the turning from affliction toward bodhi. Because it turns in this way and transforms in this way, it is able to change what precedes and transform what follows.
Regarding "changing what precedes and transforming what follows": "change" refers to the transformation of the six consciousnesses; "what precedes" refers to the first five [consciousnesses].
"Transforming" refers to the revolving of the seventh consciousness; "what follows" refers to the eighth consciousness. As for "changing what precedes":
"Transformation and illumination": the five preceding consciousnesses are, in their very essence, originally empty. "Turning back" means circling back to the source;
it refers to the original purity of the nature of the latter eight consciousnesses. Regarding "transforming and evolving":

since the five preceding consciousnesses are in their essence fundamentally empty, they transform into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is To Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*); thus, the six consciousnesses of transformation and illumination likewise [merge] with it.

Both are transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). Once the original nature of the latter eight consciousnesses is purified and transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the seventh consciousness—which revolves and returns—likewise undergoes simultaneous transformation into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
Therefore, it is said: "transforming and evolving through transformation. Regarding "transformation and turning through transformation," this refers to the former...

The latter two wisdoms are fundamentally unshakable, like space or a mirror. As for that which enables these two consciousnesses to be transformed and converted so as to realize and enter fundamental wisdom—whose power is it?
It is entirely the power of the seventh and sixth [consciousnesses] to transform and evolve.
The seventh arises in dependence upon the eighth; the sixth is produced from the fifth. Because they arise together with what is produced, they are simultaneous. As for their cessation and...

They abide together because they are both extinguished. Regarding the phrase "flame upon flame" (*yanyan*): "flame upon flame" refers to the wisdom-flame of the transformed consciousnesses becoming gnosis.
The "upper flame" indicates the preceding and succeeding moments; the "lower flame" indicates the transformational process.

This means that once the four consciousnesses have become the four gnoses, the wisdom-flames of the fifth and eighth consciousnesses and those of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are realized to be without dual characteristics; arising together with birth, yet there is no arising.
Cessation ceases together with that which it accompanies, yet there is no cessation; all are identical in being simultaneously without arising and without ceasing.
Regarding "that which has already changed" and so forth: that which has already changed is the past; that which has not yet changed is the future; and that which is changing is the present.

"Transformation" (*hua*) carries the meaning of realization and entry. Since they are realized as simultaneous and one, then the dharmas of the three periods and ten directions have no [independent existence].

It is not realized. Furthermore, regarding "attaining oneness": this means that although the causes and effects of good and evil in the past, future, and present do not go anywhere, one does not attain a "unified mark" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) for the sake of dedicating [merit] toward entering the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.
That "feeling is also like this" means that what was previously stated—that all karmic feelings are dedicated toward entering the *dharmadhātu* as a unified mark—is likewise [not realized].
This constitutes the attainment of the first stage. This explains the mental state of the second thought-moment.
○ Third, the stage of the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
The mind of dedication is precisely the profound mind of dedication. In another sutra, it is named "Dedication Equal to All Buddhas."

This refers to the nature of the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) toward which one is directed; it is profoundly still and eternally abiding, and because the wisdom that can awaken to it is equal to the awakening of a Buddha.

O Son of the Buddha, as for the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*), it is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Through the wisdom of the emptiness of real dharmas, it illuminates the existence of the true reality (*satya*). This is its function.

The continuity of the Path is the Middle Way within causes and conditions; this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The provisional designations of all phenomena—such as self, person, or master—are called the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Within these two truths, one penetrates deeply into emptiness, such that there is no coming or going. Like a magical illusion, one experiences the fruits of karma yet remains without a recipient;
thus, through this profound penetration, the mind attains liberation.
Regarding the phrase "if a Buddha’s disciple has a profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*): "profound" refers to a depth that is not merely shallow or moderately deep, but the most ultimate depth;

therefore, it is called the "profound mind. As for "the emptiness of the primary meaning" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), this refers to the principle of the Great Emptiness of the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu*).

Regarding the wisdom of the emptiness of real phenomena (*dharmas*), this is precisely the great wisdom of emptiness of the single true *dharmadhātu*. By means of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, one enters the principle of the *dharmadhātu*.

When the wisdom of principle and the principle itself are perfectly interfused, the *dharmadhātu* is unimpeded. Thus, by means of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* and its principle, one gives rise to the illumination of discernment (*prajñā*).

This illumination perceives the "real" truth; "existence" (*yu*) is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while "reality" (*shi*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). However, this ultimate truth is not...

Apart from conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there exists something else: namely, the continuity of the paths of karma, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

By illuminating these causes and conditions of arising and ceasing with the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), one brings them into accord with the principle of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), which is fundamentally neither-arising-nor-ceasing;
this is called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). As the Sūtra says: "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I..."
To speak [of it] is itself emptiness; it is also called "provisional designation" (prajñapti), and it is also called the meaning of the "Middle Way. It is precisely this.

Regarding the phrase "all dharmas as provisional designations," it means that names and words are established provisionally to designate all phenomena—calling them "self," "person," or "master"—and therefore it is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The Bodhisattva, regarding these two truths of existence, examines them with certainty and illuminates them with clarity.
They deeply penetrate into the principle of emptiness within the great empty Dharma-realm; yet they do not perceive existence, nor do they perceive reality.
Without coming or going, they manifest coming and going; like illusions and transformations, they manifest illusions and transformations.
Though there is no cause and effect, nor sin and merit, they manifest the experiencing of results. Why is this? Because fundamentally there is nothing to be experienced. Because there is none...
Because of this reception, it is only when this profound mind attains realization that one achieves liberation.

Furthermore, when Śrāvakas contemplate the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and realize the principle of the emptiness of persons, it is called "shallow liberation. When Pratyekabuddhas contemplate the Dharma of conventional truth and realize the principle of the emptiness of phenomena, [it is called "deep liberation"].

This is called "profound liberation. By means of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, the Bodhisattva contemplates that emptiness and the provisional are non-dual, and that the ultimate and the conventional are mutually integrated;
because this is profound within the profound, it is called the "liberation of the deeply deep mind. This explains the stage of the three profound minds.
The fourth is the stage of penetrating the mind (*cittāvabodha*).
"Penetrating" (*avabodha*) refers to the dedication that penetrates the mind. A separate sutra names this the "Dedication Reaching All Places" (*sarvatragāminī pariṇāmanā*).

This means that the wisdom capable of awakening previously is omnipresent, reaching everywhere; since it is now equal to the Buddha's awakening, the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) realized therein is likewise [all-pervading].
This is because the Buddha is not different [from this nature].
O Disciples of the Buddha, those who possess penetrating illumination endure and accord with all true natures. These natures are neither bound nor liberated.

They attain mastery over unimpeded phenomena, mastery over meaning, mastery over words, and mastery over teaching and transformation. They penetrate the causes and effects of the three periods of time and the faculties and practices of the roots of all sentient beings, remaining as they truly are (*tathatā*).

Conjoined, yet not dispersed; without practical utility, without function, and without the function of names. All functions are empty. Through the emptiness of emptiness, one illuminates and penetrates emptiness;
this is called penetrating the emptiness of all phenomena. Emptiness is the suchness of emptiness; its characteristics cannot be apprehended.

If a disciple of the Buddha is one who "penetrates and illuminates": "penetration" (da) means thorough understanding; "illumination" (zhao) means penetrating clarity. This refers to thoroughly understanding both phenomena and principle, and illuminating them with unimpeded clarity.
Regarding "patience and compliance" (ren-shun): "patience" (ren) means acceptance and realization; "compliance" (shun) means following along without opposition.

This means realizing the empty principle of the *dharmadhātu* through patience, and complying with the empty nature of the *dharmadhātu*. Through patience and compliance, one achieves thorough penetration.

All phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, are non-dual and indistinguishable from the fundamental essence and true nature of reality—the emptiness-principle and emptiness-nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding "the nature of natures": since this one true nature is thus, all natures of natures and their true natures are likewise so;
they are also non-dual and indistinguishable from emptiness-nature and the principle of emptiness. There is no ordinary deluded emotion that can bind them.

There is no noble liberation to be attained through liberation. Regarding "unimpeded," etc., it means that when one is able to endure and accord with the nature of things, such that there is neither bondage nor liberation, one immediately attains the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
What is unimpeded knowledge? When one penetrates and illuminates the phenomena (*dharma*), one endures and contemplates the characteristics of all dharmas:
the Four Great Elements are fundamentally empty; they are like illusions and transformations, utterly devoid of substantial reality.

This is the unimpeded wisdom regarding phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). When one attains realization and illuminates the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one patiently and compliantly contemplates the various aspects of the nature of phenomena, which pervade the ten voids;
they are from the beginning true, neither false nor empty, and no inherent nature can be apprehended. This meaning is unimpeded wisdom.
When one attains realization and illuminates the phrases of phenomena and the phrases of the nature of phenomena, one patiently and compliantly reflects with earnest contemplation.

The nature and principle of all phenomena are far removed from words and do not fall into the realm of names and expressions; they are spoken without speaking, and spoken without there being anything to speak.

This is the unimpeded wisdom of speech (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). Having personally mastered and thoroughly understood these phenomena, their principles, and all forms of expression, [one attains this].

Furthermore, by means of this analytical knowledge, one understands others and teaches and transforms sentient beings; with patience, compliance, and eloquence, one does not give rise to weariness or fatigue—this is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding "the equality of the three periods of time": it means that once the four unimpeded knowledges have been realized, then regarding the good and evil causes and effects within the ten dharma-realms across the three periods of past, present, and future, as well as the sharp and dull faculties of the sentient beings therein—
All various karmic activities are entirely suchness (tathatā), neither shifting nor changing, in accordance with the principle of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

Since no arising is perceived, how could there be conjunction? Since no ceasing is perceived, how could there be dispersion? Therefore, it is said that the three periods of time are equal, being neither conjoined nor dispersed.
Regarding "without reality" and so forth: since they are neither conjoined nor dispersed, they lack substantial reality. Since...
That which lacks substantial reality necessarily lacks practical utility. Since it lacks practical utility, it necessarily lacks the utility of names.
Since it lacks both practical utility and the utility of names, how could the nature, divisions, and principles of all phenomena—both mundane and supramundane—not be empty?
By means of this very principle of the two emptinesses of name-emptiness and reality-emptiness, one illuminates and penetrates true emptiness and reality.
In its nature, it accords perfectly and without doubt; it is non-dual and indistinguishable from the emptiness of the *dharmadhātu*.

Only in this way can one be called someone who has illuminated and thoroughly penetrated the emptiness of all phenomena. Regarding the terms "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) and "suchness" (*tathatā*):

"emptiness of emptiness" is the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, while "suchness" is the principle of the *dharmadhātu*. This means that within this wisdom of emptiness and this principle of emptiness, one seeks that which is empty.
The characteristic of emptiness cannot be apprehended; even seeking the characteristic of suchness (tathatā), it cannot be apprehended.
This explains the stage of the mind that penetrates the fourfold reach. ○ Fifth, the stage of the direct mind.
"Directly" (*zhí*) means directly dedicating the mind. In another sutra, this is called the "Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit.
This refers to the aforementioned "reaching all places," which are all worlds and so forth; these are the Tathāgatas.
Yet, the Tathāgata is the Tathāgata of all worlds, and the world is the world of all Tathāgatas. World as... [text ends]
This is because the merit of their mutual interpenetration and non-obstruction is inexhaustible.

O Disciples of the Buddha, "straight" means straight illumination: taking the conditions for the divine self (ātman) as the object, one enters the wisdom of non-arising; thus, the divine self of ignorance is empty.
Emptiness within emptiness; the mind of the principle of empty emptiness. Whether existing or non-existing, it does not destroy the seeds of the Way.
Through the single contemplation of the untainted Middle Way, one transforms and teaches all sentient beings of the ten directions, turning them all toward *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Abiding in uprightness—with an upright nature and upright conduct—those born within the three realms of emptiness encounter fetters and bonds yet do not undergo suffering.

Regarding the phrase "if a Buddha-son is upright," etc.: this refers to the meaning of being straightforward and illuminating all things, being public-spirited and without private bias, and being upright without yielding.
It means to give rise to contemplative observation from having realized and entered the Middle Way Dharma-realm of principle and wisdom.
It directly illuminates the sovereign essence-nature of all phenomena, which is entirely equal and devoid of any crookedness;
this is the direct illumination of one who is upright. As for "grasping at conditions such as the self," "grasping" refers to greedy attachment, and "conditions" refers to causes and conditions.

The "spiritual self" (ātman) is the self that discriminates through the six consciousnesses. The reason the six consciousnesses are called the "spiritual self" is that practitioners of the Two Vehicles do not understand the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;
rather, they rely on the discrimination of the six sense organs and the mental consciousness.

Because each of the preceding objects appears clearly and seemingly unimpeded, it is termed the "spiritual self. This is because the eighth storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is subtle and difficult to fathom, and the seventh...

Consciousness arises based on the eight [consciousnesses], manifesting both past defilement and past purity. Furthermore, it arises based on the six consciousnesses, manifesting both present defilement and present purity.
By means of the old sending forth the new, and the new sending forth the old, they transmit and convey one another in a continuous succession that never ceases.

This is also called "transmission" (fengzhuan) and also called "continuity" (xiangxu); this is because they are all unfathomable. These words directly illuminate without deviation; they directly grasp.
The followers of the Two Vehicles take the six consciousnesses as their object of focus and rely on the discrimination of external objects.

This "I"—which appears vividly and intelligently, resembling a spirit or a supernatural power—is pierced through by a single illumination. Fundamentally, there are no causes and conditions for greed or grasping that can arise or perish;

it is empty in its very essence. One merely realizes and enters into the wisdom of the principle of non-arising. Regarding the phrase "the ignorance and divine self are empty," this refers to ignorance prior to words.
Conditioned formations lead to suffering; they function as causes and conditions throughout the three periods of time.

When the divine self (*puruṣa*) that gives rise to views of arising and views of cessation enters this wisdom of non-arising, all existents are exhausted into emptiness. This is the emptiness of existence.

Within emptiness, even emptiness itself is emptied—this refers to the emptiness that exhausts all existents. Upon entering this wisdom of non-arising, even emptiness is exhausted into emptiness. This...
"Emptiness is non-existence. As for 'the principle-mind of emptiness and emptiness,' this refers to the principle-mind of both this particular emptiness and existence;

it is the principle-mind of universal emptiness and non-existence. When in existence, it does not cling to existence; when in existence, it possesses emptiness without destroying existence. When in non-existence, it does not realize non-existence;
when in non-existence, it possesses emptiness without destroying non-existence. Why is this? It is because this principle of the emptiness of emptiness is itself Bodhi."
It refers to the nature of the Path. How could anything—whether existent or non-existent—be able to destroy the diamond-seed?
Therefore, it is said that "emptiness is empty" and so forth; this means the seed of the Path is indestructible. Regarding "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) and so on:
"outflow-free" carries the meaning of being indestructible. Since it is indestructible, it cannot be permeated or leaked by any existence or non-existence; it does not leak into existence.
