Due to the existence of ignorance, one subsequently accumulates immeasurable and manifold minds of discursive thought and攀缘 (*pán-yuán*, object-dependent clinging), creating all manner of conditions for evil karma and inviting [suffering].
It draws forth the fruit of suffering, continuing in an uninterrupted succession. Past causes produce present fruits, and present causes invite future fruits.
Thus, through the accumulation of causes and the accumulation of causes, the causes and fruits of the three realms are gathered;
this is what is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). It is said that this cause of origination, ignorance (*avidyā*), is that which must be severed by all sentient beings.
This explains the dharma-gate of abandoning the origin [of suffering].
Right view is liberation; it is the path of the wisdom of emptiness within emptiness. Each moment of mind is designated as the path of wisdom, the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
Regarding "right view and so forth," it asks: how does one cultivate the path? It means that having already known suffering as described above, this constitutes right view.
The cessation of the origin [of suffering] is itself liberation. Why then seek a separate right view for liberation? To possess right view is to realize the emptiness of suffering;

to possess liberation is to realize the emptiness of the origin. This realization of the emptiness of suffering and the emptiness of the origin is precisely the path of wisdom that fully possesses the supreme, great emptiness.
By means of this wisdom of emptiness, one continues from mind to mind and from moment to moment...
Furthermore, one no longer undergoes the retribution of the causes for the accumulation of the fruits of suffering within the three realms;

this is precisely what is called the "further cultivation of the path of wisdom. This is used in the sense of further cultivation. As for the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), it concludes the preceding text.
This is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). This explains the dharma-gate of cultivating the path.

It exhausts all karmic retributions and exhausts all causes. It is the pure, singular illumination; its essential nature is wondrous wisdom; it is the single truth of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "exhausting all existence" (*sarvabhava*) and so forth: it asks, "How is cessation (*nirodha*) realized? The first instance of the character *you* (existence) should be understood as applying to all sentient beings who possess consciousness and a mind.
The second instance of the character *you* refers to "existence" in the sense that cause and effect are not forgotten;

[it refers to] the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the desire realm, form realm, and formless realm, which cause one to transmigrate through the three realms and prevent escape from all [sufferings].

Because it is suffering, it is called "existence" (*bhava*). One practices the Noble Path with right knowledge and right view, so that greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and doubt do not arise, nor do the various false views concerning the self and its possessions.

One exhausts the delusions of the three realms and twenty-five states of existence—such as those of seeing and thinking, and those like motes of dust in a beam of light—as well as the fruits and causes of suffering. One illuminates each of these solely by means of this pure wisdom of great emptiness.
To realize this is like blowing dust before the wind; its essential nature and wondrous wisdom are entirely identical, reaching a state of quiescent extinction without remainder.
This is what is called the Single Truth of Quiescent Extinction (*śānta-ekasatya*). This explains the Dharma-gate of realizing cessation.
The perfection of the category of wisdom is called a "root" (*mūla*). All that is of the nature of wisdom arises as emptiness and enters into contemplation; this is the first root of goodness.

Regarding the phrase "the category of wisdom and so forth," the two characters for "roots" (*mūla*) should correctly correspond to all preceding roots of goodness. The character "root" signifies the foundation of all meritorious qualities.
The character "foundation" refers to this category of great emptiness-wisdom, which is fully endowed with the immeasurable virtues of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
The Chapter on Virtue: All [virtues] take the Great Emptiness Chapter as their fundamental basis. Regarding "all wisdom-natures" and so forth:

"all" refers to the four immeasurables and the like. The statement that the wisdom-natures of all—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—likewise arise within Great Emptiness means that by entering the contemplation of wisdom through emptiness, one manifests in the six realms of existence to benefit those suffering.

To afflict sentient beings, one teaches and demonstrates the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths, enabling all sentient beings to know suffering, abandon its origin, cultivate the path, and realize cessation;
this is called the first root of goodness.

Second is the contemplation of equanimity (*upekṣā*). All modes of attachment are entirely equal and empty. One contemplates all phenomena with equanimity, without conditions, as having the single characteristic of the limit of emptiness.
I contemplate the earth and soil of all ten directions as all being the old soil used by my former bodies;
the waters of the four great oceans are my former waters; and all the fires at the end of kalpas are the fire used by my former bodies.
Fire and all wind-wheels are the breaths formerly employed by me. I now enter this earth-element; my Dharma-body is fulfilled, and I cast off my former body.
Ultimately, I shall no longer receive a defiled body composed of the four great elements and subject to segmentation. This is the perfection of the Chapter on Casting Off.

Regarding the second [section], etc.: Having already explained that one contemplates suffering, abandons the origin, cultivates the path, and realizes the truth, there is a fear that people might become greedily attached to the bliss of nirvana and fail to relinquish it;
therefore, one further exhorts the contemplation of relinquishment (*upekṣā*). Now, as for what is to be relinquished through this path: what is it? This relinquishment is not merely relinquishing;
it is the relinquishing of the deluded thoughts, craving, attachments, and unwholesome conduct of ordinary beings. Externally...
It is taught that various false views are not abandoned; rather, it is through the various causes and conditions of the Two Vehicles that they are abandoned.

With right knowledge and right view, one contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) with the equanimity of cessation, ensuring no attachment arises. One causes them all to be equal and empty, and even this "equal emptiness" is abandoned.

When there is no object (*ālambana*) to be abandoned, abandonment itself is also abandoned, as one contemplates the limit of emptiness (*śūnyatā-koṭi*) regarding all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
In this state, no characteristic can be apprehended, nor can any characteristic be abandoned; therefore, it is called "the single characteristic.

When I say, "I contemplate all things as equal," I mean that I contemplate all the earth and soil as being the old flesh and bones used by my past bodies, and the waters of the four great oceans as being the old blood and veins used by my past bodies, and all the fires at the end of kalpas as... [the old marrow and fat used by my past bodies].
The old warmth that my body formerly utilized and all the wind-circles were the old breaths formerly utilized by my body.

Now that I have realized and entered this Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*), having attained the realization of the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the perfect fulfillment of the signless Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*),
I cast off my former body, forever severing all perverse obstructions, and shall never again [be subject to them] in the ultimate sense.

Because the body receives the impure and defiled portions of the four great elements, it is [so called]; because it does not receive [them], this constitutes the fulfillment of the category of relinquishment (*upekṣā*).
This is the second contemplation on the roots of goodness of relinquishment.

The third contemplation: bestowing upon all sentient beings to be transformed the happiness of humans and devas, the happiness of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the happiness of being free from the fears of the ten unwholesome actions, the happiness of attaining the *Sukusuma-samādhi*, and even the happiness of Buddhahood. One who contemplates in this manner is fully endowed with the category of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Regarding the third equality: this means that when these Bodhisattvas teach the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, they necessarily provide them with happiness according to their individual capacities.
Therefore, they next contemplate the various faculties and natures of all sentient beings to be converted.

For those who seek the happiness of humans and devas, they provide the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Wholesome Actions, causing them to be born among humans and devas to experience superior and wondrous bliss.
Bliss. For those who seek the Bodhisattva vehicle, [the Buddha] provides the six perfections and the four means of integration, enabling them to realize the bliss of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

For those who seek the bliss of being free from the terrors of the ten non-virtues, sentient beings—who in the past committed the three impure karmas and will inevitably fall into the fears of the three miserable realms—are led to turn away from these ten non-virtues and cultivate the ten virtues, thereby attaining rebirth.
Humans and devas receive the bliss of the ten wholesome paths. Regarding the phrase "attaining the Samādhi of the Wondrous Flower" and so forth:

it means that this Bodhisattva is caused to attain the Samādhi of the Correct Concentration—the causal flower of the myriad practices of the wondrous path of the sages. By mounting this wisdom-concentration, they realize the fruit of the ten stages;
thus, they obtain the bliss of the Samādhi of the Wondrous Flower, even unto the attainment of the Buddha-fruit and Nirvana without remainder.
The ultimate bliss of parinirvāṇa. One who contemplates in this way is said to be fully endowed with the category of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Free from the fear of evil and endowed with the five joys, they are fully possessed of joy. This is the third contemplation, the root of goodness of loving-kindness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dwells within this stage; free from delusion, greed, and hatred, they enter the wisdom of the single truth of equality, which is the root of all practices.
They traverse all Buddha-worlds and manifest immeasurable Dharma-bodies, as described in the "Chapter on the Celestial Flowers of All Sentient Beings."
At that time, the Bodhisattva abides within these two stages; because the category of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) is fully perfected, there is no characteristic of delusion (*moha*).

Because the category of relinquishment (*tyāga-skandha*) is fully perfected, there is no characteristic of greed (*lobha*). Because loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy are fully perfected, there is no characteristic of hatred (*dveṣa*).

Since greed, hatred, and delusion are absent, he thereby realizes and enters the single truth of noble gnosis (*ārya-jñāna*), which is the wisdom-category of the great emptiness of equality. This is...
Taking the wisdom of the single truth of equality as the root of all practices,
one unifies this wisdom with practice to traverse all Buddha-worlds, serve all Buddhas, manifest immeasurable *dharmakāyas*,
and gather in immeasurable sentient beings. The meaning of the text explained here is as found in the great treatises.
This is explained identically in the "Chapter on the Heavenly Flowers of All Sentient Beings" within the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
Third is the Ground of the Radiance of Essential Nature (*Tattva-prakṛti-prabhāsvara-bhūmi*):
on this ground, the Bodhisattva abandons one type of obscuration of dullness and ignorance. This is precisely the innate [afflictive] aspect among the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This is so called because it arises from a partial adherence to dullness, which prevents the sublime wisdom of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, as well as the *dhāraṇī*, from manifesting.
One simultaneously abandons two kinds of deluded attachments: first, the delusion of desire and greed; second, the delusion regarding *dhāraṇī*.
These three factors can obstruct the third stage (*bhūmi*); only by severing these delusive obstructions does one ascend to the third stage. Now...
This Bodhisattva, through the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining (*śruta-dhāraṇī*) and the manifestation of the three types of wisdom (*tri-prajñā*), is able to permanently sever [the obscurations].

Because the obscurations of delusion have been severed, it is called the "Radiant Stage" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). The *tathatā* realized therein is termed the "Excellently Flowing *Tathatā*" (*viśeṣa-srotas-tathatā*), meaning that this *tathatā* causes the teachings that flow from it to be most excellent. Therefore, the Bodhisattva's station is associated with the King of the Yāma Heaven.
One provisionally cultivates dharmas such as the ten wholesome actions to transform and guide sentient beings. Among the ten *pāramitās*, the *pāramitā* of patience (*kṣānti*) is the most supreme;
it is not that the others are not cultivated, but they are practiced according to one's strength and capacity.

O sons of the Buddha, at the stage of the Bodhisattva’s luminous essential nature, by means of the wisdom that understands through samādhi, one knows all the Dharma-gates of the Buddhas of the three periods of time—the twelve divisions of the Dharma: names, phrases, syllables, repetitions, verses, prophecies, direct prose, and stanzas.
Unrequested exposition; the Vinaya precepts; parables; the Buddha-realm; past events; the formal and the marvelous;

such discourses—these constitute the essence of the Dharma and are called the differentiation of all meanings. This is explained through words, phrases, and sentences as "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

They arise sequentially: first, consciousness enters the womb; then the four great elements increase, and the growth of form and mind is called the six stages (*ṣaḍ-āśraya*). Within the sense faculties, reality arises.

When there is awareness but one has not yet distinguished between suffering and pleasure, it is called the consciousness of contact (*sparśa-vijñāna*). Furthermore, the consciousness that perceives suffering and pleasure is called the three feelings (*tri-vedanā*). One continuously perceives and becomes attached to these feelings without end.

Through desire, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), and the existence of good and evil, the beginning of consciousness is called birth, and the end of consciousness is called death.
These ten categories are the causes, conditions, and fruits of present suffering. Contemplating these modes of activity as the Middle Way, I have long since been detached from them;
therefore, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As for the "Buddha-son" (Bhikṣu), the three phrases indicate and manifest his name, virtue, and rank. Regarding the "nature of the essence of radiance," it refers to this...
The Bodhisattva accomplishes supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the great dhāraṇī of the Dharma, and is able to give rise to the light of boundless wisdom;

therefore, it is called the Ground of the Radiant Essence (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*). In another scripture, it is named the Ground of Emitting Light (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), meaning that when the defilements of dualistic views regarding identity and difference have been purified, the radiant wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) unfolds; thus it is called "Emitting Light. By means of *samādhi*...
Regarding "understanding and so forth": Samādhi is the profound Great Nāga Samādhi.

It means that from this profound great samādhi, one gives rise to the light of great wisdom, and only then can one interpret and comprehend the dharma-gates of the skillful means and transformative guidance of all Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions. Regarding "the twelve dharma-categories and so forth": "twelve" refers to the number.
"Dharma" refers to the rules of conduct and the categories of phenomena. "Names" refers to the collection of names (*nāmakāya*). "Phrases" refers to the collection of phrases (*padakāya*).

"Sentences" refers to the collection of sentences (*vyañjanakāya*). Whenever a Buddha appears in the world, he inevitably teaches these twelve dharma-gates as rules of conduct and categories of phenomena.
Within the Tripitaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—whether concerning phenomena or principles, cause or effect, or... [the text continues].

Regarding provisional and ultimate [teachings], whether exoteric or esoteric, there is not a single name, term, meaning, or phrase that does not fully encompass these twelve divisions of the Dharma; they include everything without exception. What are the twelve?

The first is called *geya* (in Sanskrit), which in Chinese is translated as "repeated verse" (*ying song*) or "repeated chanting" (*zhong song*). This is because the meaning of the prose sections is not fully exhausted, and thus it is repeated.
Verses (*gāthā*) are spoken to accommodate the capacities of future practitioners. Second is *sūtra*: the Sanskrit term *sūtra* translates into Chinese as "Scripture of Accordance" (*qìjīng*).
It accords with the principle of all Buddhas above and accords with the capacities of sentient beings below.

Those that consist only of prose (*gadya*) without verses are, for example, the *Mìtuo xīnjīng* (Amitābha-hṛdaya-sūtra) and others. Third is *vyākaraṇa*: the Sanskrit term *vyākaraṇa* translates into Chinese as...

Fourth is the *vyañjana-gāthā* (direct verse). In Sanskrit it is called *gāthā*, and in Chinese it is translated as "recitation" (*fèngsòng*) or "independent verse" (*gūqǐ*). It refers to verses that should not be spoken directly within prose; examples include the "Vajrasamādhi" and "Śūnyatā" chapters [of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*].

This is the bestowal of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), wherein the Tathāgata prophesies that various great bodhisattvas and śrāvaka disciples will become buddhas in future ages, including the adornments of their kalpas and lands.
The fifth is the *anuddesa* (unrequested discourse). In Sanskrit it is called *udāna*, which in Chinese means "self-exposition.

Without anyone posing a question, the Buddha, through his knowledge of others' minds, observes the capacities of beings and speaks spontaneously when the time is right; examples include the *Buddhapiṭaka-śikhara-sūtra* and the *Amitābha-sūtra*.
The sixth is the *vinaya-śīla* (disciplinary precepts). In Sanskrit it is called *nidāna*, which in Chinese means "causes and conditions. This is because—

The precepts are for the most part based on causes and conditions (*nidāna*). They consist of questions and answers, as well as the establishment of prohibitions regarding matters of observance and violation, gain and loss;
these include all fundamental origins, the causal conditions of good and evil, and the retribution thereof.
The seventh is *avadāna* (parables), which means comparison by analogy. Those who possess wisdom must rely upon parables to attain understanding.
This refers to the "Opening and Explaining" (Kaijie). The eighth is the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu*). The Sanskrit term is *jātaka*; the Chinese term is "Original Birth" (*ben-sheng*).

This refers to the Tathāgata’s recounting of the events of his births during his original causal stages as a bodhisattva, as well as his own narration of the events of his births during those original causal stages.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Bhikṣus, you should know that in the past, I was a deer."
These include [the Buddha] manifesting as a deer, a bear, and so forth, up to manifesting as a crown prince or a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), and so on.
Ninth is the "Past Deeds" (*itivṛttaka*); in Sanskrit, *itivṛttaka*, and in Chinese, "Original Deeds.

This refers to the accounts of the various practices and austerities performed by the Bodhisattvas and disciples during their causal stages (*hetu-bhūmi*) in their quest for the path and Dharma of enlightenment, such as gathering fruit and drawing water.

[These include] offering water, providing firewood and food, spreading one's hair to cover the mud, using one's own body as a seat, lighting lamps to seek a verse, cutting off flesh and sacrificing the body, and even [the acts of] a Golden Wheel-Turning King who sacrificed a thousand heads, and so forth. The tenth is Rectitude.

In Sanskrit, this is *vaipulya*; in the abbreviated Chinese, it is "Great, Square, and Vast" (*dà fāngguǎng*). "Great" refers to the greatness of essence; "square" refers to the greatness of characteristics;
and "vast" refers to the greatness of function. This refers to the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras preached by all Tathāgatas;
their meaning is like empty space—broad, expansive, and inclusive, reaching everywhere. The eleventh is "unprecedented" (*adbhuta*). In Sanskrit... [text ends].
The term *ābhūtam* means "unprecedented" in the language of China; it is also called "rare.

This refers to such rare events as when the Buddha was first born, pointing to heaven and earth with his hands, leaving lotus-flower footprints, illuminating the ten directions, and causing the earth to quake in six ways.
Upon seeing or hearing such rare occurrences, people marveled at their strangeness and all said, "How rare! The twelfth is "discourse"; the Sanskrit term is *vyākaraṇa*.
*Avadāna*. *Upadeśa* refers to the discourses on the meaning of various dharmas found within the sūtras, consisting of questions, answers, and debates;
for example, the discourse between the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa and Mañjuśrī regarding the wondrous Dharma in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The above are the names and characteristics of the twelve divisions of the Dharma. This is the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "the essence and so forth": it means that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these twelve dharma-gates is fundamentally identical and, in reality, without distinction.
Because sentient beings possess all [various] minds, they employ all dharmas;
for this reason, there arise all names, all meanings, and all distinctions. Thus, within the words, phrases, and sentences, such distinctions exist.

This is what is being explained. Regarding the phrase "all that exists" and so forth: the so-called distinctions are intended to clarify how all sentient beings, through delusion regarding principle, give rise to phenomena;
and through delusion regarding wisdom, give rise to consciousness. This explains the meaning of how all conditioned dharmas subject to birth and extinction undergo birth in successive stages.
It is because one wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the True is originally present while the delusive consciousness is fundamentally non-existent.
Furthermore, what is meant by "receiving birth part by part"? That which first enters the consciousness into the womb is this initial stage of receiving birth;

it is precisely the meaning of "volitional formations (saṃskāra) as the condition for consciousness. This is because, due to being shrouded by the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa) of the past, one fails to understand the principle of the true suchness (tathatā) of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu);
this is termed "ignorance" (avidyā). Because of this ignorance, one falsely commits unwholesome and evil deeds. Such is the characteristic.

Because it continues to proceed, it is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). Due to the two conditions of ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations, there is "conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness" (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam*).
Ignorance and volitional formations are causes belonging to the past; however, in the present text, all ten categories are causes and conditions belonging to the present.

At the very first moment of entering the womb, consciousness takes up defiled craving as its seed, and through the reception of mental ideation (*saṃjñā*), the embryo is formed; this is termed [consciousness].

The coagulation and thickening of the elements is thus called the initial entry of consciousness into the womb. The growth of the four great elements within the physical form and mind refers to the reception of birth through these two aspects;
this is the meaning of "consciousness conditions name-and-form. It is said that while consciousness is in the womb, it taints the semen and blood of the parents.
Through the conjunction of these three conditions, it gradually grows and develops into the physical body, thereby coming to possess the substance of name, mind, and form. [One week.]

The second week is called the *kalala* (embryo). Upon reaching the fifth week, it is termed the stage of *ghana* (solidification), during which the various sense organs, limbs, hands, and feet are produced;
thus, it is said that the four great elements increase both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). This is called the sixth abiding (*ṣaṣṭha-vihāra*), which constitutes the third stage of taking birth.

This refers to the principle of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) being conditioned by name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*); specifically, from the time after name-and-form until the seventh week, it is called the growth of hair and body hair.
The stage of nails and teeth; reaching the forty-ninth day (seven weeks), it is called the stage of the complete formation of faculties and shape.
The six sense-faculties unfold, possessing the function of entering the six sense-objects. This is the locus where the deluded mind takes its support; therefore, it is named the "Six Abodes.

Within these faculties, a real perception arises, yet one has not yet distinguished between suffering and pleasure; this is termed "contact-consciousness. These constitute the fourfold process of receiving birth, which is precisely the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The meaning of "conditioned by contact" (*sparśa-pratyaya*) refers to the period from after birth until approximately three or four years of age.

During this time, the six sense faculties encounter the six objects and give rise to a non-conceptual, direct awareness (*avikalpaka-saṃvedana*), yet they are not yet capable of discriminating between suffering and pleasure.

Therefore, this direct awareness is termed "contact-consciousness. Furthermore, that consciousness which perceives suffering and pleasure is called the "three feelings" (*tri-vedanā*); this constitutes the arising of the fivefold feeling (*pañca-vidhā vedanā*).

This refers to the meaning of sensation (vedanā) conditioned by contact (sparśa). That is to say, from the time one is five or six years old until the age of twelve or thirteen, due to the six objects (ṣad-viṣaya) contacting the six sense faculties (ṣad-indriya), one is immediately able to experience [sensation].
For instance, when encountering an object of suffering, one perceives it as suffering and thus experiences the sensation of suffering;

when encountering an object of pleasure, one perceives it as pleasure and thus experiences the sensation of pleasure; and when encountering an object that is neither painful nor pleasant, one perceives it as...
Neither painful nor pleasant, yet there exists a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant; therefore, they are called the "three sensations.

The aforementioned five factors are the present fruit. As for the phrase "continually awakening to and clinging to, experiencing them without end," this refers to the arising of the sixfold division of sensation.

This refers to the meaning of "feeling" (vedanā) as the condition for craving (tṛṣṇā). That is to say, from the age of fourteen or fifteen until the age of eighteen or nineteen, one continuously gives rise to thoughts that greedily cling to sensual objects.
Although this is called "craving," it has not yet become a broad seeking; it is still merely termed "feeling.

It is simply that the mind, through continuous awareness, becomes stained by and attached to that feeling, which is already inexhaustible. This is due to the views of selfhood (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) and the clinging to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
These seven factors constitute the process of rebirth; they correspond to the meaning of "clinging" (*upādāna*) conditioned by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

That is to say, from the age of twenty onward, due to the presence of various desires which stimulate the nature of craving, one engages in various acts of grasping and rejecting. One clings to the self, the retribution, and the person, giving rise to deep greed and grasping.

Driven by this greed, there arise hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), and clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*).

The ten afflictions (*daśa-āsrava*) are therefore named after desire, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*). Regarding "existence arising from good and evil":
these eight factors constitute the reception of birth. This is the meaning of "existence conditioned by grasping" (*upādāna-pratyaya-bhava*);

that is to say, because the six consciousnesses (*ṣad-vijñāna*) rush toward various objects and give rise to the performance of good and evil, they accumulate the causes for the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*). This draws forth the *ālayavijñāna*, which receives the fruit of birth within the three realms of existence in the future.
Therefore, it is called the existence of good and evil. These three links—craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*)—are the causes of the present.
Regarding "the first [link] of consciousness is called birth": these nine factors constitute the process of taking birth; this is the meaning of "birth conditioned by becoming.

That is to say, since there are already the causes of wholesome and unwholesome karma performed in the present, one will necessarily experience the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma in a future life; thus, the *ālayavijñāna* follows along with the wholesome [karma].
Regarding evil karma and rebirth in the six realms: this consciousness is the very first to enter the womb; therefore, it is said that the beginning of consciousness is called "birth.
That the end of consciousness is called "death" refers to this process of receiving birth in its ten stages, which is precisely the meaning of "old age and death conditioned by birth.
This means that after having received birth from a previous life, the physical form of the five aggregates matures and then decays until the single period of life comes to an end. This...
Consciousness is the last to be relinquished; therefore, it is said that the end of consciousness is called death.

Although these two dharmas of birth and death are termed the fruits of future lives, they are discussed here in terms of the present. In reality, they encompass the meaning of the arising and ceasing, the coming and going, and the successive taking of birth throughout the three periods of time.
This phrase is a general summary of the ten categories of present causes, conditions, and fruits of suffering.
This concludes the preceding section. It states that ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are the causes of the past, and that these past causes produce the effects of the present.
Now, why does the present discussion address only the causes and effects of the present, without mentioning the two causes of the past? This is because the effect encompasses the cause;
the Buddha intends for those present before him to recognize the suffering effects and the causes of suffering in the present, so as not to allow them to fall into [rebirth] again.
It creates the causes of tainted suffering and eternally extinguishes the fruits of future suffering. Regarding those who contemplate the characteristics of these formations (*saṃskāra*):
this means that within the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of all sentient beings, there are in reality no such characteristics as arising, ceasing, going, or coming.
Even when sought within delusion and awakening, they are truly unobtainable; how much more so for myself throughout the vast eons of the past?
Regarding this "Chapter on Upholding the Twelve Dharmas": amidst these various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that arise one by one, I have indeed long been detached from them.
Long ago, I entered into the wisdom of the Middle Way, which is without arising and without cessation, without going and without coming, and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Entering the supernormal power of radiance, possessing dhāraṇīs and eloquence, with every thought and action abiding in emptiness, they manifest within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions through kalpas and transformations.
For hundreds and thousands of kalpas, they cultivate their supernormal powers within those lands, paying homage before the Buddhas and receiving the words of the Dharma.

Furthermore, they manifest bodies within the six realms of existence, preaching immeasurable categories of Dharma with a single voice, while sentient beings each [perceive it according to their own capacity].
In each part, they hear the Dharma according to their own inclinations—the sounds of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and the single truth.
Though the lands differ and bodies and minds are transformed individually, within this Ground of Wondrous Flower Radiance, it is briefly opened up by the measure of a single hair-tip.
As explained in the "Chapter on the Exposition of Dharma" and the "Chapter on the Thousand Samādhis" regarding the gate of observing dharmas:
as for the phrase "entering the light," it means that this bodhisattva understands and maintains these twelve dharma-chapters, which are long free from names, phrases, and syllables;
because they are the characteristics and fruits of the causal conditions of suffering across ten chapters, he attains realization and entry into this light.
Within the ground of the essential nature, they attain the perfection of the supernormal power of the body and the samādhi of playful mastery of supernormal powers;
they attain the supernormal power of speech and the perfection of dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence; they attain the supernormal power of the mind regarding the activities of the mind.

This is the wisdom of emptiness, yet it further manifests throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, appearing through kalpas and transformations, increasing through hundreds and thousands of kalpas.
He constantly maintains the wheel of retention; within his realm, he nurtures the wheel of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

He pays homage before the Buddha, increasing the wheel of supernormal powers by receiving and studying the words of the Dharma, and increasing the wheel of the turning of the Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Furthermore, in the heavenly realms he manifests as a deva, and in the human realm he manifests as a human.
Even unto those in the realm of animals who manifest animal bodies, [the Buddha] speaks immeasurable categories of Dharma within a single utterance,
so that sentient beings of the six realms each hear, according to their own portions, the Dharma that delights their respective minds;
all are enabled to understand the sounds of the Single Truth of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self— this is what is called the "single manifestation of the perfect voice."
This refers to the equal understanding of different categories. Suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self are the four foundations of mindfulness:
body, sensation, mind, and phenomena. Regarding the contemplation that sensation is suffering: it is said that sentient beings are inverted, taking suffering for pleasure;

therefore, one causes sentient beings to contemplate that sensation is suffering so that they may attain the true bliss of quiescence. Regarding the contemplation that the body is empty: it is said that...
The internal body and the external body both consist of the gathered essence and blood of the parents; they are an accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that form the body.
From head to foot, it is entirely impure, yet sentient beings, through their inverted views, cling to it as pure.

Therefore, one causes sentient beings to contemplate the body as empty, thereby realizing the eternally abiding true emptiness. As for contemplating the mind as impermanent, this refers to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*).
"Mind" refers to this nature of mind which flows and fluctuates, arising and ceasing from moment to moment, entirely impermanent.

Sentient beings, through their inversions, mistakenly reckon it to be the true mind; therefore, they are led to contemplate the impermanence of the mind so as to realize the eternally abiding true mind.
Regarding the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*): this refers to all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.

Because sentient beings are subject to inversion and falsely recognize these phenomena as having a self, they are led to contemplate the selflessness of phenomena so that they may realize the true self of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
As for the "sound of the single truth": this refers to the four dharmas of suffering, emptiness, and so forth, which truly emerge from within this sound of the single truth.
The performance [of the teaching] is as follows: "This alone is the one reality; the other two are not true.

Regarding the statement that "the lands are different and the bodies and minds are transformed differently," this refers to the various differences—superior or inferior, pure or impure—in the lands entered by these bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas are able to manifest their bodies and minds, which likewise vary according to superiority or inferiority, purity or impurity. They divide their forms to gather and transform beings;

as for those to be transformed individually, they manifest whatever body is necessary for them to attain liberation and preach the Dharma—this is the means of gathering through "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*).
As for those such as "Exquisite Flower Radiance" (*Māndāravaprabhā*), this refers to [those who dwell] within this stage of Exquisite Flower Radiance.
The ocean-treasury of the vows and practices of boundless merit is ineffable;

herein, I have merely opened it up by a mere hair’s breadth, like a single drop of water from the great ocean taken up by a hair. Were it to be explained in detail, it would be as found in the Great Treatises.
As explained in the two sections of the *Dharmamudrā-vibhaṅga-darśana-mukha* and the *Trisahasra-samādhi-paṭala*:
Fourth, the stage of *Tathatā-jvalanā*.
At this stage, the Bodhisattva abandons one type of subtle affliction that manifests as an obstacle; this is precisely the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is so named because the subtle affliction of innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) arises therein. Furthermore, it eliminates two kinds of deluded attachments:

first, the delusion of craving for meditative attainment (*samāpatti-tṛṣṇā-moha*); second, the delusion of craving for phenomena (*dharma-tṛṣṇā-moha*). By severing these obstacles of delusion, [it is established].

One then ascends to the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). This means that this Bodhisattva, having for the first time entered into realized gnosis and having skillfully cultivated the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), is able to give rise to the fire of the wisdom of blazing wisdom.

This burns the fuel of all root afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), whereby one is able to forever sever the obscurations of ignorance. Because this fire of wisdom is most supreme once these have been severed, it is called "Blazing" (*arci*).

The Ground of Wisdom (*prajñā-bhūmi*). The *tathatā* realized therein is called the "unappropriated *tathatā*," meaning that this *tathatā* is not the basis for the grasping of self-attachment and the like.
The stage of the Bodhisattva is associated with the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, where they provisionally cultivate the dharmas of the three vehicles and so forth.
In guiding and transforming sentient beings, among the ten *pāramitās*, the *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of diligence) is the most preeminent.
It is not that the others are not practiced; rather, they are cultivated according to one's capacity and portion.
O Sons of the Buddha: within the fundamental nature of the Bodhisattva’s essence, the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti) are neither interrupted nor eternal;
they arise, abide, and cease simultaneously. Within a single world, a single moment, and a single existence, various seeds manifest as various appearances.

Thus, the Middle Way of causes and conditions is neither one nor two, neither good nor evil, and neither ordinary person nor Buddha. Therefore, the realm of Buddhas and the realm of ordinary beings are each...

This is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). As for the contemplation of the path of wisdom, it is neither one nor two. Regarding the section on the concentration of the profound path, it refers to what is called the mental activities of the Buddha:

the initial awakening, the cause of concentration, and the factors of awakening—namely, the awakening of faith, the awakening of reflection, the awakening of tranquility, the awakening of exertion, the awakening of mindfulness, the awakening of wisdom, the awakening of investigation, the awakening of equanimity, the awakening of joy, and the awakening of relinquishment. These are the skillful means of each stage, wherein every moment of mind enters the fruit of meditative absorption.
"Er" (爾) means "thus. "Yanming" (燄明) means "blazing light. The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" (若佛子) serve to manifest the names, virtues, and stages [of the ground].
Regarding "the essence-nature" (體性): it is said that within the fundamental essence and nature of this stage, there is inherently present this principle of wisdom that illuminates both sides equally.
Because it illuminates all phenomena by way of correspondence, it is called the "Essence-Nature Blazing Ground" (體性地). In other sutras, it is named... [end of fragment].
The Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). This means that when wisdom is infinitely luminous, the Buddha’s awakening is perfected.
When awakening is perfected, the radiance of wisdom blazes forth like a great mass of fire, incinerating all emotional attachments and views; therefore, it is named "Blazing Wisdom.

As for the phrase "the ultimate truth and the conventional are equal," this clarifies the meaning of the twofold illumination: it states that the ultimate truth is itself the illumination of the conventional, and that the conventional is itself the ultimate truth. Thus, they are illuminated as one.
The conventional is itself the ultimate. That conventionality is not merely conventional; that conventionality is the ultimate, and thus the characteristics of the ultimate continue in succession.
Therefore, the ultimate does not sever its conventionality. Being non-conventional yet conventional, and since all conventions are like flames, conventionality is not permanent.

Since the ultimate is ultimately uninterrupted and conventionality is not permanent, then that ultimate flame arises, that ultimate flame abides, and that ultimate flame ceases—and all of these are...
It is precisely so. Since there are arising, abiding, and ceasing, then the boundless oceans of lands are one world-age; the ten ages of past and present are one moment;
and the ultimate, the conventional, and arising-ceasing are one existence. What further distinction could there be? Regarding the differences in seeds and so forth:
the reason for these distinctions is none other than that sentient beings possess the capacity within their seeds.

This is because there is a distinction between the perfuming agent and the perfumed object. Since the seeds thus perfumed differ, the Bodhisattva, in benefiting sentient beings, cannot but manifest diverse dharmas;
hence there arise the designations of "Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha-satya) and "Conventional Truth" (saṃvṛti-satya).

Regarding the ultimate causal conditions, the boundary between arising and ceasing, and the Middle Way—the locus of these two truths—what kind of realm is this? It is like a great mass of fire [that consumes] afflictions (*kleśa*).
Entering into this, the flames of wisdom increase all the more. Whether it be one or two, good or evil, ordinary or holy—there is not a single thing that is not a flame of wisdom.

Therefore, the realm of the Buddha and the realm of ordinary beings, every single mundane and supramundane phenomenon, are all termed "worldly truth" (saṃvṛti-satya), and they all equally increase the flames of wisdom. Regarding the phrase "their wisdom and path are equal," this refers to these three.
When the firewood of deluded wisdom encounters increasing flames, the wisdom of the Middle Way’s contemplation shines upon it once, leaving nothing behind;
therefore, there is neither one nor two, neither good nor evil, neither ordinary person nor Buddha. Regarding the "Chapter on the Samādhi of the Profound Path":
since it is said that within the contemplation of the path of wisdom there is neither one nor two, how can there still be various distinctions among the categories of samādhi?
The "profound path" (*xuan dao*) is the path of supreme wisdom. The "concentration category" (*ding pin*) refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
This consists of three categories, totaling ten categories of concentration. It is said that these ten categories of concentration manifest as distinct causes within the path of wisdom.
What is called "expounding the practice of the Buddha's mind" means that these various categories of the path are indeed the Buddha's mind and the Buddha's practice. Thus it is said.
Regarding these "distinctive dharmas," they are manifested as such distinctions based on the differences between the perfuming agent and the perfumed object among all sentient beings.
Within the definitive principle of the ultimate Buddha-mind and Buddha-practice—the ten gates of certainty—there is, in reality, no difference whatsoever.

As for the "definitive cause of initial awakening," it refers to the time when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas first awaken to and enter the path of enlightenment; at that moment, they awaken to themselves...
First: The mind of initial awakening is originally and fundamentally quiescent; it is only because ordinary beings are deluded that it is not so.

Now that I have awakened to the fact that initial awakening has a source, I take this as the direct cause. Therefore, it is called the "cause of initial awakening being fundamentally quiescent. Regarding "the one who awakens through faith":
they believe that the mind of initial awakening is originally and naturally quiescent, not obtained from another person. This is a singular faith, a perpetual faith, forever...

There is no retrogression. Second, regarding "reflective awareness": although what one believes is fundamentally settled, if one does not engage in reflection and cultivation, it will ultimately remain a hollow faith;
therefore, one must practice through contemplation. Third, regarding "tranquil awareness": although one may have reflected well and practiced cultivation...
If the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is absent, that which is maintained may fall into distracted thought; therefore, it is followed by the awakening of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*).

Fourth, as for the awakening of excellence (*adhimokṣa*): although one maintains [the mind] with the seal of the power of concentration, if the power of diligence (*vīrya*) is absent within that tranquility, one fears falling into the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
therefore, it is followed by the awakening of excellence. Fifth, as for the awakening of mindfulness (*smṛti*): once speech has become refined...

One must be diligent without slackening; one should further maintain this mindfulness at every moment so as not to lose it. Therefore, the awakening factor of mindfulness follows next. Sixth, the awakening factor of wisdom:
although the mind may be mindful and free from delusion, one must still apply the faculty of wisdom to illuminate the objects of perception;

only then can things be clearly discerned without confusion. Therefore, the awakening factor of wisdom follows next. Seventh, the awakening factor of investigation: although there is illumination through wisdom...
In this state, there is no sphere of delusion; one must necessarily apply even more subtle observation before being able to enter into principle and realize the truth.

Therefore, it is followed by the awakening of contemplation (*vicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Eighth, the awakening of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): through contemplation, one enters into principle, extinguishes delusion, and realizes the truth, only then attaining physical and mental lightness and ease.
Therefore, it is followed by the awakening of tranquility. Ninth, the awakening of bliss (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): as for the term...

Since the body and its characteristics are harmonized and the mental ground is expansive and comfortable, it necessarily brings joy to both body and mind; therefore, the factor of "pleasure" (*sukha-saṃbodhyaṅga*) follows next.
As for the tenth, the factor of "equanimity" (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*): because this essence of pleasure is unerring, the joyful mind is undisturbed, and one thereby attains right view and liberation;
therefore, the factor of "equanimity" follows next. These ten factors of enlightenment, when combined, constitute seven.
Awakening consists of uniting mindfulness with thought, contemplation with wisdom, and tranquility with serenity.

Although these differ in their respective categories, they are all the ten paths of skillful means within the contemplation of the path of knowledge; for they enable the practitioner, in every thought and every moment, to realize and enter the fruit of meditative concentration.

This person abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), vividly perceiving that the activities of phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty. If they give rise to a thought of concentration, it enters the mind;
from this concentration arises attachment and compliance, and they are transformed by the Way-dharma (*mārgadharma*). This is called the patience of the joy of Dharma (*dharmaprīti-kṣānti*).

Abiding in patience, realizing patience, and attaining the patience of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*), all Buddhas appear within this Radiant Flower Samādhi (*prabhāsa-puṣpa-samādhi*), manifesting immeasurable Buddhas who stroke their crowns with their hands and preach the Dharma with a single voice.
Though they arise hundreds of thousands of times, they do not emerge from samādhi; they abide in samādhi, relishing the bliss of samādhi, becoming attached to samādhi, and craving samādhi.

They remain in samādhi for one kalpa or a thousand kalpas, seeing Buddhas seated upon lotuses preaching hundreds of Dharma-gates. These people make offerings and listen to the Dharma while remaining in samādhi for a kalpa.
At that time, the light of all Buddhas touches their crowns, awakening the categories of samādhi, so that they manifest signs of emergence and signs of progress toward their destination.

Because of these marks, one does not sink, does not regress, does not fall, and does not abide; this is the Samādhi of the Summit. The Dharma-superiority, joy, and patience are forever exhausted without remainder.
From that point on, it is truly ultimate and non-dual; this is the meaning of the dual illumination of the flames of clear wisdom. From the profound Way... [text continues]
This clarifies the cause of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Within the path of skillful means belonging to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), there exists the cause of concentration;
from this arises the fruit of entering concentration with the mind. From "this person abides" up to "without remainder," this precisely clarifies the fruit of concentration.
Regarding the phrase "this person abides in concentration," it means that a person at this stage, by practicing the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), attains abiding within concentration. Due to...
By virtue of the power of concentration (*samādhi*), one gives rise to the blazing radiance of wisdom within meditative absorption.
This radiance illuminates and penetrates the ten modes of awakening and all dharmas, such that each and every one is empty.

Regarding the phrase "if thoughts arise," it means that at the very moment a single thought arises from within concentration, do not allow this thought to take another object; rather, simply turn back upon this very thought that has just arisen within concentration.
One should nevertheless continue to fix the mind upon the arising of thought. When the state of mental ideation reaches its limit, one should investigate that very limit.
This is like a person who constantly dwells at home in sorrow, wondering what household matter remains unaccomplished; it refers to this.

Regarding "the arising of concentration" and so forth: since thought arises from concentration and returns to enter concentration, both the arising of thought and the entry of thought are entirely within profound concentration.
Is it not the case that one gives rise to a mind of affection, delight, and compliance within profound meditative concentration?

Therefore, one is able to be born through transformation within the path-dharmas of profound concentration; this is called "patience with the joy of the Dharma" (*dharmārāmatā-kṣānti*). "Abiding patience" (*vihāra-kṣānti*) means abiding securely in patience without wavering.
"Realization patience" (*sākṣātkriyā-kṣānti*) means deeply realizing this patience without turning back. "Quiescent extinction patience" (*upaśama-kṣānti*) means quiescence...

They are extinguished within patience so that they do not arise. Therefore, the Buddhas of the ten directions, while abiding in this Samādhi of the Wondrous Flower of the Light of Wisdom and the Light of Insight, manifest immeasurable Buddha-bodies, personally stroke their heads with their hands, comfort their minds, and preach the Dharma with a single voice to inspire their resolve.
And yet, by means of this Bodhisattva’s profound power of concentration—
Therefore, it is unmoving, unchanging, and unarisen, yet he does not emerge from concentration. Why is this? Because while the bodhisattva dwells in this concentration, he does not arise from it;
he relishes and delights in this concentration without weariness; he maintains this concentration without shifting;
and he cherishes this concentration without abandoning it. By means of dwelling in this concentration, even unto his craving for concentration—
Therefore, those of shallow capacity remain in meditative concentration for one kalpa, while those of deep capacity remain for a thousand kalpas.
Within this profound concentration, they behold the Buddha seated upon a lotus flower, preaching to all sentient beings the "Dharma-gate of the Hundred Dharmas of the Stages of Mind.
As for these individuals, they are bodhisattvas who, within profound concentration, offer various kinds of worship and listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.
Therefore, those of shallow capacity remain in meditative concentration for one kalpa, while those of deep capacity remain in concentration for even a thousand kalpas.

Regarding the phrase "at that time, the various Buddhas," it means that because this bodhisattva’s profound mind is vast and far-reaching, and his practice has endured through long kalpas and deep years, he moves the various Buddhas.

Consequently, within the Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom, they again bestow the empowerment of stroking the crown of his head and twice further exhort him, causing him to emerge from the state of concentration and manifest.

The body benefits sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "manifesting signs such as emergence": this means that because this bodhisattva has received the empowerment of the touching of the crown of the head and attained great mastery, they manifest the signs of emerging from meditative absorption, the signs of advancing and guiding others, and the signs of proceeding to other directions to benefit sentient beings.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "not sinking, etc.": because they have initiated [this activity], they are able to emerge without becoming submerged, and are able to advance.
It is non-retrogressive; it can proceed toward its destination without falling away. It is not merely like this.
As for the most honored, most noble Samādhi of the Summit of Wisdom (mūrdha-jñāna), even the patience of delight (kṣānti-ruci) has no dwelling or attachment therein.

Thus, both the hindrance of craving for meditative concentration (samādhi-tṛṣṇā) and the hindrance of craving for the Dharma (dharma-tṛṣṇā) are abandoned together; therefore, it is said that they are forever exhausted without remainder.
They immediately enter into all Buddha-lands and cultivate immeasurable categories of merit. Every practice they perform is luminous;
they enter into skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to teach and transform all sentient beings, enabling them to perceive the Buddha’s essential nature: permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

"Immediately entering [the state of equality]" means that because one does not abide in the pleasure of the Dharma, one immediately enters into all Buddha-fields and lands to manifest the body for the benefit of beings;

above, one serves the Buddhas, and below, one uproots the various sufferings of sentient beings, simultaneously practicing the immeasurable and boundless categories of all meritorious dharmas of the path to enlightenment. "Practicing the practices" means that each practice corresponds to each category.

Furthermore, regarding the merits of each chapter, every single practice door is able to enlighten the ignorance of sentient beings and develop the light of wisdom within each person, causing them to enter into all manner of skillful means and various subtle expedients.
These are then circulated and disseminated from one to another to teach, transform, and benefit all sentient beings; they are also able to cause all...
Sentient beings attain the realization that the fundamental essence and nature of all Buddhas are identical to their own, and they obtain the Dharma-gate of the four virtues:
true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity.
This person dwells within this stage and practices the dharma-gates of transformation, which gradually become profound and subtle.

Through the wisdom that contemplates flowers in the sky, they enter the Middle Way of essential nature. All categories of dharma-gates become fulfilled, like a diamond, surpassing the stages of the sun and moon.
The meaning of this has already been clarified.

Regarding the phrase "such persons" and so forth: it means that once these Bodhisattvas have been born into this stage and are dwelling within this stage, every Dharma-gate they establish for the sake of liberating sentient beings exceeds what came before in each and every respect; as they gradually transform and gradually practice, they become ever more profound.
Exquisite! The flower of the wisdom-flame of emptiness and the path of the wisdom that contemplates the truths all enter into this principle of the samādhi of essential nature.

Thus, all such dual-illumination dharma-gates, patience and concentration dharma-gates, the hundred dharma-gates, and the four virtue dharma-gates reach complete fulfillment herein; they are like a diamond—precious, firm, and beyond compare. Above.
Regarding the phrase "the sun, moon, and so forth": "above" refers to the beginning of this very chapter;
that is, within the preceding *Sūryacandramārga-varga*, the meaning of this stage has already been explained in detail.
Fifth is the Ground of the Wisdom that Illuminates Essential Nature (*Tattvārtha-prabhākarī-bhūmi*).
On this ground, one abandons one type of obstacle to the nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). This is a portion of the innate aspect (*sahaja*) of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

It is so named because it arises based on the aversion to the suffering of saṃsāra and the inclination toward the bliss of nirvāṇa; both [the afflictive and cognitive obscurations] are abandoned here.
There are two kinds of deluded attachments: first, the delusion of exclusively directing the mind away from birth and death; second, the delusion of exclusively directing the mind toward nirvana.
These three factors can obstruct the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*). Only by severing these delusional obstructions does one ascend to the Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*).

Now, the Bodhisattva cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); through the two wisdoms, they sever all obstacles, achieving unimpeded mastery between the ultimate and the conventional, and being able to harmonize that which is difficult to harmonize.
The path of non-differentiation is able to bring about permanent severance. Because the obscurations of delusion have been severed, it is called the "Difficult to Conquer" stage (*sudurjayā bhūmiḥ*).
The suchness realized therein is termed the "suchness of non-differentiation in categories," meaning that this suchness is [identical] with respect to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Because their nature is equal and without distinction, the Bodhisattva’s station is entrusted to the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).
Therein, he provisionally cultivates the dharmas of the three vehicles to transform and guide sentient beings. Among the ten pāramitās, the dhyāna-pāramitā is the most supreme.
It is not that they do not practice these other [perfections], but rather they do so according to their strength and capacity.

O Sons of the Buddha, for a Bodhisattva at the stage of the Ground of the Essence of Wisdom-illumination (*prajñā-avabhāsa-svabhāva-bhūmi*), there are ten kinds of powers of the arising category (*utpatti-varga*) that give rise to all meritorious practices.
By means of the single skillful means of wisdom, one knows the two types of karma—good and evil; this is the power category of distinguishing the spheres of activity (*viṣaya-vibhāga-bala-varga*).

The Chapter on the Power of Knowledge regarding the Performance of Good and Evil Deeds; the Chapter on the Power of Desire regarding all longings and wishes for the fruits of birth within the six realms;

the Chapter on the Power of Nature regarding the different natures distinguished among the six realms; the Chapter on the Power of Faculties regarding the distinct differences between each of all wholesome and unwholesome faculties;
and the Chapter on the Power of Concentration regarding those of false certainty, right certainty, and no certainty—by means of these, all causes and effects are mounted.
The cause is the vehicle; reaching the place of the fruit, one rides upon the path of the cause—this is the category of the power of the path.

Because one knows all phenomena and sees all births with the five eyes, it is the category of the power of the divine eye. Because one knows each and every event of a hundred kalpas, it is the category of the power of past lives.
In all births, afflictions are extinguished; in all sensations, ignorance is extinguished. This is the category of the power of liberation.
It is the wisdom of the category of the ten powers that knows the causes and effects of one’s own cultivation, and also knows the distinctions between the causes and effects of all sentient beings.
The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" indicate and manifest his name, virtue, and rank. Regarding "the wisdom that illuminates the ground of essence and nature":

this means that because this Bodhisattva cultivated the power of profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and vast wisdom during the causal stage, he is now able, upon reaching the resultant stage, to realize and enter the wisdom corresponding to the various truths (*satya*), thereby perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); hence it is called "wisdom."
The stage of the luminous essence of nature (*āloka-bhūmi*) is called the "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*) in other sutras.

This means that by means of the preceding "Blazing Wisdom" (*arciṣmatī*), all emotional views (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*) are incinerated and destroyed; thus, neither their differences nor their similarities can be apprehended.

Since this is the realm of all Buddhas and nothing can surpass it, it is named "Difficult to Conquer. Regarding the statement that ten kinds of dharmas arise in this stage, such as the "Chapter on Powers" (*bala-varga*), it refers to this [stage].

When a bodhisattva enters into realization, they are endowed with these ten categories of the arising of powers (*daśa-bala-jāti-pakṣa*), which give rise to all supreme and true practices of merit. By means of wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they teach and transform all sentient beings. What are the ten categories of the arising of powers? The first is "knowing good and evil," etc.; this refers to the following: [The text continues: ...this one [power], namely, the power of knowing the ripening of karma according to its causes and conditions (*karmasvakatā-jñāna-bala*). It is by means of this power that the Tathāgata knows the various karmic actions performed by sentient beings—whether wholesome or unwholesome—and understands how those actions lead to their respective maturations in the future. Furthermore, he knows which karmic actions will result in the maturation of suffering, which will result in the maturation of happiness, and which will result in neither suffering nor happiness. He also knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the human world, or the celestial realms. Moreover, he knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. He further knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth in the world-systems of the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, the zenith, and the nadir. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth in the world-systems of the small chiliocosm, the medium dichiliocosm, or the great trichiliocosm. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth in the world-systems of the four continents, the small thousand worlds, the middle thousand worlds, or the great thousand worlds. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth in the world-systems of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), a minor king, a village headman, a district magistrate, or a regional governor. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma-cakravartin*), a great minister, a high official, or a nobleman. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a householder, a merchant, a craftsman, or a laborer. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a male, a female, or a neuter. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person of low status, a person of middling status, or a person of high status. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person of little wealth, a person of moderate wealth, or a person of great wealth. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person of inferior faculties, a person of middling faculties, or a person of superior faculties. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person of dull intelligence, a person of middling intelligence, or a person of sharp intelligence. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person of little learning, a person of middling learning, or a person of vast learning. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person of little wisdom, a person of middling wisdom, or a person of great wisdom. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person of few afflictions, a person of middling afflictions, or a person of many afflictions. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person who delights in the company of householders, a person who delights in the company of renunciants, or a person who delights in solitude. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person who delights in the company of the foolish, a person who delights in the company of the wise, or a person who delights in solitude. He knows which karmic actions will lead to rebirth as a person who delights in the company of the ignorant, a person who delights in the company of the learned, or a person who delights in solitude. Through the skillful means of wisdom (*prajñā-upāya*), one understands that sentient beings who perform virtuous deeds do not necessarily obtain virtuous fruits, because they instead separately engage in evil actions and find themselves in states of retribution.

Likewise, one understands that those who commit evil deeds do not necessarily receive evil retribution, because they instead separately engage in virtuous actions and find themselves in states of reward.
Why is this? For instance, when anyone fashions Buddha images, brushes and prints sacred scriptures, or establishes assemblies to provide offerings for the Sangha—this constitutes cultivation.
This is virtuous. However, some among them falsely establish the Triple Gem for their own private gain, deceiving themselves regarding cause and effect;

thus, before heaven is attained, hell is already formed. Consequently, they cultivate virtue but do not receive its reward, instead proceeding to undergo retribution elsewhere for the evil they have committed.
Generally, when one eliminates evil people, evil beasts, or destroys external paths that disrupt harmony—

As for the killing of an icchantika, this is indeed an evil act. However, within that context, if it is done for the sake of truly afflicting and harming sentient beings [in order to prevent greater harm], such that by killing one many are saved—removing harm and promoting goodness—this is precisely what is performed through a Bodhisattva’s great compassion.
Therefore, although this is an evil act, it does not receive an evil retribution; instead, its retribution is experienced in a separate place where one performs good deeds. Such are the distinctions.

Regarding "retributive actions" (*vipāka-karma*): [the Buddha] explains each one for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of the Sphere of Distinct Actions. Regarding "skillfully performing [actions]" and so forth:

this means that through this wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), one can know that all sentient beings who perform good deeds obtain the retribution of merit, while those who perform evil deeds obtain the retribution of calamity.
Just as planting beans does not produce hemp, the causal relationship of the primary retribution (*niyata-vipāka*) is fixed and certain.
This is a mistake. [The Buddha] preaches each [teaching] for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Knowledge of Karma.

Regarding the phrase "knowing all things, etc.," it means that this single wisdom and skillful means can know everything within the minds of all sentient beings—their desires, their quests, and their aspirations.
As for "all desires," it refers to those who wish to make offerings to the Triple Gem, or who wish to revere Heaven, Earth, sovereigns, and parents.

Teachers and friends: those who harbor thoughts of wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep—those who seek anything at all, such as seeking excellent teachers and friends, seeking reputation and material gain, seeking honor, achievement, wealth, and nobility, and even seeking fine children, grandchildren, and kinsmen.
"All aspirations" refers to the aspiration to be born in the Western Land to attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings; the aspiration to be born among devas or humans;
and even the aspiration to be born within the six realms, including the hells. In each and every birth, the fruits are thus; he explains each of these for the sake of sentient beings.

Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Desire. Regarding the phrase "knowing the six realms and so forth," this means that through this single wisdom and skillful means, one is well able to thoroughly understand the fundamental natures and dispositions of all sentient beings in the six realms, discerning their various perceptions and views—whether they are sharp or dull, wise or foolish, or skillful or clumsy—each being distinct. Such differences are [discerned] one by one.
It is taught for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Nature.

Regarding the phrase "knowing all, etc.," this means that through this wisdom and skillful means, one is able to thoroughly understand all sentient beings—whether their roots of goodness or roots of evil were planted in a single lifetime, or whether they were planted over many lifetimes; and whether they are easy to transform or difficult to transform.
In teaching and transforming others, each case is distinct and different. Thus, these distinctions among faculties and realms are explained for each and every sentient being;
therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Faculties" (*indriya-bala-varga*). Regarding the sixth point, "knowing those of wrong determination," etc.:

this means that through this wisdom and skillful means, one is well able to thoroughly discern all outsiders of wrong determination, the partial determination of the Hīnayāna, the right determination of Bodhisattvas, and ordinary beings.
As for "not fixed," it means that each [wisdom] penetrates thoroughly and is taught for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Concentration.
Regarding the seventh, "all are equal," it means that this wisdom of skillful means is well able to understand the causes and effects of the Great Vehicle’s true path for all worthies and sages.
Because one practiced by mounting [the vehicle] in the past to sever hindrances, one now finally attains it by mounting [the vehicle] as such.

This wisdom illuminates and realizes the true fruit. That one has now attained this state of fruition is due to nothing other than having, in the past, relied upon such right causes and cultivated the power of such right paths. One must understand each of these points clearly.

He speaks for the sake of sentient beings; this is called the Chapter on the Power of the Path. Regarding the "eight [qualities] such as the five eyes": the five eyes consist of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which is unimpeded and supernormal;

the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), which is impeded and not supernormal; the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*), which observes only the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); and the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), which takes emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its object.
The Buddha-eye is like a thousand suns illuminating diverse forms while remaining identical in essence; it is precisely this.

It is said that these five eyes are well able to thoroughly understand all phenomena, including the distinctions between the causes and conditions of birth and cessation, as well as the good and evil karmic retributions of both the mundane and supramundane realms.

He simultaneously perceives all sentient beings at the moment of death, seeing the excellence or inferiority of their retributions and the specific places where they will be reborn according to their good or evil deeds.
He reveals each of these matters to all sentient beings; therefore, this is called the "Chapter on the Power of the Divine Eye.
Regarding the phrase "knowing a hundred kalpas," etc., it means that through this wisdom and skillful means, one is able to know the various past lives of oneself.

Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, he fully knows—down to the last detail—the deaths and births, surnames and clans, names, suffering and joy, longevity and premature death, wealth and nobility, or poverty and lowliness of sentient beings;
these are the various past lives of sentient beings. He understands each one clearly and explains them for the sake of sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Past Lives. Regarding the phrase "knowing all things, etc.," this refers to this wisdom and skillful means.
He is well able to understand that within one birth or two births, and even throughout all births, one may extinguish all afflictions and attain liberation;

likewise, through one rebirth or two rebirths, and even throughout all rebirths, from the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death, one attains liberation. He teaches this to sentient beings according to reality; therefore it is said:
This is the Chapter on the Power of Liberation. Regarding these "ten powers" and so forth:

such wisdom of the chapter on the ten powers knows, without error or mistake, the causes and effects of one's own practice; it also knows the causes and effects of the practices and cultivations of all sentient beings.
They discern and understand each part individually, without error or delusion.
Yet, they employ their body, mind, and speech differently: they take a pure land to be an evil land, and an evil land to be a land of wondrous bliss;
they can transform good into evil and evil into good; and they transform form into non-form, and non-form into form.
They take a man for a woman and a woman for a man; they take the six realms of existence for what are not the six realms, and what are not the six realms for the six realms.
Even regarding earth, water, fire, and wind, they take them for what are not earth, water, fire, and wind.
At that time, by the power of great skillful means, this person perceives within all sentient beings that which is inconceivable, which those of lower stages cannot know or perceive.
"Your Excellency’s deeds are sufficient.

As for the phrase 'body, mind, and so forth,' it means that one does not merely employ a single wisdom or skillful means to understand the knowledge of the ten powers (*daśabala*) regarding the causes and effects of oneself and others;
