rather, there are further infinite distinctions of excellence in body, mind, and speech."
Their functions are unfathomable. This is because the body can manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the mind can maintain focused mindfulness, and the mouth can preach the Dharma;
each is able to function differently through inconceivable power. Therefore, it is said that the body, mind, and mouth have distinct functions.
Regarding "by means of the Pure Land," etc., it means that by the power of these three sublime wheels, one is able to manifest the land of serene light (*śāntaprabhā*) as a pure land.

Regarding the cohabitation of the five destinies: one can manifest the land of Sukhāvatī even while dwelling amidst the cohabitation of the five destinies, as in the case of the three transformations of the pure land in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the ability to transform good into evil: this is exemplified by King Ajātaśatru.

Regarding the ability to transform evil into good: this is exemplified by the butcher Pūrṇa-mukha. Regarding the transformation of form into non-form and non-form into form: [this is likewise demonstrated].
That which manifests as the emission of light, the scattering of flowers, the hanging of canopies, and the emergence of lotuses is this. Regarding "taking a man to be a woman":
it is like Śāriputra being transformed into the appearance of a woman by a single finger-point of a celestial maiden. Regarding "taking a woman to be a man":

it is like the Dragon Girl offering a pearl and attaining Buddhahood in an instant. Regarding "taking the six realms to be not the six realms, and that which is not the six realms to be the six [realms]..."
As for the Way: the six realms are the ordinary; that which is not the six realms is the sage, such as the Great Being Mahāmaṇivimba and others.
This applies down to earth, water, fire, and wind—where "that which is not earth, water, fire, and wind" is the phrase to be supplied below.

It means that what is not earth, water, fire, and wind functions as earth, water, fire, and wind, just as in the eighteen supernatural transformations where one enters the earth as if it were water and treads upon water.
It is like the earth: fire issues from the upper part of the body while water issues from the lower part; fire issues from the lower part of the body while water issues from the upper part.
The body becomes both water and fire, such that one may carry dry grass upon it and enter [the flames] without being burned. "This person at that time" refers to such as these.

What is called "the various sovereign spiritual powers" refers to this: at that time, the Bodhisattva, through the power of a single wisdom and the power of great skillful means, performs deeds such that all sentient beings may behold them according to their own dispositions, causing them all to enter instantaneously into the inconceivable realm.
It is not only sentient beings who behold them; even those on the lower stages [of the path] find it inconceivable.
All the bodhisattvas are unable to perceive or know the manner in which this stage’s bodhisattva lifts and lowers his feet.

This person possesses great and clear wisdom; they advance gradually, with knowledge unfolding stage by stage. Infinite and immeasurable rays of light and unspeakably unspeakable dharma-gates manifest and proceed before them.

Regarding the phrase "these persons": as for why it is said that the spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) of these Bodhisattvas is unknown to those on lower stages—it is because the great wisdom and clear intelligence of these Bodhisattvas gradually increase, doubling at each successive stage.
Within a single portion of their radiant wisdom, there appear simultaneously and all at once immeasurable, immeasurable, ineffable, and unspeakable Dharma-gates.
As they practice, from the second knowledge up to the tenth knowledge, each distinct knowledge—the light of knowledge, the light of knowledge—becomes immeasurable and immeasurable;
even the unspeakably unspeakable Dharma-gates likewise manifest simultaneously before them.
Sixth, the Ground of Flower-Light (*Puṣpārāga-bhūmi*):
This ground eliminates one type of obstacle consisting of the active manifestation of coarse characteristics.

This is precisely a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) aspect of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which arises from the active manifestation of coarse characteristics regarding the distinction between defilement and purity; thus it is so named. It simultaneously eliminates two types [of obstacles].

There are two types of delusion regarding attachment to the foolish: first, the delusion of observing the flow of active formations; second, the delusion of the frequent manifestation of signs (*nimitta*).
These three factors can obstruct the severance [of afflictions] in the sixth stage. This delusion prevents one from ascending to the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Now, knowing that all phenomena are without defilement or purity, one dwells in the mental application of signlessness (*animitta-manasikāra*) to bring *tathatā* to fulfillment, whereby one is able to forever...
[The obscurations] are severed. Once the delusive obscurations have been severed, *prajñā* manifests; therefore, it is called the "Manifesting Ground" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

The *tathatā* realized therein is named the "Tathatā Free from Defilement and Purity," because the essential nature of this *tathatā* is neither defiled nor pure. The Bodhisattva’s station is entrusted to the King of the Heaven of Sovereignty (*Vaśavartin-deva-rāja*).
There, he provisionally cultivates the dharmas of the three vehicles and so forth to transform and guide sentient beings. Regarding the ten *pāramitās*:
Among these, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the most supreme. It is not that the others are not practiced; rather, they are practiced according to one's strength and capacity.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva reaches the stage of the "Flower-Light" (*kusumita*) within their essential nature, they are able to manifest the ten supernormal powers and the category of clear wisdom throughout all worlds for the sake of all sentient beings. Through various transformations, they employ the clear wisdom of the divine eye.
One knows all forms within the lands of the three periods of time, as numerous as atoms, dividing each into the bodies of sentient beings of the six realms;
one knows each individual body, from its subtle atomic forms to its gross forms, part by part.

With the wisdom of the divine ear, one knows the sounds of suffering and joy of sentient beings in the six realms throughout the ten directions and three periods of time—sounds that are neither non-sounds nor non-noises, the sounds of all phenomena.
By means of the wisdom of the celestial body, one knows all forms—whether form or non-form—and those that are neither male nor female in shape;

within a single thought-moment, one pervades the lands and the measure of kalpas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, manifesting bodies as numerous as atoms within both large and small lands.

By means of the celestial knowledge of others' minds, one knows the mental activities of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, including all sentient beings within the six realms of the ten directions.

Regarding the mental states and mental concomitants—such as suffering and pleasure, good and evil—he uses his celestial and human wisdom to know all sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
he knows each and every instance of their past lives, their experiences of suffering and pleasure, and their lifespans, even those extending for a hundred kalpas.
The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" indicate and manifest the name, virtue, and rank [of this stage]. Regarding "the stage of the Flower-Light Essence":
it means that when this Bodhisattva enters this stage, the flowers of great wisdom and practice bloom all at once, and their light illuminates all things.
Therefore, it is named the Ground of Flower Radiance (*Puṣpārāga-bhūmi*). In another sutra, it is named the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

This means that because the characteristics of difference and identity can no longer be apprehended, the pure nature of *tathatā* (suchness) clearly manifests before one; hence, it is called the Ground of Manifestation.
Regarding the phrase "able [to act] in all worlds," etc., it means that this Bodhisattva, dwelling in this ground, is able [to manifest] throughout the ten directions.

Within all worlds, they employ the ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the light of wisdom, and the categories of knowledge to teach and guide all sentient beings, manifesting various extraordinary transformations and inconceivable realms.
What are the ten kinds of categories of clear wisdom? First, "the clear wisdom of the divine eye," and so forth; this refers to the divine...

This refers to the supernormal power of the eye (*cakṣur-abhijñā*). Because this bodhisattva has attained this supernormal power, he is able to know all subtle forms—equal in number to the atoms within the lands of the three periods of time:
past, future, and present—including both large segmented bodies and small segmented bodies, all of which are composed of atoms.
This includes human bodies, celestial bodies, and even the large and small segmented bodies of animals.
It is formed from atoms. Each and every sentient being’s body is known to be such a mechanism.
Subtle forms of atoms form a single physical body; the same applies to gross forms. One understands each and every characteristic of the gross and subtle parts of form without error.
Second, "by means of the wisdom of the divine ear" refers to the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*). This means that by attaining this power...

One is immediately able to hear and know the sounds produced by sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether they produce sounds of suffering due to being oppressed and afflicted, or sounds of pleasure due to experiencing ease and comfort.

One clearly understands that these sounds of suffering and pleasure are neither sounds of suffering and pleasure, nor are they sounds that are not suffering and pleasure; this extends even to all mundane and supramundane sounds of phenomena.
It is not non-sound, because each is known individually. Third, "by means of the celestial body and wisdom" refers to the supernormal power of the form-body (*rūpakāya-abhijñā*).

This means that by attaining this supernormal power, one is able to know that all external forms—the six sense-objects of the environment (*pratyaya*)—and all internal forms—the six sense-faculties and physical bodies of the primary retribution (*vipāka*)—are all not truly form, yet are designated as "form. They are not male.

Female form; this is called the male and female form. Furthermore, in a single thought-moment, this bodhisattva completely pervades the lands and the measure of kalpas throughout the ten directions across the three periods of time—whether large or small—including the bodies of sentient beings as subtle as the finest atoms within those lands.
Because in a single thought-moment they thoroughly know each and every body, [this is] the fourth, by means of the divine power of others.
"Knowledge of the minds of others," etc., refers to the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*). This means that by attaining this power,

one is able to know all that occurs within the minds of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time— past, present, and future— including the thoughts and mental factors of all beings in the ten directions,
from gods and humans down to animals within the six realms of existence, as well as matters such as their experiences of suffering and pleasure, and the causes of their good and evil karma.
Because each is known individually. Fifth, "by means of the knowledge of gods and humans" refers to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).

This means that by attaining this power, one is able to clearly know the experiences of suffering and happiness throughout all past lives—from one life, two lives, up to hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions of lifetimes—for all sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time. It is called "knowledge of past lives."
First, there is the thorough knowledge of the continuity of the duration of one's lifespan for a hundred kalpas and so forth;

because each of these is thoroughly known, it is demonstrated to all sentient beings. The first five wisdoms know the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of dependent origination, wherein no defiled characteristics can be found;
the latter five wisdoms know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of liberation, wherein likewise no pure characteristics can be found.

By means of the divine knowledge of liberation, one knows the liberation of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, severing all afflictions—whether many or few—from the first stage up to the tenth stage, until they are extinguished and exhausted. By means of the divine concentration and mental wisdom, [one knows this].

He knows the minds of sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether they are concentrated, unconcentrated, neither concentrated nor unconcentrated—and the methods for inducing concentration.
He possesses the samādhis of "that which is grasped" and the "one hundred samādhis.

By means of his celestial awakening-wisdom, he knows all sentient beings—those who have already attained Buddhahood and those who have not—even down to every single mind of every person throughout the six realms of existence; furthermore, he knows the ten directions.

The Dharma spoken from within the Buddha’s mind: by means of the wisdom of celestial recollection (*divyasmṛtijñāna*), he knows the lifespans—both long and short—of all sentient beings throughout hundreds and thousands of kalpas, as well as the intermediate and great kalpas;

and by means of the wisdom of celestial vows (*divyapraṇidhijñāna*), he knows the individual practices and vows within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and thirty minds of the noble ones (*ārya*), whether they seek suffering or happiness, or that which is Dharma and non-Dharma. All of this...
Seeking the fulfillment of the ten vows and the hundred thousand great vows.
Regarding the phrase "sixth, by means of celestial liberation" and so forth, this refers to the supernormal power of cessation (*nirodha-abhijñā*).

From this point downward, the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*) collectively refers to worthies and sages (*ārya*), which differs from its usage above. This means that because this Bodhisattva has attained this supernormal power, he is able to thoroughly know the ten...

The noble beings of the three periods of time follow the path of liberation according to their capacity and portion, severing all afflictions and the obstacles of ignorance—whether in great measure or in small measure.
From the partial severance of the first stage, they proceed through successive stages until the great measure of the tenth stage is severed and ultimately extinguished;
this extinction is total, leaving nothing remaining. Such are these various [stages].

Liberation, because each is thoroughly understood. Seventh, "by means of the divine power of concentration and wisdom" refers to the supernormal power of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*).
This means that by attaining this power, one is able to know the minds of the noble ones and ordinary beings within the lands of the ten directions and three periods of time;
or how their minds enter right concentration, remaining unmoving and unshakable, thus abiding in such a state; or [at other times]...
In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one contemplates and realizes [the truth], makes offerings to the Buddhas, and listens to the Dharma; such is "not fixed.
Or, within concentration, one manifests walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, manifesting the performance of all activities; such is "not fixed.
Or, within the state of non-concentration, regarding all matters and at all times, one enters concentration according to one's will; such is "not non-fixed."

Furthermore, regarding those who emerge from meditative absorption and preach the Dharma in various directions to benefit sentient beings, because they know each and every form of encompassing samādhi, up to the one hundred and eight samādhis and all states of correct meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), they enter with the wisdom of celestial awakening;
this is the supernormal power of speech and sound. Because they have attained this supernormal power, they are able to understand all things as one.

All the deeds of the worthy and holy ones—those who have already severed obstacles and realized the truth, those who manifest the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] and have swiftly attained the path of Buddhahood, as well as those who have not yet attained the path of Buddhahood—he knows them all.
Furthermore, he knows the minds and mental objects, the thoughts and actions of beings in the six realms, and the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Because one knows each and every Dharma for teaching and benefiting sentient beings that was contemplated and spoken within [the present], ninth, by means of the wisdom of recollecting past lives (*jātismara-jñāna*),
this is precisely the supernormal power of the future (*anāgata-abhijñā*). Because one attains this supernormal power,

one is able to clearly know how all worthy sages and sentient beings receive the Buddha’s life of wisdom (*prajñājīva*) throughout hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, and great and small kalpas, thereby teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Benefiting all beings, such a life of wisdom may remain for one *kalpa* or two *kalpas*;
if it remains longer, it may abide in the world for ten *kalpas*, or even for hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions of *kalpas*. This is because each [instance] is known.

Tenth, as for the "wisdom of celestial vows," this is the unconditioned supernormal power (*anabhisaṃskāra-abhijñā*). It means that by attaining this supernormal power, one is able to thoroughly understand one...

Regarding the practices and vows of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the noble ones and all great-minded sentient beings, as well as each of the gates of practice and each of the great vows generated within the thirty minds:
if one seeks [to demonstrate] suffering, then one manifests the burning of the body, arms, and fingers as an offering to the Buddhas— such as the Medicine King (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*) burning his own body,
or the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*) being struck by a staff— and the vow of Ānanda regarding the five turbidities of this evil age.
Seeking happiness refers to such instances as Śākyamuni’s vow to enter [nirvana] first and so forth.
Seeking the Dharma refers to manifesting and expounding the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of scripture to transmit the Buddha’s intent.
Seeking what is not the Dharma refers to manifesting the four Veda scriptures and the heterodoxies of non-Buddhist paths.
The treatises include the Four Books, Five Classics, *Daodejing*, *Nanhua jing*, and the various heterodox schools of this land.

These are studied as a supplement to the power of learning the True Dharma of the Mahāyāna practitioners; they are studied in order to subdue those who are icchantikas, as well as those with worldly wisdom and clever eloquence.
Both are termed "unrighteous. All seeking culminates in the ultimate seeking; transforming those above and below, there is nothing one does not seek.
The ten vows are the ten great practices and vows of Samantabhadra. The phrases of the ten inexhaustible treasuries are the hundreds of thousands of great vows;
they are the boundless, vast, and solemn vows of all Bodhisattvas. Such are the practices and vows in this chapter; for each and every [vow], the Bodhisattva on this stage...

Because they are fully perfected and known individually, these persons dwelling within the stages manifest immeasurable distinct functions of body, mind, and speech through the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Even if one were to explain their virtues for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, they could not be exhausted; yet Śākyamuni has here briefly opened up these supernormal powers and insights.
Chapter. As explained in the "Chapter on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination," regarding those who "dwell in the stages" and so forth:

this means that these Bodhisattvas, dwelling within this Flower Radiance Stage (*Puṣpārāga-bhūmi*), are already able to manifest immeasurable wheels of the body through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) among the ten kinds of supernormal knowledge and wisdom, as well as immeasurable forms of mnemonic retention (*dhāraṇī*).
The mind-wheel and the immeasurable dharma-teaching mouth-wheel manifest distinct forms and functions.
To explain the various merits, practices, and vows of this stage would be impossible to exhaust or finish even after hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
yet, Śākyamuni Tathāgata has here only provided a general outline of these ten supernormal powers and clear wisdoms. Within the great section [of the scripture], there is...
The "Chapter on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination" explains that, as stated in that chapter, there is neither duality nor distinction.
○ Seventh, the Stage of Fulfillment of Essential Nature (*svabhāva-paripūri-bhūmi*):

the Bodhisattva of this stage abandons one type of subtle obstacle regarding the manifestation of signs (*nimitta-pravṛtti-āvaraṇa*). This is precisely the [obstacle] associated with the cognitive hindrance (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
A portion of birth arises; because it is produced by the manifestation of subtle marks of arising and ceasing that are grasped as existing, it is so named.

One simultaneously abandons two kinds of deluded attachments: first, the delusion regarding the manifestation of subtle marks; second, the delusion of exclusively applying mental attention to seek the signless (*animitta*).
Because these three factors can obstruct the Far-Reaching Ground (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*), one must sever these delusive obstructions before ascending to this [ground].

The Seventh Ground. Now, one is far removed from the three realms and near the station of the Dharma King. One’s practice surpasses that of the two vehicles, and one skillfully cultivates the signless (*animitta*), reaching the limit of the signless.

As the effortful application (*prayoga*) reaches its ultimate, it is vastly superior to what preceded it; therefore, it is called the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*). One is then able to permanently sever the obstacles of delusion.
Once these are severed, the *tathatā* realized is termed the "Tathatā of Non-Differentiation of Dharmas. This refers to this *tathatā*...

Just as one can understand that all various teachings are identical to True Suchness (tathatā) because they are without marks (animitta), the Bodhisattva’s stage is entrusted to the King of the First Dhyāna Heaven.

Therein, he provisionally cultivates the dharmas of the Three Vehicles and so forth to transform and guide sentient beings. Among the ten pāramitās, the pāramitā of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā) is the most preeminent;
it is not that the others are not cultivated, but rather they are practiced according to one's power and capacity.

O sons of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva reaches the stage of the perfected nature and enters into these dharmas, they possess the eighteen categories of noble wisdom that are not shared with those of the lower stages.
These are: the body is free from outflows and faults; speech is free from verbal transgressions; mindfulness is free from lapses;

one is detached from the eight worldly dharmas; one maintains equanimity toward all phenomena; and one constantly abides in samādhi. This constitutes the fulfillment of the six categories of the first stage.

Furthermore, from this wisdom arises the sixfold wisdom (*ṣaḍpāda-jñāna*). Because the fetters and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the three realms are ultimately never again received, there is the fulfillment of desire;
because all merits and all dharma-gates are sought after and fulfilled, there is the fulfillment of vigor;
because all matters of dharmas, all matters of kalpas, and all matters of sentient beings are known simultaneously within a single mind, there is the fulfillment of mindfulness. This...

Regarding the characteristics of the two truths: because all dharmas pertain to the sentient beings of the six realms, there is the "sufficiency of wisdom," which knows the ten destinies of persons up to all Buddhas, being free from fetters and habitual tendencies.
Because one perceives all sentient beings and knows others as oneself and as disciples, being free from outflows and the habitual tendencies of afflictions, there is the "sufficiency of liberation.
Through wisdom, one knows the bodies of others; this is the "sufficiency of the six supernormal powers."
This person enters into the sixfold fulfillment of clear wisdom and thereby gives rise to the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*).

Following the mental activities of sentient beings throughout the six realms, they eloquently expound immeasurable categories of Dharma-doors (*dharmaparyāya*) for the sake of revealing them to all sentient beings.

Following the mental activities of all sentient beings, they constantly enter samādhi, causing the great earth of the ten directions to tremble and flowers to manifest in the void; thus, they are able to cause sentient beings—
Regarding mental activity: through the perfection of great clear wisdom, one perceives the appearance of Buddhas in all past kalpas;
this also demonstrates the minds of all sentient beings. Through unattached wisdom, one perceives all lands within the ten directions in the present.
By means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of the movements of the minds of all Buddhas and all sentient beings,
one perceives within all kalpas of the future the appearance in the world of all Buddhas and all sentient beings who, from these Buddhas, receive the Way and hear the Dharma.
"If a Buddha's disciple" (the three phrases) indicates the name, virtue, and stage [of this ground].

"The Ground of Fulfillment of the Nature-Stage" means that because this Bodhisattva has extensively cultivated the *pāramitās* as skillful means during the causal stage, they realize and attain them as the fruit;

thus, all the practices of the Tathāgata’s omniscience are completely fulfilled and perfected, hence it is called "Fulfillment. In other sutras, it is named the "Ground of Far-Going," meaning that the true...
The realm of suchness is vast and boundless; although suchness manifests before one, partial realization remains limited. Only when its limits are fully exhausted does one reach the ultimate state;

therefore, it is called the Far-Reaching Ground (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*). Regarding "entering into this dharma," it means entering into the dharma of essential nature (*dharmatā*), having already attained the categories of wisdom of the eighteen noble ones (*ārya*), which are not shared with the provisional and inferior vehicles of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
It is shared [only by the Buddhas]. It is not only that which is not shared by those of provisional capacity or the Lesser Vehicle; it is also not shared even by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages.
Why is it called "the category of the eighteen kinds of noble ones' wisdom"? First, what is meant by "the body being free from outflows and faults" is that the body is without error.
This means that from time immemorial, this Bodhisattva has constantly practiced non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexuality.
He cultivates his body until all afflictions are purified and exhausted without remainder. Because this bodily karma is pure, he attains great supernormal powers;
thus it is said that his body is free from outflows and faults. Second, regarding "no verbal transgressions," this means his speech is without error.
It refers to how this Bodhisattva, from immeasurable kalpas past, has constantly employed the five modes of speech of the Tathāgata in accordance with the various sentient beings.

He gives rise to skillful means and preaches the Dharma, enabling others to attain the fruits of the Path. Because his verbal karma is thus pure, it is said that there is no fault of speech in his mouth.

Third, "no loss of mindfulness" refers to the absence of lapse in mental activity. This means that this Bodhisattva, from time immemorial, has constantly cultivated morality, concentration, and wisdom;
he has eradicated greed, anger, and delusion, benefiting both himself and others, and remains settled in meditative absorption.

By subduing the poisons, one attains purity of the sense faculties; thus it is said that mindfulness is free from loss of mindfulness. Fourth, regarding "being free from the eight worldly dharmas," this refers to a mind devoid of discriminatory thoughts.
There are many varieties of these eight dharmas, categorized according to the Shared Teaching, the Distinct Teaching, the Perfect Teaching, and so forth.
The eight dharmas, in general, do not transcend the categories of teaching, principle, wisdom, severance, practice, stage, cause, and fruit; yet each possesses distinct characteristics.
Since this stage is eternally free from these and does not share them with the lower stages, it is said to be "free from the eight dharmas.

Regarding the "equanimity toward all phenomena" among the five [perfections], it refers to the mind of equanimity that knows nothing [it does not know]. That is to say, since beginningless time, this Bodhisattva has...
The great *prajñā* of emptiness illuminates and examines all mundane and supramundane phenomena—both defiled and pure—and finds them to be entirely empty in their very essence.
Because there is no thought of craving whatsoever, it is said that "one practices equanimity (*upekṣā*) among all phenomena.
Sixth, "always abiding in samādhi" refers to the absence of an unconcentrated mind; this means that from time immemorial, this bodhisattva has never been separated from profound...

Regarding the profound and great samādhi: even when establishing transformations according to the capacities of beings, or remaining hidden or manifest to benefit sentient beings, one never departs from this samādhi;

therefore, it is said that "one is constantly in samādhi. As for the phrase "entering the stages" and so forth, it means that once this Bodhisattva has fully perfected these six categories, they further give rise to the six types of supernormal knowledge (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) from the continuous flow of these six wisdoms. What are these six?
Are you endowed with wisdom? Regarding the phrase "the fetters of the three realms and so forth," this refers precisely to the non-diminution of desire.

It means that for many eons, this Bodhisattva has constantly cultivated the three gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—entering the three realms to perform common activities and transform sentient beings, causing them to abandon the fetters, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all states of existence (*bhava*), to resolve upon Bodhicitta, and to realize the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
How could there be any principle by which a bodhisattva would further undergo the habitual tendencies of the fetters within the triple world?
Because they ultimately do not undergo them, they attain the fulfillment of right liberation; thus it is said that they "desire to be complete. Second, regarding "all merits being equal":

This refers to the non-diminution of diligence (*vīrya*). It means that regarding all the merits of benefiting sentient beings and all the Dharma-gates for benefiting sentient beings belonging to all the worthy ones and sages (*ārya*), whatever this Bodhisattva diligently seeks with joy, there is nothing that is not fulfilled and perfected;
therefore, it is said that "the mind of progress is sufficient. Third, "all dharmas are equal" refers to the non-diminution of mindfulness (*smṛti*). That is to say:
This Bodhisattva constantly contemplates all Buddhas and sages establishing all dharmic activities;

contemplates all matters regarding the duration, length, magnitude, and brevity of all kalpas; and contemplates all matters regarding the arising and ceasing of sentient beings through causes and conditions, as well as the uprooting of suffering and the bestowing of happiness.
Because of this constant contemplation, within a single mind there is no need for laborious calculation. One.

Knowing this at that time, it is said that "the mind of mindfulness is sufficient. Regarding the phrase "the four [perfections] are equal to the two truths": this refers to the non-diminution of wisdom.
It means that this Bodhisattva is able to thoroughly comprehend the two aspects of existence and non-existence within the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.
This is the Prajñā-emptiness dharma that destroys all ignorance of sentient beings throughout the six realms. By means of the emptiness of Prajñā, one illuminates...

Because the ultimate and the conventional, existence and non-existence, are non-dual, it is said that his "wisdom is complete. Regarding the "knowledge of the five and the ten stages of departure," this refers to the non-deficiency of liberation.

That is to say, this bodhisattva is able to know the ten stages of departure (*daśa-niryāṇa*), the nurturing of the diamond-like stage (*vajropama-bhūmi*), the ten stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*), and the sublime equality of the sages;
he knows how the Buddhas emerge from meditative concentration to manifest their virtues, and how they give rise to wisdom to benefit sentient beings.
He manifests to all sentient beings the habitual tendencies of shared activity (*sabhāga-karman*), yet in reality he has neither fetters nor habits; therefore, it is called the "foot of liberation.

Regarding the sixth point, "seeing all things as equal," this refers to the non-diminishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation. This means that this bodhisattva is fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*):
the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), miraculous powers, and the power of mastery over circumstances.
This is because he clearly perceives all worthy sages, the Great Way, and sentient beings;

he is further able to fully know all others and his own disciples whom he has transformed, such that they all attain the severance of false views, realize untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and remain far removed from the subtle habitual tendencies of the one hundred and eight afflictions. It is for this reason that I am thus able to fully comprehend.
Regarding "knowing the matters within the bodies and minds of others": why is it that one knows the bodies of others through the wisdom of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*)?

Therefore, it is called the "perfection of the six supernormal powers. As for the phrase "such persons," it means that when these bodhisattvas enter into this great, perfect, and luminous wisdom, they further become fully endowed with the functional applications of six kinds of knowledge. What are these six knowledges? First:
"Then he gives rise to the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*) and so forth" means that his bodily action (*kāyakarman*) follows after wisdom.

This refers to the bodhisattva’s mobilization of the six bases of supernatural power (*ṣaḍabhijñāpāda*); by means of the bodily action of pure supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), he manifests miraculous signs to discipline the various mental activities of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva. Therefore, it is called "following one."
This refers to the mental activities of all sentient beings. Second, regarding "eloquence in speech and so forth," this refers to the vocal karma following the movement of wisdom.

It means that this bodhisattva, by means of pure and subtle vocal karma and the eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna*), can preach immeasurable categories of dharma-gates, skillfully guiding the mental activities of all sentient beings in accordance with them, causing them to resolve upon and practice the Great Mind (*mahācitta*).

This is the practice of a bodhisattva; hence it is said that they "accord with the mental activities of all sentient beings. Third, "constantly entering samādhi" means that the mental karma (manas-karma) follows the movement of wisdom.
This refers to how this bodhisattva, by means of a pure and luminous mental karma, constantly enters the meditative absorption of right reception (samāpatti).
By the power of this samādhi, the earth of the worlds in the ten directions shakes in six ways.

"Zhen. Within the void, the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers. By virtue of this majestic spiritual power, he is able to cause all sentient beings to give rise to a mind of superior advancement and to practice the deeds of all Buddhas; therefore, it is said that he "enables the minds and practices of sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "with great illumination," etc., this refers to the unimpeded wisdom of the past. That is to say, this Bodhisattva...
Because they are fully endowed with great clear wisdom, they are able to see the past, reaching to the very limits of the past.

Throughout all kalpas, they behold the Buddhas descending to take birth, attaining enlightenment, appearing in the world to benefit sentient beings, and likewise guiding the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to enter the path of Buddha-wisdom.
For this reason, it is said that they "reveal the minds of all sentient beings. Fifth, by means of...
"Non-attached wisdom" (*asaṅga-jñāna*) and so forth refers to the unimpeded wisdom of the present. This means that because this bodhisattva has perfected non-attached wisdom,
they are able to see all Buddhas throughout all lands in the ten directions within the present—
those who have descended to take birth, attained enlightenment, appeared in the world to benefit sentient beings, and guided all beings through every moment of their minds.
Because they continue to practice the path of Buddha-wisdom, it is said that "all sentient beings' minds and mental factors proceed [in this way].
Sixth, regarding "by means of supernormal powers" and so forth, this refers to unimpeded wisdom regarding the future.

This means that because these bodhisattvas have fulfilled the knowledge of the path of supernormal powers, they are able to see the future—that is, throughout all kalpas within the limits of the future. All...

The Buddha descended to be born in this world and attained enlightenment; he appeared in the world to benefit sentient beings, enabling all worthy sages and living beings to receive the Way and hear the Dharma from this Buddha.
By means of this, they in turn transform and deliver all sentient beings, thereby continuing the path of the Buddha’s wisdom.
For this reason, it is said that they "receive the Way and hear the Dharma from this Buddha."
Abiding among these eighteen noble ones, with every thought-moment in samādhi, he contemplates that the forms of the three realms, as numerous as motes of dust, were his own bodies in the past;

all sentient beings were his parents. Now, having entered this stage, he perceives all merits, all divine radiances, and all the dharmas practiced by the Buddhas, even those pertaining to the eighth and ninth stages. All dharmas [are thus perceived].

Regarding the Chapter on the Gates: because I have already entered them all, I manifest as a Buddha within all buddha-lands—attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, manifesting entry into parinirvāṇa, and transforming others in lands of the past, future, and present.
Regarding "dwelling in these eighteen," etc.: it means that this Bodhisattva dwells in these eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Within the category of the noble ones' wisdom, his mind at every moment is never separated from right concentration (*samādhi*).

By means of the wisdom of concentration, he contemplates the subtle forms within the triple world, such as atoms, seeing that not even so much as the point of a needle is not-self. Thus, by means of concentration, his body...
With wisdom he contemplates. He further contemplates all sentient beings, great and small, within the three realms;

there is not one who has not been his own father or mother throughout his successive births. Now that they have entered this stage of fulfillment, he perceives them as possessing all the merits of all Buddhas, all the divine powers and wisdom-light of all Buddhas, and the skillful conduct of all Buddhas.
The Dharma of wondrous skillful means, up to all the great vidyā-mantra gates of emptiness within the eighth and ninth stages,
reaching as far as the hundred-thousand gates of liberation and the gates of mastery over the eighty minor marks and thirty-two major marks—
because I have entered these stages, I have attained and entered all such Dharma-gates simultaneously. Regarding this:

Regarding "all lands" and so forth: because they have already attained entry into all [realms], they are able to manifest birth, renunciation, ascetic practice, the realization of the Way, the attainment of Buddhahood, and the turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma to extensively deliver sentient beings within all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.
Having completed these tasks for those with whom they share a karmic affinity in a single day, they then further manifest entry into parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he transforms and teaches others in other directions, manifesting all manner of inconceivable displays within all lands of the past, future, and present.
The eighth stage, the Stage of the Buddha’s Lion’s Roar (*Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-bhūmi*):
On this stage, the bodhisattva abandons one type of obstacle to application (*prayoga-āvaraṇa*).

This is a portion of the innate aspect (*sahaja*) within the cognitive obstacles (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), which prevents the signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*) from arising spontaneously; for this reason, it is so named. Furthermore, two types of deluded attachments are abandoned.
First is the delusion of exerting effort regarding the signless; second is the delusion of lacking mastery over signs.
These three factors can obstruct the eighth stage. Only by severing these delusional obstructions does one ascend to the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

This means that this Bodhisattva now enters the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*), attains the illumination of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) which flows on spontaneously and continuously, and their conduct born of maturation (*vipākaja-caryā*) becomes fully refined.
Abiding in the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-darśana*), one is not moved by the afflictions of any phenomena and is thus able to sever them forever.

Because ignorance and obstructions have been severed, it is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*). The *tathatā* realized therein is termed the "neither-increasing-nor-decreasing *tathatā*," meaning that this *tathatā*, while abiding in the contemplation of signlessness, does not undergo increase or decrease according to defilement or purity. The stage of the Bodhisattva is entrusted to these two [grounds].
The Celestial King Dhyāna is the sovereign of a small chiliocosm. He transforms and guides sentient beings through the One Vehicle Dharma.
Among the ten pāramitās, the pāramitā of power (bala) is his most profound; he does not fail to cultivate the others, yet he practices them according to his strength and capacity.

O Sons of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva attains the stage of the Buddha’s Roar of the Essential Nature and enters the Samādhi of Entering the Rank of the Dharma King, their wisdom becomes equal to that of a Buddha due to the Buddha’s Roar Samādhi.
Consequently, the ten grades of the Great Illumination Gate of Emptiness are constantly manifest before them.

Through the Flower-Light Sound Entering the Mind Samādhi, that wisdom of emptiness refers to the gate of internal emptiness-wisdom, the gate of external emptiness-wisdom, and the emptiness of the conditioned.
The gate of wisdom; the gate of wisdom of unconditioned emptiness; the gate of wisdom of intrinsic emptiness; the gate of wisdom of beginningless emptiness;

the gate of wisdom of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) emptiness; the gate of wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness; the gate of wisdom of the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness; and the gate of wisdom of the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness.
These ten gates of emptiness are each unknown to the lower stages. In the stage of the equality of space, they are ineffable and inexpressible.

He speaks of the wisdom of the supernormal powers: by means of the wisdom of a single thought-moment, he knows all phenomena in their distinct and particular differences, enters immeasurable Buddha-lands, receives the Dharma before each and every Buddha, and turns the wheel of Dharma to deliver all sentient beings.
Bestowing the medicine of the Dharma upon all sentient beings, he acts as a great Dharma teacher and a great guide.
Having destroyed the four māras, his Dharma-body is fully perfected; through successive transformations, he leads others into the Buddha-realm.

The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" indicate and manifest the name, virtue, and stage [of this level]. Regarding "the stage of the Buddha’s roar (buddha-ghoṣa-bhūmi) as the essential nature":
it means that when this bodhisattva preaches the Dharma without fear, they are equal and without distinction from the roar of the Great Teacher; therefore, it is named the Stage of the Buddha’s Roar.

Another sutra names this the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*). This means that once the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) has reached its ultimate limit and its essence is fully realized, it becomes truly constant and tranquil, incapable of being shaken; hence it is called the Immovable Ground.
Regarding the phrase "entering the samādhi of the rank of the Dharma King," it means that this Bodhisattva realizes and enters the supreme, self-awakened, noble wisdom of the Dharma King.

Delighting in samādhi, he correctly receives the precious throne; among all dharmas, he possesses mastery in accordance with the Dharma. Whether emerging or submerging, his mind is always in meditative concentration;
therefore, it is said that he has entered the samādhi of the rank of the Dharma King. As for his wisdom being equal to that of a Buddha:
It is said that his wisdom and skillful means are immeasurable, encompassing all dharmas and extensively delivering sentient beings;

he is no different from a Buddha, being non-dual and indistinguishable from him. Why is this so? It is because this bodhisattva has attained the Buddha’s Roar Samādhi (Buddhagarjita-samādhi), and it is due to this that such is the case.
Regarding the "Ten Chapters of the Great Illumination" and so forth, it refers to the fact that this bodhisattva, by virtue of attaining the Buddha’s Roar Samādhi...
Furthermore, the ten-stage Dharma-gate of the Great Illumination of Emptiness-Wisdom is entirely without deficiency and is constantly present before them.
To benefit sentient beings, their Flower-Wisdom-Light and the Sound of the Dharma surpass those of the past;
they all enter into the samādhi of profound mind and right reception, which is why they are able to roar the lion’s roar. As for that emptiness-wisdom, what is it called?
Does the tenfold great illumination of the wisdom of emptiness constantly manifest before one? First, regarding the gate of the wisdom of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*):
this means that this bodhisattva constantly uses the wisdom of *prajñā* to illuminate their own internal body and mind.

[They perceive that] the four great elements do not exist and the five aggregates are fundamentally empty, like illusions and like dreams; thus, this gate of the wisdom of internal emptiness constantly manifests before them. Second...

Regarding the gate of wisdom of external emptiness: it means that this bodhisattva constantly illuminates all external phenomena with wisdom, such that every verdant bamboo is none other than *prajñā*, and every lush yellow flower is entirely *tathatā*.
Being without gain and without loss, they thus attain the realization of this gate of wisdom of external emptiness, which is ever present before them.
Third is the gate of wisdom of the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*): it means...
This bodhisattva constantly uses wisdom to illuminate all conventional, conditioned phenomena (*saṃvṛti-dharma*), seeing them as false and unreal, entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, he attains the realization of this gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of the conditioned, which is ever-present before him.

Regarding the fourth, the gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā-jñāna-mukha*): it means that this bodhisattva constantly uses wisdom to illuminate all ultimate truths (*paramārtha-satya*).

Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is not empty, as it is their true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), this gate of wisdom regarding unconditioned emptiness is realized and remains constantly present before him.
Fifth is the gate of wisdom regarding the emptiness of both natures: this means that this bodhisattva constantly uses wisdom to illumine both the conditioned and the unconditioned;
both natures are empty, entirely without obstruction, and perfectly equal. Thus he attains...
This means that the wisdom-door of the realization of this emptiness of nature is constantly present before him. Sixth is the wisdom-door of the emptiness of the beginningless:

it means that this bodhisattva constantly uses wisdom to illuminate the afflictions of the ground of ignorance (avidyā-āśraya) which have been beginningless; [he realizes that] they fundamentally have no root.
Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, he attains the realization of the wisdom-gate of beginningless emptiness, which is constantly present before him.

Seventh, as for the wisdom-gate of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā): this bodhisattva constantly uses wisdom to illuminate both the two truths—the conventional and the ultimate—and sees that they are identical to true nature (*dharmatā*).
Since no characteristic can be apprehended, he does not abide in the two extremes, nor does he maintain a middle way; thus, he attains the realization of the first...
The gate of the wisdom of emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is constantly present before him. Regarding the gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*):
it means that this bodhisattva constantly uses wisdom to illuminate both the emptiness that is able to empty the emptiness of the ultimate truth and the emptiness that is emptied;
since these two principles of emptiness also do not persist, he attains the realization of the gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness, which is constantly present before him.
Regarding the ninth gate of wisdom, the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-śūnyatā-jñāna-mukha*):

it means that this bodhisattva constantly uses wisdom to illuminate emptiness, such that both the subject and object of emptiness are emptied, and even that emptiness itself is further emptied. Thus, one attains the realization of the gate of wisdom—the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness—which is perpetually present before them.

Regarding the tenth gate of wisdom, the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-śūnyatā-śūnyatā-jñāna-mukha*): it means that this bodhisattva constantly uses wisdom...

Illuminating emptiness, both subject and object are empty. Since the emptiness of emptiness is itself empty, then emptiness has nothing further to empty. This refers to the emptiness that has nothing to empty;

because this emptiness is also again empty of emptiness, one attains the realization of the wisdom-door of "emptiness of emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā), which is repeatedly empty of emptiness, such that this door is constantly present before one.
Regarding "such as these," it means these ten categories of the wisdom-door of emptiness; only these [are so].
That which is realized in the eighth stage is something that all Bodhisattvas of the lower stages do not individually know.
Regarding the phrase "the equality of space": why is it said that those of the lower stages do not individually know this?

It is because within the gnosis of the stage of the equality of space realized by these Bodhisattvas, there is not merely the ten kinds of emptiness; furthermore, there is that which is ineffable and beyond expression.
He explains the principles of majestic spiritual power, transformations, and wisdom; yet even the bodhisattvas of the lower stages cannot know them.

Regarding the phrase "by means of a single thought-moment," it means that by means of ineffable spiritual powers, paths, and knowledge, one is able to use wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment to know all the most excellent dharmas, discerning their various distinctions and differences, and thus observes them.
Adapting their skillful means to the teachings, they enter the realms of immeasurable buddhas to serve them.
Before each and every buddha, they inquire and receive instruction, listening to the essentials of the Dharma.

They transform and deliver beings in succession so that the lineage shall never be severed, transmitting the Dharma to all worthy sages and sentient beings of great resolve, acting as Great Physician Kings. And with this...
Bestowing the medicine of the Dharma upon all ordinary beings, he heals their mental afflictions;
as a great Dharma master, he instructs sentient beings so they may distance themselves from defilements; as a great guide, he leads sentient beings to forever transcend the realms of suffering.
He destroys the four māras and takes refuge in the Triple Gem. His Dharmakāya is fully perfected, lacking nothing and with nothing remaining.
He manifests transformation bodies to propagate the teaching, an unceasing succession of transformations, so that all sentient beings may enter the realm of the Buddha.

This is the number of all Buddhas. Within this enumeration of the ninth and tenth stages (*bhūmi*), one nurtures the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) through hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates, hundreds of thousands of samādhi gates, hundreds of thousands of *vajra* gates, hundreds of thousands of supernormal power (*abhijñā*) gates, and hundreds of thousands of liberation (*vimokṣa*) gates.
Thus, within these hundreds of thousands of gates of equality with space, one attains great mastery in a single thought-moment and at a single time.
They may speak of kalpas as non-kalpas, and non-kalpas as kalpas; speak of what is not the Path as the Path, and the Path as what is not the Path;
speak of beings of the six realms as beings of the six realms, and beings of the six realms as beings who are not of the six realms;

speak of those who are not Buddhas as Buddhas, and Buddhas as those who are not Buddhas, while entering and emerging from the Samādhi of the Essential Nature of all Buddhas, reflecting back, reflecting forward, and reflecting in reverse.
It illuminates what precedes and what follows; it illuminates cause and fruit; it illuminates emptiness and existence; it illuminates the ultimate meaning of the Middle Way.

This wisdom is realized only in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and is beyond the reach of lower stages. It is unmoving, neither arriving nor departing, neither entering nor exiting, neither arising nor ceasing.

Regarding the phrase "equal in number to these Buddhas": this means that once the Bodhisattva of this stage has manifested in various places to deliver sentient beings, they are then accounted among the ranks of the Buddhas. They are, in fact, included among the noble ones of the ninth and tenth stages;
however, they merely manifest transformations according to circumstances to nourish their wisdom-life and bring fulfillment to the Dharma-body. Their hundreds...
One attains great mastery within the gate of the equality of empty space regarding a thousand gates of dhāraṇī-retentions, a hundred thousand gates of right concentration-samādhis,
a hundred thousand gates of indestructible vajras, a hundred thousand gates of transformative supernatural powers,
and a hundred thousand gates of skillful means and liberation— such various dharma-gates numbering in the hundreds of thousands. Within this one [gate],...
Within mindfulness, at one time, there is not even the slightest moment of rest, for [the practitioner] is able to practice them all.
Regarding "saying an eon is not an eon, or saying what is not an eon is an eon": the Sanskrit term *kalpa* is translated here as "time-period" (*shifen*).

This refers to the fact that eons have varying lengths and scales, and their durations differ: the eon of the gods' brushing away of stones, the eon of the hells' mustard-seed-filled city, and the human eon of the waterwheel.
"Kalpa. When a bodhisattva has practiced for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and completely severed ignorance, they finally attain Buddhahood;
this is what is called a "kalpa. Such kalpas as these are fundamentally not truly existent and are therefore called "non-kalpas.
Thus it is said: "A kalpa is spoken of as a non-kalpa, and a non-kalpa is spoken of as a kalpa. Regarding "speaking of non-path as path," etc., this refers to this bodhisattva.
One is able to clearly perceive that the worldly conditioned dharmas—such as false views and non-paths—are fundamentally empty and devoid of intrinsic substance.

By directly awakening to and seeing the dharmas of the Bodhi-path, it is called "speaking of the path where there is no path. Furthermore, one is able to clearly perceive the supramundane unconditioned dharmas—such as the Noble Truths and the True Path.
Although these are called the "True Path," the true is established in dependence upon the false; thus, the true is likewise [empty].
It is wrong. Since both the wrong and the right are neither, it is said that "the Way speaks of what is not the Way.
When those of the six realms of existence speak of the beings of the six realms, the Sage is one who has awakened from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

When ordinary persons speak of those who are not of the six realms of existence, the ordinary person is one who has not awakened to the state of a Sage. When those who are not Buddhas speak of the Buddha:
Māra is not different from the Buddha. When the Buddha speaks of what is "not Buddha," the Buddha is also Māra.

This is precisely what is meant by the saying that those who speak of "is" and "is not" do not recognize [the truth]; whether they act in opposition or in accord with the Way, even the heavens cannot fathom them.

As for the phrase "entering and emerging equally," it means that since this bodhisattva has already entered the ranks of the Buddhas, they can enter meditative absorption while speaking horizontally or vertically, and acting either in opposition or in accord with the Way.
Emerging from meditative absorption, one attains great mastery within the samādhi of the essential nature of all Buddhas and becomes fully endowed with ten kinds of wisdom-illumination.
What are these ten? First, "reflecting back" means reflecting back upon oneself:
that the four elements and five aggregates, subject to both birth-and-death and transformation, are not even one that is real, nor one that is unreal, nor one that is empty.
There is not one that is not empty. Who is it that acts for the benefit of living beings? Who is the "benefactor of living beings"?

Second, "conformative illumination" refers to acting in accordance with the nature of sentient beings so that they may be easily transformed and delivered without generating weariness, thereby embracing them through compassion.
Third, "contrary illumination" refers to acting in opposition to the nature of sentient beings; though difficult to tame, one is able to tame them through skillful means and majestic power.

The "divine subjugation" refers to this. Regarding the fourfold "prior illumination": it exhaustively covers the past lives, from the initial aspiration of an ordinary person until entering this stage, thereby illuminating them.
Regarding the fivefold "subsequent illumination": it extends from this stage until the attainment of Buddhahood and the benefiting of sentient beings.
It illuminates throughout the entirety of future worlds. Sixth, illumination of causes:

it illuminates the causes of suffering—the beginningless non-awakening of oneself and others—along with the causes of bliss, which is initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) and purity. Seventh, illumination of fruits:

it illuminates the fruits of suffering—the bondage of karma within the cycle of birth and death for oneself and others—as well as the ultimate fruits of bliss, which is original awakening (mūla-bodhi). Eighth, illumination of emptiness:
The first is the illumination that illuminates the True [Reality]. It is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). The ninth is the illumination that illuminates the conventional;

it is the illumination of all phenomena (*dharma*). The tenth is the illumination of the meaning of the supreme Middle Way Truth (*paramārtha-satya*): it means illuminating the True as not-True, and illuminating the conventional as not-conventional.
It does not abide in the two extremes, nor does it exist as a "middle. It is free from both identity and difference; therefore, it is called "supreme."
The meaning of the Middle Way is illumination. Regarding the phrase "this wisdom is equal," it means that these ten kinds of wisdom-illumination are realized only in the eighth stage;
they are not within the reach of Bodhisattvas in the lower stages. Why is this?
It is because the *tathatā* (suchness) realized by these Bodhisattvas is neither moving nor arriving, as it is free from the characteristics of movement and arrival; it neither goes out nor enters.

Because it is free from the characteristics of entering and exiting, it is neither arising nor ceasing; because it is free from the characteristics of arising and ceasing, within this wisdom-concentration, both the illumination and the illuminator are simultaneously quiescent and extinguished.
This is the section on the Dharma-gates of the Grounds (bhūmi). It is immeasurable beyond measure, ineffable beyond the ineffable.
Now, I shall briefly open up but a single hair-tip’s worth of the hundreds of thousands of divisions within these grounds, as has already been clarified in the section on the Arhats.

Regarding this dharma-gate of the stages: it refers to all the dharma-gates realized by these bodhisattvas, which consist of immeasurable, immeasurable, unspeakable, unspeakable categories; they are without limit and beyond the reach of verbal expression.
Now, this has been briefly set forth from among the hundreds of thousands of millions of parts of the merits within the stages;
it is merely like a single drop of water, or a hair-tip's worth, from the great ocean. This meaning has already been clarified within the "Arhat Chapter" of the Great Treatise.
Ninth, the Ground of the Nature of the Flower Ornament (*Avataṃsaka-bhūmi*).
On this ground, the Bodhisattva abandons one type of obstacle to the lack of desire for practice.

This is a portion of the innate grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) within the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which arises from a lack of diligent application toward activities that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings; therefore, it is so named.
Furthermore, they simultaneously sever two kinds of ignorant attachments: first, ignorance regarding *dhāraṇī*; second, ignorance regarding mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
These three factors can obstruct the ninth stage; only by severing these ignorant obstructions does one ascend to the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
This means that this Bodhisattva now attains ten kinds of unimpeded intellectual application (*jñāna-prayoga*) which manifest before them; among all forms of knowledge, these are the most supreme.

It is preeminent. Because the function of this wisdom is unimpeded, one is able to permanently sever [obstructions]. Once the obstructions of ignorance are severed, one is able to turn the great wheel of the pure Dharma.
Thus, because one skillfully employs this wisdom, it is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). The *tathatā* realized therein is termed the *tathatā* of mastery over wisdom;
that is to say, the function of wisdom regarding this *tathatā* is sovereign by virtue of the four kinds of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Because he is the locus of wisdom, the Bodhisattva takes his station as a celestial king of the third dhyāna, acting as the sovereign of a middle chiliocosm.
He transforms and guides sentient beings through the Single Vehicle Dharma; among the ten pāramitās, the pāramitā of skillful means (upāya) is most preeminent.
It is not that he does not cultivate the others, but he does so according to his power and capacity.
O Sons of the Buddha! The Bodhisattvas possess the ground of the essential nature of the Flower Ornament of the Buddhas.
With the deportment of a Buddha and the Sovereign King Samādhi of the Tathāgatas, they enter and emerge from meditative concentration at no fixed time.

Throughout the ten directions, across three thousandfold world systems, with ten billion suns and moons and ten billion sets of four continents, they simultaneously attain Buddhahood, turn the wheel of Dharma, and even pass into parinirvāṇa—all these Buddhas.

With a single mind, he simultaneously manifests to all sentient beings all manner of physical bodies, the eighty minor marks, the thirty-two major signs, sovereign bliss, and a radiance equal to space.
Adorned with the marks and signs of immeasurable great compassion, he is neither god nor human, nor does he belong to the six realms;
yet, transcending all phenomena, he constantly traverses the six realms, manifesting in infinite ways.

With an immeasurable body, immeasurable speech, and immeasurable mind, he expounds immeasurable Dharma-gates, able to transform the realm of Māra into the realm of the Buddha, and the realm of the Buddha into the realm of Māra.
Furthermore, he transforms all views into the view of the Buddha, and the view of the Buddha into all views;
he brings the Buddha-nature into the nature of sentient beings, and the nature of sentient beings into the Buddha-nature. The radiance of that ground shines with light; wisdom shines with wisdom.
Brilliant flame, brilliant flame! Fearless and immeasurable; the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, liberation, and nirvāṇa—the unconditioned, singular path of purity.
The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" indicate and manifest his name, virtue, and rank. Regarding "the Flower Adornment (Avataṃsaka) body-nature ground":
it means that the adornment of the realm realized by this Bodhisattva is equal to that of a Buddha, without any distinction. "Flower" refers to the flower of practice.
"Adornment" (*vyūha*) refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. It is so called because one adorns the fruit of Buddhahood by cultivating the flowers of the causes, which are the myriad practices.

In other sutras, this stage is named the "Stage of Excellent Wisdom" (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). This means that once the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) has been attained, one immediately gives rise to wondrous function;

whatever is illuminated and realized is entirely *tathatā*. Therefore, it is named the Stage of Excellent Wisdom. Regarding the phrase "by means of the Buddha’s majestic deportment," this refers to its function. That is to say, this...
A bodhisattva is able to employ the majestic deportment of a Buddha amidst both movement and stillness. To speak of "majesty" (wei), it is awe-inspiring;
it subdues all māras and restrains all heterodox teachers, bringing to discipline those who ought to be disciplined. To speak of "deportment" (yi), it is worthy of contemplation.
He transforms and edifies humans and devas, guiding all classes of beings; he gathers in and sustains those who are to be gathered. Regarding the term "Tathāgata":

"Tathā" (Thus) refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), and "Gata" (Come) refers to initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*). Because the original and the initial are non-dual, it is called Tathāgata.

Furthermore, as for "coming," there is nowhere from which one comes; as for "going," there is nowhere to which one goes. Because there is neither coming nor going, it is called Tathāgata. Samādhi... [self-]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Awakening of Faith*, specifically concerning the etymology of "Tathāgata" and the nature of samādhi.)
Regarding "King of Samādhis": it refers to the King of Samādhis among the one hundred and eight samādhis, namely the Samādhi of Stable Establishment (*vyavasthāna-samādhi*).
This is because [the bodhisattva] is able to dwell with mastery over all samādhis. That is to say, whether this bodhisattva is moving or still, coming or going, sitting or lying down—
In all cases, they manifest the majestic demeanor of a Buddha. When entering stillness, they abide with sovereign mastery within all samādhis by means of the King of Samādhis;
when emerging into activity, they enter and exit at will and without obstruction through the King of Samādhi concentration in accordance with their minds.

Whether for a brief moment or for a long duration, there is no fixed time. Regarding the phrase "in the ten directions," it means that this Bodhisattva, having attained this King of Sovereign Samādhi, is no different from a Buddha.

Throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions, they exercise mastery according to their will by means of the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Transformation-body, across all great trichiliocosms, billions of suns and moons, and billions [of worlds].

In the midst of the four continents, without relying on external power, he simultaneously manifests the descent into birth, the renunciation of the world, the subduing of Māra, the attainment of the Way, the turning of the Great Dharma Wheel, and even the entry into Nirvāṇa.
All these Buddha-activities are manifested before all sentient beings at once within a single thought-moment. He manifests all forms of golden bodies...
Their marks are all complete with the eighty secondary characteristics and the thirty-two major marks.
That which they manifest is the sovereign enjoyment of incomparable great bliss, as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimately identical to space, and without any difference.
Yet these various immeasurable great compassions, various radiances, various marks and signs of excellence, and various adornments—
He manifests as identical to the devas, yet is not a deva; he manifests as identical to humans, yet is not a human;
he manifests as identical to the six realms of existence, yet is not of the six realms. He stands far beyond all phenomena, yet does not abandon any phenomenon.

Constantly moving within the six realms, he manifests immeasurable wheels of the body through various supernatural powers, immeasurable wheels of speech through infinite eloquence, and immeasurable...
The wheel of the wisdom-mind expounds immeasurable dharma-gates of skillful means and ultimate reality.
It is that which can turn the realm of Māra into the realm of the Buddha. Thereupon, the Māra King said to the World-Honored One:

"Gautama, I shall wait until all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood, until the realm of sentient beings is exhausted and the very name 'sentient being' no longer exists; only then will I resolve to attain Bodhicitta."
Furthermore, regarding "the Buddha-realm entering the realm of Māra," this refers to when Devadatta said to Ānanda:
"Since the Buddha has no portion of falling into hell, how could I have any portion of escaping from hell?

Regarding "being able to turn all views into the Buddha-view," when one perceives the perception itself, that perception is not [ultimately] a perception. Regarding "the Buddha-view entering all views," as for that perception...
It transcends views; it is beyond the reach of vision. When the Buddha-nature enters the nature of sentient beings, it constantly accords with them, attaining the wondrous by following the flow.
When the nature of sentient beings enters the Buddha-nature, it transforms the ordinary into the holy, like alchemically turning iron into gold.
In brief, this Bodhisattva, through the Samādhi of the Sovereign King of Buddha-Dignity and Grace, manifests great spiritual power and function. Extensively...
The performance of Buddha-work is such as this. From the ten directions and so forth, all together elucidate the meaning of the Sovereign King of Freedom (*Vasavartin*).
As for the "light of the ground," it is the primordial, fully perfected radiance inherent to the *Avataṃsaka* ground.

As for the "light-illuminating light," it refers both to the wisdom-light that is capable of reflecting and illuminating, and the wisdom-light that is reflected and illuminated; these lights shine upon one another.
It is illumination. Regarding "wisdom illuminating wisdom": this refers both to the emptiness-wisdom that is capable of clear illumination and the emptiness-wisdom that is clearly illuminated;
thus, wisdom and wisdom illuminate one another. Regarding "the brilliance of the flame, the brilliance of the flame":

the upper "brilliance of the flame" is the brilliance-flame of the light of wisdom (*jñāna*), while the lower "brilliance of the flame" is the brilliance-flame of emptiness-wisdom (*śūnyatā-prajñā*). This refers to the brilliance-flame of this light of wisdom and...

The brilliant flames of the wisdom of emptiness continue one after another in succession, serving as the lamp of the inexhaustible. As for "fearlessness," this refers to the four fearlessnesses of a Buddha:
first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path;
and fourth, fearlessness regarding the path that exhausts suffering. Furthermore, these ten fearlessnesses are fully contained within the enumeration of dharmas.
The "immeasurables" refers to the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). The ten powers (*daśabala*) and eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are both explained as previously seen.
"Liberation" (*vimukti*) refers to the liberation in which the active manifestation of the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) is forever suppressed, as described in the preceding stage.
"Nirvāṇa" refers to *nirupadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder). It is said that the radiance of this stage is not only brilliantly and inexhaustibly blazing, but that the Buddha—
From fearlessness up to the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all are unconditioned, a single path of purity. As the Sūtra says:
"The light of wisdom illumines the immeasurable; skillful means are inexhaustible. This is precisely what that refers to.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings as one's own parents and siblings, one preaches the Dharma for them until the end of all kalpas so that they may attain the fruits of the Path.
Moreover, manifesting bodies in all lands, one regards all sentient beings as one would look upon one's own father or mother.
Regarding "the celestial Māras and non-Buddhists regard one another as father and mother,
yet [the Bodhisattva] treats all with equality": this refers to the Bodhisattva who, having realized the light of this stage and attained the fearlessnesses of a Buddha,
and having fully purified the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, again gives rise to compassion and manifests inferior conduct throughout the ten directions and the four...
Regarding all sentient beings born within the six realms, one regards them as one’s own parents and serves them with filial piety;
one regards them as one’s own brothers and loves them with respect. Through various skillful means, one preaches the Dharma for them without ever becoming weary or fatigued.

Even throughout the duration of all kalpas, one must ensure that they all attain the Buddha-way and realize the fruit of Buddhahood before ceasing. Furthermore, one manifests in the form of a Honored One...
This is the supreme practice: within all lands, manifesting every form for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to regard one another as fathers or mothers;

even celestial Māras and followers of external paths likewise regard one another as fathers or mothers, cherishing each other with parental love as if they were all one child, and ensuring that they attain the Way and its fruits before finally coming to rest.
Abiding in this stage, from the limit of birth and death up to the adamantine limit,
one manifests such events within a single thought-moment and is able to enter the realms of immeasurable sentient beings. Such immeasurability is, in brief, like a single drop from the ocean.
Regarding the phrase "dwelling in this stage," it means that when a Bodhisattva dwells within this Flower Ornament (Avataṃsaka) stage,

they begin from the initial awakening of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*)— arising from the limit of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) through the non-awakening of ordinary beings— and continue until the ultimate awakening at the limit of the Vajra-wheel.
Within this interval, all the various dharmas of what is cultivated, what is practiced, what is severed, and what is realized are included.

Gate: Within a single moment of mind, one is able to manifest such phenomena as these, and furthermore, can enter into the realms of immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation and the ultimate fruit of the Path.

Thus, these infinite gateways to the Buddha-dharma are ultimately inexhaustible to describe; this has been but a brief exposition, like a single drop from the ocean or a mere hair-tip’s worth of the matter.
○ Tenth: Entering the Ground of the Buddha-realm through Essential Nature.
On this stage, the Bodhisattva abandons one type of obstacle to mastery (*vaśitā-āvaraṇa*).

This arises from a portion of the innate clinging to phenomena (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*) within the cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), which functions as an attachment to the "flavor" of phenomena.
