It obstructs the manifestation of the great cloud of Dharma-knowledge (*mahā-dharma-jñāna-megha*) and the activities arising therefrom; therefore, it is so named. Furthermore, two types of deluded attachments are abandoned. The first is...
First is the delusion regarding the manifestation of great supernatural powers; second is the delusion regarding subtle secrets. These three factors can obstruct the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Only by severing these delusional obstructions can one ascend to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), where the Bodhisattva’s *dharmakāya* is perfected, intrinsic wisdom is purified, both emptiness and existence are forgotten, and the principle of the Middle Way is fully realized. Once these delusional obstructions are severed, they are exhausted forever.
Therefore, the clouds of wisdom pervade the entire dharma-realm and rain down the great rain of Dharma, fully satisfying all withered sentient beings;
hence it is called the Ground of Dharma-Clouds (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). The suchness (*tathatā*) realized therein is named the "Suchness of Sovereignty over Karma.
All karmic afflictions are completely liberated, and one accords with the principle of suchness; thus, the Bodhisattva takes the four *dhyānas* as their provisional station.
O Celestial King, as the sovereign of the great trichiliocosm, you expound the Dharma of the Single Vehicle to transform sentient beings.
Among the ten pāramitās, the pāramitā of wisdom is the most supreme; all other pāramitās and every merit reach complete fulfillment and perfection therein.
If, O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas enter the ground of the essential nature of the Buddha-realm, their great wisdom is empty, empty again, and yet further empty;
it is like the nature of space. With the wisdom of equality, there is the Tathāgata-nature. The ten qualities of merit are fully endowed with emptiness and share a single characteristic.
Their essential nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the spirit is void and the substance is one. Dharmas are identical to the Dharma-nature; therefore, they are called Tathāgatas.

One should accord with the Four Truths and the Two Truths, exhausting the limits of the wheel of birth and death. Since the Dharma-nourishment and the Dharma-body are non-dual, one is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).

Because one possesses right knowledge that universally covers all worlds and all phenomena, as well as noble liberating wisdom that knows the existence and non-existence of all dharmas and the faculties of all sentient beings, one is the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha). This is the clear and luminous cultivation at the time of the Buddha-fruit.

Because he is complete in these [bases of power], he is the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*). The *sugata* (Well-Gone) possesses the Buddha-dharmas of the three times; his dharmas are identical to those of the Buddhas of former times.
When the Buddha departs, it is excellent; when he comes, it is excellent—thus he is named *sugata*. This person practices these supreme virtues and enters into the world.
He transforms and edifies sentient beings, causing them to be liberated from all fetters and bonds; therefore, he is called the "Liberator of the World.
This person, standing above all dharmas, enters the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha; his physical demeanor is like that of a Buddha.

As one who dwells in the sphere of practice of a Great Being, he acts as the Liberator of the World, taming and harmonizing all sentient beings; thus he is named a "Great Man" (Puruṣa). Among devas and humans, he transforms and edifies all.
Because sentient beings consult and receive his words of Dharma, he is the Teacher of Gods and Humans. His wondrous foundation is non-dual;
the Buddha-nature is profound awakening, eternally and ever-present, perfectly full. Because all sentient beings prostrate to him and revere him, he is the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Because all people of the world consult him, receive his teachings, and honor them, he is the Buddha-ground. This ground is the place entered by all sages.
Therefore, it is called the "Buddha-realm ground.
The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" indicate and manifest the names, virtues, and stages. Regarding "entering the essential nature-ground of the Buddha-realm":
this refers to the treasury of all merits—wisdom, principle, practice, and vows—realized by this Bodhisattva, which is identical to those of the ten directions.

The realm realized by all Buddhas is equal and without distinction; therefore, it is called the Stage of Entering the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu-bhūmi*). In another sutra, it is named the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
This means that when a Bodhisattva reaches this tenth stage, their cultivation of merit is fulfilled, and they devote themselves solely to transforming and benefiting sentient beings.
Their great compassion is like a cloud, capable of universally shading and covering all; hence it is called the Cloud of Dharma Stage. Its great wisdom is empty.
"Emptiness further emptied" means that this Buddha-realm is precisely the Great Wisdom-emptiness of emptiness further emptied.
This Great Wisdom-emptiness reaches the ultimate of ultimates; emptiness is further emptied, such that there is no emptiness remaining to be emptied.
"Emptiness further emptied, like the nature of empty space" means that this Great Wisdom-emptiness is itself further emptied, and so forth.
It is not the same as the empty void of non-existence or the emptiness of annihilation;

rather, it is the nature of space itself—perfectly interfused and all-pervasive, leaving nothing out whether great or small, an emptiness-nature that is neither deficient nor redundant. This is precisely the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
The assembly of principles is perfectly consummate; this is the realm of the Dharmakāya. Regarding those who possess the Tathāgata-nature within their wisdom of equality:

it is said that this Buddha-realm is fundamentally equal and inherently possesses this wisdom. Therefore, within this wisdom of equality, the essential nature of the Tathāgata is already fully present.
This is precisely the wisdom-assembly of the Wisdom of Equality, the perfectly luminous realm of the Saṃbhogakāya.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Ten Qualities": it is said that when a bodhisattva realizes and enters this stage, they immediately attain the ten titles of qualities in their complete perfection.
This is precisely the realm of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), wherein the accumulation of merits of the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is fully perfected.
It is only when the three bodies are perfectly manifested and the ten titles are simultaneously revealed that one may be said to have entered the realm of the Buddha.
Furthermore, what are the ten qualities of the chapter? First, regarding "emptiness being of one identical characteristic":

this means that within this Great Wisdom emptiness (*mahāprajñā-śūnyatā*), although there are ten different names and titles, in reality they originally possess no form or shape; every title is empty, and they share the single characteristic of emptiness.
Regarding "the essential nature being unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*): this means that since every title is equally empty and fundamentally lacks any distinct characteristics, then...
This essence is without arising or ceasing, and is devoid of deliberate action. Regarding the phrase "the spiritual is empty and the substance is one":
it means that since the essence of the Dharma-body is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the spiritual mechanism of the reward and transformation bodies is empty, luminous, and all-pervasive.
The three bodies are one body; their functioning is undivided, yet they manifest everywhere without hindrance. Phenomena are the Dharma-nature; the Dharma-nature...
This is precisely the Dharma. For this reason, it extends through the three periods of time without facing toward or away from them, and pervades the ten directions without coming or going;
therefore, it is called the Tathāgata. Second, regarding "conforming to the Four Noble Truths" and so forth:

the Four Noble Truths refer to the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) Four Noble Truths, the non-arising (anutpāda) Four Noble Truths, and the immeasurable (apramāṇa) Four Noble Truths. The Two Truths refer to the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti).
This refers to the Truths (*satya*). "Exhausting birth and death" means exhausting the limits of beginningless saṃsāra;
it is the ultimate limit of the Vajra-wheel. "Dharma" refers to the aforementioned dharmas of the Truths. It is said that a Bodhisattva who has entered this stage is worthy of offerings (*arhat*);

this is not like the humans, devas, or followers of the Two Vehicles who are worthy of offerings consisting of limited, segmented food. Rather, such a one is worthy of extensively transforming sentient beings by employing the Four Truths.

The Dharma consists of the two truths. From the very beginning of beginningless saṃsāra, until reaching the limit of the vajra-circle, by means of such dharmas, one nourishes the dharma-body in accordance with it;
being neither identical nor different, it benefits and receives the offerings of humans and devas, and is therefore called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
Regarding the third point, "pervasive covering," it means that the Bodhisattvas of this stage are able to universally and completely cover [all beings].
What is it that enables one to thoroughly and universally know all things—both mundane and supramundane—within all worlds?
It is, in short, the possession of this right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). What is right knowledge? It is the noble knowledge of liberation (*ārya-vimukti-jñāna*).
By means of this very right knowledge, one universally knows that for all phenomena (*dharma*), "existence" is liberation, and for all phenomena, "non-existence" is likewise liberation. Both are...
By means of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), one universally knows that the faculties of all ordinary and noble beings—whether dull or sharp—are empty in every respect;
there is nothing that is not liberated. Therefore, it is called "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). Regarding the four illuminations (*vidyā*) and so forth:

"illumination" refers to the limb of wisdom (*prajñā-sambhāra*), while "cultivation" refers to the limb of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*). It is said that since this Bodhisattva first gave rise to the Great Mind (*mahā-citta*), he has clearly illuminated his cultivation.
Wisdom. Having practiced and planted merit, once this stage is entered, one finally attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because the two adornments of merit and wisdom are simultaneously fulfilled and complete, this is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna).

Fifth, "The Sugata" means that this Bodhisattva is skillfully able to come and go within the triple world, manifesting birth, leaving home to practice, attaining enlightenment, preaching the Dharma, and transforming sentient beings.
To deliver sentient beings and enter into nirvana—this is the path and Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. The Way of every Buddha is the same;

it is the ritual and Dharma of the ancient Buddhas, identical to the Dharma of the Buddhas of the past. When a Buddha departs, he does so with excellence; having completed his conditions, he passes away.
He manifests entry into nirvana, yet departs without going anywhere. When he comes, it is well; he comes in accordance with conditions, manifesting birth and the attainment of enlightenment.
He comes from nowhere, and his coming and going are auspicious; this is called "well-well" (*śaṃ-śam*). As for the sixth point, "those people who practice these things":
this refers to those of the stage of the person (*pudgala-bhūmi*) who can practice these supreme, unsurpassed merits of the Buddha, and thus manifest their bodies [in the world]. Entry...

Within the world, he extensively establishes teachings to benefit sentient beings, so that all sentient beings may attain liberation from all worldly fetters and bonds and enter the Buddha-way; this is called "liberation in the world.
Seventh, regarding "this person is equal in all respects": it means that this noble one is able to manifest [the truth] upon all phenomena.

The principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) enters the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*prabhāva*), manifesting the body of the nature of phenomena with a physical form and demeanor identical to that of a Buddha.
Therefore, wherever a Great Being (*mahāsattva*) travels, those who behold his countenance find their delusions dissolved; in every place they visit, all attain worldly liberation.

There is nothing superior to this; therefore, he is named the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*). Regarding the "eightfold discipline" (*aṣṭāṅga-samyama*), "discipline" (*samyama*) has three meanings:

regulation (*pariṣkāra*), harmony (*saṃskāra*), and submissiveness (*anuvidhāna*). Regulation means that the body does not engage in killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, and its substance is naturally pure.
Harmony means that the mouth is free from contentious debate and always maintains the five forms of speech. Submissiveness means that the mind is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and...

This refers to the generation of concentration, wisdom, and so forth. It means that this Bodhisattva is able to thus discipline the body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings within the entire dharma-realm, causing them to distance themselves from the ten unwholesome paths of action and attain the fruits of the Path.

For this reason, he is called a "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi). "Taming" (damya) is like taming a horse; it carries the meaning of training according to their inherent nature. Ninth, regarding gods, humans, and others...

This means that this Bodhisattva is able to manifest in various places throughout the heavens and among humans, teaching, transforming, and benefiting all sentient beings, causing them to inquire about and listen to the Buddha-dharma; because his words penetrate deeply and reach their hearts, they obtain great benefit.
Therefore, he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans. Regarding the phrase "The ten wonders are fundamentally non-dual": "Wondrous" (Miao) refers to...
This is the wondrous function; the "origin" is the fundamental substance. This refers to the Bodhisattva’s fundamental substance of Buddha-nature, profound awakening, and wondrous function.
Upon reaching this realization of the fruit, awakening is perfected. Regarding both substance and function, there is neither one nor two;
it is unconditioned and signless, perfectly full and eternally abiding. Constantly and ever-filling, without deficiency or excess, this is what is called a Buddha, for the sake of all worlds.
Because the supramundane noble beings prostrate to and gaze upon him with reverence, and because they honor and respect him, he is therefore named the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The above clarifies the Chapter on the Ten Merits; below, it correctly clarifies the entry into the stage of the Buddha-realm.

Regarding the phrase "all worldly beings and others": it means that this Bodhisattva, being fully endowed with the ten merits, is one whose Dharma is consulted and upheld by all worldly and supramundane sages and saints;

they receive it into their hearts, follow his instructions, and rely upon him as their refuge. Therefore, this is called the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). Regarding the phrase "in this ground": it means...
The realm within this Buddha-ground is not the realm of lower grounds;
rather, it is the sphere of all Buddhas, the place where the sages of every ground enter and realize. Therefore, it is called "entering the Buddha-realm ground."
At that time, he sat upon a precious lotus flower; all were filled with joy as they received their prophecy. The Dharma-Body hand stroked his head.
Regarding the phrase "at that time, he sat": at that very moment, he entered the ultimate limit of the Buddha-realm.
When the fruit of Buddhahood is attained, it is said that this Bodhisattva, having achieved ultimate perfection at that time, shall sit upon this precious lotus flower.
This is the entry into the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

All Buddhas of the ten directions then bestow upon this Bodhisattva of the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) the prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood, including the adornments of the eons and lands, as well as the matters of attaining the great bliss, mastery, and joy of a Buddha.
They all likewise stroke his head with the light-net marks and radiant hands of their pure *dharmakāya*.

This is an exhortation to turn the wheel of Dharma. These three constitute the praise of the dharma-gate. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the praise of the primary figures and their retinues in the native land;
second, the praise of the primary figures and their retinues from other directions.
The bodhisattvas who share the same vision and study praised [the Buddha] with one voice and in unison, their praise being non-dual.
Those who share the same vision possess the same understanding; that is, they are those who see the reality of the *dharmakāya* and the true mark (*tathatā*).

Those who share the same study are those who study under the same teacher; that is, they are those who study the bodhisattva path together. Those who have received the same empowerment are those who have been conferred the same office. This refers to that time.
All the bodhisattvas who share the same views and study together are filled with joy; with one voice and in unison, they praise and extol him.
Their companions are entirely identical, without duality or distinction. This is the praise of his native companions.
Furthermore, from hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds, all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas gathered together like clouds at once,
requesting that the ineffable Dharma-wheel— the Dharma-gate of the transformative guidance of Ākāśagarbha— be turned.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and hundreds of thousands," it means that not only have the Buddhas placed their hands upon his head and the Bodhisattvas offered praise,
but moreover, all the Buddhas and all the Bodhisattvas from hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields have gathered together at once like clouds,
requesting the Bodhisattva of the Dharma-Cloud Stage to turn the wheel of the ineffably ineffable [Dharma].
He preaches the vast wheel of Dharma, including the inexhaustible and boundless Dharma-gates for transformation and guidance of the *Gaganagañja* (Space-Treasury),
so that this Way may circulate forever and its transformative influence continue unceasingly among gods and humans.
This is the praise and request from the principal and retinue of other directions to turn the wheel of Dharma.
This stage contains unspeakably wondrous Dharma-gate chapters, marvelous triple super-knowledges (*traividyā*), gateways of samādhi, and gateways of dhāraṇī.
These are not known by the mind-consciousness of ordinary beings in lower stages; they are known only by the immeasurable body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas.
One may exhaust its source. As stated in the "Chapter on the Light-Sound Heaven" (*Ābhāsvara-deva-varga*), the ten fearlessnesses (*daśa-vaiśāradya*) are identical to those of the Buddha’s path.

Regarding the phrase "those who are equal to this stage," it means that the Bodhisattvas of this stage skillfully expound all dharmas in order to eliminate the notion that there are others who can equal the Tathāgata.
For this reason, there exists the "Chapter on the Ineffable, Wondrous, and Vast Dharma-Gates. It is wondrous.

This is the Dharma-gate of the wisdom of the three types of clear knowledge; the Dharma-gate of the wondrous and marvelous samādhi of right concentration; and the Dharma-gate of the wondrous and marvelous dhāraṇī of total retention.
It cannot be known by the mental consciousnesses of bodhisattvas of the lower stages or by ordinary beings who have merely resolved their minds upon awakening;
it can be known only by Buddha after Buddha, with their immeasurable bodies of supernormal powers, their immeasurable eloquence of speech, and their immeasurable wisdom.
One may fully comprehend its underlying essence and origin through reflection.
What is explained here is identical to the teaching on the ten dharmas of fearlessness found within the "Chapter on the Ābhāsvara Heaven" in the Great Sūtra;
it is precisely the same as the path for entering the stage of the Buddha-realm, without any difference whatsoever. This is a praise of supreme merit.
The Buddha-Spoken Brahmajāla Sūtra with Concordant Annotations, Volume Upper;
The Buddha-Spoken Brahmajāla Sūtra with Concordant Annotations, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Shu Yu Hua Yan Ji er Guan Sheng Ke De Yu,
Shun Zhu Ci Yun Si Jia Nan Hui Xian, Transcribed from the "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Chapter," Part Two.

At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened up within the Dharma-gates of the hundred-thousand Ganges-sands of ineffable teachings the Ground of the Mind (Cittabhūmi), even as much as the tip of a hair.

"At that time" refers to the moment when the exposition of the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi) has been completed. "Vairocana" is the Retribution Buddha (vipākabuddha) who is the speaker; in the language of the Huā (Chinese), it means "Pure and Full.
"Pure" means that the five abodes (pañcavihāra) have been thoroughly exhausted and the two deaths (dvimṛtyu) have forever ceased;

because all afflictions have been purified to the point of exhaustion, this is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). "Full" means that the fruit of the three awakenings is complete and the causes of the ten thousand practices are perfected; because of [this] merit...
Because of the perfection of wisdom, it is the *saṃbhogakāya*. When these two meanings are combined, it is called "pure fulfillment.
It is also said that "various radiances shine everywhere. Here, radiance signifies the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya*, while shining everywhere signifies the meaning of the *dharmakāya*.
Furthermore, the *dharmakāya* is Vairocana; in the Chinese language, this means "pervading all places. To pervade all is precisely the meaning of shining everywhere.
Therefore, know that the Dharma is itself the retribution, and the retribution is itself the Dharma; the Dharma and its retribution are not divided, and principle and wisdom are darkly one.

When these two meanings are spoken of together, there should be no doubt. As for "this great assembly," it refers to the gathering at the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*), a great assembly where ordinary beings and sages intermingle.
"Briefly revealing" means to manifest this Dharma-gate of the mind-ground, which is profoundly deep, vast, and inexhaustible.

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "as many as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers," this employs a metaphor to clarify the Dharma and precisely explains the sense of the brief opening [of the teaching].

It means that what was previously described—the thirty minds and ten stages—is merely a general summary when compared to the gates of the Dharma that are as ineffable as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers; it is like a minute fragment, perhaps the size of a single hair-tip.

These two clarify the third [section], the Precepts of the Mind-Ground. First, the summary that reveals the Dharma-gate; second, the entrustment and exhortation to propagate; third, the transformation through propagation after having received [the teaching].
These were spoken by all Buddhas of the past, will be spoken by the Buddhas of the future, and are now being spoken by the Buddhas of the present. Thus, throughout the three periods of time...

"Bodhisattvas have already studied, shall study, and are now studying"—this refers to those who draw forth the fruit in the past and so forth, establishing a commonality of realization and explanation to encourage faith. Regarding "the three times and so forth":
This is cited to encourage others to receive [the teaching] by showing that those who practice and study together with the practitioner will likewise do so.

It is said that although the "mind-ground" (cittabhūmi) described above may seem as minute as a single hair-tip, its merit is exceedingly great. The Buddhas of the three periods of time have realized this very thing;
what they have taught is this very thing. The Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time have cultivated this very thing; what they have studied is this very thing.
"I have cultivated this mind-ground for a hundred kalpas; thus I am named Vairocana. Regarding the phrase "I have [cultivated]":
the first clause cites the cause to clarify the fruit, while the second clause cites the fruit to clarify the cause.
This means that what has been realized, taught, cultivated, and studied by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time is neither different nor false.
This is precisely what I have practiced, studied, realized, and taught over the course of these hundred kalpas; how could it possibly be in vain?
You may see that the realization of the fruit is fundamentally not caused by anything else, but resides solely within this mind-ground. These are the three preceding sections.
This concludes the exposition of the Dharma-gate.
"You, my sons of the Buddha," [means] that you shall propagate what I have taught to open the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings.
"You, my sons of the Buddha" refers to the Compassionate Honored One, Śākyamuni, who exhorts the thousand Buddhas to propagate the Dharma and transform living beings.
Regarding "turning for us," it means turning what I have taught. I have cultivated the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*) for a hundred kalpas;
such is the profundity of its cause that I am titled Vairocana. Such is the ultimate path of its fruit, which I now bestow upon you.
You should turn and teach it to all deluded sentient beings, causing them to awaken to the mind-ground and to realize the vast opening of their original nature.
There is the Way of the Radiant Vajra Jewel Precepts.
At that time, in the Lotus-Womb World (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*), upon the majestic lion throne of celestial light, Vairocana Buddha emitted rays of light.
These rays addressed the Buddhas upon the thousand petals, saying: "Take this Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground and depart. They then further transmitted it to the thousand [Buddhas].

"Billion Śākyamunis and all sentient beings" refers to the secondary retribution (*upabhoga*) supported by the environment. "The brilliant celestial light" refers to the primary retribution (*vipāka*).

"Vairocana emits light" manifests the excellence of the one who proclaims; "the light proclaims [them] equally" manifests the excellence of those to whom it is proclaimed. "Uphold me... [and so forth].
The term "etc. correctly clarifies the words addressed [to the assembly]. Regarding the "lion throne" (*siṃhāsana*): the lion is the king among beasts;

with a single roar, the brains of the hundred beasts are split open. This symbolizes that when the Dharma King sits upon this throne, he is without fear, for the celestial Māras and non-Buddhist heretics lose heart and are struck with terror upon seeing or hearing him.
Regarding "the light emitted by Rocana Buddha is equal to the light," this refers to the light.

"This Buddha emits" refers to the announcement made by this light; it means that not only is the primary reward body (the physical form) well able to preach the Dharma, but even the light of the secondary reward (the lotus flower) is also able to preach the Dharma, thereby announcing it to the Buddhas upon the thousand petals.

Regarding "uphold my mind-ground," etc., it means that once Vairocana has announced it to the thousand Buddhas, he further desires those thousand Buddhas to successively transmit and receive it from one another.
Therefore, the thousand Buddhas upheld this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground and departed, subsequently transmitting it in succession to the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamuni Buddhas.
These hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamuni Buddhas entrusted and exhorted its transmission to all sentient beings.
This is the joyful and straightforward path.
I shall now explain, in sequence, the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Superior Ground-Mind. You all should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and practice it with single-minded devotion.
Regarding the phrase "in sequence," this refers to Vairocana Buddha’s light informing the thousand Buddhas, who in turn inform the hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas.
I entrust this to you with earnest instructions. When you expound this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, you must not speak it erroneously or in reverse order;
you should teach it according to the sequence of the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, and the Ten Grounds.
You all should likewise receive, uphold, read, and recite it in proper succession. With single-minded focus, apply yourselves with diligent effort. Thus shall you be moved [to realization].
To transform sentient beings means that those above act and those below follow. This is the entrustment and exhortation to turn the wheel [of Dharma].
At that time, the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses—the hundreds of thousands of myriads of Śākyamunis—rose from their majestic lion thrones in the Lotus Treasury World and each withdrew.
From their entire bodies, they emitted inconceivable light; every ray of light transformed into... (no limit).
The Buddhas of the Ten Directions, at one time, offered immeasurable flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white to Vairocana Buddha.
Having completed the reception and upholding of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as expounded above, they departed.
"At that time" refers to the moment when Vairocana exhorted and transmitted [the teaching] for the sake of transformation. Regarding "the thousand flowers" and so forth:

once Vairocana had completed the transmission, at that time the thousand Buddhas—the ten hundred billion Buddhas who were the appropriate recipients—received his instructions and each took leave to return to their respective worlds of origin and manifestation, departing to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings in accordance with conditions. "Lifting the entire body" and so forth signifies the manifestation of the mind.
The Buddha of immeasurable and boundless wisdom is born from the light of the precepts of the ground.

All these Buddhas—the original Buddhas, the trace Buddhas, and the Buddhas of the traces—are all issued forth from within the light of the precepts of the mind-ground. This light cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed in words.
Regarding the "equal lights": the upper light is the light of the thousand Buddhas; the lower light is that of the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis.
The Buddha’s light: because each ray of light is immeasurable and inconceivable, the Buddhas manifested by that light are likewise immeasurable and inconceivable.
Regarding the phrase "at one time," it refers to a thousand Buddhas, ten billion Buddhas, or immeasurable Buddhas all appearing simultaneously.
By means of the flowers of subtle and wondrous causes, they are plucked forth from the hand of faith within the mind-ground. Green symbolizes the Ten Abodes; yellow...
Red represents the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). White represents the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

These are further offered as worship to the Śākyamuni Buddha of fruition who appears within the mind-ground, thereby repaying the Dharma by means of the Dharma and acknowledging and returning its grace. Regarding "receiving and upholding" (*udgrahaṇa*), etc.:
this concludes the passage on the thirty minds and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) in order to introduce the subsequent meaning; hence it says, "receive and uphold the Dharma of the mind-ground."

The Chapter on the Gates concludes. These three types of reception have already been transformed into two: first, the initial reception has already passed away from the teacher; second, each returns to its own realm.
This refers to the initial reception having already passed away from the teacher.

Each of them vanished from this Lotus Treasury World. Having vanished, they entered the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature and returned to their original source world, to the foot of the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa.
Regarding the phrase "each and every one," this refers to thousands of Buddhas, billions of Buddhas, and immeasurable Buddhas.
Each of these has withdrawn from this Lotus Treasury World, which is the dependent retribution adornment of the fundamental Buddha Śākyamuni. Their initial withdrawal constitutes their disappearance;

once they have finally withdrawn and disappeared, they enter into the nature of reality (dharmatā). This passage precisely clarifies the locus where they disappear. It is said that wherever there is a place of disappearance, there must necessarily...
There is an entrance, namely at the moment of passing away; one immediately enters the samādhi of the Flower-Light of the Dharmatā-Space, which is the fundamental essence.

Regarding "returning to the world of the source": thousands and billions of Buddhas each emit light from their respective native lands to manifest before the assembly, and each receives those beings who were previously in doubt, leading them all together to the presence of their original teacher, Śāstṛ Buddha.
Because the *cittabhūmi-śīla-dharma* (the precepts of the mind-ground) which were heard have been fully received;

furthermore, each returns to their original source world (*mūla-lokadhātu*) upon which they rely, seeing that what was concealed and what was revealed do not depart from their respective places—hence it is said they "return to their original source world.
Jambudvīpa is the southern continent of Aparagoyānī within the Sahā world-system. Bodhi-flower...

It is called the "Path of Awakening" (*bodhimārga*) and is also named the "Tree of the Path" (*bodhidruma*). This is because whenever a Buddha appears in the world, they all rely upon this tree to realize the Unsurpassed Way.
Regarding these two [aspects], each revolves within its own realm: first, entering meditative absorption and returning to the source; second, emerging from absorption and preaching the Dharma.
This [passage] refers to entering absorption and returning to the source.
"Emerging from the Samādhi of the Body-Nature’s Flower-Light of Emptiness. Regarding "having emerged":
since it is said that one has entered from this samādhi, one must necessarily emerge from it; there is both concealment and manifestation.
The initial manifestation is called "emerging," and once the manifestation is complete, it is termed "having emerged. Second, emerging from concentration to preach the Dharma, in two parts. First:
This explains the teaching of the horizontal [dimension]. Second, it explains the teaching of the vertical [dimension]. Regarding this explanation of the horizontal teaching, there are two parts:

first, the manifestation of the signs of emerging from meditative concentration; second, the actual teaching of the Dharma-gate. This is the first: the manifestation of the signs of emerging from meditative concentration.
He sat upon the Vajra-Thousand-Rays King Throne and in the Hall of Sublime Light, where he expounded the ocean of dharma-gates of the ten worlds.
Rising again from his seat, he went to the palace of Śakra and expounded the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Rising again from his seat, he went among the Yāma devas and expounded the ten practices (*caryā*).
Rising again from his seat, he went to the fourth heaven (*Tuṣita*) and expounded the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). Rising again from his seat, he went to the Heaven of Transformation...

Nāgārjuna taught the ten dhyānas in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati). Rising again from his seat, he went to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) and taught the ten stages (daśabhūmi).

Then, returning to the first dhyāna, he taught the ten vajras; returning to the second dhyāna, he taught the ten patiences (daśakṣānti); and returning to the third dhyāna, he taught the ten vows (daśapraṇidhāna).
Regarding the phrase "sits squarely" (*fangzuo*): "squarely" (*fang*) means upright and correct. "Vajra" signifies being both sharp and firm; "thousand lights" signifies being vast and expansive;

and "king" (*wang*) conveys the sense of supreme dignity. This refers to what kind of seat the Buddha should occupy after emerging from meditative absorption beneath the Bodhi tree, and how he should sit in sequence to preach the Dharma.
He should sit upon a vajra-seat that is most firm, most sharp, and possesses a thousand lights.
The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s first assembly at the Bodhimaṇḍa describes how the King of Most Vast Radiance (*Vairocana*) preached the Dharma while seated upon his most honored and noble throne;

it also includes Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s exposition of the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World" (*Gandavyūha-loka-dhātu-parivarta*), wherein the Tathāgata reveals the gates of the primary and secondary dharmas (*śāsanadharma*).
Regarding "this very place" and the "Hall of Sublime Light": the hall is the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-maṇḍala*).
In the second assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) in the Hall of Universal Radiance;

this is precisely what is explained below in the section on the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), as these are collectively situated within the human realm and constitute a single abode. As for the exposition of the ocean of Dharma-gates of the ten worlds:
This refers to the Flower Treasury Adornment (*Puṣpa-kośa-vyūha*) of the ten oceans of worlds. The "Dharma-gate" refers to the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
The term "ocean" signifies that there is nothing it does not contain—whether a hundred rivers or a thousand streams—and nothing it does not produce—whether a hundred jewels or a thousand treasures.

Likewise, among the hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates, there is not one that does not flow forth from this ocean of merit, which is the source of faith. Thus, it is called the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths.
The ocean fills the entire dharma-realm, equal to the ten Flower Treasury Adorned World-Oceans.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "rising from his seat," this second location explains the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*). The Palace of Śakra refers to the inner court where the Heavenly King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven resides.
In Sanskrit, he is called Śakradevendra; in Chinese, this means "Lord of Gods. In Sanskrit... [text ends]

Trāyastriṃśa (忉利), here translated as "Thirty-three. This heaven resides upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. One is born therein by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) in their superior degree.
It presides over the Heaven of the Thirty-three. The two characters *Dishi* (帝釋) are a hybrid term combining the Sanskrit and Chinese.

The World-Honored One next taught the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*) in this palace in order to enable Bodhisattvas who have already entered the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) to enter the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes.
Regarding "up to the Yāma Heaven," this is the third location where the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*) are taught.
The Yāma Heaven is the Yāmāntaka Heaven; in the language of China, it means "Time-Division" (*kāla-bhāga*). This heaven dwells supported by space, and because of its lotus...

Because the opening and closing of the flowers distinguish day from night, one is born there by practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade while concurrently dwelling in the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) meditative concentration.

When the World-Honored One subsequently taught the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*) at this location, it was in order to enable Bodhisattvas who have already entered the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) to enter the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices. Regarding "reaching the fourth heaven," etc., this...
The fourth location teaches the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). The four heavens refer to Tuṣita Heaven;

in the language of China, this means "Contentment" (*tuzu*), because [the beings there] know contentment regarding the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). This heaven also dwells supported by space. Their practice is the same as before.
The World-Honored One taught the ten dedications here in order to enable bodhisattvas who have already entered the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*) to enter the ten dedications.
This refers to the Dharma-gate [of the Ten Directions]. Regarding "up to the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations" (*Nirmāṇarati*) and so forth: this fifth stage explains the ten dhyānas.
As for "Delighting in Emanations," it means that one personally emanates the five objects of desire to enjoy them; they also dwell in the sky (*ākāśa-vihārin*). Their practice is the same as before.
The reason the World-Honored One next taught the ten dhyānas in this place is to cause those who have already entered the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) [to further progress].

The Bodhisattva attains the dharma-gate of entering the ten meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Regarding the phrase "up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations" (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), this sixth section explains the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
There are two types of beings in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations: first, those who correctly cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).
Furthermore, they practice the dhyāna of the "not-yet-attained" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), relying on what is accomplished therein to naturally experience bliss.

Second, there are those who exclusively cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action, relying on what is transformed by others to achieve their own bliss; these are the Heaven of the Māra Kings. Both of these heavenly kings dwell in dependence upon space.
The World-Honored One subsequently taught the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) at this location in order to cause those who have already entered the ten dhyānas [to progress].
This is the dharma-gate through which bodhisattvas enter the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, regarding the arrival at the first *dhyāna*:
this seventh location explains the ten vajras. The Heaven of the First *Dhyāna* is the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion.

Because the beings of this heaven have already abandoned the desires and evils of the lower realms and rejoice in the sublime meditative concentration above, the World-Honored One subsequently taught the ten vajras in this place.

This is for the purpose of enabling Bodhisattvas who have already ascended to the seventh stage to realize the wisdom of the adamantine contemplation and enter the ocean-like fruition of wondrous enlightenment.

Furthermore, regarding the arrival at the second dhyāna: this eighth station explains the ten patiences (*kṣānti*). The second dhyāna is the stage of "joy and bliss born of concentration" (*dhyānajapratīsaṃvedasukha*).
The devas of this heaven have already abandoned the joy of the first dhyāna; they collect their minds in meditative absorption, remaining serene and tranquil.

Because it gives rise to superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the World-Honored One next taught the ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) at this stage, in order to cause those Bodhisattvas who have already attained true non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) to practice the dharma-gate of the ten patiences and thereby enter the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, regarding the arrival at the third *dhyāna*: this is the ninth stage where the dharma-gate of the ten vows is taught. The third *dhyāna* is...

The Stage of Sublime Bliss Free from Joy: Because these devas have already transcended the agitation of joy and rapture found in the first and second dhyānas, they enter meditative absorption with total composure and attain a superior, sublime bliss; therefore, the World-Honored One next taught the ten vows to these devas.

It is for the sake of enabling those Bodhisattvas who have already realized the ninth stage to further attain the power of the ten great vows and enter the ocean-like fruition of the Tathāgata’s wondrous enlightenment. Thereupon,
he proceeded to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara within the Fourth Dhyāna and spoke of his own source, the Lotus Treasury World.

The Realm. Regarding the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" taught by Vairocana Buddha, which further reaches the fourth dhyāna and so forth: this tenth section is a general exposition of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" taught in the Brahma Net Sutra by Śākyamuni (Vairocana).
The preceding nine sections were gradual and sequential expositions; this one is a sudden exposition. Thus it is said.
Because this is the "Mind-Ground" (citta-bhūmi) of the Mahāyāna, sixty [stages] are omitted and only the thirty minds and ten grounds are taught.

The four dhyānas constitute the Ground of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*). In these heavens, one abandons the joy and mindfulness of the second dhyāna and the bliss and mindfulness of the third dhyāna;
the mind is free from aversion and attachment. With a single thought of equanimity, it is pure and unmixed. Abiding in this dhyāna, emptiness is luminous and tranquil, and all...

Because all [the stages] appear as an elephant, the World-Honored One next taught the *Cittabhūmi* (Mind-Ground) in its entirety at this location in order to cause those Bodhisattvas who have fully realized the ten stages to enter the ocean of the fruit of *Sūkṣmajñāna* (Subtle Awakening).
The remaining thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are likewise thus; they are non-dual and without distinction, as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpika-parivarta).
Regarding the phrase "the others and so forth": since that which was spoken by the thousand Śākyamunis is thus, it applies to the remaining thousands of billions of Śākyamunis.
The Kāśyapa Buddha likewise emerged from samādhi and preached the Dharma in the Hall of Sublime Light;
he then rose again and proceeded through ten locations, including the Palace of Śūra, preaching both gradually and instantaneously. In all these respects, he was identical to the thousand Śākyamunis.

They are non-dual and without distinction. This teaching is identical to what is explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpika-parivarta). These two above constitute the primary gateways for teaching the Dharma.
This concludes the explanation of the transverse teaching.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having first appeared in the world of Padmagarbha and come from the east to enter the celestial palace, preached the *Māraparivarta Sūtra*.
Thereafter, he descended to be born in Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu; his mother’s name was Māyā and his father’s name was Śuddhodana.
My name is Siddhārtha; I left home at the age of seven and attained the Way at thirty. Thus am I named.

As for Śākyamuni Buddha: the above clarifies that the thousand Śākyas and the hundreds of billions of Śākyas all, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, preach the chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
From here below, it clarifies how one Śākya, within a single world, preaches the Dharma of the Mind-Ground.
This is the Chapter on the Gateways. "At that time" refers to the time when he came from the Lotus World in the eastern direction.

At that time, having come from there, he entered the Tuṣita Heaven palace; first, while remaining in this heaven, he subdued Māra, and after teaching the *Sūtra on the Conversion of King Māra*, he next observed the sentient beings of the lower realms—those whose karmic obscurations made them difficult to liberate. There were... [some who... possessed such obstacles.

One whose faculties are fully matured and easily liberated will, from this very heaven, conceal the superior and manifest the inferior, descending to be born as a crown prince in the royal house of King Śuddhodana in the kingdom of Kapilavastu in Jambudvīpa.

When the Tathāgata descends his spirit, five portents first appear, followed by the manifestation of the eight signs; specifically, his descent from Tuṣita Heaven into the imperial palace is the first sign.
The mother’s name was Māyā; in the Sanskrit language, this means "Great Illusion" (Mahāmāyā), because she manifested all Buddhas through great illusory arts.
Thus, whenever the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest their birth, she serves as their mother. Her father’s name was Śuddhodana; in the Sanskrit language, this is *Uttaradanta*.
When the World-Honored One was about to be born, he observed that King Śuddhodana’s nature and conduct were benevolent and virtuous. Māyā... [text continues]
Lady Ya is the mother of a Bodhisattva for five hundred lifetimes; you ought to go there to take conception in her womb.

What is called "entering the womb," "dwelling in the womb," and so forth refers to the two signs and three signs. My name is Siddhārtha in Sanskrit, which in this language means "Sudden Auspiciousness."
Because at the time of the Prince’s birth, his treasuries were entirely empty, yet having been empty, they became full once more, he was named Dungi (Sudhana).
At that time, the Prince emerged from the right side of Queen Māyā and stood upon a lotus flower.
Pointing one hand toward heaven and the other toward earth, he gazed in the four directions and walked seven paces, declaring: "In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am supreme."

"Venerable One, among all worldly and world-transcending dharmas, this is the foremost. This demonstrates the four signs encountered by the one who emerged from the womb. At the age of seven, he left the household life;
the Prince possessed great wisdom and, observing the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, grew weary of the five desires of the world."
He cast aside his precious position as a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) like spittle or mucus, and with a mind intent on renunciation, went to inform his father the King.

When the father the King would not permit it, on the seventh day of the second month, he emitted light from his body that universally illuminated the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings and even those of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
When the devas saw this, they came to the Prince’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, and said: "O Bodhisattva..."
The practices cultivated by the Bodhisattva over immeasurable kalpas have now reached full maturity.
Thus, at midnight, he leaped over the city wall to renounce the world and enter the forest of austerities; these are the five signs.

As for what is called "attaining enlightenment after thirty years" and being titled Śākyamuni Buddha, this signifies that the World-Honored One’s meritorious conduct was complete, his Way perfected, and his virtues fully realized.

This demonstrates that the Buddha’s prophecy by the Tathāgata Pradyota was not in vain; it shows him attaining enlightenment upon seeing the morning star and subduing Māra—these are the six characteristics.
Below this, the second part clarifies the two ways of teaching the Dharma in a vertical sequence: first, preaching the Way among the devas;
second, preaching the precepts among humans.
In the place of the tranquil site of enlightenment, sitting upon the Vajra-flower-light-king throne, and extending even to the palace of the heavenly king Maheśvara—
within these successive stages of dwelling places, that which was taught.
Regarding "in the state of quiescence (*śānti*) and so forth": in terms of principle, "quiescence" refers to the principle of pure quiescence;

in terms of phenomena, it refers to the true site of *araṇya* practice. This is because it is said that the Buddha sat at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (*mahābodhimaṇḍa*) and turned the Great Wheel of Dharma within this pure *araṇya*.
Regarding "seated upon the vajra and so forth," this describes the aforementioned [state] of Bodhi...
From emerging from samādhi beneath the *tāla* tree, sitting upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King Throne,
and up to the Hall of Sublime Light and the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara— in the interval between these, there are ten successive teachings given in order.

The *Avataṃsaka* consists of seven locations and nine assemblies, while this sutra consists of ten locations and ten assemblies; the teachings of these two sutras are largely the same with minor differences.
Specifically, that which manifests the attainment of enlightenment and the turning of the Great Dharma Wheel refers to the seven aspects. There are no eight aspects.
This is because they have not yet attained *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the Buddha observed the net-like banners of the Great Brahmā Kings and, for their sake, spoke of the infinite worlds as being like the mesh of a net;
each and every world is distinct from the others, differing in infinite ways. The gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so.
"At that time" refers to the occasion when this Dharma-gate on the essence of the precepts of the Mind-Ground was being taught within this Brahma Heaven.

It is said that the Buddha observed the "net-banner" (*jāla-dhvaja*) as a metaphor to explain the mental activities and the environments and inhabitants of sentient beings throughout immeasurable worlds.
Their distinctions are like the meshes of a net; each and every world is different from the others.
These differences and variations are likewise immeasurable and each is distinct. The teachings and the established gateways of the various Buddhas are also just like this.
I have now come to this world eight thousand times. For the sake of this Sahā world,

from sitting upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King Throne up to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, I have finished briefly opening the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground for all the great assemblies therein.

"Regarding 'I have now [come] likewise': the Buddha said that I have come to this Sahā world and sat upon the Great Jewel Throne to preach this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for the benefit and deliverance of sentient beings; this has already occurred not just once, but as many as eight thousand times.
Regarding 'even unto' and so forth: it means that from preaching the Dharma here until reaching the palace of Śūraprabha, there were ten locations in total."
"Among these" refers to being among the ten realms of sentient beings, devas, humans, worthies, sages, and all living beings.
"Briefly opening [the teaching]" means that the above constitutes a concise exposition of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground; it is not particularly extensive or detailed.
"Concluded" (*jing*) signifies the completion of the preceding text’s meaning. This concludes the discourse on the Path above the first heaven.
[The Buddha] then descended from the palace of the Heavenly King to the Bodhi tree beneath the Jambū tree in Jambudvīpa.

For the sake of all sentient beings upon this earth—ordinary people shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—he spoke of the initial aspiration within the mind-ground of his original self, Vairocana Buddha.
The single precept that is constantly recited within the mind is the Radiant Vajra Jewel Precept.
It is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all Bodhisattvas, and the seed of Buddha-nature. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
all consciousness, form, and mind—whether emotional or mental—all enter into the Buddha-nature precept, for there is always a cause at every moment. At every moment...
It shall abide eternally as the Dharma-body. Thus, these ten *prātimokṣa* emerge in the world;

they are the Dharma-precepts that all sentient beings of the three periods of time should receive and uphold upon their crowns. Now, for the sake of this great assembly, I shall again proclaim the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Precepts, which is the source of the precepts for all sentient beings and is pure by its very nature.

Regarding the phrase "again from the heavens," etc.: previously, it was said that he ascended from the earth to the heavens, where he sequentially expounded ten dharma-gates and the essence of the precepts to benefit the devas.
Now, however, he descends from the heavens; he expounds the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts to benefit human beings.
Having descended from the celestial palace to this foot of the Bodhi tree, for what kind of people does he preach the precepts?
Indeed, this is spoken for the sake of all sentient beings with minds upon this great land of Jambudvīpa.
As for ordinary people who do not know the precepts: "delusion" refers to ignorance obscuring the mind; "darkness" refers to the eye of wisdom being unclear.
When I speak of my own Teacher’s precepts, it is precisely because their mental eyes are thus shrouded that I specifically grant them [these teachings].
It is for the purpose of destroying darkness and eliminating delusion. Furthermore, what dharma is taught for their destruction?
It is taught that when my original teacher, Vairocana Buddha, first gave rise to the mind of enlightenment, there was a single precept he constantly recited within his mind:
the Jewel Precept of Wisdom-Light, Firm and Sharp as a Vajra, which is fully endowed with all virtues. This Jewel Precept is precisely that which destroys darkness.
The bright lamp is the sword of wisdom that eliminates delusion;

it is the fundamental source of all Buddhas, the fundamental source of all Bodhisattvas, and the seed of the Buddha-nature that equally aligns with the Buddhas of the three periods of time above and reaches down to all sentient beings of the three periods of time below. Therefore, it is said to dispel all the darkness of ignorance.
All sentient beings who possess a mind have the Buddha-nature; it is fundamentally not lacking in anyone. Regarding "all mental faculties" (*manas*) and so forth:

that which deliberates is called the "mind," which refers to the seventh *manas*-consciousness; that which discriminates is called "consciousness," which refers to the preceding six evolving consciousnesses.

That which is the object of perception is called "form" (*rūpa*); this refers to the five sense organs and the six sensory objects. That which is the aggregate of arising is called "mind" (*citta*); this refers to the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*.
This consciousness is termed "Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*) among sentient beings, and "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) among non-sentient beings.

It is said that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is inherently complete; it is merely due to the failure of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to comprehend form and mind that such [delusion] occurs.

Now, by the power of our Original Teacher, the Buddha, all these sentient and insentient beings, as well as those with minds, shall all enter into the precious precepts that are the source of Buddha-nature.
Regarding the phrase "constantly, one should constantly," it means that all sentient beings whose faculties are dull must give rise to this correct cause for entering the precepts. All...
Those who possess a mind and have sharp faculties should all give rise to this primary cause for entering the precepts.
Since both these emotions and this mind can enter the precepts, one should naturally always maintain such a primary cause for reciting the precepts.

Since one must naturally possess this primary cause for the practice of reciting the precepts, one will inevitably possess the primary cause for realizing and entering the eternally abiding Dharma-body.
This is the result. The phrase "in this way" connects what precedes with what follows. *Prātimokṣa* is a Sanskrit term;
here it is translated as "preserving liberation. This means that one who upholds these precepts protects the three karmas and the six sense faculties, thereby attaining great liberation.
Regarding these ten precepts of liberation, which emerge from within both the mundane and the supramundane:

they are the true Dharma precepts through which the Buddhas of the three periods of time practiced to achieve Buddhahood; they are the fundamental nature-precepts (prakṛti-śīla) inherent in all sentient beings of the three periods of time.
One should prostrate to them, wear them upon oneself, receive, uphold, and maintain them, recognizing them at every moment and never neglecting them.

It is forgotten. When I say "I shall now equally," it means that I shall now, for the sake of this great assembly of the fourfold congregation and the eight classes of beings present before me, expound and unfold this teaching in successive layers:
from the one precept, I shall open up the ten precepts; from the ten precepts, I shall open up the forty-eight precepts;
and so on, until the infinite and inexhaustible categories of all precepts, numbering thirty thousand and eight hundred thousand, none of which are not subsumed herein.

They all return to the single precept within the ten *pratimokṣa*. Regarding the phrase "all these are equal," it means that by attaining the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*), one must necessarily attain their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Having understood the characteristics of the precepts, one does not forget the essence of the precepts; therefore, it further specifically points out the path:
this is the mind-precept of all sentient beings, the inherently pure essence of the original nature. Fundamentally, it does not arise from...

This is for those who have attained [the path]. Within these two sections on the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) between humans, there are first the fundamental source of ordinary beings and sages, and second, a summary of the characteristics of the precepts.

Regarding the first, the fundamental source of ordinary beings and sages, there are three parts: first, the distinct recitation of the precepts; second, a verse summarizing the preceding and introducing the subsequent;
and third, the formal conclusion of the chapter on the precepts. This is the first: the distinct recitation of the precepts.
I, now as Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal; Surrounding me on a thousand petals, there appear another thousand Śākyamunis.
Upon each petal are ten billion lands, And in each land is a Śākyamuni, Each sitting beneath a Bodhi tree.
One attains the Way of Buddhahood; Thus are there hundreds, thousands, and tens of billions.

The Vairocana himself and the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis, each leading hosts as numerous as motes of dust, have all come together to my abode to hear me recite the Buddha’s precepts; the gate of ambrosia now opens.
At that time, the hundreds of thousands of millions return to their original sites of enlightenment and each sits beneath a Bodhi tree.
I recite the precepts of my original teacher, the ten grave and forty-eight minor ones.
The precepts are like the sun and moon, and also like a string of precious pearls. By means of them, the multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust attain perfect enlightenment.
This is what Vairocana recited; I likewise recite them. You, newly initiated bodhisattvas, [should do the same].
I receive and uphold these precepts; having received and upheld these precepts, I transmit them to all sentient beings.
Listen attentively as I correctly recite the treasury of precepts within the Buddha-dharma, the Prātimokṣa, which the great assembly should believe with a sincere heart.
You are those who shall become Buddhas; I am one who has already become a Buddha.
Always maintaining such faith, one is already fully endowed with the precepts. All who possess a mind should receive the Buddha’s precepts;
when sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Once their rank is equal to that of Great Enlightenment, they are truly the children of the Buddhas, and the great assembly shall all pay them reverence.

"Listen with a sincere mind as I recite what I have now [attained]" is a general verse that explains the Dharma of the Mind-Ground Precepts from beginning to end; it concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one, serving as a broad outline for praising and exhorting others to accept and practice them.
"I am the Buddha" is a self-designation by the Buddha himself; it is not the same as [the claims of] ordinary people or non-Buddhists.
The "self" that is the self of the vehicle, the self of the person, the self of the deity, and the provisional self—this is precisely the self of non-self, the self of the eight masteries.
Now is the time to speak of this. Vairocana is the primary reward-body Buddha (dharmakāya). He sits squarely, meaning he is seated in perfect composure.
The lotus pedestal is the Buddha’s land of dependent retribution; the pedestal is situated therein, surrounding...

"Enveloped all around" means it is surrounded on every side. "Upon the thousand petals" means that outside the perimeter of this great lotus pedestal, there are a thousand petals, and upon each petal there is another lotus flower.
"In each" refers to the center of each of those thousand flowers. "Furthermore, they appear" means that within each of these flowers, a thousand Śākyamunis again appear, seated upon them. One.
Regarding "flowers and so forth": it means that upon each single petal of a flower, there are ten billion lands.
Regarding "one land and so forth": it means that within each single land, a Śākyamuni Buddha descends from heaven;
this is the case for every land, each manifesting sitting beneath a Bodhi tree, all simultaneously manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood and realizing the Unconditioned.

The Supreme Way: seated upon the Vajra-flower throne, he proclaims the Vajra Jewel Precepts. Such statements mean that each manifestation appears according to specific circumstances, yet none is without its fundamental source.

Thus, among these thousands of billions of Śākyamunis, the thousand Śākyamunis take one Śākyamuni as their fundamental body, and those thousand Śākyamunis take Vairocana as their fundamental body. The former represents the arising of function from essence; this, however, [represents...]
This summarizes the function back into the essence. The preceding section provides a general verse for the first nine chapters of the Great Sūtra.

The five lines beginning with "The thousand-billion Śākyamunis" summarize this current volume. From the point where the Buddha Śākyamuni emitted rays of wisdom from his body, illuminating and stirring the humans and devas so that they conceived doubts, the Lord of Mysteries gathered the assembly to inquire about the characteristics of the light. Śākyamuni then led the assembly to his dwelling.
That place: one Śākyamuni thus receives a thousand Śākyamunis, and a hundred billion Śākyamunis likewise receive them;
therefore, it is said that "each receives. "Multitudes as numerous as motes of dust" refers to the multitude who have conceived doubts.

"All come together" means that both the Buddhas who receive [the disciples] and the beings who are received all come to the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*) to hear me, Vairocana, constantly recite [this teaching].
The "One Precept" is the Vajra Jewel Precept, the radiance of all Buddhas. "Amṛta" (Nectar) praises this precept for possessing such virtues;

it means that the feverish afflictions of birth and death experienced by sentient beings who harbor doubts will be instantly extinguished upon hearing this precept, just as with the moisture of amṛta which revives what is parched and withered, restoring the dead to life. "The gate opens immediately" refers to this...
This is the Dharma-gate of the Virtue of the Ambrosia Precepts. Because of this assembly, it was immediately and extensively propagated, being chanted and transmitted from one to another.
At that time, the four lines beginning with "The thousand [Buddhas]" and so forth praise Śākyamuni Buddha;
having led the multitude of thousands of billions of Śākyamuni Buddhas to the abode of Vairocana to receive and hear the precepts, they then each returned to their own original world-systems.
At the Bodhimaṇḍa, having finished preaching the Dharma in ten abodes while ascending to the celestial palaces, he again descended from the celestial palaces to the human realm.
For the people of this land, he preached the precepts that my Original Teacher first constantly recited, up to the passage on "Intrinsic Purity.
At that time, he immediately conferred the Dharma of the Mind-Ground Precepts upon the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis.

"At that time" refers to the occasion when, having already attained the precepts, they return to their own lands within the *bodhimaṇḍa* of quiescence to preach the precepts for the benefit of sentient beings. "Each sat" means that one Śākyamuni sat beneath the Bodhi tree.
He turns the Great Dharma Wheel. The remaining ten billion Śākyamunis each sit beneath a Bodhi tree and likewise each turn the Great Dharma Wheel.
Those who recite the precepts of my Original Teacher represent this dharma of the precepts as having been transmitted from Buddha to Buddha with an original source and a basis for authority;
it is not a false tradition. The preceding verses comment on the previous text, while the following verses comment on the subsequent text. [The Ten Grave Precepts and Four]...
Eighteenth: This reveals the characteristics of the precepts. Regarding the phrase "The precepts are like the sun and the moon," this speaks of the merit of the precepts.
One who attains them is like the sun and moon illuminating the void, moving without obstruction; they are also like a necklace of precious jewels, the most honored and magnificent of ornaments.

Regarding the phrase "as numerous as motes of dust," one should connect each of the preceding items with the expression "as numerous as a multitude of motes of dust," numbering in the hundreds and thousands.

The multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust, who were received by billions of Buddhas, attained the benefit of the precepts and thereby perfected the path of unsurpassed bodhi-awakening;
thus it may be said that their merit was not bestowed in vain. As for the phrase "Rocana and others," this refers back to what was stated above:

it means that this dharma of the precepts was recited by my own Teacher, and I likewise recited it in accordance with him; it does not mean that I did not recite it myself but taught others to recite it.
"Furthermore, you who are newly initiated learners," and so forth—this is an exhortation for those who both bestow and receive the precepts.

It states that since bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust have attained the precepts and thereby achieved Buddhahood, you who are newly initiated bodhisattvas should single-mindedly receive and uphold these precepts, and furthermore, you should in turn transmit them to all sentient beings to extensively benefit all living beings. "Listen attentively," and so forth—this...
This is an exhortation to listen attentively. It means that one should examine it clearly with the ears and comprehend it within the mind.
This recitation of the precepts is not like the heterodox views of external paths, nor the partial and non-universal precepts of the Two Vehicles;

rather, it is the recitation of the Mahāyāna Precepts of True Reality (dharmatā) bestowed by all Buddhas. Regarding "the Buddha-dharma and so forth," this refers to the threefold treasury of the Dharma taught by the Buddha. This...

This is the Basket of Precepts (*Vinaya-piṭaka*) among the Three Baskets. Regarding terms such as *pāramitā* and so forth, it means that this precept for maintaining liberation can, through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, ultimately bring great benefit to the great assembly. One must not merely hear it with the ears;
nor should one hear it without it entering the heart, or fail to examine it with deep faith. To have heard much without practicing is equivalent to not having heard it at all. You—
Regarding the phrase "you who are thus equal": it means that you who are able to uphold [this precept] in this way will certainly attain Buddhahood in the present and the future.
As for me, having practiced this precept with deep faith over kalpas of long duration, I have already attained Buddhahood.

As for those who have already attained Buddhahood: it is because they constantly practiced such thorough, genuine, and profound faith with diligent effort that they were able to perfect and fulfill the category of precepts pertaining to the stage of the mind (*cittabhūmi*).

If even those who have already attained [Buddhahood] must constantly maintain such faith, how much more so for those who have not yet become Buddhas? Regarding the phrase "all beings" and so forth, this is an exhortation to receive [the precepts]; that is to say, all...
Those who possess a mind are not the same as wood or stone. All who have a mind shall become Buddhas;

they are subsumed within the precepts of Buddha-nature—how could this be a minor cause or a minor fruit? Regarding the phrase "sentient beings receive [the precepts] equally," it means that there is no Buddha outside of the mind.

Outside the ground of the mind, there is no ground of the Buddhas. Since sentient beings have already received the dharma of the precepts of the Buddhas' mind-ground, do they not immediately enter the rank of the Buddhas?
Regarding those whose rank is equal [to the Buddhas]: once their rank is equal to that of Great Enlightenment, they are merely able to be true sons of the Buddha family;
they must still pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* until the fruit is fulfilled and the merit of the ten thousand practices is perfected, at which point they can truly succeed [the Buddhas].

The Buddha manifested his birth to realize unsurpassed *bodhi*. As for "the great assembly," this refers to the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings who are present before him to receive the Buddha’s precepts—the pure assembly of both noble and ordinary beings—all of whom give rise to profound reverence.
Exhausting the utmost sincerity of mind and refraining from all verbal debate, everyone shall listen with single-minded devotion as I recite the one precept that I constantly recite:
"The Radiant Vajra-Jewel Self. These two verses precede and conclude [the recitation].
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unexcelled enlightenment, first formulated the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa:
to be filial toward one’s parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem; to be filial toward the Dharma of the Ultimate Path.
Filial piety is called the precepts; it is also called restraint. At that moment, the Buddha emitted immeasurable light from his mouth.

Then, a great assembly of hundreds of millions of bodhisattvas, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire, and the sixteen great kings joined their palms and listened with single-minded devotion as the Buddha recited the Mahayana precepts of all Buddhas.
"At that time" refers to when he descended again from the heavens to the human realm to manifest the attainment of enlightenment and the preaching of the precepts.
Śākyamuni Buddha is the name of the Buddha who is the teacher of this Sahā world. He first sat beneath the Bodhi tree.

At the very place where he first sat at the site of enlightenment and attained unsurpassed awakening—that is, the awakening of the Perfectly All-Knowing One—he transcended all other levels of Equal Awakening and Sublime Awakening, such that none could surpass him.
Regarding the initial formulation of the precepts and so forth, this demonstrates the urgent necessity of turning the wheel of Dharma.
The Buddha’s fundamental intention was originally to uproot the suffering of sentient beings, causing them to leave suffering behind and attain happiness.
Therefore, the World-Honored One reflected: "Ultimately, by what teaching can I cause sentient beings to leave suffering and attain happiness?
For this reason, he first expounded the *Prātimokṣa* at the outset, so as to protect the three karmas and six sense faculties of sentient beings, enabling them to attain great liberation.
When sentient beings are freed from suffering, the Buddha’s vow is fulfilled. Thus, he first established such a Mahāyāna [precept].
The precepts universally deliver sentient beings; they are not like the precepts of the Śrāvaka-vehicle of the Hīnayāna, which benefit only oneself and cannot benefit others.
Regarding "filial piety and obedience" and so forth: filial piety is *kṣānti* (reverence); obedience is *anuvidhāna* (compliance). "Parents" refers to those who gave one physical birth.

"Teacher" refers to the Preceptor (*upādhyāya*) from whom one receives the precepts; they are the parents of one's Dharma-body. "Sangha" refers to fellow students. The Three Jewels are as follows: [the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha].
The Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are the parents of one’s wisdom-life. It is said that they are all like one's own parents;

therefore, one should serve them with filial piety and reverence, never being arrogant, and comply with their will without ever disobeying. For this reason, one must be filial and obedient. This Prātimokṣa is the dharma of the ultimate Way;
filiality is itself what is called the Precepts (*śīla*). Among the three thousand offenses categorized under the five punishments, there is no crime...
This is greater than filial impiety. How could that which is filial impiety be called a precept?

It is also called "restraint" (or "prohibition"), which means that the Buddha, in accordance with the varying capacities of sentient beings—whether great or small—formulated regulations and prohibitions.
How could one who receives the precepts fail to be obedient toward parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem, and yet obtain the precept of restraint? Therefore, it is said: "Also..."
This is called "restraint. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha is equal [to them]," this signifies the auspicious response of the Dharma of the Mind-Ground Precepts.

In this sutra, light is emitted from six locations: first, the body of Śākyamuni emits the light of wisdom; second, the body of the Mysterious Lord (Vairocana) emits light the color of white clouds of vajra;
third, the body of Śākyamuni emits the light of space; and fourth, the body of Śākyamuni emits light when entrusting the teaching.

The five Buddhas emit light, and from each ray of light emanate transformation Buddhas. From their six mouths they emit immeasurable radiance and proclaim the Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Precepts (*cittabhūmi-śīla*).
