This clearly demonstrates that the Buddhas personally proclaimed these teachings with their own mouths;
ultimately, one must rely upon the light of the mind-ground precepts as the supreme cause for practice, and only then attain the supreme fruit of the light of the mind-ground precepts.

Furthermore, the "assembly of one hundred trillion beings" at that time is a general designation for the multitude of humans, devas, ordinary persons, and sages who have a karmic affinity with the light of the precepts.
The "various bodhisattvas" refers to the bodhisattvas of the inner and outer stages of worthiness (*pṛthagjana*) as well as those on the *bhūmi* stages.

The "eighteen Brahma heavens" refers to the heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*): the three heavens of the first dhyāna, the three heavens of the second dhyāna, the three heavens of the third dhyāna, and the [four heavens of the fourth]...

The heavens of the dhyānas are nine; together with these, there are eighteen heavens in total. As for the "Sons of the Six Heavens of Desire," these refer to the six heavens within the realm of desire:
the Four Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*), Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin.

Regarding the "Kings of the Sixteen Great Kingdoms," there were sixteen great kingdoms in the Western Regions in total. Since the rulers of these great kingdoms received and upheld the precepts, as for the others...

O King, it may also be understood that the method for receiving the precepts is as follows. The two phrases "with palms joined" and "with a sincere mind" clarify the reverent intention of the recipient.
Joining the palms signifies the sincerity of the bodily action (*kāyakarman*); having a sincere mind signifies the sincerity of the mental action (*manaskarman*);
and remaining silent without speaking signifies the sincerity of the verbal action (*vākkarman*). Through this sincerity of the three actions, regarding this Great...
Riding upon the light of the Bodhisattva Precepts of the Mind-Ground, he understood immediately upon hearing them once, attaining a sudden and thorough penetration.

○ This is the second section, the formal conclusion of the Chapter on the Precepts. First, the heading and narrative concerning the conferral; second, the characteristics of the precepts. Regarding the first, the heading and narrative concerning the conferral, there are two parts:
first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler; second, the narrative by the Buddha himself. This is the first: the narrative by the sūtra compiler.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "I now recite the Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas every half-month.

You all, bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment], should likewise recite them; even the bodhisattvas of the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the ten bhūmis should recite them.
For this reason, the light of the precepts issues from my mouth. This light exists because there is a condition; it does not arise without a cause."
This light is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black; it is neither form nor mind, neither existent nor non-existent, and not a phenomenon of cause and effect.
It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas, the root of practicing the bodhisattva path, and the foundation for all you sons of the Buddha in this great assembly.
Therefore, sons of the Buddha, you should receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and study it well. Sons of the Buddha!
Listen attentively. Those who receive the Buddha’s precepts— whether they be kings, princes, ministers, high officials,
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire, commoners, eunuchs, lecherous men, lecherous women, slaves,
the eight classes of spirits and deities, vajra-spirits, animals, or even transformed beings— as long as they understand the words of the Dharma Master, all may receive them.
"Precepts: all are called the foremost purity.
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas, and even the bodhisattvas up to the tenth stage recited this single passage; thus he used his own example to exhort others.
He said: "I am already a fully awakened Buddha, yet every half-month I personally recite the precept-dharma of all Buddhas."
How much more so for you, bodhisattvas who have only recently resolved to attain enlightenment!

On the thirtieth day of the dark fortnight and on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, those who recite the precepts before the Triple Gem should examine themselves and discern within these ten grave and forty-eight light precepts whether they are pure or impure.
It is like a person looking into a mirror; they will feel joy at seeing their own beauty.

[The assembly] responded with solemnity. The recitation of the precepts is likewise. This is the Heart-Mind Precept Dharma transmitted by all Buddhas, established by Śākyamuni Tathāgata every half-month.
It is a grand standard for ten thousand ages; who would dare to violate it?
Since even all Buddhas have already recited it, how much more so those of lesser rank? Therefore, you who have first resolved upon the Great Mind and perfected the precepts—
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) all enter into principle and realize the truth;

Bodhisattvas of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), and the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) should likewise recite [this] every half-month, just as the Buddhas do.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "the precepts and so forth," it means that because the Buddhas themselves recited this, and the new and old Bodhisattvas also recite it, [it is thus established].
The light of the precepts of the mind-ground flows forth entirely from the Buddha’s mouth. Since this light issues from his mouth, there is a karmic affinity.
Where there is such an affinity, there must be its cause; it does not arise without a cause. Therefore, he emits this light.
This light does not belong to the categories of sensory objects such as blue, yellow, red, white, or black, nor does it belong to the illusory phenomena of the four great elements.
The Dharma of the form-body does not belong to the mental phenomena that are the causes for the accumulation of the five aggregates;

it does not belong to the dharmas of existence, non-existence, annihilation, or permanence held by external paths; nor does it belong to the dharmas of cause, effect, cultivation, and realization of the two vehicles.
Since it is none of these dharmas, what dharma is this light of precepts? It is precisely the unsurpassed bodhi and nirvana without remainder originally realized by all Buddhas.
The Dharma that is the fundamental source of the *pāṭha* (vows) is the root Dharma for those who practice the bodhisattva path. Moreover, this is not only the case for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
it is also the root Dharma for all the sons of the Buddha in the present assembly who have newly resolved their minds toward enlightenment.
Therefore, when it says "the assembly and so forth," it means that since the light of the precepts (*śīla-prabhā*) is the very foundation, it is thus [great].
"O sons of the Buddha, regarding this ground of the mind and its precepts, you should receive, uphold, and maintain them; you should read and recite them;
and you should study them well. 'Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively' means to encourage them to listen with careful scrutiny and sincerity.
'If one receives the Buddha-precepts,' etc., refers generally to the multitude of people capable of receiving the precepts."
Whether they be kings, princes, high officials, ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, the eighteen Brahmā heavens,
the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire, commoners, eunuchs, male libertines, female libertines, slaves, the eight classes of beings, ghosts and spirits, devas, or nāgas—
Yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, vajrapāṇi spirits, animals,
and even transformed beings— whosoever among these can comprehend the language of the Dharma-preacher.
One must not discriminate. This means that although their forms may differ, their nature is fundamentally no different.
Each and every one of them shall receive the Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Precept Dharma and depart; all are called those of the foremost purity.
It is said that before these people have received the precepts, they are defiled and impure; once they have obtained the precepts, they are purely [so].
It is pure and free from defilement. With a single thought, one turns the light back within; it is as if returning to what was originally attained.
Therefore, it is said that all are called "the foremost purity. These two [statements] are the Buddhas' own narration.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddha, saying: "There are ten grave *prātimokṣa* precepts.
If one has received the Bodhisattva precepts and does not recite these precepts, they are not a Bodhisattva; they are not the seed of a Buddha. I, too, have recited them in this way;

all Bodhisattvas of the past have studied them, all Bodhisattvas of the future shall study them, and all Bodhisattvas of the present are studying them. I have now briefly explained the Bodhisattva [precepts]."
Regarding the characteristics of the *prātimokṣa*, one should train in reverently upholding them.

As for the Buddha’s statement "one should [recite]," this follows from the previous point that having received the Buddha's precepts as the cause for attaining Buddhahood, one must recite those Buddha-precepts.

This is for the sake of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. "Announces" refers to summoning those capable of receiving [the precepts]. "There are ten levels," etc., clarifies the Dharma that is received.
"If one violates two phrases" clarifies the person who violates the Dharma. "Not a Bodhisattva," etc., defines the fault of violating the Dharma;
that is to say, the *Prātimokṣa* is the fundamental practice of a Bodhisattva, and it is the means of accomplishment.
The Buddha’s true dharma is not being recited now; this is to abandon one's fundamental practice and lack the seeds of truth.

If even the original seed cannot be obtained, how can one benefit sentient beings and be called a bodhisattva? Therefore, it is said that such a person is neither a bodhisattva nor a seed of the Buddha.
When I say, "I too am one who recites thus," I cite those who have attained the fruit to encourage those on the causal path to recite. (1)

Regarding the phrase "all bodhisattvas and so forth," this cites those who have attained the fruit as an exhortation to recite. It means: "I am one who has already realized the fruit, yet I still recite in this manner;

how much more so should those who are still on the path of cause? Furthermore, all bodhisattvas of the three periods of time—those who have already studied and recited, those who shall study and recite, and those who are currently studying and reciting—even these bodhisattvas who are already fully matured still train in such recitation; how much more so should you?

"Is it that newly initiated bodhisattvas do not study recitation? Regarding the phrase "I have briefly explained," this means that while the precepts of the śrāvakas have limits, the precepts of the bodhisattvas are limitless.
Now, from within these limitless [precepts], I have merely cited one or two; therefore, it is called a "brief explanation.
As for the term "characteristics" (laksana), it means that the essence of the precepts (śīla-svabhāva) originally has no characteristics, yet this does not preclude their existence.

By upholding the precepts, one attains the characteristics of one who upholds the precepts; by violating the precepts, one attains the characteristics of one who violates them—this refers to those whose minds maintain the seal-mantra and whose gaze is heroic and resolute.
Regarding the phrase "one should train," it means that even the bodhisattvas of the three times who have reached maturity still train;
therefore, you new bodhisattvas should practice with urgency; you ought to train and revere [the teachings].
Engrave this precept upon your heart and do not forget it; receive, uphold, and maintain it without loss.

Regarding these two aspects of the recitation of the precepts: first, the general exposition of the characteristics of the precepts; second, the specific exposition of the characteristics of the precepts. This is the initial general exposition of the characteristics of the precepts.
Below follows the specific exposition of the characteristics of the precepts, which has two parts: first, the exposition of the ten grave precepts; second, the exposition of the light precepts.
The forty-eight precepts.
○ First, the precept against killing.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, if one kills by one's own hand, causes another to kill, employs the means of killing, praises killing, or rejoices upon seeing it being committed."
Even down to incantations for killing—the cause of killing, the conditions for killing, the methods of killing, and the karma of killing—one must not intentionally kill any living being whatsoever.
This Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of constant compassion, a mind of filial obedience, and employ skillful means to rescue and protect all sentient beings;
yet, if they instead indulge their own desires and take pleasure in killing, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva.

When the Buddha says "Son of the Buddha," he addresses that person directly. He tells them that as a son of the Buddha who has received and upholds the Buddha's precepts, they must practice in accordance with those precepts;
for one must not lightly violate the regulations established by the Buddha. The following passages are to be understood in this same manner.
If one kills this body oneself, it is killing by the body (*kāya-vadha*). To instruct others through skillful means or to praise such acts is killing by speech (*vāk-vadha*).

To rejoice upon seeing [the act] being committed, or even to kill through incantations, is killing by mind (*manas-vadha*). The cause of killing consists of the accumulated karma from beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that have not been forgotten;
even if one were to undergo hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the karma one has created would not be forgotten. The conditions (*pratyaya*) for killing are those of the present.
The gathering of enemies serves as the condition; "when causes and conditions meet" refers to this.
The method of killing is likewise the present act of taking another's life by means of weapons, nets, or snares; "the retribution is received by oneself" refers to this.
The karmic action of killing is accomplished through the conjunction of these three factors, thereby producing the fruit of future killing. As for the phrase "and so forth," it means:

Whether sentient or insentient—beings that wriggle, fly, or crawl, insects, plants, trees, and all things possessing life—one must not inflict injury or harm upon them without cause, much less upon those with great life.

Just as kings and high officials may kill one to save many, promoting good and eliminating evil, this is great compassion; thus there are permissions and prohibitions. However, one must never act intentionally [to harm].
A selfish mind constitutes killing. Only when one can practice and maintain [the precepts] in this manner may one be called one who upholds the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint).
Regarding the phrase "there is no evil that does not cease" for those who are equal to Bodhisattvas:

this refers to a Bodhisattva who has received the precepts, who should give rise to a mind of constant abiding and non-forgetfulness, constantly dwelling in loving-kindness and compassion as if protecting an infant.
The mind of the child constantly dwells in a state of filial piety and obedience, ever following the heart that regards others as one's father and mother.
By such skillful means and by thus protecting all sentient beings, it is only then called the "precept of gathering virtuous dharmas" (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

There is no virtue that is not cultivated; by thus uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness, it is only then called "benefiting sentient beings" (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). [There is] no non-arising.

Regarding "those who do not deliver [others]" and "instead indulge their minds," this means that if one sees sentient beings suffering yet fails to provide rescue or extraction, instead indulging and giving free rein to one's mind to willfully satisfy one's own desires by killing and harming sentient beings—how could such a person be considered a Bodhisattva who upholds the precepts?
This is one who does not maintain [the precepts] but is rather a violator of them. As for "this Bodhisattva," it refers to...
To commit the offense of killing a Bodhisattva is to incur one’s own guilt; one shall receive the *pārājika* offense.
In the Sanskrit language, *pārājika* means "extreme evil" and is also called "the abandoned offense," because one will fall into the three evil realms.
For anyone who upholds this precept, this is the first thing they must be cautious of.
○ Second, the Precept Against Stealing:
If a Buddha’s disciple steals themselves, teaches others to steal, employs expedient means to steal, or steals by incantation;

whether through the causes of stealing, the conditions of stealing, the methods of stealing, or the karmic acts of stealing—even down to the property of ghosts and spirits that has an owner, or the goods of bandits, or any material wealth, even a single needle or a single blade of grass—one must not...
If a bodhisattva, having obtained [the means], steals, yet should fail to give rise to a mind of filial obedience toward the Buddha-nature and a mind of compassion,

and instead constantly fails to assist all beings in generating merit and happiness, but rather goes on to steal another's wealth and property— this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that bodhisattva.
If a disciple of the Buddha intends as previously described, they may personally commit theft, instruct others through speech using expedient means,
or employ incantations with the mind. Whether regarding past causes, present conditions and methods, or future karmic fruits—

whether it be various stolen goods, even the ritual vessels within temple halls, the property of spirits and deities, or all items that were once offerings given by owners or obtained by bandits— they shall not take them.
Regarding all manner of wealth and property, one must never take what is not given.

Regardless of whether it is noble or base, large or small—not even a single needle or a blade of grass—one must not take it under any pretext if it has not been given, for there is no theft that remains unbroken.
Regarding the phrase "and the bodhisattvas, etc.": it means that these bodhisattvas should give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience, viewing all sentient beings as their fathers and mothers;
they should give rise to a mind of compassion, viewing all sentient beings as their sons and daughters;
and they should constantly assist and support all sentient beings, so that they may cultivate the field of merit, receive its blessings in this body, and develop the requisites for happiness.

The mind attains peace and happiness because there is no virtue that is not cultivated. Thus, by assisting in merit and assisting in happiness, one causes all people to leave suffering and attain joy;
only then can one be called "one who does not fail to deliver those who have not yet attained birthlessness. As for the Bodhisattvas and others:
If one sees those in dire distress yet fails to provide relief, and instead steals their wealth and property, how can such a person be considered a Bodhisattva who upholds the precepts?
Therefore, the determination of the offense is the same as before, and the resulting downfall is likewise the same. Should one not be cautious?
○ Third Precept on Sexual Misconduct:

O Disciples of the Buddha, one must not engage in sexual misconduct oneself, nor teach others to engage in sexual misconduct, even with any woman whatsoever. One must not intentionally commit sexual acts, which are the cause of such transgression.

Regarding the conditions for sexual misconduct, the nature of sexual misconduct, and the karma of sexual misconduct— even engaging in it with female animals, female devas, or female spirits, or practicing it through improper orifices—
a bodhisattva ought to give rise to a heart of filial obedience and rescue all sentient beings by bestowing the pure Dharma upon them.
Yet, instead, they further incite sexual desire in others, making no distinction between animals or even their own mothers, daughters, sisters, or other members of the six degrees of kinship.
Sexual misconduct. One who lacks a heart of compassion commits a *pārājika* offense against the Bodhisattva precepts.

If a disciple of the Buddha personally engages in sexual conduct, speaks with the mouth to instruct others in sexual matters, or even harbors a single thought of lust toward any woman—whether regarding past causes of lust or present conditions of lust—he commits an offense.
This is the accumulation of dharmas: the future fruit of sexual karma that creates all manner of fetters, from which there is no time of liberation.
This includes engaging in sexual intercourse with female animals, making no distinction between birds and beasts; with the females of devas and ghosts, being ignorant of what is right or wrong;
engaging in unwholesome ways; regardless of day or night, season, the two sexual organs of male and female, or whether they are large or small, old or young—all such acts are termed "unrighteous."
The Way: one must not commit even a single transgression, for it is because of the failure to sever lust that [suffering arises].
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva should give rise to filial piety and obedience, cultivating the mind that regards all men as his fathers and all women as his mothers.
In this way, he protects and delivers all sentient beings, teaching them to sever the root of craving and desire, so that they may become pure and undefiled.
To bestow upon others the dharma of liberation from defilement is the fundamental practice of a bodhisattva, for there is no goodness they do not cultivate.
Only by thus uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness can one be called a bodhisattva who does not fail to deliver beings from the state of non-arising.

If a bodhisattva does not provide such instruction and benefit, they instead cause all sentient beings to arise [in further suffering], making no distinction between species, noble or lowly, mother or daughter.

To engage in sexual misconduct with sisters, close relatives, or those who are not one's proper path, and to lack even a single point of compassionate and pure mind—how could such a person be a Bodhisattva who upholds the precepts?
Therefore, the penalty for this offense is the same as before, and the resulting downfall is likewise the same.
Should one not be cautious?
The fourth precept against false speech:
O disciples of the Buddha, [if one] speaks falsely oneself, teaches others to speak falsely, employs skillful means to speak falsely, or provides the causes and conditions for speaking falsely.

Regarding the dharma of false speech and the karma of false speech: from claiming to have seen what one has not seen, to claiming not to have seen what one has seen—this is physical and mental false speech.

If a Bodhisattva, while constantly producing right speech and also producing right speech and right view for all sentient beings, instead gives rise to wrong speech, wrong view, and wrong karma for all sentient beings, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva.
If a Buddha’s disciple speaks untruthful words themselves, or teaches others through skillful means, causal conditions, or karmic actions;

or if, being anything but a sage, they claim to be a sage; or if, not having truly attained the dharmas of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), they claim to have attained them—thus deceiving simpletons and seeking fame, reputation, profit, and offerings—such is physical falsehood.

To act with mental delusion and speak with verbal delusion—when the three karmas are not grounded in reality and all speech is false, whether light or grave—all such things must be severed by a Bodhisattva who upholds the precepts, for there is nothing false that they do not sever.
As for the "Bodhisattvas and others," this means they should constantly give rise to the five utterances of the Tathāgata; through such correct speech, they also cause all [beings] to...
Sentient beings should constantly give rise to right speech, so as not to be seduced by the false speech of ordinary or inferior people;
they should constantly give rise to right view, so as not to be deluded by the false views of non-Buddhists. Only when one is thus authentic oneself can one inspire confidence in others.
Only when one makes others truly authentic can one be called "one who does not fail to cultivate any virtue.
Likewise, only when one is oneself authentic and makes others authentic can one be called "one who does not fail to deliver any being from birth. As for the opposite case:
if a bodhisattva is themselves not upright in speech or view, yet instead gives rise to all manner of improper words and biased, deviant views among all sentient beings.

Such views lead one to create various kinds of deluded karma, deceiving both oneself and others; the transgression is no small matter. Therefore, the determination of the offense is the same as before, and the resulting retribution for falling into [an evil state] is likewise the same.
Exceptions apply in cases of urgent distress where one unties a net or employs skillful means to release someone from suffering; in such instances, there is no offense.
In other matters, one should be cautious.
○ Fifth, the precept against selling alcohol:

If a Buddha’s disciple sells alcohol themselves, teaches others to sell alcohol, or provides the causes for selling alcohol, the conditions for selling alcohol, the methods for selling alcohol, or the [means] for selling alcohol...
Regarding the liquor trade: one must not sell any kind of intoxicant. Such liquor is a causal condition for the arising of transgressions;
yet, a bodhisattva should give rise to the wisdom of clarity and penetration in all sentient beings, rather than instead giving rise to the minds of delusion and inversion in them.
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
If a disciple of the Buddha sells liquor and the like, "selling" refers to brewing and selling alcohol.
To sell it oneself, or to instruct others to sell it, arises from a past motivation of greed for profit; by means of this cause, one obtains rice and wheat [to brew].

Regarding the conditions for brewing: by obtaining grain and yeast and fermenting them, one establishes the method of brewing; through the conjunction of these three factors, the business of brewing is established.
This is the evil fruit of intoxicating others. As for "all kinds of liquor" and so forth, this means that not only the aforementioned types are forbidden to be produced.
This extends even to sugarcane, grapes, waxplums, jujubes, and the like; none of these may be used to produce [alcohol]. Indeed, the harm caused by alcohol is no small matter.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that there are thirty-six faults associated with alcohol, including being unfilial toward one's parents.

Those who do not revere the Triple Gem will fall from chariots or horses, throw themselves into rivers or leap into fires, and bring ruin to their nations and families; there is no calamity they will not encounter.
The Confucians say that wine possesses three virtues and seven evils. Yu detested fine wine, yet he acknowledged that "wine has no limit, provided it does not lead to disorder.
Thus it is said that wine gives rise to the causes and conditions for transgression, for there is no evil that cannot be severed by abstaining from it. And so one maintains [the precept].

A person who observes the Bodhisattva precepts should give rise to the mind that teaches and transforms sentient beings, developing the inherently existing wisdom within each individual so that they may thoroughly understand the roots of all ignorance. One must not allow them to drink this poisonous medicine of madness;
rather, one should enable them to attain wisdom and ensure there is no virtue left unpracticed. Is it not thus that, by eliminating ignorance and establishing wisdom, [one fulfills the purpose]?
Is there any sentient being to be benefited who would not be delivered? Yet, as for those who act contrary [to this], it means they are unable to practice these skillful means;

instead, they further give rise to the deluded and inverted minds of all sentient beings, causing them to sell and drink [alcohol], thereby plunging people into a state of extreme suffering. How could this be the concern of a Bodhisattva who upholds the precepts? Therefore—
The offense is established and one shall fall [into hell]; this is identical to what was stated previously.
○ Sixth, the precept against speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly:
If a son of the Buddha, with his own mouth, speaks of the faults of lay or ordained Bodhisattvas, Bhikṣus, or Bhikṣuṇīs, or teaches [others to do so]...

When people speak of transgressions—the causes of transgression, the conditions for transgression, the phenomena of transgression, and the karma of transgression—and when Bodhisattvas hear heterodox practitioners or those of the two vehicles speaking what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya within the Buddha-dharma, they always give rise to a heart of compassion.
They teach and transform these wicked people, causing them to develop wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna; yet the Bodhisattvas, conversely, further speak for themselves...
In the Buddha-dharma, that which constitutes a transgression is a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
If a disciple of the Buddha speaks of it himself, it means he slanders it with his own mouth. "Those who have left the home life" refers to the two communities of the ordained;
"those who remain at home" refers to the two communities of the laity. All of them have given rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna and have received the Mahāyāna precepts.
Therefore, they are called Bodhisattvas. As for the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, these are specifically distinguished as the two assemblies of those who have left the household life;
they are those who gradually enter the Mahāyāna from among the śrāvaka’s ten precepts and two hundred and fifty precepts, rather than those who receive them all at once.
For this reason, they are separately distinguished. These four assemblies together sustain and maintain the Triple Gem and propagate the Dharma.
Being fellow sons of the Buddha, one must not air one's own family’s disgrace by speaking of another's transgressions.

Nor should one teach others to speak of another's transgressions, including their past causes for transgression, their present conditions and dharmas, and the future results of the karma of speaking of transgressions formed through the conjunction of these three. One must not commit any of the above offenses. There is no [exception].
This is because evil has not been severed. As for the phrase "Bodhisattvas and others," it refers to Bodhisattvas who maintain the precepts;

that is, when they hear of those among the outsiders who are evil people with inverted and false views, as well as those among the followers of the Two Vehicles who are evil people with the narrow-minded view of seeking only their own benefit.
If one who has not attained the Mahāyāna境界 (state) of the direct and inverse [realms] speaks of what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya within the Mahāyāna teachings of the Buddhas,
a Bodhisattva who hears this should always give rise to a heart of compassion and pity, and should teach and transform such non-Buddhists, followers of the Two Vehicles, and evil persons,

causing them to turn from the heterodox toward the orthodox, abandon the Small Vehicle for the Great, and give birth to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna. If they lack such wholesome [faith], [the Bodhisattva should continue to guide them].

It may be that they do not practice; such teaching is indeed beneficial. Is this not precisely the way to benefit sentient beings who have not yet attained non-arising and have not yet been delivered?
If one is unable to do so, one already lacks compassion; how could one go so far as to speak of the faults within the Buddha-dharma oneself?
Whether speaking of them oneself or causing others to speak of them, the offense incurred is the same as before, and the downfall is likewise the same.
...Furthermore,
the seventh [precept] regarding praising oneself and disparaging others:

If a Buddha’s disciple praises themselves and disparages others with their own mouth, or teaches others to praise themselves and disparage others— this is the cause for disparaging others, namely, disparaging others.
Regarding these conditions: if others disparage the Dharma or disparage their own karma, a bodhisattva should instead undergo all such abuse and humiliation on behalf of all sentient beings.
They should direct evil toward themselves and give good to others; if they were to praise their own virtues or conceal the good deeds of others, [they would fail in this].
To cause another to suffer defamation is a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
"If a son of the Buddha, by means of speech and so forth," refers to a bodhisattva who praises his own virtues while disparaging the faults of others,
or who instructs others to praise him as virtuous while disparaging others as lacking virtue, as well as in the past...
If habitual tendencies from beginningless time are not eliminated, mutual disparagement acts as the cause; the manifestation of envy and jealousy leading to disparagement acts as the condition;
and skillfully disparaging others while gaining their trust acts as the method. Through the convergence of these three factors, the karma of slandering others is formed.

As stated above, each of these must not be transgressed, for there is no evil that would not be severed thereby. Regarding the phrase "Bodhisattvas and so forth," this refers to those who uphold the precepts.
Sā. If you see others at fault, you should take upon yourself all the abuse and humiliation they receive for the sake of all sentient beings.
You should direct evil matters toward yourself and give good matters to others; there is no virtue that you should not cultivate.
To say that one directs evil matters toward oneself means that one should not praise oneself; to say that one gives good matters to others means that one should not disparage others.
One who acts with such a mind to benefit others is truly called one who is unborn and does not cross over [the world].
If, however, one exalts one's own virtues while concealing the good deeds of others, thereby causing others instead to suffer humiliation, [one is not so].
How could this be the way a Bodhisattva applies the mind? Therefore, the offense is concluded as before; the falling [into hell] is likewise as before. ○ Eighth:
The Precept Against Stinginess and Malicious Slander.
"Stingy" (*mātsarya*) means being parsimonious; "cherishing" (*rakta*) means being attached. "Malicious slander" refers to unjustly attributing offenses to others and thereby harming them.
This brings affliction to sentient beings.

If a disciple of the Buddha is himself stingy, teaches others to be stingy, or possesses the causes of stinginess, the conditions for stinginess, the methods of stinginess, or the karma of stinginess, then when that Bodhisattva sees any poor person coming to beg, he should give them everything according to what that person requires. And yet, the Bodhisattva...
If, with an evil mind and a mind of hatred, one does not give even a single coin, a single needle, or a single blade of grass; and if, when there is a seeker of the Dharma,

one does not explain even a single word, a single verse, or a portion of the Dharma as small as a mote of dust, but instead reviles and insults them— this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
"Regarding 'if a Buddha’s disciple is personally stingy,' etc.: this means being personally stingy and personally parsimonious, not bestowing gifts or providing relief to others;
teaching others to be stingy, causing them to be miserly so as to shield oneself. The cause of stinginess (*mātsarya*) is the habitual harboring of a stingy mind from time immemorial;

the condition (*pratyaya*) for stinginess is the shielding and guarding of the wealth of the Dharma. Regarding stinginess regarding the Dharma, it consists in skillfully devising pretexts for not relinquishing it."

Regarding the dharma: through the combination of three factors—the act of stinginess, the volition, and the formation [of the karma]—one brings about the fruit of karmic retribution as a hungry ghost in the future.
Not a single one of these may be transgressed, for there is no evil that is not severed thereby. As for "bodhisattvas and others," this refers to bodhisattvas who uphold the precepts;
when they see any person in poverty, regardless of whether they are kin or strangers, noble or lowly, coming to beg.

One should provide whatever clothing, food, and other necessities are required according to the wishes of others, giving them all without stinginess, for there is no virtue that one should not cultivate.
It is by thus abandoning evil and cultivating good that one is called a "benefactor of sentient beings" who leaves no one unredeemed.
As for the phrase "Bodhisattvas and so forth," it means that if a Bodhisattva, by means of their own...

Because of the evil mind that seeks private profit; because of the hateful mind that loathes the trivial begging of others—not only failing to give much, but not giving even a single coin, a single needle, or a single blade of grass, withholding even a hair’s breadth.
Furthermore, there may be those who seek the Dharma, yet out of stinginess regarding the Dharma, one does not grant them even a single word, a single verse, or so much as a speck of dust.
Dharma. Such a mind has already lost the path of a bodhisattva’s compassion and has already fallen into the fault of stinginess;

how much more so when one further adds insults and humiliation toward others? Therefore, the determination of the offense is the same as before, and the falling away [from the precepts] is likewise the same as before.
○ Ninth: The Precept Against Anger and Refusing Apologies.

If a Buddha’s disciple becomes angry themselves, teaches others to be angry, or engages in the causes of anger, the conditions for anger, the methods of anger, or the karmic actions of anger, that Bodhisattva should instead cultivate roots of goodness and non-contentiousness among all sentient beings, constantly giving rise to a mind of compassion and a mind of filial obedience.
If, on the contrary, one reviles and insults all sentient beings— and even non-sentient things— with harsh speech, further assaulting them with the hands,
knives, or staves, and still does not cease; and if, when the other person seeks reconciliation and offers an apology with kind words,
one’s anger remains unresolved— this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
"If a Buddha's disciple becomes angry himself," and so forth: "becoming angry oneself" means harboring resentment toward others personally.

"Teaching others to be angry" means instructing another person to be angry with someone else in order to avenge one's own resentment. The cause of anger is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of harboring resentment from the past;
the condition (*pratyaya*) for anger is the person currently being the object of one's resentment; and the phenomenon of anger is the arising of the mind.

To calculate and cause another to suffer humiliation for the sake of the Dharma—this karmic action of hatred, formed by the conjunction of these three factors, constitutes the bitter fruit of retribution in the three miserable realms in the future. None of the above may be transgressed, for there is no evil that is not severed.
As for "the Bodhisattvas and so forth," it means that Bodhisattvas should give rise to equanimity within the minds of all sentient beings.
...these roots of goodness. For those of dull faculties, it shall cause them to be free from contention; for those of sharp faculties, it shall cause them to attain the Samādhi of Non-contention.
Furthermore, such matters shall always cause them to give rise to a mind of compassion, regarding all sentient beings as equal to an only child;
and they shall always cause them to give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience, regarding men and women as equal to one's own parents. Without...
This is because one has failed to cultivate virtue. Thus, only by severing evil and cultivating goodness can one be said to benefit sentient beings;

there are none who do not cross over [to liberation]. If one is unable to do so, yet instead reviles and insults all sentient beings as well as non-sentient things with harsh speech, one’s verbal karma becomes unwholesome, and furthermore—
Whether by striking with the hand, or with sword and staff, one commits unwholesome physical karma; if the mind still does not cease, one commits unwholesome mental karma.
Because these three types of karma are equally transgressions, there is no way to escape them.

Even if the person toward whom one was angry comes to seek repentance, one should use kind words to apologize, humble oneself, and resolve the anger. If, however, one raises one's eyebrows or glares with an angry look...
One who harbors anger and does not resolve it—how could such a person be one who practices and maintains the Bodhisattva precepts? Therefore, the determination of the offense is the same as before;
the falling away [from the precepts] is likewise the same as before.
○ The Tenth Precept: Slandering the Triple Gem.

If a disciple of the Buddha slanders the Triple Gem themselves, or teaches others to slander the Triple Gem— whether through the causes of slander, the conditions of slander, the methods of slander, or the karma of slander— and if that Bodhisattva,

upon seeing a non-Buddhist or an evil person utter even a single word of slander against the Buddha, feels as though three hundred spears are piercing their heart, how much more so when they themselves slander with their own mouths?
Yet they fail to give rise to a mind of faith or a mind of filial obedience, and instead further assist such evil people and heterodox views.
To see someone slandering [the Triple Gem] and to slander them oneself is a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
"If a disciple of the Buddha, himself," etc., means to slander the Triple Gem oneself; this is because one's own views and understanding are not upright.

To see someone slandering and then to follow suit by slandering and engaging in false criticism and defamation is to join in the slander. "To teach others to slander" means to cause others to engage in malicious slandering.
The desire for a faction is the cause. Slander has past habitual tendencies harboring malice as its cause;
it has the convergence of improper speech as its condition; and it has skillful words used for false slander to delude the ignorant as its method.
Slanderous karma is the fruit of suffering in the three evil realms, produced by the conjunction of these three factors. None of the above [conditions] may be obtained individually.
This constitutes an offense, for there is no evil that is not severed [by such a mind].

As for the phrase "Bodhisattvas and others," it means that if a Bodhisattva sees a heretic with false views, or a person who slanders the Triple Gem, and hears even a single word or half-verse of blasphemy against the Buddha enter their ears, it is as if three hundred spears and lances were piercing the very center of their heart. Its...

There are sufferings more difficult to endure than these. To hear slander is a heart-piercing pain; yet one should cultivate every virtue, teach others to give rise to faith, and surely vow to deliver all beings from the state of non-arising.
How much more so when the slanderous words issue from one’s own mouth? The Buddha is the Teacher of Gods and Humans; he has opened the clouds of my delusion.
One ought to give rise to a mind of faith and reverence, yet instead one fails to do so. The Buddha is the Great Compassionate Father.
"You should have developed a heart of filial piety toward me, who have pulled you from suffering; yet you did not develop such a heart.
Thus, you are no longer a child of the Buddha, for you instead assist evil people and those with false views to slander the Triple Gem and to spread malicious talk.
You are like a rebel, or like a worm within a lion's body that devours the lion's own flesh."
As for meat-eating, how could one who is a bodhisattva upholding the *prātimokṣa* do so?
Such a bodhisattva commits a *pārājika* offense and shall fall into the three evil realms. Should one not be cautious?
○ Summary of the Tenfold Text:
O virtuous practitioners who study well, these ten *pātimokkha* precepts of a bodhisattva should be studied.

Within them, one must not commit even a single transgression so slight as a mote of dust, much less commit all ten precepts in their entirety. If there is one who commits [a transgression], they shall not...
Though they have manifested the bodhicitta in this present body, they shall lose their status as a king, as well as their status as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).

They shall also lose their status as a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, and lose the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the Buddha-nature—the eternally abiding, wondrous fruit.
Having lost all these, they will fall into the three evil realms, where for two or three kalpas they shall not hear the names of their parents.
Regarding the names of the Three Jewels, for this reason one must not transgress each and every one of them.

You, all you bodhisattvas—those who are currently training, those who will train, and those who have already trained—should thus train in these ten precepts and reverently uphold them. The eighty thousand categories of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) shall be explained in detail.
O virtuous learners, this Buddha praises those bodhisattvas who well maintain the precepts as being benevolent ones who love all sentient beings.

Regarding these bodhisattvas, it is said that they should diligently study, practice, and uphold the *prātimokṣa*, the code of individual liberation, consisting of the ten categories of pure precepts. Within that—
In the interim, one must not commit even a single transgression so minute as a speck of dust.
Since even a speck of dust is not permitted to be transgressed, how much less so the full commission of the ten precepts? This is a definitive statement that they must not be transgressed.
As for the phrase "if there should be those who transgress," it means that if there were such transgressors, they would be unable to give rise to [the aspiration] in this present life.
One who has set their great aspiration upon seeking the path to unsurpassed bodhi not only fails to give rise to that great mind, but if a king commits such an offense, he loses his royal throne;
if a wheel-turning monarch commits it, he loses his status as a wheel-turning monarch.
If a bhikṣu commits an offense, he loses his status as a bhikṣu; if a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense, she loses her status as a bhikṣuṇī.

Having already lost their positions regarding merit and wisdom in both the mundane and supramundane realms, they likewise lose the stages of the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*), the ten adamantine stages (*daśa-vajra-bhūmi*), and the ten noble stages (*daśārya-bhūmi*).
Since all causal stages have been lost, [they remain only with] the Buddha-nature, which is eternally abiding and the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.
"How could the state of the ocean be attained? Everything is lost as well. Regarding "falling into the three [lower] realms":

this means that since the states of all causes and effects have been lost, where will one fall? It refers to falling into the places of extreme suffering within the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"Two kalpas or three kalpas" indicates the vast duration of time spent in those places of extreme suffering.
Furthermore, those who have not heard the names of their parents or the Three Jewels are shown to be in a state of extreme suffering, where their obstacles are heavy and their karma is deep.

Since such is the distance of their time of suffering and such is the gravity of their retribution for suffering, you should know by this that you must not violate even a single one of these precepts, not even as much as a speck of dust. "All of you" refers to you all.
All bodhisattvas— whether they have not yet studied, are now beginning to study, are currently practicing and training this very day,
or have already practiced for a long time— should, regarding these ten precepts, train as they were received, uphold them with a reverent mind,
and never forget them until the end of their lives. The phrase "eighty thousand," etc., refers to what is summarized here.
It is said: Within the eighty thousand chapters on dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) in the Great Collection Sūtra, this meaning has already been explained in detail.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "The ten *prātimokṣa* have now been fully expounded; the forty-eight minor precepts shall now be explained."
"The Buddha addressed the various bodhisattvas" refers to our Buddha, the World-Honored One, calling out to the bodhisattvas present in the assembly—
those who have received the precepts, including the three grades of worthies, the ten stages of sages, and the fourfold assembly and eight classes of beings.
Having already explained the forty phrases that conclude the preceding ten grave prohibitions, the forty phrases that initiate the subsequent forty-eight minor precepts shall now be set forth.
It is said: First is the precept against disrespecting one's teachers and friends.
Teachers possess the grace of guidance; friends possess the virtue of mutual refinement. These are those whom one ought to revere and honor. Should one dwell in arrogance...
Pride prevents the seeds of merit and the sprouts of wisdom from flourishing throughout one's life; therefore, it must be restrained.
O disciples of the Buddha, when you are about to receive the position of a king, the position of a universal monarch (cakravartin), or when the various officials receive their positions—
One should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts. Then all ghosts and spirits will protect the person of the king and the persons of his officials;
all Buddhas will rejoice. Having received the precepts, one should give rise to a mind of filial obedience and a mind of reverence.

Upon seeing elders, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), those of great virtue, fellow students, those of the same view, or those of the same practice, one should rise to welcome them, prostrate, and inquire after their well-being. And as for the Bodhisattva...
He instead gave rise to a mind of arrogance, conceit, delusion, and anger; he did not rise to welcome him or pay him homage, nor did he provide each with offerings according to the Dharma.
Rather than doing so, he offered his own body, his kingdom, cities, sons, daughters, the seven treasures, and hundreds of other things as provisions for him.
If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the phrase "if a disciple of the Buddha wishes to receive [the precepts]," etc.: kings are the benevolent rulers of their respective realms.
There are four types of wheel-turning kings (cakravartin): the gold, silver, copper, and iron wheel-turning kings; they respectively govern over the four, three, two, or one continent of the world.
The sovereign is the ruler, and the various officials, both civil and military, are the great ministers.
When such a sagely sovereign and virtuous minister wish to receive the rank of king or the position of official, they should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

By harboring compassion and altruism, and cherishing filial piety and obedience, when the sovereign is sagely and the ministers are virtuous, they will naturally invoke the protection of all spirits and deities for the person of the king and the persons of the officials.

Thereby the national destiny will be sustained and noble rank and glory made eternal. Not only will spirits and deities respond in this way, but one will also move the Buddhas of the ten directions to rejoice, protect, and keep one in mind, so that the realm shall be peaceful and the people happy.
Having received the precepts through the guidance and exhortation of teachers and friends, you should recognize their kindness and repay it, honoring your precept master as you would your own father.
Toward one's mother, one should give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience, not daring to disobey;

toward virtuous friends, one should regard them as elder brothers, giving rise to a mind of reverence and not daring to be arrogant. Upon seeing elders and the like, one should immediately manifest the intent of filial piety and respect.
"Upādhyāya" (上座) is an honorific title for a senior elder who possesses the Way and virtue; it is a Chinese rendering of the Sanskrit term "Upādhyāya," which means "one who gives birth by power.
Because one's Dharma-body and wisdom-life are born through the power of the teacher, he is the Preceptor of Precepts (*śīlācārya*). "Ācārya" is a Sanskrit term.

This refers to the "preceptors" (*ācārya*), namely the three officiating masters (*karmācārya*) and the seven witnessing masters (*śraddhācārya*). The term "Virtuous One" (*bhadanta*) refers to the aforementioned masters.
A person devoid of virtue can certainly not serve as such; they must all be fully endowed with both merit and wisdom.
Those who possess such great virtue are such that upon seeing them, everyone should give rise to a heart of filial obedience, as toward one's own parents. They are fellow students of the same...
Regarding "teachers and students": those who have attained the principles of the precepts through the same vision and the same instructions of a teacher;
those who practice together in the same pure and white *brahmacarya*. This refers to the aforementioned friends, all of whom are vessels for the Three Jewels;
upon seeing them, one should always give rise to a mind of reverence, as toward an elder brother. Toward such teachers and friends, regardless of whether they come from afar or nearby, one should...
One must rise to welcome them, pay homage with a sincere heart, prostrate and inquire after their well-being, and make offerings according to the Dharma;
only then can one be called a person who recollects and upholds the precepts.

As for those such as bodhisattvas, it means that if such a bodhisattva encounters a teacher or a friend, they not only fail to show respect, but instead give rise to a haughty mind of self-importance and arrogance, treating them with contempt.
One gives rise to a mind of arrogance toward one’s predecessors; a mind of folly that fails to personally attend upon the worthy and the noble;

and a mind of aversion and anger toward the strict instructions of teachers and friends. Having given rise to such states of mind, one fails to rise to greet them, pay homage, or inquire after their well-being.
Thus, the three karmas of body, speech, and mind become unwholesome, extending even to matters such as food, drink, clothing, bedding, and bathing water.
[They] offered medicine, yet none of these were provided in the proper sequence or according to the Dharma.

Now, the method for serving one's teachers and friends is that one should offer internal wealth—such as one's own body—and external wealth—such as kingdoms, cities, men, women, the seven treasures, and all manner of goods—to prepare whatever is required for their support.
How could one fail to provide such offerings, only to instead give rise to arrogance?

Is it not that one should maintain an impartial mind? If a Bodhisattva does not act in this way by rising to welcome and making offerings, that Bodhisattva will certainly commit a minor defilement offense (*laghu-pāpa*).
This offense is one grade less than the ten preceding grave offenses; it is not to be called a trivial or insignificant matter.
The second precept against drinking alcohol states:
"A person who drinks alcohol shall fall into the Hell of Burning and Boiling for five periods of five hundred years. For the first five hundred years, they shall be in the Hell of Saline Dregs;
for the second five hundred years, in the Hell of Boiling Excrement; for the third five hundred years, in the Hell of Crookedness..."
They become maggots; for four or five hundred lifetimes they dwell among flies and gnats, and for another four or five hundred lifetimes they remain in the hell of delusional fever and ignorance.
Such is the retribution of their karma; therefore, one must exercise restraint.
If a Buddha’s disciple intentionally drinks alcohol, the transgressions arising from such drinking are immeasurable.

If one passes a vessel of alcohol with their own hand to another person so that they may drink it, they shall be without hands for five hundred lifetimes; how much more so if they drink it themselves?
Furthermore, one must not instruct any person or any sentient being to drink alcohol, let alone drink it oneself. One must not drink any kind of alcohol whatsoever. If...
Therefore, to drink [alcohol] oneself or to teach others to drink it constitutes an offense of light impurity.

If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally drinks alcohol and the like, the Vinaya provides an exception for cases of serious illness where a physician says the disease can be cured by using wine as a vehicle for medicine;
such provisional use does not constitute an offense. However, to drink without cause, or to drink under the pretext of being ill, is what constitutes intentional drinking.
As for the fact that the faults of alcohol are immeasurable, this clarifies that one must absolutely not drink it.
Because alcohol deludes the mind and disturbs the nature, immeasurable faults arise from it; therefore, one must absolutely not drink it.

Regarding the phrase "with one's own hands" and so forth, it means that one should not only refrain from drinking it oneself to avoid committing a fault, but furthermore, one must not pass it through one's own hands.
Regarding wine cups and vessels: even one who provides others with alcohol to drink will incur the retribution of being born without hands or feet for five hundred lifetimes;
how much more so for one who drinks alcohol oneself without cause? Since one may not drink it oneself, one must not teach all people to drink it either.
Since neither oneself nor all people may do so, this applies to the drinking of alcohol by all sentient beings as well.
This is likewise not permitted. Since one may not even teach others to drink, how much less may one drink oneself?
All wines made from rice, wheat, and the like, as well as those made from *yángméi* (Chinese bayberry), jujubes, and grapes, are forbidden.
This is stated with repeated and earnest emphasis because it is absolutely and definitively impermissible to drink or to teach others to drink. If one does not comply...
Because of this precept, if a Bodhisattva drinks [alcohol] themselves or teaches others to drink it, or if they err themselves or cause others to err, they commit a minor offense.
○ The third precept: abstaining from eating meat.
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally eats meat, no kind of meat whatsoever may be eaten. Indeed, those who eat meat sever the seeds of great compassion and the Buddha-nature;
all sentient beings will see them and depart in revulsion. For this reason, no Bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any sentient being.
To eat meat incurs immeasurable sin. If one intentionally eats it, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally eats meat: long ago, when the Buddha was in the world, there occurred a year of famine and no vegetables grew.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, he manifested five kinds of pure meat from the tips of his five fingers, temporarily appearing them all at once to sustain people;
yet these were not actually flesh and blood. How could a Bodhisattva who upholds the precepts intentionally eat the flesh of sentient beings? This is so.
Therefore, the flesh of the bodies of all sentient beings must not be eaten. Indeed, those who eat meat sever the seeds of the Buddha-nature of great compassion.
It is said that whatever possesses blood and breath necessarily possesses consciousness; that which possesses consciousness is the seed of the Buddha-nature.
All that possesses consciousness is of the same essence. If one eats the flesh of that which is of the same essence, one severs great compassion. Therefore...
It is said that those who eat meat sever the seeds of great compassion and the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the phrase "all [sentient beings]," it means that when living beings see a person who eats meat, they feel fear; they will not cease until they distance themselves from such a person.
This is like the seagulls departing because of the sea-farer’s artifice, or the pigeons fleeing at the shadow of the Arhat. For this reason, all Bodhisattvas who have received the precepts must—
One must never eat the flesh of any sentient being. Though their forms differ, their substance is the same; as for the seed of their Buddha-nature, there is likewise no distinction.

Regarding the acquisition of immeasurable sin from eating meat, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that there are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat, because all sentient beings have, from the very beginning, always been...
Because they are one's own six kin; because they are produced from impure elements;

because when sentient beings smell their scent, they all become terrified, just as *caṇḍālas* and *ḍombas* [flee] or as dogs bark in alarm upon seeing them; and even in secluded forests, tigers and wolves are startled by the scent.
For these reasons, one should not eat the flesh of sentient beings. If one should nevertheless eat it, such a person is no longer a bodhisattva.
One commits a minor offense.
○ Fourth, the precept against eating the five pungent roots:
If a Buddha’s disciple, one must not eat the five pungent roots—garlic, leek, scallion, onion, and asafoetida. These are the five.
Species. Among all foods, one must not eat these; if one intentionally eats them, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

Regarding the phrase "If a Buddha’s disciple shall not... and so forth: it refers to the five pungent roots (*pañca-gandhaka*), which are the five *huǎn* (aromatics), not the five *xīng* (meaty substances).
These are: first, garlic (*rājasarṣapa*), also called *hú*; this refers to the *húcōng* (garlic scallion). Second, *gècōng*, which is the *xiècài* (wild onion/garlic chive). Third, *cícōng*...

1. *Gṛñjana* is the onion. 2. *Laśuna* is the garlic. 3. *Kalāya* is the vetch. 4. *Laśuna* is the small garlic (*kṣudra-laśuna*). 5. *Hingu* is the asafoetida; this species does not exist in this region.
Regarding the prohibition against eating these: if these five pungent plants are eaten cooked, they arouse lust; if eaten raw, they increase anger.
Furthermore, there are five occasions when one should not eat [the five pungent vegetables]: first, when life is exhausted; second, when the heavens are distant; third, when ghosts are near;
fourth, when merit is being consumed; and fifth, when Māras gather. Among all foods, if even a hair’s breadth of these five pungent vegetables is mixed therein, one must not eat them.
If one intentionally eats them, this Bodhisattva commits a minor offense (light defilement).
○ The Fifth Precept: Not Teaching the Repentance of Sins.
If a Buddha’s disciple sees any sentient beings who have violated the eight precepts, the five precepts, or the ten precepts;

who have breached prohibitions, committed the seven heinous acts, or encountered the eight difficulties—having committed any such offenses against the precepts—they should be taught to repent. Yet, if a Bodhisattva does not teach them to repent, but instead dwells with them...

If one partakes of the Sangha’s offerings and participates in the *poṣadha* together with them, dwelling within the same community for the recitation of the precepts, yet fails to expose their transgressions or instruct them to repent,
one commits a minor offense of defilement.
"Regarding the phrase 'if a Buddha's disciple sees,' etc.: this refers to seeing all sentient beings, including those who have received the lay precepts.
The 'eight precepts' refers to the eight precepts of an upāsaka; the 'five precepts' refers to the first five of those eight. There are two types of the 'ten precepts.'"
First, the ten pure precepts of a śrāmaṇera; second, the ten grave precepts of a bodhisattva. "To destroy" means to break and ruin; "to prohibit" means to cease and extinguish.
This refers to the correct precepts established by the Tathāgata for ceasing evil and extinguishing transgressions—to violate and destroy them with all one's heart.
The seven reversals are: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing one’s upādhyāya, killing one’s ācārya, and disrupting the *karmavācanā* (the formal ritual procedure).
The *dharmacakra-saṃgha* refers to those who, with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha or murder an arhat.
To sell images of the Buddha, images of bodhisattvas, or the sūtras and vinaya constitutes shedding the blood of a Buddha; to murder a bhikṣu-saṃgha is equivalent to murdering an arhat.
Regarding the "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states they are the eight difficulties outside the [Buddha’s] realm. Among these, there are those that remain...
The thirty minds constitute the three evil realms. Abiding in the dharma of non-self is equivalent to the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru).
The craving for dharmas prior to the stages is like the long-lived gods. Not yet possessing the ten kinds of sixfold wisdom of the first stage is called "having incomplete faculties.

Wisdom prior to the stages is shallow, like worldly cleverness and eloquence; it does not exhaust the central principle, being like the period before or after a Buddha’s appearance. These eight [categories] are outside this realm.

Question: One who upholds the Mahāyāna precepts should instruct those who have committed an offense to perform repentance (*pratideśanā*). To fail to so instruct them is also a transgression of a defiled offense (*mala-āpatti*). If one sees such individuals who have violated the precepts, one ought to give rise to a mind of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*) and instruct them to repent and eliminate their prior faults, ensuring they do not commit them again thereafter. If a Bodhisattva fails to instruct them to repent, would this not constitute a transgression on his own part? Answer: It is difficult to say. If there is no suitable person capable of guiding them toward repentance, or if the offender is of a stubborn nature and will not accept instruction, then the Bodhisattva is not at fault. Furthermore, if the Bodhisattva were to instruct them but the offender were to harbor resentment or feel malice toward the instructor, the Bodhisattva would instead incur a transgression by causing the other to fall into further affliction. Therefore, if one perceives that the offender’s disposition is such that they would not accept the teaching, it is permissible for the Bodhisattva to remain silent; he does not thereby commit a transgression. However, if the Bodhisattva knows that the offender is capable of repenting and yet deliberately fails to provide the necessary instruction, then he does indeed commit a transgression. Thus, while the primary responsibility lies with the offender, the Bodhisattva must exercise wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) in accordance with the circumstances. If he acts out of a compassionate heart, seeking only to benefit others, he incurs no fault. But if he acts out of negligence or a lack of concern, he is guilty of a transgression. Therefore, one must carefully examine the situation before deciding whether to intervene. If one fails to act when intervention is required, one commits a defiled offense. If one acts when intervention is unnecessary, one likewise commits a defiled offense. Hence, the Bodhisattva must always maintain equanimity and act with discernment. If he can skillfully guide others toward repentance without himself falling into error, he fulfills his duty. Otherwise, he may inadvertently cause harm. Therefore, the Bodhisattva must never abandon the practice of compassion, yet he must also never neglect the application of wisdom. Only by uniting these two can he avoid transgressions and bring true benefit to sentient beings. If he fails to instruct in repentance when it is appropriate, he certainly incurs a transgression. How much more so if he fails to do so when the conditions are favorable! Thus, the Bodhisattva must always strive to lead others toward purification and reform. If he fails to do so, he cannot claim to be fulfilling the path of a Bodhisattva. Therefore, one must be diligent in both self-cultivation and the guidance of others. If one can ensure that others repent and reform, one’s own merit will increase immeasurably. If one fails to do so, one’s own virtue will decline. This is why the Bodhisattva must never neglect this duty. If he fails to instruct in repentance, he will surely incur a transgression. How could he possibly avoid it? Therefore, the Bodhisattva must always be mindful of this principle. If he fails to act, he is at fault. If he acts appropriately, he is without blame. This is the essential standard for the conduct of a Bodhisattva. If he fails to instruct in repentance, he certainly incurs a transgression. How could he possibly avoid it? Do you not instruct them to repent for their offenses? Moreover, since they dwell in the same place, partake of the same monastic food and offerings, and observe the *poṣadha* together, sitting and dwelling within the same pure assembly of the Sangha, and reciting the *Mahā-śīla* in unison—yet you do not raise up or examine the faults and transgressions of those monks, nor do you instruct or admonish them to repent for their misdeeds; this is...
A Bodhisattva commits a minor offense (light impurity).
○ Sixth Precept: Not Providing for Those Who Request the Dharma.
If, O Son of the Buddha, you see a Mahāyāna Dharma Master, or a fellow student of the Mahāyāna who shares the same views and practices, entering the monastic quarters—

Whether from their own homes, cities, or from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li*, whenever anyone came, he would immediately rise to welcome them and see them off, prostrating and making offerings.
He made offerings three times every day, consuming three *liang* of gold daily for food and drink of a hundred flavors.

He provided the Dharma Master with seats, bedding, and medicine, attending to all his needs and supplying everything required. He constantly invited the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma during the three periods of the day.

One should perform prostrations three times each day, without giving rise to anger or a mind of resentment or affliction. One should sacrifice one's body for the sake of the Dharma and request the teachings without weariness.
If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense.
"If a disciple of the Buddha sees [such a person]," and so forth, refers to a Dharma Master of the Mahāyāna. This is not one who follows the Hīnayāna for solitary benefit alone;

rather, it is a Dharma Master who possesses great faith and understanding, penetrates the principles of the Buddha, and practices the method of the simultaneous cultivation of compassion and wisdom for the sake of both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
"Mahāyāna fellow students" refers to those who study under the same teacher and learn the Mahāyāna precepts together. They share the same views and the same...
Regarding those with clear insight who practice the precepts of the Bodhisattva’s mind-ground, and those who practice the pure precepts of the Bodhisattva’s mind-ground in common with others:
it is said that if one sees such teachers or friends entering a monastery, a house, a city, or any such place, [one should act accordingly].
Regardless of distance—whether they come from a hundred *li* or a thousand *li*—the presiding Bodhisattva should give rise to a heart of supreme respect.

Those who come must be welcomed, and those who depart must be seen off. One should prostrate with utmost sincerity and make offerings according to the Dharma, ensuring that these are not lacking during the three periods of every day.
As for what is used for these offerings: one may use the three portions of food consumed each day.
One should use the two kinds of gold to prepare a hundred flavors of food and drink as offerings; one should provide offerings of fine couches, seats, and bedding;
and one should serve the Dharma Master with the four requisites of clothing, food, bedding, and medicine. Whatever the Dharma Master may require, one should provide it all without any stinginess.
Regarding the phrase "constantly invite those who are equal," this means that such offerings are not made for the sake of seeking human rewards.
Is it merely for the sake of the minor fruits and blessings of the heavens? It is truly for the purpose of seeking the Great Dharma of Prajñā;
by means of pure verbal karma, one requests the Dharma Master to expound the wondrous Dharma three times every day, so that the life of wisdom may never be severed.
With pure physical action, they prostrate three times each day; with pure mental action, they do not give rise to even a single thought of anger, anxiety, or affliction.

Not only are their three karmas sincere, but they are truly persons of the Great Dharma who would not begrudge even burning their bodies or severing their arms to request the preaching of the Dharma, never failing to do so.
This refers to a mind of weariness and indolence. If one does not act accordingly, this Bodhisattva commits a minor offense (light defilement).
The Seventh Precept: Against Indolence and Not Listening to the Dharma.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, there is the preaching of the Dharma, the Vinaya, the Sutras, or the Shastras in any place—whether in a great residence or at a site where the Dharma is being taught—
A newly initiated bodhisattva should carry the scrolls of the sutras and vinaya to the place where the Dharma Master resides to listen, receive, and inquire about them.
Whether it be in mountain forests, beneath trees, on monastic grounds, within rooms, or at any place where the Dharma is preached, they must go to all such places to listen and receive the teachings.
If one fails to go there to listen and receive them, one commits a minor offense.
"If a Buddha’s disciple [encounters] all [who are equal]," means that it is not only when a teacher comes to one's own place that one should provide offerings and request the Dharma;
rather, wherever there is a place where the Dharma is being taught, one should go there to listen and receive it.
"In all places" refers to those where the Mahāyāna Vinaya, sūtras, and śāstras are expounded, which extinguish evil and give rise to goodness.

The Great Dharma. *Vinaya* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Subduing" (*tiáofú*). This means to subdue the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, and to subdue the six sense faculties, thereby eliminating evil and increasing goodness.

While the *Sūtras* elucidate the principles of essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the *Vinaya* restrains both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

Thus, they are called the *Sūtra* and *Vinaya*. Regarding "within the great mansion": this refers to when the Buddha was in the world, constantly receiving [offerings from] kings, ministers, and others.
Please remain in residence within this house to preach the Dharma; this is a place for expounding the Dharma within a great mansion.

When a newly initiated bodhisattva sees such a place where the Dharma is being preached, they should personally take the scrolls of the Sūtras and Vinaya and go directly to the location where the Dharma Master is lecturing. There, with a sincere mind, they should listen attentively and receive the teachings. If...
If there is something not yet understood, one should consult and inquire in order to resolve one's doubts. Regarding "in mountain forests and the like," this uses the distant to illustrate the near;

it means that it is not only the case for those living at home, but even if one is in a secluded monastic site among mountains and forests, or in a solitary dwelling in the wilds, one must go to every place where a teacher preaches the Dharma to listen to and receive his teachings.
The youth Sudhana traveled south on his pilgrimage, traversing a hundred cities; Dongshan went up nine times, and Touzi ascended three times.
All these were done for the sake of the Dharma—how could one dare to avoid such toil and fail to go and listen?

If one does not go there to receive instruction, it means that at first they are arrogant toward the Dharma and indolent, and in the end, they are a person who commits every kind of evil. This is a Bodhisattva’s transgression of a minor defilement.
Offense. ○ Eighth, the precept against turning one’s back on the Great Vehicle and heading toward the Small Vehicle:

If a disciple of the Buddha, in their heart, turns their back on the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas that abide eternally, claiming they were not spoken by the Buddha, and instead accepts and upholds the teachings of the Two Vehicles—
Those who hold the evil views of śrāvakas and non-Buddhists, and who follow the heterodox precepts and the sutras and vinayas of false views, commit a minor offense (light impurity).
If a disciple of the Buddha is "equal-minded," yet turns his back—that is, he is in opposition and does not turn toward—the Mahayana eternally abiding sutras and vinayas;
that is, the *Mahāpūrṇa-nityasthita-vajra-ratna-śīla-citta-bhūmi-nimitta-dharma-paṭala-sūtra-vinaya*. It says:

Those whose faculties and resolve are narrow and inferior fear its difficult practice; their minds consequently become discordant, and they turn their backs on the Great Dharma rather than inclining toward it—this is to turn one's back on the Great [Vehicle].

Instead, they incline toward and uphold the provisional and inferior dharmas of the two vehicles of the śrāvakas, as well as the various evil and heterodox views, prohibitions, and false views of external paths, and the sūtras and vinayas that possess signs (*sanimitta*). This is...
