That which the Mahayana should face, one instead turns away from; that which the Hinayana should turn away from, one instead faces.
This is why the Bodhisattva incurs a minor offense (light defilement).
○ Ninth Precept: Not Tending to the Sick.
If a disciple of the Buddha sees anyone who is ill, they should always provide for them with offerings no different from those made to the Buddha himself.
Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit of tending to the sick is the foremost. If one’s parents, teachers, monks, or disciples fall ill, and their faculties are impaired—

Even when there are those afflicted by the hundred kinds of diseases and sufferings, whom one should provide for and cause to recover, the bodhisattva, out of a mind of anger and resentment, does not look upon them;
this extends to failing to rescue or provide for those seen with illness within monasteries, cities, wildernesses, mountain forests, or on the roads.
One commits a minor offense (light impurity).
Regarding the phrase "if a Buddha’s disciple sees," etc.: this refers to those above, such as parents and teachers; those below, such as children and disciples;
those in between, such as brothers and the six types of relatives; and those outside, such as enemies—whenever anyone among these is ill, one should always...
One should honor and make offerings to them just as one would to the Buddha; there is no difference between them.
For instance, when Master Yan personally stayed in an infirmary for lepers and Master Kuan returned home with a sick person in his carriage—these acts are all worthy of being taken as models.

Indeed, among the eight fields of merit, nursing the sick is the foremost field of merit. The eight fields of merit are: first, the Buddhas; second, the sages; third, fathers; fourth, mothers; fifth...

First, the Upādhyāya; second, the Ācārya; third, the six Ācāryas; fourth, the Saṃgha; fifth, the Śrāvakasaṃgha; sixth, the Pratyekabuddhasaṃgha; seventh, the Bodhisattvasaṃgha; eighth, the sick. Among these eight, only the sick constitute a source of affliction.
Because those who can rescue them from suffering will themselves obtain the fruit of happiness, nursing the sick is the foremost field of merit.
Whether it be those above, such as parents and teachers; those in the middle, such as the Sangha;

or those below, such as disciples who are ill—whether their faculties are impaired or incomplete, or they suffer from various ailments and afflictions numbering four hundred and four—one should, regardless of their status as superior, middling, or inferior, with a single flavor of an impartial mind, provide them all with the four requisites in accordance with the Dharma.
May they be restored to health, becoming exactly like the Buddha, without any difference. As for those who are "bodhisattvas" [in name only]:

this refers to those who, having been constantly supervised and disciplined by their parents or teachers, develop feelings of weariness and aversion, giving rise to resentment and abandoning them without a second thought—whether they be in monasteries, cities, towns, wildernesses, mountain forests, or on the roads.
Among these, regarding all such illnesses, one should exert every effort to provide relief even for those with whom one has no acquaintance or familiarity;
how much more so for parents, teachers, elders, and close relatives?
If a Bodhisattva sees a sick person and fails to employ skillful means to provide relief but instead abandons them, this constitutes a minor transgression for the Bodhisattva.
○ Tenth: The Precept Against Possessing Instruments of Killing.
If a Buddha’s disciple, they must not possess any swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, axes, or implements for combat;

nor nets or any other devices for killing living beings. Nothing of this kind may be possessed. Yet, even if a Bodhisattva were to kill their own parents, [it would still be better than possessing such things].

One shall not retaliate; how much less should one kill any sentient being? One must not keep implements for killing sentient beings. If one intentionally keeps such things, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
If a disciple of the Buddha does not [act] as described, it means that those who are disciples of the Buddha ought to keep weapons for cutting off demons and slaying [them].
The sword of wisdom for love, the staff of valor, the bow of great power, the arrow of diligence, the spear of patience, and the axe of meditative concentration—
along with the spreading of the great Dharma net to ensnare the sentient beings of the three realms and lead them out of the river of craving—
one who possesses such things as these is fit. Furthermore, Deshan’s staff for protecting life and Shigong’s bow for saving from death are precisely what should be maintained.

Furthermore, one should not keep any weapons for fighting or killing—such as swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, or axes—nor any evil nets or instruments for taking life; none of these, which are unfit for a son of the Buddha, may be kept.
Moreover, a bodhisattva should even retaliate against those who have killed his own parents. Furthermore...
One must not seek retribution; how much less could one who kills all sentient beings receive retribution? One must not even keep the instruments of killing.
One must not allow a single thought of murderous intent to sprout within the mind, let alone act upon it with the body.
If one intentionally keeps these inauspicious instruments of killing, this Bodhisattva commits a minor transgression.
"These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind.
These "ten precepts" summarize the preceding ten precepts. The two phrases "should be studied" and "upheld" collectively exhort one to practice and learn them.
This precept should be received upon the crown of the head and practiced with a reverent mind; uphold and maintain it, neither forgetting nor losing it.
○ The eleventh is the precept against serving as a state messenger.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, for the sake of profit or out of an evil mind, you must not serve as a messenger between states to facilitate military arrays or assemblies."
When armies are raised and they strike one another, killing immeasurable sentient beings, even a bodhisattva is not permitted to enter the midst of the army to come and go;
how much less so for one who intentionally acts as a traitor to the state? If one does so intentionally, one commits a minor offense.
When the Buddha says, "O sons of the Buddha," he means that as sons of the Buddha, you must fulfill the mission of a Buddha by transmitting the seal of the Buddha’s mind (*buddha-citta-mudrā*).

Like Deng Yinfeng, who resolved a conflict by flying his staff, or Master Chen, who broke the siege by throwing his shoe, you should be able to eliminate the thieves of affliction for sentient beings and bring an end to the suffering of war.
If, however, you merely seek fame, reputation, profit, and sustenance, plotting for personal merit...

Receiving rewards; plotting with malicious intent; causing one family to prosper while another family to perish; and acting as a state emissary for matters such as treaties and the scheduling of battles—these are absolutely forbidden.
Regarding military arrays and the like: it is said that twelve thousand men constitute an army (*senā*); when these troops are formed in ranks, it is an array (*vyūha*).
To join in combat, to assemble forces, to mobilize a host, and to strike one another down, resulting in injury and slaughter—[these are likewise forbidden].
Such evils as these committed against immeasurable sentient beings—how could they possibly be the deeds of a bodhisattva?
Even a novice bodhisattva is not permitted to enter a military camp to come and go; how, then, could it be tolerated for them to act as a state envoy?
It is certain that even a dangerous place or a lethal weapon must not be approached, let alone intentionally acting as a traitor to the state to harm sentient beings. If...
Therefore, the author [of this transgression] commits a minor offense for a Bodhisattva.
○ The Twelfth Precept Against Selling:
If a Buddha’s disciple intentionally buys and sells free persons, male or female slaves, or six types of domestic animals; or trades in coffins, planks, or wood used for containing the dead;

These implements one should not even make for oneself, much less teach others to make them. Therefore, if one makes them oneself or teaches others to make them, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

If a Buddha’s disciple intentionally engages in "buying" and so forth—buying meaning to acquire something cheap and sell it as expensive, and selling meaning to take goods out and obtain wealth in exchange—[this is likewise forbidden].
A "good person" refers to the children of a respectable family. "Six domestic animals" refers to oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, chickens, and dogs.
Coffin planks are materials for containing the dead. To treat them as if one were selling goods is inhumane.
It would cause great harm to the mind of compassion; therefore, one must not sell it.
As for the phrase "it should not even be done by oneself," this means that doing it alone is already impermissible, let alone teaching many others to perform such an uncompassionate act.
If one intentionally performs such an act oneself or teaches others to do so, this constitutes a transgression for a Bodhisattva.
A light offense of defilement.
○ Thirteenth: Slandering and Defaming the Precepts.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders others—whether they be virtuous people, good people, Dharma masters, teachers, or monks—without cause; or [slanders] the state...

O King and noble ladies: regarding those who commit the seven rebellions and ten grave offenses—toward parents, siblings, and the six classes of kin—one ought to give rise to a mind of filial piety and compassion;
yet, if instead one further commits acts of rebellion and harm against them, thereby falling into an undesirable state, this constitutes a transgression of the secondary precepts.

Regarding the phrase "If a disciple of the Buddha," etc.: "With an evil mind" clarifies that although slander originates from the mouth, it is driven by the mental ground—that is, by jealousy, greed, and anger—and is therefore called an "evil mind. "Slandering without cause" means to slander another despite the absence of any fault;

this refers to those who are mild and kind, those who are virtuous and gentle, Mahāyāna practitioners, those who observe the twenty-one-day precepts, Dharma masters, and the sixfold harmonious Saṃgha.
Furthermore, the holy lords and worthy ministers who have received the Mahāyāna precepts all bring great benefit to the Triple Gem;
they ought to be honored and revered. Yet, on the contrary, you engage in groundless slander, claiming that they have committed the seven heinous offenses and the ten grave transgressions.
Now, teachers and monks possess the relationship of parents toward one another, and good people and virtuous men possess the relationship of brothers.

Regarding the meaning: A person of noble status possesses the relationship of the six kin. Within that context, one ought to give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience, a mind of compassion, and offer praise and encouragement to bring about their fame and virtue, ensuring that each of their wishes is fulfilled.

To do the opposite—further aggravating their feelings, harboring harmful intentions, destroying their fame and virtue, and causing them to fall into an undesirable state—is for a bodhisattva to commit a light offense.
A Tainted Offense.
○ The Fourteenth Precept on Setting Fires:
If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind, sets a great fire to burn mountains, forests, wildernesses, or open lands for four months up to nine [months], [it is a transgression].

The Moon releases fire. If one burns the houses and dwellings of others, cities and towns, monastic quarters, fields and trees, as well as the property of spirits, deities, or officials—indeed, any property belonging to another—one must not burn it intentionally.
If one burns it intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
"If a disciple of the Buddha," and so forth, refers to those with an evil mind—meaning one who harbors resentment or gives rein to their passions—all of which are uncompassionate thoughts.
These produce a great, fierce fire that burns mountains, forests, and wildernesses, causing much injury to insect life.

Therefore, from the fourth month to the ninth month, while large creatures such as birds and beasts are incubating their eggs and hatching their young, even the smallest insects are undergoing transformation throughout the summer. One summer...
During the autumn months, if one were to set fire [to the fields], how could the injury and loss of living beings ever come to an end? It does not stop at this alone;

should the fire spread to the houses, dwellings, cities, and towns of others, as well as monastic quarters, fields, trees, objects belonging to spirits, or official property—in short, any object with an owner—the damage would be even greater and the loss of virtue even more severe, regardless of the specific items involved.
Whether life is at risk or not, one must never intentionally burn [the scriptures]. If one intentionally burns them, one commits a minor offense.
○ The Fifteenth Precept Against Deviant Teachings:
If a Buddha’s disciple—whether toward fellow disciples, non-Buddhists, evil persons, the six types of relatives, or all spiritual friends—should...

One by one, they were instructed to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, taught the principles and meanings thereof, and led them to resolve upon the bodhicitta—the ten minds of setting forth, the ten minds of nurturing, and the ten adamantine minds. Within these thirty minds, each was made to understand the sequential application of their methods.
Yet, out of malice and anger, the Bodhisattva arbitrarily taught the sūtras and vinaya of the two vehicles, the śrāvakas, to outsiders.
To advocate for heterodox views, wrong views, or such theories constitutes a minor transgression.
Regarding the phrase "if a Buddha’s disciple" and so forth: "one's own" refers to the disciples of the Buddha, who are members of the internal assembly of the Triple Gem;

"external paths" and "evil persons" refer to those whose minds wander among the heterodox views of external paths, and who are called "evil persons" because they follow such heterodoxy. As for the "six relations," they are...
These include parents, brothers, children, and spouses; all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
and those among one's acquaintances and associates who possess the roots of nature for the Mahāyāna and are good friends.

Thus, whether they be internal or external relatives and friends, one should guide each and every one of them to receive, uphold, and train in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, leading them to faith, understanding, and thorough penetration.
Regarding the principles: cause them to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, as well as the minds of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications;

within these three levels of the stage of the worthy (śaikṣa), cause each of them to understand and enter them according to their sequential order, including the methods for the visualization of dharmas.

When faith is fulfilled, one enters the stage of abiding; when abiding is fulfilled, one enters the stage of practice; when practice is fulfilled, one enters the stage of heading toward [enlightenment].
One must provide such instructions for each and every meditative practice; only then can it be called "right teaching," which benefits both oneself and others.

If a bodhisattva, out of an evil mind, jealousy, or contempt, fails to teach; or if, out of anger or resentment, they abandon someone who has not yet followed their instruction—[this constitutes a transgression].

To abandon [the Mahāyāna] or to perversely teach the sūtras, vinayas, and all heterodox treatises of wrong views belonging to the two vehicles of śrāvakas—this is like using fine timber for a crooked purpose or employing a beautiful vessel for a vile use. It misleads students and severs the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom.
Such perverse teaching is truly not the intent of a bodhisattva; therefore, it is defined as a light secondary offense (āpatti) for perverse deviation. "Perverse" (héng-pì) means deviant.
The sixteenth [precept] concerns explaining the precepts erroneously for the sake of profit:
"O Sons of the Buddha, one should with a sincere heart first study the Mahāyāna Vinaya and Sūtras regarding dignified conduct, extensively opening up and understanding their meanings and flavors.
When one sees a newly initiated Bodhisattva who has come from a hundred or a thousand li to seek the Mahāyāna Sūtras and Vinaya, one should act in accordance with the Dharma."

He shall preach all forms of ascetic practice for them: whether it be burning the body, the arms, or the fingers; or, if one does not burn the body, arms, or fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, they are not renunciant bodhisattvas.
Even unto hungry tigers, wolves, lions, and all hungry ghosts, one should relinquish one's own flesh, hands, and feet to offer to them.
Only after that should one preach the True Dharma to each of them in due order.
To cause the mind to open and the intellect to be liberated, yet for the sake of gain and profit, or for the sake of fame and reputation,

one fails to answer when one should answer, misinterprets the words of the Sūtras and Vinaya, presents them without proper sequence, and slanders the Triple Gem— such a speaker commits a minor offense.

Regarding the phrase "If a Buddha-son should be equal," the term "good mind" refers to first taking as one's resolve the pure Dharma of the Mahāyāna to practice for the benefit of both self and others.
One must first study the system, scope, and methods of body and mind regarding the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva precepts.
Having extensively opened up and mastered the categories of the Mind-Ground Dharma, and having understood the meaning and flavor of each individual point, only then may one establish the rules.
To model oneself for later students: having first benefited oneself, one then benefits others.

Regarding the phrase "seeing those who come later," it means that since I am already an elder student, when I see new students of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) who have traveled from as far as a hundred or a thousand li to seek these Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas—this is truly a sincere heart—I should guide them according to the Dharma in proper sequence. For...

He previously spoke of all methods of ascetic practice. What are these ascetic practices? They include burning the body, burning the arms, or burning the fingers as offerings to the Buddhas—such as the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana burning his body, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja burning his arm, and the World-Honored One burning a lamp—all of whom may serve as witnesses.
If one does not thus burn the body, arms, or fingers as offerings to the Buddhas, [one will not attain the goal].
This constitutes being an ordinary person attached to signs; since the physical body has not yet been emptied of its characteristics, how could one be an ordained bodhisattva?

Therefore, it is said that such a person is "not an ordained bodhisattva. Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it means that one should not only perform offerings such as burning the body for the Buddhas, but should also do so even when encountering hungry tigers, wolves, lions, or any hungry ghosts, and in all such cases, one should relinquish [the body].
One should offer this body—its flesh, hands, and feet—as an offering, without discriminating among its various features.

Thereafter, one should explain the profound principles of the Mahāyāna True Dharma to them one by one in sequence, so that their minds may open without obstruction and their understanding may be liberated without bondage.
To teach in this manner is called "correct teaching" and is called "the sequence of the good intention."

It is said: "As for 'bodhisattvas and the like,' it refers to cases where a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and profit or for the sake of fame and reputation, seeks that which cannot be attained, and consequently gives rise to the thought of either answering or not answering.

Even when they do answer, they do not explain in proper sequence; instead of explaining correctly, they explain perversely regarding the words, meanings, and principles of the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas."
In the past, there was nothing from which it arose; in the future, there will be nowhere to which it returns. To oppose the intent of the Buddhas above is to slander the Buddha;
to turn one's back on the purport of the Sūtras and Vinaya in the middle is to slander the Dharma; to deviate from those who seek the truth below is to slander the Saṅgha.
One who speaks thus, slandering the Triple Gem, commits a minor offense against the Bodhisattva precepts.
○ The Seventeenth Precept on Begging by Abusing One’s Power:
If a disciple of the Buddha, for the sake of food, drink, wealth, offerings, or reputation, associates with kings,
princes, ministers, and officials, and relying upon their influence, begs, extorts, beats, or drags others, thereby taking money and property by improper means— all such acts [are forbidden].
To seek profit, to be called a "wicked seeker," to seek much, to teach others to seek, and to be entirely devoid of a heart of compassion or a heart of filial piety—
these constitute a minor transgression.
Regarding the phrase "if a Buddha’s disciple for himself," what does "for oneself" mean? It distinguishes this from acting for the sake of the community or seeking to protect the Dharma;
rather, it refers to seeking fine food, drink, wealth, offerings, and a good reputation for the sake of one's own peace and comfort.
Regarding "intimacy" and so forth, it means that for this reason, they become intimate with one another, affectionate toward each other, and dwell in close proximity.
Morning and evening, they were full of affection for the families of kings, princes, ministers, and high officials, treating them as close kin.

Relying on the power of their noble and wealthy status, they affected airs of refinement; using their influence to covet and greedily seek gain, they would resort to beating and striking those from whom they could not obtain what they begged.
When such violence failed to yield results, they would then drag, pull, and forcibly coerce others, taking their money by force.
Wealth is not obtained through human wishes; even all forms of greedy seeking are called unwholesome. Such seeking for evil dharmas is called improper.

This is the excessive seeking of greed. If one has not yet obtained it oneself, yet teaches others to seek it as well—seeking in such ways causes people to give rise to resentment and hatred, being utterly devoid of a heart of compassion and a heart of filial piety.
This constitutes a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
○ The Eighteenth Precept: To Act as a Teacher Without Understanding.
If a Buddha’s disciple should study the twelve divisions of the scriptures and recite the precepts, they should uphold the Bodhisattva precepts six times every day and understand them.

Regarding the principle of the Buddha-nature, if a bodhisattva does not understand even a single sentence or verse, nor the causes and conditions of the precepts, yet falsely claims to understand them, they are deceiving themselves and deceiving others; they do not understand any of it.
If one does not understand all dharmas, yet acts as a teacher for others and bestows the precepts upon them, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
"If a Buddha-son should be equal," means that one should study and practice the Prajñāpāramitā. There are three types of Prajñā.
First is the Prajñā of a Single Syllable; this refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Second is the Prajñā of Contemplative Insight;
this refers to upholding the Bodhisattva precepts. Third is the Prajñā of the True Mark; this is the understanding of the nature of Buddha-nature.

It is said that a Son of the Buddha must first study the twelve divisions of the scriptures to give rise to the wisdom of understanding. If one possesses the wisdom of understanding yet fails to practice, there is a fear that it will result in madness.
Wisdom: One should recite the precepts in order to stabilize the foundation of wisdom. One must, without the slightest laxity, perform this six times every day.
One must uphold the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Precepts" of the Mahāyāna and practice the actual conduct of a bodhisattva according to the Dharma.
Since one already possesses the conduct of the precepts, if one does not understand their ultimate purpose, one will be unable to reach the final fruition of Buddhahood; therefore, one should...

Only by understanding their meaning, flavor, and principles, and by penetrating to the very depths of the Buddha-nature, becoming self-illuminated and free from delusion, can one clarify others and serve as a teacher and model for humanity.

As for the phrase "Bodhisattvas and others," it means that if a Bodhisattva does not understand even a single sentence or a single verse of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, nor the causal conditions of the Bodhisattva’s mind-ground precepts; [they cannot fulfill their role].
This is not possible. To falsely claim, on the contrary, that one can understand and realize it—is this not self-deception? Is it not also deception of others?

One may truly be called a person of great audacity, grave transgression, and shamelessness. Regarding the nature of Buddha-nature and each of its doctrinal principles, there is not the slightest comprehension;
one knows nothing of the teachings, practices, principles, fruits, or any of the dharmas, yet still [to act thus] is delusory.
To act as a teacher for others and transmit the precepts with such [malice] constitutes a light offense for a Bodhisattva.
The Nineteenth Precept: Against Divisive Speech.
If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind, sees a precept-keeping Bhikṣu holding an incense burner and practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva...
To incite strife between two parties, to slander and deceive the virtuous, and to commit every kind of evil—this constitutes a transgression of a light impurity.

If a disciple of the Buddha, with an evil mind, speaks of those who uphold the precepts as being different from himself, praising them for others while harboring jealousy, envy, and other such malicious intentions;
or if one sees a bhikṣu upholding the precepts and does not acknowledge him by name [as such]—this constitutes a transgression.
He is styled a śramaṇa; he possesses the virtue and conduct of a worthy and holy Jewel of the Saṅgha.
Holding a censer of incense in his hand, he practices the true path of a bodhisattva. If he were not a worthy and holy member of the Saṅgha, who else could he be?

As a person who aspires to be a bodhisattva, he ought to promote the excellence of others and join in encouraging the transformation through the Dharma. How could he possibly incite strife, engage in factionalism, or act as a mediator between two parties?
To seek pleasure and profit within this [teaching] so as to corrupt one's own mental faculties—regarding "deceitful slander" and the like:

it means that although this bhikṣu was originally a worthy and noble person, one raises groundless slanders to deceive him, conversely claiming he has committed every kind of evil, thereby causing him distress.
One who thus slanders and deceives a worthy person commits a minor offense against a Bodhisattva.
○ Twenty: The Precept Against Failing to Practice Releasing Living Beings.
If a Buddha’s disciple, out of a heart of compassion, practices the act of releasing living beings, they should form this thought:
"All men are my fathers; all women are my mothers. In every successive birth, there is none from whom I have not received life. Therefore, [the sixth...]
I take all sentient beings to be my parents. To kill and eat them is to kill my own parents, and it is also to kill my former bodies.
All earth and water were my previous bodies; all fire and wind are my fundamental essence.
Therefore, one should practice the karma of releasing living beings in every successive birth. If you see people of the world killing animals, you should employ skillful means.
One should provide protection and deliverance, relieving them of their suffering and hardship. One should constantly teach and expound the Bodhisattva precepts to save and deliver sentient beings.

On the day of the death of one’s parents or siblings, one should invite a Dharma Master to lecture on the Sūtras and Vinaya of the Bodhisattva precepts, so that the merit may assist the deceased in seeing the Buddhas and being reborn among humans or in the heavens. If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense.
"If a Buddha-son [practices] with compassion," and so forth, means that in cultivating the ten thousand practices of a bodhisattva, compassion is taken as the foundation.
One who possesses compassion personally practices benevolence and love; one who possesses benevolence and love, toward all sentient beings suffering in the throes of death, [extends this care].
One should practice the vow of rescue and protection; this is precisely the fundamental activity of a bodhisattva’s practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Having performed this activity, one should further cultivate contemplation to strengthen the resolve for the release of living beings. What kind of contemplation should be practiced?
One should contemplate that all men are my fathers and all women are my mothers. Why is this known to be so? Because throughout my successive births...
There is not one who has not received birth from them; thus, we know this. If we extend and apply this principle further, all sentient beings of the six realms have been our own parents.
If one were now to kill their body and eat their flesh, would this not be killing our parents from many kalpas and many lifetimes? It is likewise the killing of our parents from many kalpas.
Why is this body that has been born many times so cherished? All earth and water are the flesh and blood of my many past lives;
all fire and wind are the essential warmth of my many past lives. Thus, they are the closest kin of one's parents and the most beloved parts of one's own self;
these things are identical for both. Since there is fundamentally no difference between the Buddha and sentient beings, how can one not act with urgency?

One should urgently and constantly practice this karma of releasing living beings. Regarding the phrase "life after life" and so forth, it means that one should not merely practice the karma of releasing living beings for one or two lifetimes;
rather, one should constantly practice this karma of releasing living beings throughout every successive birth from lifetime to lifetime.
When seeing worldly people killing or injuring large or small animals, one should employ skillful means.
One should employ skillful means and gentle persuasion to rescue and protect them, causing them to leave suffering behind and attain peaceful happiness.
While such efforts may save one life from its pain, they cannot provide universal protection for all;

therefore, one should constantly establish extensive teachings and expound the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra to deliver all sentient beings, so that they may forever be free from all sufferings and attain peaceful happiness.
Regarding "if it concerns one's parents and so forth," this means that when parents, brothers, or others have passed away— their breath stilled and their spirits departed—

leaving no peer in this world on the day of their death— one who is a filial son or a virtuous younger brother ought to respectfully invite a Mahāyāna Dharma Master to lecture upon the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtras and Vinaya.
By means of these merits and blessings, one should dedicate them to the deceased, so that they may behold the ten [directions].
When the Buddhas have thus been honored, sins are extinguished and blessings arise; one is reborn among humans or in the heavens, and is liberated from the sufferings of the three miserable realms.
To provide such protection and salvation is called a Bodhisattva repaying the kindness of the Buddhas. If one does not do so, that Bodhisattva commits a minor offense.
These ten precepts should be studied and reverently upheld. As explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Extinction of Offenses," each of these precept-characteristics is clarified.
These ten precepts serve as a summary of what precedes; "should be studied" is the exhortation to practice, while "reverently uphold" is the instruction.
One should uphold these with a heart of reverence, honoring and maintaining them without forgetting or losing them.
These ten grave and twenty light precepts constitute a complete prohibition for ordained bodhisattvas, whereas for lay bodhisattvas there are both allowances and prohibitions.
All who act as teachers should study these deeply; the same applies to the twenty-eight light precepts that follow.
○ The Twenty-first Precept: Against Retaliating with Anger or Blows. The Buddha said:
"O Son of the Buddha, one must not repay anger with anger, nor repay a blow with a blow.

Even if one's parents, brothers, or six types of kinsmen are killed, one must not seek retribution. Even if a sovereign is killed by another, one must likewise not seek retribution. If one kills... [text ends]

Regarding retribution in this life: to fail to follow the way of filial piety, even to the point of not refraining from keeping slaves and mistreating them with beating and abuse—thus daily giving rise to the three karmas and committing immeasurable verbal offenses—is already a transgression.
How much more so for a renunciant bodhisattva to intentionally commit the seven grave offenses (*ānantarya-karma*)?
If one harbors a mind of resentment and seeks revenge, even against one's own six types of close relatives, by intentionally seeking retribution, one commits a secondary offense of impurity.
The Buddha’s address as "Son of the Buddha" (Buddhaputra) serves to designate his name; he then calls out to him by means of the ten precepts, one after another.
The two phrases beginning with "must not" are intended precisely for the Bodhisattva to achieve emptiness of mind and stillness of environment, such that both self and other are forgotten.
"Must not harbor an unkind heart" means one must not strike back in anger to seek revenge. "If [one commits] killing, etc. refers to cases such as parents, siblings, or the six...
One must not seek retribution even against one's closest relatives or one's own flesh and blood.
Even if a king’s sovereign is killed by another, one must likewise not seek retribution. It is said that the enmity between ruler and subject, or father and son, cannot be shared under the same sky;
yet while such principles dictate that these must all be avenged, Buddhism does not permit retribution, let alone other forms of vengeance. For what reason does the Buddha not [permit it]?
Granted. For the retribution for killing causes all sentient beings to kill one another incessantly from lifetime to lifetime.
When a Bodhisattva regards all men and women as his own parents, then to kill them is to kill one's own parents.
If this were so, how could it conform to the principles of filial piety? "Not even equal" refers to the cultivation of the Way.

If humans do not even dare to beat, strike, or insult their own domestic slaves, yet they daily give rise to physical karma of beating, verbal karma of insulting, and mental karma of anger—among these three types of karma, it is speech alone that is the gateway to calamity and gives rise to the greatest number of transgressions.
How much more so, then, for the physical commission of the crimes of killing one's parents, the seven heinous offenses, or filial impiety? It can be known that such acts are even more grave.
Furthermore, regarding those who have left the household life: it is said that a bodhisattva who has renounced the world should treat enemies and kin with equanimity, forgetting both self and others.
How could such a person harbor a desire for retribution? This would merely resemble the view of self and other held by worldly people.
If a renunciant bodhisattva, lacking a mind of compassion, were to seek revenge for themselves, or even for their parents, brothers, and so forth...
If one’s six kin seek revenge, it constitutes a minor offense.

**The Twenty-second Precept: The Prohibition Against Arrogance and Refusing to Request the Dharma.** O Sons of the Buddha, when you have first left the home life and have not yet attained any understanding, if you rely on your own cleverness or intelligence, or rely on...

There are those of noble age and seniority who, perhaps relying on their prestigious lineage and high status, or their great learning and immense wealth, and being arrogant due to their abundance of the seven treasures, do not consult or receive the sūtras and vinaya from learned Dharma masters.

These Dharma masters may be of humble lineage, young, or from lowly families; they may be poor, low-born, or physically impaired, yet they truly possess virtue and have mastered all the sūtras and vinaya.

It is explained: If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not inquire of or receive instruction from a Dharma Master regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) because they judge the Dharma Master’s lineage or social standing, they commit a minor offense (āpatti).

"Regarding the phrase 'if a Buddha-son, from the beginning,' etc.: it means that when this Buddha-son first resolves his mind to leave the household life and depart from the secular world, he has never yet understood the meaning, flavor, and principles within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of non-self and dharmas.
Yet, relying on his own cleverness and intelligence, he does not realize that this worldly wisdom and eloquence act as an obstacle to right knowledge and right view."
Some rely on the high status and nobility of their names and positions; some rely on their advanced age;
some rely on their family being of great lineage and noble descent, their extensive learning and understanding, or their vast wealth and abundance of the seven treasures.
All such things are esteemed by the worldly, yet none are valued by those who practice the Way. Thus, when a son of the Buddha who has newly left the household life relies [on these],...
Because of this arrogance, they do not inquire with an open mind nor receive the sūtras and vinaya taught by the learned Dharma masters.
It is as if, when a lethal poison has already been drunk and the true medicine is present before them, they are unable to swallow it.
As for those Dharma masters, they may be of humble lineage rather than noble families, young rather than venerable elders, or lowly rather than exalted.
He is poor rather than wealthy; lowly rather than noble; his faculties are incomplete and he lacks the marks and signs of a great man.
Although this Dharma Master is inferior to others in every respect regarding worldly matters, in terms of the stages of transcendence, he is in fact possessed of virtue.
Furthermore, his learning penetrates all sūtras and vinayas, understanding them thoroughly; he is fit to be a teacher for others, yet because he is a bodhisattva who has newly begun his training—
One must not give rise to a mind of arrogance by viewing this Dharma master as being of lowly lineage;
yet, if one ultimately fails to come to inquire of and receive from the Dharma master the exposition of the primary truth (paramārtha-satya), one commits a minor offense (āpatti).
○ Twenty-third: Arrogant and Deviant Preaching of the Precepts.

If, O Sons of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts with a sincere heart, one should take the vow to receive the precepts before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva.
One must repent before the Buddha for seven days until a favorable sign is seen; only then may one obtain [the precepts].
Regarding the precepts: if one does not obtain a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*), one should practice for two weeks, three weeks, seven weeks, or even up to one year, until a favorable sign is obtained.

Once a favorable sign has been obtained, one may receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or a Bodhisattva. If a favorable sign is not obtained, although one receives the precepts before an image of a Buddha, the precepts are not attained.
Alternatively, one may receive them first from a living person or before a Dharma Master who administers the Bodhisattva precepts.
When receiving the precepts, it is not necessary to see auspicious signs. Why is this? Because these Dharma masters have transmitted them from teacher to teacher;

therefore, auspicious signs are not required. For this reason, one obtains the precepts immediately upon receiving them before a Dharma master. Because one gives rise to a mind of profound respect, one attains the precepts.
If there is no capable preceptor within a thousand *li*, one may take the vow before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva.
Upon receiving the precepts, one must seek auspicious signs. If a Dharma Master relies on his own mastery of the sutras and vinaya,

studies the Mahayana precepts, and acts as a virtuous friend to kings, crown princes, and high officials, yet when a newly initiated Bodhisattva comes to inquire about the meaning of the sutras or the vinaya,
he responds with a light, malicious, or arrogant mind and does not answer each question well, he commits a secondary offense.

Regarding the phrase "If a Buddha’s disciple... equal to the Buddha," the expression "the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa" serves to distinguish this from the period when the Buddha was still in the world. During his lifetime, one took the Buddha as one's teacher;
now, however, after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, one takes the Dharma of the precepts as one's teacher, and regards the Precept-Master as the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "desiring to do so with a sincere mind" and so forth: it means that since the Buddha is not present before one and there is no teacher, if one desires to receive the Bodhisattva Great Precepts with a sincere mind, one may only do so by making a vow before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva.
This involves establishing the ten great vows and the four great vows, and further establishing the thirteen vows, as follows: [text continues below]
One must not fail to make the vow that is the pledge within the precepts. Once the vow has been made, one should further repent before the Buddha for seven days to eliminate karmic obstacles.
Having eliminated the offenses, one will perceive auspicious signs and thereby know for oneself that the precepts have been obtained.
Should one fail to perceive such auspicious signs within the first seven days, one ought to [continue] for a second...
For as long as seven days, three weeks, or even up to one year, one must necessarily obtain a good sign (*lakṣaṇa*).
Once a good sign has been obtained, one may then take the vow to receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva; only then does one obtain the precepts.
If a good sign is not obtained, even if one were to receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, one certainly would not [obtain them].
One may obtain the name of having received the precepts, yet lack actual attainment; one’s entire life will be in vain, and one’s essential nature remains that of a layperson.
If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there is currently a Bodhisattva Dharma Master who has previously received the precepts, one should receive the precepts before such a master.
At the time of receiving the precepts, it is not necessary to see auspicious signs. Why is this? Because...

When both the speaker and the recipient are present before one another, it is not a case of receiving [the precepts] at a distance, receiving them on behalf of another, or receiving them before an image.
This is because this Dharma Master has descended from the seven Buddhas of the past, transmitted from teacher to teacher, possessing a source and a foundation.
Thus, there is no need to require the appearance of auspicious signs; this Precept Master is none other than the Buddhas of the past dwelling in the world.
Generally speaking, one receives the precepts immediately before the Dharma Master and thereby attains them.

This is because the disciple seeking the precepts generates a mind of profound respect prior to the formal recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), viewing the Precept Master as a Buddha; for this reason, they immediately attain the precepts.
As for the phrase "if within a thousand *li*," it means that if there is no capable Dharma Master to bestow the precepts within a distance of a thousand *li*.
If one sincerely desires to seek the method for receiving the precepts, one may take the vow to receive them before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva.

Once a favorable sign has been obtained, one may obtain the precepts without fault. However, if there is a Dharma Master capable of conferring the precepts within a thousand li, to bypass that Dharma Master and follow an image instead will not only prevent one from obtaining the precepts, but furthermore, it will cause [one’s own]...
This refers to the sin of inciting arrogance, perverse teachings, and perverse adherence.
As for the phrase "if a Dharma Master," it means that if a Dharma Master internally relies on his own ability to understand the sutras and vinaya and upholds the Mahayana precepts,
yet externally relies on the kings, crown princes, and officials with whom he associates as virtuous friends, and [consequently] looks down upon a newly initiated Bodhisattva...
When others come to inquire about the meaning of the Sūtras or the Vinaya, if one relies on those with whom one has social ties and, out of such self-reliance, gives rise to a contemptuous mind,
a mind of disdain, a malicious mind of jealousy, or a mind of arrogance that leads to negligence— failing to answer each question properly and thoroughly—
this Dharma Master incurs the fault of arrogant and deviant teaching and commits a secondary offense (light defilement).
○ Twenty-fourth: Not Practicing the Buddha’s Precepts.

If, O sons of the Buddha, there exist the Buddha’s sūtras and vinaya, the Mahāyāna Dharma, right view, right nature, and the true Dharma-body, yet you are unable to diligently study and practice them, but instead abandon the seven treasures to study the false views of the two vehicles, the heterodox paths, secular classics, and the Abhidharma—this is a transgression.

The *Tanzalun* (Discourse on Miscellaneous Matters) states: All written records that sever the Buddha-nature and act as causes and conditions for obstructing the Path are not the practice of a Bodhisattva.
If one intentionally produces such works, one commits a minor offense (*laghu-āpatti*).

Regarding the phrase "If you, O sons of the Buddha," it means that there exists the pure Jewel of the Buddha to whom one may take refuge; there exist the pure Jewel of the Dharma—the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Mahāyāna teachings—to which one may pay reverence;
and there exists the pure Jewel of the Saṃgha—the Sangha of Right View, Right Nature, and the Right Dharma-body—upon which one may rely.
One ought to be diligent and devoted to learning, cultivating such treasures as these; yet instead, one is unable to study them and abandons these seven treasures:

the treasure of the Buddha, the treasure of the Sūtras, the treasure of the Vinaya, the treasure of the Mahāyāna Dharma, the treasure of right view, the treasure of right nature, and the treasure of the true Dharmakāya.
Turning one's back on awakening and uniting with the defilements, one fails to study right knowledge and right view, but instead—
They study wrong knowledge and wrong views, rather than studying the Mahāyāna Dharma; they instead study the Śrāvaka vehicle.

They do not study the Sūtra-piṭaka, Vinaya-piṭaka, or Abhidharma-piṭaka, but instead study the secular texts of external paths, the Abhidharma, miscellaneous treatises, and all manner of written records.
Those of such a sort are like those who abandon sweet mangoes to climb the mountains and pluck sour pears; they are truly pitiable.
"Those who sever [the roots]" refers to these followers of the Two Vehicles—withered sprouts—and those of the external paths—ruined seeds.
All are people deluded by their own ignorance, who sever the Buddha-nature and act as the causes and conditions for obstructing the Right Path. How could they ever achieve the Mahāyāna?
This is the true practice for a Bodhisattva on the right path who possesses the seeds of their nature.
If one does not study the Buddhas, nor even study the True Dharma-body, yet intentionally acts in such a manner, they commit a minor offense.
○ Twenty-fifth: Not Knowing the Precepts for the Assembly.

If a disciple of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, serves as a master of Dharma, a master of monastic quarters, a master of instruction, a master of seated meditation, or a master of administrative affairs, they should give rise to a heart of compassion.
They should skillfully reconcile disputes and skillfully guard the property of the Triple Gem; they must not fail to do so.

To use [the property] as if it were one's own, and instead to cause disorder among the assembly, engage in strife, and recklessly use the property of the Triple Gem, constitutes a minor transgression.
Regarding the phrase "If a Buddha’s disciple," this refers to the final age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; such a person acts as a master of the Dharma.
Those who advocate the path of the Dharma shall serve as masters of the monasteries; those who maintain the forest retreats shall serve as masters of instruction;
those who employ skillful means to instruct and benefit sentient beings shall serve as masters of seated meditation;

and those who have thoroughly penetrated the principles of Chan and are able to discern and understand right concentration and wrong concentration shall serve as masters of conduct. These masters must be well-acquainted with both the distant and the near.

Regarding the matters of welcoming and seeing off guests: it is said that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, since one has become such a leader among the assembly, one should give rise to a heart of benevolence and love for the multitude. One should use kind words to harmonize them so that there is no strife;
ensuring that those who have not yet quarreled do not begin to do so, and that those already quarreling bring their disputes to an end. Furthermore, one should skillfully provide protection.
Guard the wealth and property of the Triple Gem so that it is not intermingled, lost, or damaged by those who reside permanently [at the monastery].
Do not use them recklessly; let the property of the Buddha be used for the Buddha, the property of the Dharma for the Dharma, and the property of the Sangha for the Sangha.

Do not treat these as if they were your own private possessions and use them indiscriminately at will. If one can harmonize well and guard them well, such a person is a true child of the Buddha. If, however, one...

If one is capable [of maintaining the precepts] yet instead causes disorder among the assembly, engages in strife and contention, fails to maintain harmony, acts according to one's own whims, misappropriates the property of the Triple Gem,
or fails to protect it, one commits a minor offense of defilement.
The Twenty-sixth Precept on Receiving Offerings Alone:

If a disciple of the Buddha is already residing in a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), and sees a visiting Bodhisattva Bhikṣu entering a monastery, a private residence, a city, the palace of a king, or even a place of summer retreat (*varṣāvāsa*) or a great assembly; [if that visitor]...

The resident monks should welcome them upon arrival and see them off when they depart. They should provide food and drink, as well as dwellings, bedding, rope beds, and wooden beds, supplying every necessary item.
If they lack material goods, they should sell their own bodies or even the bodies of their sons and daughters;

they should cut their own flesh to sell, providing whatever is required and giving it all to them. If there are donors who invite the community of monks, the guest monks [should likewise be provided for].
Regarding the portion of offerings and sustenance: the master of the monastery should assign visiting monks in turn to receive invitations.
If the resident monks alone accept such invitations while failing to assign visiting monks, the monastery master incurs immeasurable sin;
he is no different from a beast, not a śramaṇa, and not of the Śākya lineage. This constitutes a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).
Regarding the phrase "If a son of the Buddha," etc.: those who have previously resided within a monastic compound (*saṃghārāma*) are naturally the masters;

they ought to fulfill the duties of a master to the fullest extent. If, however, one sees visiting Bodhisattvas or Bhikṣus entering to reside in a monastic compound, or entering the residences of lay devotees (*gṛhapati*), or entering the dwellings of cities and towns, or entering the palaces of kings—

Within these [monasteries], including those places where the summer retreat is observed for seated meditation and within the great assemblies—in such dwellings as these, the resident monks who have been there first must fully exercise their duties of hospitality, which differ from the ordinary. Upon seeing someone arrive, they shall welcome them; upon seeing them depart, they shall see them off.
They shall provide offerings of medicinal decoctions, drinks, and meals according to the Dharma, as well as rooms, bedding, rope beds, and wooden beds. All...
Whatever things are required, one must provide them without being stingy.
Even if one lacks the means and is unable to make offerings, a practitioner of the bodhisattva path should sell their own body or even the bodies of their children and wife.
One should make offerings not merely by selling one's body, but should even cut the flesh from one's own body to provide what is required, giving it all away.
How much more so should one provide external possessions; how could one give rise to a mind of stinginess?

Regarding the phrase "if there are [such people]": it means that even if the host has no possessions and must sell his own body or cut his own flesh, he would still endure such hardship to make offerings.
How could it be that when a donor invites a meal, one would not assign guest monks in due order to receive the invitation?
Therefore, if there are those who come to invite the assembly of monks, the guest monks have a share of the offerings, while the resident monk who heads the monastery does not.

One should appoint visiting monks in succession to attend the invitation. If one accepts the host’s invitation alone and does not appoint visiting monks to accept it, then the resident master of the monastery will incur immeasurable transgressions.
Those who are like animals are said to be contrary to human sentiment; they are no different from beasts. Because they lack the six points of harmony within, they are not [true monks].
Śramaṇa: To deviate from the Buddha’s mind above is to not belong to the lineage of Śākyamuni; therefore, to accept [an invitation] alone constitutes a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).
○ The twenty-seventh precept: Accepting Special Invitations.
If a Buddha’s disciple accepts special invitations for offerings and takes them for personal use, they commit an offense of secondary defilement.
For such offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions; yet by accepting a special invitation, one takes the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself.

Among the eight fields of merit, this constitutes using for one's own benefit the goods belonging to the Buddhas, the sages, the teachers and preceptors, parents, and the sick. Thus, one commits an offense of secondary defilement.

Regarding the phrase "If a Buddha’s disciple," etc.: it means that whenever any donor invites the Sangha for a meal, one must not privately accept an individual invitation, thereby causing these offerings to enter only one's own person rather than being shared with others. These offerings belong entirely to the Sangha of the ten directions;
all have an equal share. If a resident monk privately accepts an individual invitation and does not share it with visiting monks, [he commits an offense].
It is the same. For instance, it is like taking property belonging to the Sangha of the ten directions and using it for one’s own private benefit;

how could such a sin possibly be escaped? As for the eight fields of merit: first, the Buddhas who have attained the fruit; second, the noble ones who are on the path; third, the preceptor (upādhyāya); fourth, the teacher (ācārya);
fifth, the community of monks; sixth, one’s father; seventh, one’s mother; eighth, the sick. Thus, from the Buddhas above down to one’s parents...
The seven types of mothers are called the "Field of Reverence" (*guru-kṣetra*). The one type of sick person is called the "Field of Compassion" (*karuṇā-kṣetra*).

These eight together constitute the excellent fields for planting merit and cultivating wisdom. Regarding the items within these eight fields of merit: they belong to the Sangha of the ten directions.
Using them for public purposes yields merit; using them for private purposes incurs sin. This is because receiving a private invitation and using it for oneself constitutes a transgression.
This constitutes the transgression of a minor offense.
○ The twenty-eighth precept: Regarding the separate invitation of monks.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, there are ordained Bodhisattvas, lay Bodhisattvas, or any donors who invite the Sangha for the sake of merit...

When seeking to fulfill a vow through a field of merit, one should enter the monastery and inquire with the administrative official (*karmadāna*), saying, "I now wish to invite the Sangha to fulfill my vow.
The official shall reply, "If you invite according to the established order of succession, you will obtain the assembly of worthy and holy ones from the ten directions.

However, if worldly people separately invite five hundred arhats or bodhisattvas, it is not as good as inviting even a single ordinary monk (*pṛthagjana*) according to the monastic order. If one invites monks individually..."

This is the teaching of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Among the Seven Buddhas, there was no practice of separate invitations; it does not accord with the way of filial piety. If one intentionally invites the Sangha separately, one commits a minor offense (*āpatti*).

Regarding the phrase "if a son of the Buddha" and so forth, it means that there are Bodhisattvas who have shaved their hair, donned the dyed robes, and left the household life, and who have received the six grave precepts.
When a lay bodhisattva observing the twenty-eight minor precepts, or any donor who delights in practicing generosity,
makes a prayer or vows to be reborn in the heavens, among humans, or in the Western Land,
and requests the Sangha to fulfill this aspiration within the field of merit of the Triple Gem, they should enter the monastery and ask the administrator, saying: "I..."
"Such-and-such a person now wishes to invite a certain number of monks to offer prayers and seek the fulfillment of their vows. The administrator should reply:
"If you wish to invite monks, you must follow the protocol for sequential invitations. Since it is difficult to distinguish between ordinary persons and sages, one cannot select them arbitrarily.
By following the sequence, one effectively invites the assembly of worthy and holy monks from the ten directions. As for worldly people..."

To specifically invite five hundred arhats and bodhisattvas with a discriminating mind—thus selecting names and inviting individually—is not equal to the merit of inviting a single ordinary monk (pṛthagjana) from among the monks invited according to their established order. Why is this?
Because it involves a mind that dwells upon signs (nimitta). As for those who are invited individually...
This is the teaching of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Within my Buddha-dharma, there is no mind of discrimination, for it does not cling to signs (*nimitta*).

Furthermore, since the time of the Seven Buddhas, there has been no practice of requesting special invitations. To request the Dharma through such special invitations is to be contrary to the way of filial piety;
it violates the teachings of the Seven Buddhas above, deviates from the impartial mind of a Bodhisattva in the middle, and [contradicts... below.
One loses the merit of benefiting sentient beings. Therefore, if one intentionally invites the Sangha for separate offerings, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

**The Twenty-ninth Precept: Against Living by Wrong Livelihood** If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind and for the sake of profit and sustenance, sells the beauty of men or women; or prepares food with their own hands; or...

Grinding [grains], husking by hand, interpreting the signs of male and female [infants], deciphering the auspiciousness or misfortune of dreams, determining whether a child will be male or female, practicing incantations and crafts, training hawks,
compounding hundreds or thousands of varieties of poisonous drugs, snake venom, raw gold and silver poisons, and *gū* poisons—
doing these things entirely without a heart of compassion or filial piety; if one intentionally commits such acts, it constitutes a minor offense (*āpatti*).

Regarding the phrase "If a Buddha’s disciple," etc., it means: if a Buddha’s disciple does not practice the Bodhisattva path with a good heart, but rather, out of an evil mind, seeks wealth and profit to provide for themselves, engaging in various forms of wrong livelihood to sustain their own lives.
First, the trafficking of men and women in sexual favors severs the bonds of flesh and blood and defiles the family reputation.

Second, preparing food with one's own hands—grinding and pounding them oneself—is contrary to the monastic code of a bhikṣu, wherein a *śrāmaṇera* or lay attendant (*upāsaka*) performs the service of giving and receiving.

How could one permit such manual labor for one’s livelihood, thereby losing the dignified demeanor expected of a monk? However, if one has resolved to practice the Bodhisattva path and provides for others through physical labor, this may perhaps be permissible.

Third, they practice divination to distinguish male and female, determine fortune and calamity, and judge success and failure. Fourth, they interpret the auspiciousness and inauspiciousness of dreams;
they analyze human dream omens to ascertain good or bad fortune, and falsely determine whether a child will be male or female based on the principles of the Six Jia cycles.
Fifth, they employ incantations and arts to exorcise ghosts and spirits, perform various magical illusions and skilled crafts, and produce exquisite works of calligraphy and painting.
Sixth, the methods for training hawks: skillfully training hawks and dogs so that they can seize prey. Seventh, the compounding of a hundred kinds of poisonous drugs:

although there are hundreds of thousands of types of poison, here only two or three are briefly set forth. Snake venom harms humans, yet it also harms snakes. Regarding the production of gold and silver poisons:
the compounding of these poisonous drugs refers to causing copper and iron to produce gold and silver. [Poison] by means of *gū* (sorcery).
Various poisonous insects are combined to form a *gū* (a magical poison), which is then used as *gū*-poison to harm people and living beings.

Regarding these seven aforementioned types of transgressions committed intentionally, there is not a single thought of compassionate pity that views others as one's own sons or daughters, nor is there a single thought of filial obedience that views others as one's own father or mother. If one transgresses...
To do so intentionally constitutes a minor offense of defilement.
○ The thirtieth precept: Not Respecting Auspicious Times.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders the Triple Gem themselves while feigning intimacy and attachment, and speaks of emptiness with their mouth—
To engage in worldly affairs, acting as a go-between for laypeople to facilitate the sexual union of men and women, creating various bonds and attachments; or,

on the six days of fasting and during the three months of the long fast, to commit acts of killing, robbery, or theft, thereby violating the fast and breaking the precepts— these constitute minor offenses.

"If a Buddha’s disciple, with an evil mind," and so forth, means that they do not practice the bodhisattva path with a good heart, but rather because of an evil mind, they themselves slander the Triple Gem;
their physical karma is impure. They feign intimacy, and thus their mental karma is impure.
They speak of emptiness while their conduct remains within existence; thus their verbal karma is impure. Such are the three impurities of karma.

This purity is entirely a thorough penetration of an evil mind directed toward men and women, engaging in sexual union, and indulging in lustful sounds and beautiful forms—performing such acts that bind ordinary people.
Such persons are by no means liberated; they are those who slander the Triple Gem through their speech, their thoughts, and their bodies.
Regarding the six fast days and so forth, it is said that for this reason, one does not respect them.
It is the proper time. On the six days of the monthly fast and during the three months of the annual long fast, these are auspicious times and virtuous days and months;

one should exhaustively cultivate merit and practice goodness, for this is superior to other times and months. As for the six days of the monthly fast, they are the eighth and twenty-third of each month;
these are the days when Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, presides over the Southern Continent. The fourteenth... [and so forth].
19. As for the moon, the twenty-eighth day is the crown prince of the heavenly king; the fifteenth and the thirtieth days are the heavenly king himself.
Regarding the three months of the long fast (*trīṇi dīrghopavāsa-māsāni*), these are the first, fifth, and ninth months of each year.
These three months are called the "Three Auspicious Months" (*tri-śubha-māsāḥ*). They are the months when Śakra Devendra conducts his circuit of inspection. Within this celestial palace, there is...
The Great Precious Mirror: from the first month of the year, it illuminates Jambudvīpa in the south; in the second month, it illuminates Aparagoyānī in the west;
in the third month, it illuminates Uttarakuru in the north; in the fourth month, it illuminates Pūrvavideha in the east;
and in the fifth month, it again illuminates Jambudvīpa in the south. In this manner, it examines the good and evil of human beings three times over. As for ordinary people—
Every movement of thought and every stirring of the mind naturally manifests clearly within the mirror.
Therefore, during these days of the sun and moon, one ought to exhort others to observe the fasts and precepts, release living beings, and perform various meritorious deeds.
To do the opposite at such a time—committing acts of killing, robbery, breaking the fast, or violating the precepts—is why one incurs a minor offense.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind, as explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Formulation of Precepts" (Śīlasaṃvara-varga).
These ten precepts summarize the preceding text; they should be studied to encourage their cultivation and upheld with a reverent mind.

One should, from time to time, respectfully revere, uphold, and maintain [the precepts] so as not to lose them. Within the Great Collection (Mahāsaṃnipāta), there is a chapter on the formulation of precepts (*śīla-vinaya*) which further elucidates this meaning in detail.
○ The thirty-first precept: Not practicing redemption.

The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, after my parinirvāṇa, in this degenerate age, if you see non-Buddhists, various evil persons, or bandits who sell images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or one's parents;
or who sell the sūtras and the Vinaya; or who trade in bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
or even sell those bodhisattva-practitioners who have resolved their minds for enlightenment, making them servants or slaves for all manner of people, or employing them as officials' messengers—"
When a Bodhisattva sees such things, they should give rise to a mind of compassion and employ skillful means to rescue and protect them.

They should go everywhere to teach and transform others to acquire objects for the purpose of redeeming images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as all the sutras and vinayas of the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
If one does not redeem them, one commits a minor offense.

"Regarding 'after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa': this means that while the Buddha was in the world, such things did not exist; it is only after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, within this degenerate age, that such things occur.

If one sees those who do not realize their own minds, such as heterodox practitioners with false views, those who constantly disparage the Triple Gem, all manner of evil people, as well as plunderers, robbers, and thieves, who sell images of the Buddha."
The appearance of a Bodhisattva is like that of a father, while the appearance of a Buddha is like that of a mother.
Yet they destroy the Jewel of the Buddha; they sell the Sūtras and Vinaya, thereby destroying the Jewel of the Dharma; and they sell Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs, thereby destroying the Jewel of the Saṅgha.

It is not only the Three Jewels that they ruin; they also sell those who have resolved their minds for enlightenment—whether Bodhisattvas, laypeople, the fourfold assembly, or practitioners of the Way. Or...
They are sold to official families to serve as low-ranking attendants, or sold to all manner of people to be made into slaves.
When this bodhisattva perceives such suffering and hardship, he should give rise to a heart of compassion that seeks to uproot suffering and bestow happiness;
employing various skillful means, he should provide urgent rescue and protection in every way.

O donors, you should teach and transform others to take their wealth and property to redeem the forms and images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, making offerings to them according to the Dharma to protect the Buddha-jewel;
to redeem the various sutras and vinayas, circulating them according to the Dharma to protect the Dharma-jewel;
and to redeem bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, enabling them to leave behind suffering and hardship to practice the Way in peace and security, thereby protecting the Sangha-jewel. Thus it is.
Only by providing rescue and protection can one be called a child of the Buddha. If, upon seeing such matters, one does not act to redeem them, one commits a minor offense.

**The Thirty-second Precept: Against Harming Sentient Beings.** If a disciple of the Buddha, they must not keep swords, staves, bows, or arrows; nor may they sell with light scales or small measures, nor exploit their official status or power.

To seize the property of others; to bind others with a malicious intent; to ruin successful undertakings; or to raise cats, wildcats, pigs, and dogs—if one intentionally raises such creatures, one commits a minor offense.
"If a son of the Buddha does not [act] equally," it means that a son of the Buddha should take compassion as his fundamental principle.
He must not keep or store weapons such as swords, staves, bows, or arrows—evil instruments for harming living beings.

He must not engage in trade by buying low and selling high, using light scales and small measures, or practicing open deception and secret fraud to afflict and harm sentient beings. He must not rely upon the authority of government officials.
One must not, by leveraging power and influence, forcibly demand or greedily seize the wealth of others.
One must not further exploit official authority to commit evil harms or to bind and restrain individuals. One must not damage sentient beings once one’s own undertakings have been accomplished.
One must not keep cats or mongooses to catch mice as malevolent animals, nor raise pigs for profit, nor keep dogs to seize property. All of these [are forbidden].
To harbor an enemy within one's own kindness, to sustain life only to harm it, and to lose the thought of compassion—these are not things that a child of the Buddha should do.
If one intentionally sustains such a being, they commit a minor offense.
○ Thirty-third: The Precept Against Wrongful Mental Activity and Discursive Thought.
If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind, observes all men and women fighting, or armies, generals, and bandits fighting;
nor shall they listen to the blowing of conchs, drums, horns, or the playing of lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, or *konghou* lutes, nor to singing, shouting, or the music of courtesans.

One must not engage in the sounds [of gambling]. One must not play with *chūpú* (dice), *wéiqí* (go), *bōluósè xì* (Brahmasaṃsparśa), *tánqí* (board games), *liùbó* (six-sided dice), *pāi qù* (ball games), *zhìshí tóuhú* (stone-throwing and arrow-casting), *qiāndào bādào xíngchéng zhuàojìng* (games involving pulling paths, eight-row cities, or mirrors).
One must not use *shīcǎo* (millet stalks), willow branches, alms bowls, or skulls to perform divination.
One must not act as a messenger for thieves. None of these may be done; if one intentionally does so, it constitutes a light offense (*duṣkṛta*).
Regarding "defilements and offenses":

if a son of the Buddha, as one who is "equal to [those with] evil," refers to a bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind and is contemplating and observing within the mind, yet has not yet attained proficiency;
for fear that they might pursue external objects and give rise to emotional attachments, thereby giving rise to an evil mind—for this reason, they release...
One should contemplate all forms of play, dancing, and the like involving men and women;

one should contemplate all battles between two armies, as well as the fighting of soldiers, generals, plunderers, thieves, and so forth. These are things that a son of the Buddha ought not to contemplate.
Furthermore, one must not give oneself over to listening to the blowing of conch shells and horns, the beating of drums and cymbals, or the sounds of lords, ministers, commoners, and subjects.
The five-stringed *qin*, the twenty-five-stringed *se* made by Emperor Shun, the thirteen-stringed *zheng* made by Meng Tian,
the seven-holed bamboo flute, and the twenty-four-stringed *konghou* made by Shi Yan—
all such musical instruments, songs, shouts, and every sound of performance music as mentioned above— [are...]
Those things which a Son of the Buddha ought not to hear, nor ever engage in: gambling with dice; playing Go;
the game of *pārasika*; playing chess; the game of *tánqí* (striking balls) or cosmetics-box games; the sixfold game (*liùbó*) or *shuānglù*;
clapping balls, kicking round balls, throwing stones into pits, tossing arrows into jars, and tug-of-war.

Horses; the eight paths for selling weapons; the procession through the city, which is a dramatic performance from the Western Regions; the claw-mirror medicinal finger that reveals light; the milfoil stalks used for divining good and ill fortune;
the willow branches that immediately report calamities and blessings; and the alms bowl that reflects water to determine right and wrong.
The recitation of spells over skulls to predict fortune and calamity, as well as the aforementioned practices such as divination and geomancy, are things that a son of the Buddha ought not to do.
One must not accept commissions or orders from thieves; even at the cost of one's life, one must absolutely not engage in such acts.
As stated above, none of these should be performed by one who is not a son of the Buddha. If one should intentionally [engage in them]...
The author commits a minor offense.
○ Thirty-fourth: The Precept Against Briefly Thinking of the Lesser Vehicle.

If a Buddha’s disciple protects and upholds the prohibitive precepts, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, during the six periods of day and night, they shall read and recite these precepts. Just as...
Like a diamond; like one wearing a life-preserving float wishing to cross the great ocean; like a bhikṣu bound by grass.
One should constantly give rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna, knowing for oneself: "I am a Buddha-to-be," while the Buddhas are Buddhas who have already attained realization.

One should resolve upon bodhicitta, never letting it depart from the mind for even a single thought-moment. If one gives rise to a single thought of the Two Vehicles or of non-Buddhist paths, one commits a minor secondary offense.

Regarding the phrase "If a Buddha’s disciple protects and upholds," etc., it means that a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva guards and firmly maintains [the precepts], restraining the five sense faculties and ceasing [unwholesome] mental activity.

Amidst the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—and throughout the day and night, during the twelve periods of time, they should constantly and thoroughly read and savor the meaning, reciting and upholding them from memory; these are the Bodhisattva Precept Root Texts. Just as...
It is like a vajra: it can destroy all things, yet nothing can destroy it. Such is the firmness of this mindfulness.
Furthermore, it is like a merchant of old who, carrying a life-preserving float, crossed the sea. A rākṣasa came and begged for the float; the man would not give it to him.
Even when asked for a single coin or even a single strand of silk, he would not give it. Why? Because his life depended upon that float.
This is like a person who upholds the precepts wishing to cross the bitter sea of birth and death.

Even if they encounter the rākṣasa of craving and desire who offers a single boon, they will never comply. Why is this? Because their life depends upon the precepts. Therefore, the protection of the precepts is such as this.
Furthermore, it is like a bhikṣu of old who was plundered by bandits; the bandits bound this bhikṣu with grass. The bhikṣu...
One who upholds the precepts does not harm even a blade of living grass. Only when the King happened to pass by was he finally released and set free.
If this is the case for one who upholds the precepts of the Hīnayāna, how much more so for a Bodhisattva of the Mahāyāna? Therefore, one should always give rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna.

In every thought-moment, one has self-confidence; in every thought-moment, one has self-knowledge. One decides with certainty: "I am not yet a Buddha, but in the present and the future, I shall certainly become a Buddha.
