All Buddhas have already attained the perfection of the three bodies, are complete in the ten thousand virtues, and have exhausted the five stages of dwelling.
Second is death. This refers to one who has already become a Buddha. One who resolves upon the bodhicitta does so precisely because of this decisive faith and understanding;

for because this bodhicitta is firm, one holds it constantly in mind, never forgetting it, and is determined never to abandon the aspiration. How could there be any falling back into the two vehicles?
...the principle of this. Should one give rise to even a single thought of the Hīnayāna or non-Buddhist paths, one is no longer a child of the Buddha and will certainly commit a minor offense.
○ The Thirty-fifth Precept: Not Making Vows.
If you are a disciple of the Buddha, you should always make all manner of vows: to be filial toward your parents and respectful toward your teachers and the Sangha;

to pray for excellent teachers, fellow students, and virtuous spiritual friends who will constantly instruct you in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, as well as the Ten Stages of Departure, the Ten Stages of Nurturing, and the Ten Stages of Vajra-like Perfection.
The Ten Grounds. May I attain understanding and realization, practice according to the Dharma, and firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
Even at the cost of my body and life, may these never depart from my mind for even a single thought-moment. If any bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.
"Regarding the phrase 'If a Buddha-son always should,' etc.: it means that for a Buddha-son, making vows is not difficult; rather, one only fears a lack of constancy.

Therefore, one should always make vows, because the afflictions, karmic retributions, and obstacles of all sentient beings are inexhaustible, and thus the Bodhisattva’s making of all vows is likewise inexhaustible.
First, one should constantly vow to be filial and obedient to one's parents; second,"

First, may I always vow to be filial and obedient toward my teachers and the Sangha—where "teachers" refers to the three masters and "Sangha" refers to the seven witnesses—and likewise serve them with filiality as if they were my own parents.
Second, may I always vow to obtain a good teacher who provides guidance, and good fellow students who provide assistance and support.
Third, may I vow to encounter good spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who constantly instruct me and are thoroughly versed in the Mahayana sutras and vinaya.

Fifth, I vow to enter the Ten Abodes and attain the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Sixth, I vow to enter the Ten Practices and attain the cultivation of the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).
Seventh, I vow to enter the Ten Dedications and attain the perfect Middle Way contemplation.

Eighth, I vow to enter the stages of the Ten Sages and cultivate all practices perfectly, entering the Buddha-realm at an early date. Ninth, I vow that I may achieve thorough understanding in every detail and practice in accordance with the Dharma.
And they shall swiftly realize the fruit of Buddhahood. With ten vows, they firmly uphold the precepts and Dharma of all Buddhas;

even if they encounter adverse conditions, they would rather sacrifice their bodies and lives, even unto the point of death, never daring to depart from this mind that resolutely maintains the Buddha-precepts.
If a Bodhisattva does not make such vows as these, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
○ Thirty-sixth: The Precept Against Making Vows [to Renounce the Precepts].
If a Buddha’s disciple, having made the ten great vows, upholds the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha, they should make this vow, saying: "I would rather, with this very body..."

I would rather cast myself into a great pit of blazing, fierce fires or onto a mountain of knives than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time by engaging in impure conduct with any woman. Furthermore, I make this vow:
I would rather have my body bound all around by a thousand layers of glowing iron mesh than, with this body of broken precepts, ever accept anything from a faithful donor.

Regarding clothing, he further made this vow: "I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and endure great, raging flames with this mouth for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever, with this mouth of broken precepts, eat the food of a hundred flavors offered by a faithful donor.
He further made this vow: "I would rather lie upon this body on a floor of red-hot iron within a net of fierce, blazing fire..."
One should not, with this body of broken precepts, accept the hundreds of kinds of seats offered by faithful donors. Furthermore, one should make this vow:

"I would rather have this body pierced by three hundred spears for the duration of one kalpa or two kalpas, than ever, with this body of broken precepts, accept the medicines of a hundred flavors offered by faithful donors. Furthermore, one should make this vow: "I would rather..."
This body shall be cast into a cauldron of molten iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas;
one shall never, with this body of broken precepts, accept the thousand kinds of dwellings, houses, gardens, groves, fields, and lands offered by faithful donors. Furthermore, one makes this vow:
"I would rather have this body smashed to pieces with iron hammers, from head to foot until it is like fine dust, than ever again accept such offerings with this body of broken precepts."
While receiving the respectful prostrations of faithful donors, he further made this vow:
"I would rather have my two eyes gouged out with hundreds of thousands of hot iron knives and spears than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, look upon the beautiful forms of others."

He further made this vow: "I would rather have my sense organ of the ear pierced by a hundred thousand iron awls for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, listen to pleasant sounds. He further made this vow:
"I would rather have my nose cut off by a hundred thousand sharp blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily smell various fragrances. He further made...
I make this vow: I would rather have my tongue cut off by hundreds of thousands of sharp blades than ever, with a mind that has broken the precepts, eat the hundred-flavored pure food of others.

Again, I make this vow: I would rather have my body hacked and mangled with a sharp axe than ever, with a mind that has broken the precepts, crave pleasant tactile sensations. Again, I make this vow: may all sentient beings attain Buddhahood.
If a bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the phrase "if a son of the Buddha does not make [these vows]," etc., this refers back to what was stated above: having already made these ten kinds of great vows.
Furthermore, one is able to firmly uphold the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, never abandoning them from moment to moment.
One should further make these thirteen kinds of vows as follows. How does one make these vows? First, one makes this vow and strengthens it by saying:
"I would rather cast this body into a blazing, fierce fire than engage in impure conduct. This is the first kind of firm resolve.
I vow not to engage in unchaste conduct. Second, he further makes this vow to strengthen it, saying:
"I would rather respectfully prostrate before hot iron than [refuse] these six things: first, clothing; second, drink; third, food;
fourth, bedding and seats; fifth, medicine; sixth, houses, fields, and gardens. Regarding these six kinds of things, I firmly vow that my resolve shall not be in vain."
He accepted the offerings. Eighthly, he again made this vow to strengthen his resolve, saying:

"I would rather endure hundreds of thousands of instances of intense attachment to pleasant tactile sensations—namely, (1) the eye, (2) the ear, (3) the nose, (4) the tongue, and (5) the body—than allow these five types of objects to defile my six sense faculties.
Of the twelve kinds mentioned above, these are for one's own benefit; the following kind is for the benefit of others. Ten.
Repeating this three times, he further made this vow to strengthen it, saying: "May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood;

my words do not mean that I seek only my own purity and liberation. It is fundamentally for the sake of universally delivering all sentient beings so that they may all attain purity and liberation and fully realize Buddhahood. To thus establish such a vow and aspiration is called...
If a Bodhisattva does not make these four categories of thirteen kinds of vows, they commit a minor offense (light垢罪).
○ The thirty-seventh precept: Against Traveling During Times of Peril.

If a Buddha’s disciple, one should always practice *dhūta* during two periods of the year, sitting in meditation during winter and summer, and observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*). One should always use the *yǎng*...
A staff, soap powder, the three robes, a water flask, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, a mendicant’s staff, an incense burner, a water filter, a hand towel, and a knife.
Fire-sticks, tweezers, a corded bed, the Sūtras, the Vinaya, images of the Buddha, and images of Bodhisattvas—
these eighteen kinds of items always accompany the person when a Bodhisattva practices the dhūta austerities or travels abroad, journeying hundreds or thousands of li.

Regarding the dhūta practitioner: from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month—during these two periods—the eighteen items must always accompany the body like the two wings of a bird.
On the uposatha days, the newly initiated bodhisattva observes the uposatha every half-month and recites the ten grave precepts and the four...
Regarding the eighteen minor precepts: when reciting the precepts, one should do so before images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Whether it is a single person performing the *poṣadha* or one, two, three, up to a hundred thousand people, only one person shall recite them.

The reciter shall occupy a high seat while the listeners remain on lower seats. Each person shall don the nine-strip, seven-strip, or five-strip *kāṣāya* robe. This applies even during the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
In each case, act in accordance with the Dharma. When practicing *dhūta* austerities, do not enter dangerous places.

Whether it be national turmoil, an evil king, uneven terrain, dense vegetation, lions, tigers, wolves, water, fire, wind, calamities, bandits on the road, venomous snakes, or any other such perilous locations—none of these must be entered.
This applies whether one is practicing the *dhūta* path, or even during the summer retreat (*varṣā*). These are all dangers.
[He] shall not enter [such places]. If he enters intentionally, he commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the phrase "If a Buddha’s disciple should always... and so forth: "always" means one should constantly act in this manner. "The two seasons" refers to the two seasons of spring and autumn.
*Dhūta* is translated here as "shaking off"; it means to shake off adventitious afflictions (*kleśa*) and seek the Unsurpassed Way.

Regarding "winter and summer alike": this means that during the winter, when the cold is severe, and during the summer, when the heat is scorching, it is precisely the proper time to practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and sit in meditation.
One should observe the winter retreat (*hemanta*) and the summer retreat (*varṣā*), dwelling in a place of peaceful sustenance to cultivate the Buddha-way with diligent effort. Regarding "daily use":
this refers to the eighteen items, from the *śīrṣa-prasāda* (tooth-stick) up to the image of the Bodhisattva; these are the items regularly used by the sons of the Buddha (*buddhaputra*).

These items are not used only during the summer and winter retreats; rather, even during the two seasons of spring and autumn, when a bodhisattva practices *dhūta* (asceticism) by traveling far to other regions—whether journeying back and forth over distances of a hundred or a thousand *li*—these articles are always carried with him for practical use.
Regarding the *dhūta* practices, from the second section to the first part of the third, it correctly clarifies the *dhūta* observances for these two seasons.
These are the items for daily use. The two lines beginning with "Spring" clarify the spring season; the two lines beginning with "August" clarify the autumn season.
During these two seasons of spring and autumn, these eighteen kinds of objects must always be kept ready at hand, like the two wings of a bird.
With them, one may soar high and travel far without any hindrance. If...
Regarding "the *poṣadha* and so forth": *Poṣadha* is translated here as "performing the ritual to accomplish the task," and it is also called "confessing offenses face-to-face.

This refers to repenting one's transgressions before an image of the Buddha. It is said that because newly initiated bodhisattvas have inferior wisdom and strong habitual tendencies (*vijñāna*), they should perform the *poṣadha* every half-month during both the dark and light phases of the lunar cycle, constantly reciting the ten grave precepts and the forty-eight light precepts. Should they [fail to do so] when reciting...
One must certainly purify one’s own body and mind. One should recite the precepts before the physical images and forms of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the phrase "from one person to the *kāṣāya*," etc., this clarifies the ritual for reciting the precepts; it is essential to rely upon this method.
The two lines concerning the summer retreat (*varṣā*) express a sense of earnest care; they state that even during the two periods of *dhūta* practice, one should remain thus.
This also applies to the matters of entering the winter retreat (*hemanta*) and the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Each and every detail must further be performed in accordance with the Dharma.
As for those who practice *dhūta* austerities, this further clarifies that during these two seasons of *dhūta*, one must not travel about while disregarding hardships.

What is meant by "difficult places where one should not enter"? If a country is beset by calamities, such as the presence of venomous snakes and other perils, one must not enter any such dangerous locations.
It is not merely that one may not travel there for leisure when there is no business;

even if one is traveling for the sake of practicing *dhūta* austerities, upholding the Buddha-dharma, or relying on the Way, one should not approach such places—even during the winter retreat (*varṣā*) or summer retreat. One should remain far removed from them.

These various states of difficulty are places where one must not enter at all. If a disciple of the Buddha does not observe the Buddha’s precepts and yet deliberately enters them, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
"All" (*yi*) is a term signifying universal pervasion; "entirely" (*qie*) is a word denoting the ultimate limit.
Although the national calamities, the venomous snakes, and so forth are divided into the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), it is feared that this would not suffice to encompass them all.
...also. ○ The thirty-eighth precept concerning violating the order of seniority:
If a Buddha’s disciple should sit according to the proper sequence, those who received the precepts earlier shall sit in front, and those who received the precepts later [shall sit behind].
When sitting in the assembly, regardless of whether one is old or young— whether a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, a person of high status, a king, a prince, or even a eunuch or a slave—
one who has received the precepts first should sit in front, and those who have received them later should sit in order according to their seniority.
Do not be like the foolish outsiders, who sit without regard for age or precedence, lacking any sense of proper order.
Regarding the regulations for military slaves: within our Buddha-dharma, those who arrive first sit first, and those who arrive later sit later.
If a Bodhisattva fails to sit according to this sequential order of propriety, they commit a minor offense.

"If a disciple of the Buddha should act according to the 'equal' [rule]" means that acting "according to the Dharma" refers to sitting in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions. That is to say, regarding the precepts:

those who received them earlier should sit in front, and those who received them later should appropriately sit behind. This is not based on worldly distinctions of seniority such as age or birth year;
rather, one sits strictly according to the sequence of the ordination. This is explained clearly from the bhikṣus down to the slaves.
Those who receive the precepts are each categorized into distinct groups; the term "group" (類) signifies that each individual has their own specific meaning.
It is said that within the class of *bhikṣus* there is a sequence, and within the class of *bhikṣuṇīs* there is likewise a sequence.
Even among the classes of nobles, kings, princes, and even eunuchs or slaves, each must respectively sit according to the order of their prior reception of the precepts.

"Furthermore, 'there is nothing like the method of reaching [the goal]' and so forth clarifies the principle of violating the proper order of honor and status. This is precisely what one must guard against;
it means that one should not act in such ways. These ignorant and deluded outsiders—whether old or young—have neither seniority nor juniority."

Sitting without order is like the manner of soldiers or slaves. As for "my Buddha’s Dharma" and so forth, it means that within my Buddha’s True Dharma, those with seniority in precepts must certainly sit first, and those with juniority in precepts must sit later.
There is old and young; there is before and after; sitting follows a sequence, each point being in accordance with the Dharma. However, [the Bodhi...]
If one does not sit according to the Dharma in the proper sequence, whether once or repeatedly, one commits a minor offense.
○ The thirty-ninth precept: Not Cultivating Merit and Wisdom.
If a Buddha’s disciple, they should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings, establishing monastic dwellings, mountain forests, gardens, and fields. They should establish...
One should establish Buddhist stupas, places for winter and summer retreats and seated meditation, and all sites for the practice of the Way.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings, whether in times of illness or national calamity.
In times of peril from bandits; on the days of the passing away of one’s parents, brothers, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), or teachers (*ācārya*);
during the periods of seven days, fourteen days, twenty-one days, up to forty-nine days; as well as for all assemblies for offerings and seeking merit;

when traveling or engaging in livelihood; and in cases of being burned by great fires, swept away by great floods, or when ships are driven by black winds upon rivers and great oceans—[in all such instances, one should likewise recite Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya].
In the face of the perils of sea-rākṣasas, one should likewise recite, chant, and expound this sutra and its vinaya.
Even for all karmic retributions of sin—the three evil realms, the eight difficulties, and the seven heinous offenses; for those whose bodies are bound by cangues, shackles, pillories, and fetters;

and for those with excessive lust, anger, ignorance, or illness—all such persons should expound this sutra and its vinaya. If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not do so, they commit a minor offense.

Regarding defilements and transgressions: if a disciple of the Buddha constantly teaches and transforms all beings, he should lead them until they are all established [in the Way]. This encourages the cultivation of merit.
It means that one should always instruct and transform all sentient beings who possess consciousness, causing them to establish and construct monasteries.
One should extensively cultivate forests, mountains, gardens, orchards, fields, and lands; erect Buddha-stūpas; assemble the Saṃgha from the ten directions;
establish periods for retreat and Chan meditation; set up places for precepts and concentration; and establish all locations for the extensive practice of the path of wisdom.
By practicing merit in this manner—truly and without obscuring the law of cause and effect—one fulfills the *dāna-pāramitā* for both oneself and others.
Because it is like honey. Furthermore, a bodhisattva should, for those who are afflicted by many illnesses, lecture upon this sutra and its vinaya;
this is the cultivation of wisdom (prajñā-bhāvanā). It is said that a bodhisattva should expound and proclaim the Mahayana sutras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings.
Not only this, but when a person is afflicted by illness, or during times of great national calamity, or the threat of bandits and thieves;
on the days of the death of one's parents, brothers, preceptors (upādhyāya), or teachers (ācārya);
and on the first, second, and even the seventh week—on these occasions, one should likewise lecture upon and propagate this Mahāyāna sūtra and vinaya, or [practice] all forms of cultivation.
Those who hold fast-day assemblies seeking blessings and merit, those who travel to and fro, those engaged in livelihoods and industries,
and even those facing the calamities of being consumed by great fires, swept away by great floods, having their ships tossed by black winds,

or encountering the perils of rākṣasas in rivers, streams, and the great ocean— should likewise read, recite, explain, and expound this Mahāyāna sūtra and vinaya, and [protect themselves] from all evils.

Regarding the karmic causes, effects, and retributions—the three evil realms, the eight difficulties, and the seven obscurations; being bound by handcuffs and fetters, with hoods and shackles upon the neck, and constrained at the five points of the body;
abounding in lust, anger, and delusion, and suffering many illnesses—for each of these hardships, one should lecture upon this Mahāyāna Sūtra and Vinaya.
Such is the cultivation of wisdom through reality, which brings benefit to infinite beings and fulfills the *paramitas* for oneself and others.
If, for the sake of the *pāramitās*, a newly initiated bodhisattva does not thus cultivate the two kinds of adornments—merit and wisdom—they commit a minor offense (*laghu-pāyantika*).
These eight difficulties refer to the eight difficulties of the "Crown Stage" (*mūrdha-bhūmi*); as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, these are the eight difficulties within the realm (*dhātu*).
They are: the three evil destinies, the northern continent (*Uttarakuru*), lack of sensory faculties, being before the Buddha, and being after the Buddha.
Worldly wisdom, eloquence, and brilliance—these belong to the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva).
These nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind; they shall be explained in the Chapter on the Brahma-Altar (Brahmāyatanika-varga).
Thus, these nine precepts conclude the preceding section. One should train oneself to respectfully cultivate them, uphold them with reverence, and guard them with care so as not to lose them.
The final sentence states that within this major work there is a "Chapter on the Brahma-Altar," which shall be explained in detail later.
[Section] Forty: On the Prohibition Against Discrimination in Bestowing the Precepts.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, when bestowing the precepts upon others, one must not practice discrimination.
This applies to all kings, princes, ministers, officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, laywomen, male and female libertines, and even the eighteen Brahmā heavens."
The devas of the six heavens of desire, those without sexual organs, those with both sexual organs, eunuchs, male and female servants, and all spirits and ghosts may all receive the precepts.
One should instruct them that the robes they wear must all be of dyed colors to correspond with the Way;
they should be dyed blue, yellow, red, black, or purple. All dyed garments, even down to bedding and mats, must be of dyed colors; as for the robes worn on the body, they must likewise be so.
Regarding all dyed colors: in whatever kingdom one may be, whatever clothing the people of that land wear, a bhikṣu must always differ from their secular attire.
When wishing to receive the precepts, one should ask: "In this present life, have you not committed any of the seven heinous crimes?

A Bodhisattva Dharma Master must not confer the precepts upon someone who has committed one of the seven heinous crimes in this present life. The seven heinous crimes are as follows: [text continues].

Drawing blood from the body of a Buddha; killing one’s father; killing one’s mother; killing one’s preceptor (upādhyāya); killing one’s teacher (ācārya); causing a schism in the Saṃgha that obstructs the turning of the Wheel of Dharma;
and killing an arhat—if one possesses these seven heinous offenses, one cannot receive the precepts in this present life. All other persons may fully receive the precepts.
According to the dharma for those who have left the household life, one does not prostrate to kings, nor does one prostrate to parents, nor to the six types of relatives.

If one lacks respect and fails to honor the spirits and deities, yet understands the Dharma Master’s words, and there are those who come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* seeking the Dharma,
yet the Bodhisattva Dharma Master, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, does not immediately bestow the precepts upon all these sentient beings,
they commit a minor offense.
The Buddha said: "O Sons of the Buddha," when bestowing the precepts upon all people, one must not give rise to a mind of discrimination.
From kings and princes down to all spirits and ghosts, there is no one who cannot receive the precepts;
they must not be discriminated against, and the precepts should be bestowed upon them all. One should instruct them regarding the reach of their own bodies.

Regarding the differences in secular dress: since one has already received the precepts, what kind of appearance and demeanor should one adopt? One should be taught to wear robes of "ruined color" (kasāya) as a representation of a practitioner.

Because such a person corresponds with the Way, all items—specifically the *kāṣāya*, but including all meditation garments, meditation skirts, and bedding—are dyed with colors that blend the five primary hues.
It is not only the *kāṣāya* that must be dyed in ruined colors; everything else is likewise so treated.
Whatever one wears upon the body should all be dyed with a color that signifies transformation.

While the clothing worn by people in all lands naturally employs the five secular colors, most people dye them in only one of those colors. We, the bhikṣus and sons of the Buddha, must all be distinct from others.
The laity have their own lay garments, and the Saṃgha has its monastic robes; we should always differ from them.

Furthermore, if one wishes to reach the point where the precepts cannot be obtained: although the preceding section did not specify what was to be excluded, even within that lack of exclusion there are certain things that ought to be excluded.
How should they be excluded? At the time of receiving the precepts, one should ask:
"Have you, in this present life, ever committed any of the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) or other such sins? If they answer "No," then they are not excluded. If they answer...

It is said that there are. A Dharma Master must not bestow the precepts upon those who have committed the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*). The seven heinous offenses are: first, shedding the blood of a Buddha;
second, killing one’s father; third, killing one’s mother; fourth, killing one’s *upādhyāya*; fifth, killing one’s *ācārya*;

sixth, disrupting the *saṃgha* that performs the *karmavācanā* and turns the wheel of the Dharma; and seventh, killing a noble being (*ārya*). If one possesses these seven heinous offenses, one does not obtain the precepts. This is so.
One must exercise discernment regarding these. Beyond this, all other persons may receive the precepts; therefore, there is no need for such discernment.

As for those who have left the household life and so forth, it is said that since they are children of the Buddha, they transcend worldly dharmas and thus ought not to perform worldly acts of prostration toward kings or parents. This does not mean they should not see kings or their parents.
It is out of this that arrogance arises toward one's mother. One does not revere the six types of kin, nor does one engage in frequent social visits with them.

One does not revere ghosts and spirits, nor does one perform acts of flattery or profane ritual. This is not to say that one should give rise to contempt toward the six types of kin or toward ghosts and spirits;
rather, it means that as a son of the Buddha, one should transcend the mundane world and not be constrained or bound by worldly etiquette. However—

Regarding "one who understands the Dharma Master’s speech": this refers simply to one who understands extensively and comprehensively, and who is able to fully comprehend the language of the Dharma Master.
If someone comes from as near as a hundred *li* or as far as a thousand *li* to request the precepts, the Bodhisattva Dharma Master should grant them the ordination.
However, if [the Master] acts with an evil mind, jealousy, anger, resentment, or regret, and does not...
To immediately bestow the precepts upon all sentient beings [without due cause] constitutes a minor offense (light defilement). **Forty-first:
The Precept Against Acting as a Teacher for the Sake of Profit.** If a Buddha’s disciple, when teaching and inspiring faith in others, acts as a teacher of instruction for another person—
When one sees a person who wishes to receive the precepts, one should instruct them to request two masters: an Upādhyāya and an Ācārya. The two masters should ask:
"Do you have any of the seven obstructing offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*)? If the candidate currently possesses any of the seven obstructing offenses, the masters should not confer the precepts upon them.

If they are free from the seven obstructing offenses, they may confer the precepts. If there are those who have violated the ten grave precepts (*daśa-uttarāpatti*), they should be instructed to perform repentance.
Before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, one should recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts during the six periods of the day and night.

With utmost sincerity, one should prostrate before the thousand Buddhas of the three periods of time until a "good sign" (*lakṣaṇa*) is seen. This may take one week, two or three weeks, or even up to a year;
one must see a good sign. A good sign is when a Buddha comes to rub the crown of one's head, or when one sees radiance, flowers, and various extraordinary phenomena.
One will then be able to extinguish the offense. If there are no auspicious signs, although one performs repentance, it is of no benefit;

such a person shall not receive the precepts in this present life, yet they will gain increased merit from the act of receiving them. If one has violated any of the forty-eight minor precepts, one may repent before another person (pratimukha-vinaya), and the offense will then be extinguished.
This is not the same as the case of the seven grave prohibitions (*saptāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, the instructor in this Dharma must understand each of these matters thoroughly. If...
They do not understand the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, nor the characteristics of what is light or heavy, or what is right or wrong.

They do not understand the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the nature of the stage of practice through habituation (śikṣā-mārga-gotra), the nature of growth and nourishment (caryā-prakṛti-gotra), the nature of the lineage of the essence (gotra-bhūta-gotra), the unbreakable nature (abhedyatva-gotra), the nature of the path of cultivation (mārga-gotra), and the nature of perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi-gotra).

Furthermore, they do not attain any of these dharmas regarding the various degrees of meditative practice and its entry and exit, the ten factors of dhyāna (daśa-dhyānāṅga), or all the dharmas of conduct.
This is acceptable. However, if a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and fame, seeks and demands excessively through improper means, greedily coveting disciples,
and falsely pretends to understand all the sutras and vinayas for the sake of offerings— thus deceiving both themselves and others—
then one who bestows the precepts upon such a person commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the phrase "if a Buddha-son teaches and transforms others," it means that when a Bodhisattva wishes to instruct,
transform, and open the minds of all people so that they give rise to faith, the Bodhisattva provides such exhortation to others.
As one who acts as a guiding Dharma Master for others, upon seeing someone who desires to receive the precepts, the Dharma Master should first instruct that person to request [the precepts].
The two masters—the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya—should ask the candidate for ordination: "Do you have any of the seven obstructing offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*)?
If the candidate has committed any of the seven obstructing offenses in their present life, the masters should not confer the precepts upon them.
If one is free from the seven obstacles (*saptāvaraṇa*), one may be granted the precepts. The above clarifies that conferring the precepts upon others must not be done arbitrarily;

it must necessarily be performed by two masters together. Regarding those who have committed transgressions: once the precepts have been received, even if one should happen to violate them, how should one proceed?
One must not act as a master for the sake of profit, nor fail to clarify the gravity of the offense and perform repentance.
Regarding these rituals, it is improper to indiscriminately equate them with the seven grave offenses (saptātyaya) and thus abandon them without instruction; neither approach is acceptable.

Furthermore, if one has committed the ten major transgressions, when instructing them on repentance, they should stand before images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas during the six periods of the day and the six periods of the night, constantly reciting the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts.
With a heart of supreme sincerity, they must offer earnest and fervent prayers and perform prostrations.
Prostrate before the thousand Buddhas of the three ages and seek a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*).
Whether it appears after one seven-day period, or two or three, up to seven seven-day periods, or even a year, you must ultimately see a favorable sign. As for these favorable signs:

whether at the place where you perform repentance, or at the place where you practice seated meditation, or within a dream while sleeping, there may be a manifestation such as a Buddha personally touching your crown, or you may behold radiant light and flowers.

By means of these various extraordinary signs, one may verify that one’s own flowers of transgression have withered away, that karmic obstructions have been eliminated, and that the precept-body has been restored.
If such auspicious signs do not appear, then even if one prays with diligent earnestness, the mind will not be single-minded and nothing will be moved;
thus, the repentance will be of no benefit, and this person shall not attain [liberation] in their present body.
Furthermore, although one may merely be able to increase the benefits of receiving the precepts in the future, this explains the method for repenting the ten grave offenses (*daśa-guruka-āpatti*).

As for those who have committed the forty-eight [light offenses] and so forth—should they happen to commit any of these forty-eight light offenses—they must simply, before the ten masters and the presiding head, earnestly pray with supplication and repent of their transgressions. Immediately...
It is then extinguished and removed. This clarifies the method for repenting the forty-eight minor transgressions.
It differs from the "seven prohibitions" (saptāvaraṇa) in that it states both these grave and minor offenses can be repented of, unlike the seven prohibitions where repentance is not permitted.
Thus, within each of these methods of repentance, the preceptor should properly and thoroughly [instruct] one by one.

Only after one has contemplated and understood [the teachings], and attained clear and correct realization, may one act as a teacher for others. Regarding the phrase "if one does not understand" and so forth:

it means that if one acts as a teacher for others merely for the sake of gain and offerings, yet lacks understanding of the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, then one will mistake the light for the heavy and the heavy for the light, taking what is right to be wrong and what is wrong to be right.

Furthermore, they do not understand the principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way. They do not understand the nature of the seeds cultivated during the ten stages of the beginner (*ādikarmika*);
the nature of growth during the ten practices of the intermediate stage (*madhyama-kalyāṇika*); the nature of the seeds during the ten dedications of the superior stage (*uttama-kalyāṇika*);
the indestructible nature during the ten stages of the noble state (*āryabhūmi*); and the nature of the seeds on the path of equal enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*).

Within the Middle Way of Wondrous Enlightenment lies the nature of Perfect Awakening. One who does not understand these six natures will remain uncertain regarding the extent of their contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) throughout the stages of the three sages, the ten saints, and the two awakenings.
For instance, within the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) predominates while the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) is slight;

within the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), the contemplation of the provisional predominates while the contemplation of emptiness is slight; and within the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*) predominates while the contemplations of emptiness and the provisional are slight.

Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), from the first stage up to before the sixth stage, non-conceptual observation (*animitta-vipaśyanā*) is slight while conceptual observation (*sanimitta-vipaśyanā*) is predominant.

From the fifth stage up to before the seventh stage, conceptual observation is slight while non-conceptual observation is predominant. From the eighth stage onward, including the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*), there is exclusively non-conceptual observation.
At the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), it is the observation of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*). Therefore, it is said that [the observations] are "more or less."

This refers to the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). "Entering and exiting" means emerging from and entering into meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The ten factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*) have been explained previously;

these are the methods of contemplation cultivated within the four dhyānas. Thus, it is said that one enters and exits these ten types of contemplative methods within the ten factors of dhyāna-concentration.
Regarding all such dharma-gates of contemplative practice, if one does not penetrate, understand, or attain the essential meaning within these dharmas,
how could one possibly serve as a teacher for others? As for those referred to as "bodhisattvas" who, failing to understand such dharmas,
nonetheless act as teachers to others out of a desire for gain and sustenance— they are so called [only in name].
Because they have heard [these things], they give rise to a mind of evil seeking and excessive craving. The teacher initiates it, and the disciples harmonize with it.
Both teacher and disciple, for the sake of greed for profit, both manifest hypocrisy: they do not understand but claim to understand;

they are not proficient in the sūtras and vinaya but claim to be proficient in the sūtras and vinaya. For the sake of clothing, food, and offerings, they deceive themselves and deceive others. Therefore...
To bestow the precepts upon another person [who is not a fit candidate] constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).

**The Forty-second Precept: Prohibiting the Exposition of the Precepts for Evil Persons.** If a Buddha’s disciple, for the sake of receiving offerings, should expound the Bodhisattva precepts before those who have not yet received them—whether they be followers of external paths (tīrthikas) or others—[it is a violation].
One must not preach these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas before wicked people. One must also not preach them before those with false views, except for kings;
to all others, they must not be preached. Such wicked people do not receive the Buddha’s precepts and are called "beasts";
life after life they do not see the Triple Gem, being like wood or stone, devoid of mind. They are called "heretics," for such people with false views are like wooden stumps.
It is different. If a Bodhisattva, before such wicked people, preaches the seven admonitions of the Buddha, they commit a minor offense (light impurity).
Regarding the phrase "If a disciple of the Buddha must not, etc.," it means that one who is capable of explaining the Dharma must not preach indiscriminately out of greed for profit.
To give drink to one who is thirsty, the flavor of the water is sweet; to seek clarity in the darkness, the function of the lamp is essential.
It is great. For this reason, one must never preach these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas before those who have not received the full ordination or before non-Buddhists and evil persons.
Not only in these cases, but even before those with false views, one must likewise refrain from preaching them.

"Excluding kings" means that the Tathāgata has previously entrusted the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha to kings and ministers to protect them, so that they may abide long in the world, extinguish evil and give rise to good, and cause both the royal way and the Buddhist way to flourish together.
Regarding all Buddhist activities performed, it is not appropriate to conceal or suppress them; therefore, kings are excluded. All other heterodox and erroneous [teachings]...
Why is it that one must not preach this in the presence of others? It is because such people are a class of evil persons who do not receive the Mahāyāna precepts and teachings of all the Buddhas;
though they have eyes, they are like the blind; though they have ears, they are like the deaf;
they are like animals, lacking wisdom and failing to understand human principles; they are destined to fall into the three miserable realms, life after life and age after age.

They do not hear the names of the Triple Gem; they are like wood or stone, for they do not recognize nor give rise to the mind that is neither born nor extinguished—the indestructible essence of the vajra.
For this reason, they are called non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Such people of false views are no different from pieces of wood or lumps of stone.
Just as the dragon heard the Dharma and awakened to the Way, so too did the python hear the *chán* (repentance) and [attain realization].
He was reborn in heaven. When Master Sheng preached the Dharma, even the stubborn rocks nodded their heads in response. Can a human being truly be less than an animal or a stone?
Yet, if a Bodhisattva were to preach these Great Precepts of the Seven Buddhas and the Thousand Buddhas before such evil people, they would commit a minor offense (light impurity).
○ Forty-third: The Precept Against Receiving Alms Without Shame.

If a disciple of the Buddha has left the household life with faith and received the Buddha’s true precepts, yet then gives rise to the thought of violating these holy precepts, they shall not receive the offerings of any donors (*dānapati*).
Furthermore, they shall not walk upon the ground of the kingdom, nor shall they drink from the waters of the kingdom.
The King’s Water. Five thousand great ghosts constantly block his path ahead. The ghosts cry out, "Great thief!
Whether he enters a room, a city, or a house, the ghosts further sweep away his footprints. All people of the world revile him, saying, "A thief within the Buddha-dharma.
No sentient being wishes to see him with their eyes; such a person who violates the precepts is no different from a beast, no different from a block of wood. If...
Therefore, one who destroys the right precepts commits a minor offense.
As for the phrase "if a Buddha-son with faith," it means that when a Buddha-son first resolves his mind to leave the household life, he is able to abandon all biased and heterodox views;
at the time he comes to receive the great, bright, precious precepts of all Buddhas, his mind is fundamentally upright.
It is fitting that such a person should receive the offerings of devas and humans. However, as days and years pass, they become lax in their observance and give rise to arrogance;
thus, conceiving faithless thoughts and biased, deviant notions, they violate the great precepts of the Buddhas.
How could such a person still be entitled, as before, to receive the offerings of kings, princes, ministers, lay devotees, elders, and householders?
"Regarding the various offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine provided by donors:
'nor may one accept them as equals' means that it is not merely inappropriate to receive such offerings; furthermore, one must not set foot upon the land of a king."
One walks upon this ground; there is no other place for one's feet to rest. One must not drink even a single drop of the king’s water, for it is difficult to digest.

Regarding the "five thousand" and so forth: it means that if the five root precepts are maintained with purity and not violated, then five thousand benevolent spirits will provide protection and assistance.
If one is negligent and commits transgressions, then five thousand malevolent ghosts will [take their place].
Because it subdues demons, [the deity] constantly blocks its path, turning blessings into calamities. When the ghost says, "A great thief has arrived;
his footprints, etc.," this expresses the extreme degree to which the spirit loathes it—such that even its tracks are not tolerated, let alone its physical form.
When it says, "All people of the world... do not wish to see it, etc.," this expresses the extreme degree to which humans loathe it. As for its...
One does not even wish to see the physical form of such a person with one's own eyes, much less associate or dwell with them.
Therefore, those who violate the precepts are detested by both spirits and humans; they are loathed by non-humans as well.

Such people find no place in the human realm and ought to fall into the three miserable realms, where they are indistinguishable from animals or mere pieces of wood. If one willfully abandons right faith and destroys the precepts...
Regarding the precept of right morality: if one lacks a sense of shame and remorse yet accepts the offerings of others, one commits a minor offense.
The forty-fourth: The Precept Against Not Making Offerings to the Scriptures.

If a disciple of the Buddha, they should always with a single mind receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas. Even if they must flay their own skin to serve as paper and pierce...

Using blood as ink and marrow as water, one shall break bone to fashion brushes and transcribe the Buddha’s precepts. One should likewise transcribe and maintain them upon birch bark, rice-husk paper, silk, or bamboo slips.
One should always use the seven precious gems, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels to construct cases and bags for the volumes of the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Should one fail to make such offerings in accordance with the Dharma, one commits a minor offense.

"O sons of the Buddha, you should always... and so forth, means that the sons of the Buddha should constantly and single-mindedly take up this Mahāyāna sutra and vinaya, receiving and upholding it, upholding and reading it, reading and reciting it, and thus disseminate this profound and wondrous Dharma according to the Dharma.
How does one disseminate it? There are two ways to disseminate it: first, one should be prepared to sacrifice body and life, even flaying one's own skin...

One should use paper as the substrate, draw blood for ink, use marrow as water, and break bones for pens to transcribe each and every one of these Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, so that they may be circulated.

Second, one should relinquish wealth and treasures, and instead use tree bark, grain, paper, silk, bamboo, or cloth to transcribe and uphold them, so that they may be circulated. How should one make offerings?
One should constantly provide offerings using the seven treasures— gold, silver, coral, conch-shell, amber, rose-colored gems, and lapis lazuli—
as well as priceless and most precious incense, flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels,

fashioned into boxes and bags to store and preserve the volumes of the Sūtras and Vinaya for the purpose of making offerings. To thus circulate and make offerings [to the Dharma] is truly to make offerings to the Buddha.
Disciple, if one does not circulate and make offerings [to this teaching] in accordance with the Dharma, one commits a minor offense. **The Forty-Fifth Precept:
Not Transforming Sentient Beings.** If a Buddha’s disciple constantly gives rise to a heart of great compassion, and upon entering any city, town, house, or dwelling, sees any sentient being...
When giving birth, one should proclaim: "All you sentient beings, you should all receive the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts.
If one sees cattle, horses, pigs, sheep, or any other animals, one should mentally contemplate and verbally say: "You are animals; arouse the Bodhicitta.
Thus, wherever the Bodhisattva enters—whether in mountains, forests, rivers, or fields—he causes all sentient beings to arouse the Bodhicitta. This is...
If a bodhisattva does not teach and transform sentient beings, they commit a minor offense.

Regarding the phrase "if a son of the Buddha constantly arouses [compassion]," it means that when a son of the Buddha constantly arouses great compassion to uproot the suffering of others, should he enter any city, town, or dwelling and see sentient beings, he ought to proclaim: "You all..."

Sentient beings each possess the precept-body of Buddha-nature. From beginningless time until this present life, because you did not uphold the precepts, you have transmigrated through the various realms of existence.
Now that you have awakened to your former errors and abandoned evil for good, [you shall attain liberation].
Everyone should receive and uphold the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Precepts, prohibiting such actions for the future so that they never arise again as evil karma.

If one sees cattle or other such beings, it is said that not only should humans be instructed, but even animals such as oxen, horses, pigs, and sheep should be addressed with the thought and words: "Although you are..."
"Beasts and birds all possess the Buddha-nature and the essence of the precepts; they should therefore give rise to the aspiration for supreme Bodhi, lest they fall into further delusion.
As for the phrase "Bodhisattvas and others," it means that such instruction does not stop merely with humans and domestic animals.
He shall travel afar to all places— mountains, forests, rivers, and fields— and whenever he sees any sentient being,
he shall cause them all to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhicitta, so that they may never again fall into delusion.
If this Bodhisattva sees any sentient being and fails to teach and transform them so as to cause them to resolve their minds [on enlightenment], he commits a minor offense (light defilement).

**The Forty-sixth Precept: Teaching the Dharma Unlawfully** If a disciple of the Buddha constantly practices teaching and transformation, giving rise to a heart of great compassion, and enters the homes of donors or among all the noble classes, they must not stand while preaching the Dharma to laypeople.
They should sit upon a high seat before the assembly of laypeople to preach the Dharma.

A preceptor bhikṣu must not stand upon the ground to preach the Dharma to the fourfold assembly or laypeople. When preaching the Dharma, the Dharma-preacher shall occupy a high seat, provided with offerings of incense and flowers;

the members of the fourfold assembly who listen shall sit on lower seats, showing filial obedience to their parents and respectful compliance with the teacher’s instructions, just as a Brahmin serves the sacrificial fire.
If the one preaching the Dharma does not preach in accordance with the Dharma, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
"Regarding the phrase 'if a Buddha-son constantly practices,' etc.: it means that when a Buddha-son constantly performs the bodhisattva practice to teach and transform all sentient beings,
and gives rise to this great compassion to uproot their suffering, whether he enters the homes of noble patrons who are fond of giving and practices renunciation,
or stands among the vast assembly of the fourfold community, he must not stand upon the ground himself [without treading on mats]."
When preaching the Dharma to laypeople, how should one preach? One should prepare a high Dharma-seat before the assembly of laypeople and show respect for the Dharma-preacher.
It is appropriate that the Dharma-preacher ascends the seat and preaches according to the Dharma.

A bhikṣu who is a Dharma-preacher must by no means remain standing on the ground in a state of self-deprecation while preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly and laypeople, causing them to [conceive]...
This is pride. If one truly intends to preach the Dharma for the sake of the assembly, it is only proper that the Dharma Master sit upon a high seat.
The listeners should arrange incense and flowers as offerings according to the Dharma and maintain sincerity in their three karmas;
only then may the Dharma Master preach in accordance with their capacities. The fourfold assembly of listeners should each be categorized by their type and arranged in successive order below.
One should sit as if serving one's parents with filial piety—revering the teacher without arrogance and following their instructions without opposition.
Furthermore, one should be like a Brahmin tending the sacred fire—diligent without indolence and respectful without negligence.
When both speaker and listener act in this manner, they benefit both themselves and others, and their efforts will not be in vain. If, however, the person who speaks...
To preach in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
○ The forty-seventh precept on unlawful restrictions:
"If, O Sons of the Buddha, there are those who have received the precepts with faith—including kings, crown princes, officials of the hundred ranks, and the fourfold assembly—"
My son, relying on your own noble status, you have brought about the destruction of the Buddha-dharma and its precepts.

You have openly established restrictive laws to control my fourfold assembly of disciples, forbidding them from leaving the household life to practice the Way, nor permitting the creation of images, stupas, or the scriptures and Vinaya.

You have established a central authority to govern the masses, requiring monks to register their names and records, while placing Bodhisattvas and Bhikṣus on the ground and allowing laypeople to occupy high seats—thus widely propagating what is contrary to the Dharma.
This is contrary to the Dharma. It is like a soldier or a slave serving a master; yet a Bodhisattva, who ought to receive the offerings of all people, instead becomes a messenger for officials.
This is neither Dharma nor Vinaya. If kings or high officials have good intentions and receive the Buddha’s precepts, they must not commit such a sin of destroying the Triple Gem.
To intentionally act as a destroyer of the Dharma constitutes a minor offense (light impurity).

"If all Buddha-sons are equal" means that whether monastics or laypeople, as soon as these Buddha-sons take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the Great Precepts with right faith and a sincere heart,
they are all persons within the Buddha-realm and not those excluded from it.
Whether they be kings, crown princes, officials, or disciples of the fourfold assembly, it is only right that they provide protection and assistance, enabling them to enter [the Way].

Regarding the practice of the Way: should one, relying on the high status and nobility of one’s own position, give rise to a mind of arrogance (*māna*), thereby destroying and severing the Buddha-dharma and the precepts;
should one manifest ostentatious activities and impose restrictive regulations that constrain my fourfold assembly of disciples, causing the Three Jewels not to flourish;
should one prohibit those who have left the household life from practicing the Way, thereby severing the Sangha Jewel; nor should one fail to permit it—[such actions must be avoided].

To construct images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas while severing the Buddha-Jewel; to prohibit the construction of Buddhist stupas and the copying of the sutras and vinaya while severing the Dharma-Jewel;

and furthermore, to establish official ranks for administration, to regulate the fourfold assembly, to arrange registers, and to record the names of monks so that not a single one may possess autonomy—this is what Bodhisattva-bhikṣus ought to [oppose].
The high seat is instead placed on the ground, while the white-robed laypeople—who ought by right to stand on the ground—are instead made to occupy the high seat.
In this manner, such perversions and widespread unrighteous acts contrary to their own interests proceed, much like soldiers toward their commander or slaves toward their master.
This brings my fourfold assembly to a state where there are those who cannot bear to see or hear it, and as for the Bodhisattvas...
"Kū, it is only right that you should receive the offerings and alms of kings, crown princes, and all officials; this is the correct principle.
Yet, instead, you act as a servant for secular and official households—this is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya.
How could this be reasonable? If kings and officials have cultivated good intentions and entered this Dharma-gate to receive the great precepts of the Buddha,"
Do not, under any circumstances, commit such transgressions as destroying the Triple Gem, which will bring about inexhaustible evil retributions in the future.
If one deliberately creates the conditions for the destruction of the Dharma in violation of this, one commits a minor offense (light垢罪).
Forty-eighth: Violating the Precepts of the Dharma.

If a disciple of the Buddha has left the household life with a sincere heart, yet for the sake of fame and profit preaches the Buddha’s precepts before kings and high officials, and arbitrarily subjects bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or disciples of the bodhisattva precepts to acts of restraint and bondage.
It is like the law for prisoners or the law for military slaves; it is like worms within a lion’s body devouring the lion’s own flesh, rather than other external insects.
In this same way, O Son of the Buddha, one destroys the Buddha-dharma oneself; it is not externalists or celestial Māras who can destroy it.
Those who have received the Buddha-precepts should protect the Buddha-precepts as they would cherish an only son or serve their parents; they must not violate or break them. And...
When a bodhisattva hears the sound of non-Buddhists and evil persons slandering the Buddha’s precepts with malicious words,
it is no different from three hundred spears piercing their hearts or a thousand swords and ten thousand clubs beating their bodies.

They would rather enter hell and remain there for a hundred kalpas than hear even a single malicious word that breaks the Buddha’s precepts, much less break the Buddha’s precepts themselves or teach others to do so.
These are the causes and conditions for destroying the Dharma, and they also lack a heart of filial piety. If one intentionally commits such acts, one incurs a minor offense (light impurity).

Regarding the phrase "if a Buddha’s disciple with a good [mind]," etc.: it means that when a Buddha’s disciple first resolves their mind to leave the household life, there is no thought that is not upright and no conduct that is not dignified.
What kind of good intention was this? Yet, as the Dharma persists over time, corruptions arise, and it gradually...
Through mutual defilement and habituation, they likewise transform into what is called "fame. For the sake of seeking fame and profit, their wholesome mind immediately vanishes;

they then preach the Buddha’s precepts before kings and officials, relying upon that power to suppress their own companions and arbitrarily grant the two assemblies of monastics—bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—as well as the bodhisattva precepts to others.
My son, while living at home, the two assemblies [of monks and laypeople] engage in various activities that create bonds, entanglements, and lack of liberation;
like a prisoner in a jail, they cannot escape suffering. Like soldiers or slaves, they cannot act according to their own will.
It is also like the parasites within a lion’s body that eat the lion’s own flesh—no other external parasites can eat the lion’s flesh. Thus it is with the lion.
The lion is the king among beasts; what creature would dare approach to eat the lion’s flesh?
It is the worms within the lion’s own body that eat the flesh of the lion’s body, not other external worms.
Such examples correctly explain the destruction of the Dharma, clarifying the meaning of the lion metaphor. Thus it is said: "O Son of the Buddha."
It is those who destroy the Buddha-dharma themselves; how could it be that external paths or celestial Māras outside the Triple Gem can destroy this Buddha-dharma?
Rather, it is those within the Buddha-dharma who destroy it themselves, just like the worms within a lion's body that eat the lion's own flesh.
If one "receives from the Buddha," this refers to a person who has received the Buddha-precepts and ought to protect them.
Relying on the Buddha’s precepts for protection is like being connected by the ancestral bloodline to an only son;
it is a matter of supreme urgency—how could one ever lose them? To lose them would mean having no refuge. Protecting the precepts is also like serving one's parents;
to violate or break them is unfiliality, and the gravity of such a sin is beyond words. Yet, as soon as a Bodhisattva hears of external [distractions]...
When a wicked person utters a single evil word slandering the sound of the Buddha’s precepts, it is just like three hundred spears piercing one's heart;
its pain is as difficult to endure. It is no different from a thousand blades and ten thousand staves striking and beating one's body—their pain is equally unbearable.
Rather than [suffering such], one would prefer to take responsibility and enter hell oneself to undergo [retribution] for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of...

Eons are long and extremely painful; one would not even wish to hear the suffering sound of slandering the Buddha, let alone personally destroying the Buddha-dharma or providing the causes and conditions for others to destroy it.
This is further an act of extreme lack of filial piety and a state devoid of a filial heart. If one intentionally commits such an act, they incur a minor offense of defilement.
These nine precepts should be studied; they should be reverently upheld.
Thus, the nine precepts are concluded. One should study them with the intent to practice them;

one should reverently uphold them, being exhorted to act with respect and caution, and to maintain them firmly without loss. The above concludes the explanation of the forty-eight minor rules. Below is the summary.
The Characteristics of the Precepts: O Sons of the Buddha, you should receive and uphold these forty-eight minor precepts. All Bodhisattvas of the past have recited them;
all Bodhisattvas of the future shall recite them; and all Bodhisattvas of the present are now reciting them.
The various Buddha-sons collectively address the person: these forty-eight phrases summarize the Dharma in order to exhort them to receive and uphold it.
The preceding several phrases cite those of like practice to encourage recitation; this refers to the forty-eight minor precepts.
It is not that I alone am exhorting you new learners to recite and uphold this;
rather, all bodhisattvas of the past have already recited it, all bodhisattvas of the future shall recite it, and you, the bodhisattvas of the present, are now reciting it.

This concludes the text of the "Section on the True Doctrine. This corresponds to the second part of the "Recitation of the Precepts" (Uposatha) for human beings, which summarizes the characteristics of the precepts. Below...

The section on the dissemination of the teaching has three parts: first, the dissemination of the fundamental precepts; second, a summary of this chapter; and third, a general praise of the dissemination. Listen, O sons of the Buddha!
These ten grave and forty-eight light precepts have been recited by all Buddhas of the three periods of time—those of the past, those of the present, and those yet to come. Now...

Recite: I now recite in this same manner. You, the entire great assembly—including kings, princes, the hundred officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, and laywomen who have received and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts—should receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe this scroll of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature precepts.
Let it circulate through the three periods of time, transforming all sentient beings, generation after generation.
It shall not be severed. You shall behold a thousand Buddhas, with each Buddha extending a hand to the next. In every lifetime you shall not fall into the evil realms or the eight difficulties;
you shall always be reborn among humans or in the heavens. Now, beneath this tree, I briefly expound the Dharma-precepts of the Seven Buddhas for you, the great assembly.
"You should single-mindedly study the Prātimokṣa and joyfully practice it, as explained in detail in each instance within the 'Exhortation to Study' in the *Vimaladevaputraparivarta*.
At that time, the three thousand scholars who were seated listening heard the Buddha recite this himself;
they took it to heart with every thought, receiving and upholding it with leaping joy."
"O sons of the Buddhas, listen," and so forth, means: "O sons of the Buddhas, you must listen to what I shall say.
This dharma of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts has indeed been transmitted and recited by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The Buddhas of the past have already recited it; the Buddhas of the future shall recite it; and the Buddhas of the present are now reciting it. Therefore, I..."
Now, following the example of all the Buddhas, you should likewise recite it in this manner. How could all of you in this great assembly not recite it thus?

Whether they be benevolent rulers such as kings and princes, virtuous ministers among the civil and military officials, the pure community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, or faithful laymen and laywomen—everyone [should do so].
Those who receive and uphold these ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of the Bodhisattva should internalize them all within their hearts, maintaining them without loss.
They should study and read them every morning, recite them every day, and explain their meaning to others.

Whether by hand-copying or transcribing this scroll of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature precepts, they should cause it to be widely propagated and circulated, so that for those of the past, present, and future—
How is it that all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time are transformed and transformed by one another in succession,
never allowing this process to be severed? It is because one desires to enable all sentient beings to behold a thousand Buddhas, with each Buddha extending a hand to the next,

so that they are certain not to fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficult conditions, and are certain to be constantly reborn within the human and celestial realms, extinguishing their sins, acquiring merit, and attaining greatness.
It is for the benefit of others; it is for the sake of both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
As for the phrase "I, now," it means that I, Śākyamuni, am currently here beneath this Bodhi tree, manifesting the attainment of enlightenment and turning the Great Wheel of Dharma.
This is merely a brief exposition of the wondrous and virtuous precepts transmitted by the seven Buddhas of the past. You, the great assembly, should apply yourselves single-mindedly to this.
You should train your minds in this Prātimokṣa, which preserves the precepts of liberation. For this reason, I exhort you:
joyfully practice it and do not be indolent. This has been but a brief explanation;

the meaning is fully and extensively elucidated in the "Chapter on the King of Non-Form" within the Great Section, specifically in the section on exhorting study. Three thousand scholars were present in the assembly.
The bodhisattvas— referring collectively to the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, as well as monastics and laypeople— along with those listening in the assembly at that time,
all received the Buddha’s recitation of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts upon their hearts and heads with deep reverence.
Rejoice and receive this with diligence, guarding it well so that it is not lost. This concludes the first section on the circulation of the fundamental precepts.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha finished preaching the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Precepts within the Section on the Mind-Ground Dharma-Door of Vairocana Buddha in the World of the Superior Lotus-Pedestal Treasury. The same applies to the thousands of billions of Śākyas.

It is said: from the palace of the celestial king Maheśvara down to this dwelling place beneath the Bodhi tree, the discourse on preaching the Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas and the inexpressibly vast assembly is likewise to be received, upheld, recited, and its meaning explained.
Throughout the worlds of hundreds of thousands of millions, the Lotus Treasury World, and worlds as numerous as motes of dust—

the heart-treasury of all Buddhas, the earth-treasury, the precept-treasury, the treasury of immeasurable practices and vows, and the eternally abiding treasury of the Buddha-nature of cause and effect—
when all such treasuries of immeasurable dharmas spoken by all Buddhas were completed, they were received and upheld by all sentient beings within those hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds.
They joyfully received and practiced it. As for the detailed characteristics of the mind-ground, they are as explained in the "Seven Practices" chapter of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-rāja-sūtra*.
The phrase "at that time" refers to the occasion when the aforementioned entrustment was made to the great assembly to hear and receive the Dharma of the mind-ground precepts. It says:
The Tathāgata who is the emanation of Śākyamuni, the Teacher of this Sahā world, has thus fully expounded the principles and phenomena of each individual practice—

the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of the Precepts— from within the chapter on the Mind-Ground Dharma-Door transmitted by Vairocana Buddha in the World of the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury. Now, the thousand billion Śākyamunis...
The emanated Buddhas likewise all taught without deviation from what was spoken by the Teacher of this Sahā world. Yet,
they all proceeded from the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara to this site beneath the Bodhi tree and to their various dwelling places,
where they preached the Dharma-discourses for the sake of all bodhisattvas and an inexpressible multitude of great assemblies— such as these great assemblies.

Each shall receive, uphold, read, and recite it; each shall understand and expound its meaning and flavor, no differently than the great assembly in this Sahā world receives, upholds, and explains it.
Not only this, but all the Buddhas who speak throughout the thousands of billions of worlds, even down to the Buddhas within worlds as small as motes of dust—all these Buddhas speak thus.
The treasury of the thirty minds; the treasury of the ten grounds; the treasury of the one hundred and eight precepts consisting of the ten grave and forty-eight light offenses;

the treasury of the immeasurable practices performed by sages and saints; the treasury of immeasurable vows; the treasury of causes cultivated through a hundred kalpas; the treasury of the fruit of attaining equal and perfect enlightenment;
and the treasury of the eternal abiding nature of the Buddha-nature within all sentient beings. These eight kinds are collectively referred to as the [eight] treasuries.
Regarding "Treasury" (Pitaka): it means that these eight treasuries are vast and expansive, encompassing all; they are perfectly integrated and universally inclusive.
Thus, they represent the ultimate culmination of all the immeasurable Dharma-treasuries taught by all Buddhas, such as this *Cittabhūmi* [Mind-Ground].
Within hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds, all sentient beings receive, uphold, and rejoice in them, practicing each one accordingly, just as in this case.

The realms and sentient beings are equal and without distinction. Such is the general outline of how the Original Buddha, the Traces-Buddha, and the Buddha of the Traces of Traces preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
If one were to extensively open the ground of the mind and explain each and every aspect of these meanings, it would be found within the great scriptures;
for instance, it is explained in detail in the "Seven Practices Chapter" of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-rāja-saptapada-paṭala*.
Each and every aspect of the stages of the mind (*cittabhūmi*) and the aspects of immeasurable practices and vows (*caryāpraṇidhāna*) are fully perfected.
These two [verses] summarize this chapter.
One who possesses strong patience and wisdom, And is able to uphold such a Dharma as this, Until the attainment of the Buddha-way—
One securely obtains five kinds of benefits: First, the Buddhas of the ten directions Compassionately regard and constantly protect one.
Second, at the time of death, With right view, the mind is joyful. Third, in every place of rebirth, one becomes A companion to all bodhisattvas.
Fourth, the accumulation of merit— The perfection of ethical discipline—is fully accomplished.
"Fifth, in this life and future lives, / The nature-precepts, merit, and wisdom will be fulfilled. / These are the sons of the Buddhas;
/ The wise and those of clear insight reflect well.
This praises and encourages the benefits of maintaining the precepts. "Those of clear insight" refers to those who have transcended [the mundane].
Transcending the category of ordinary beings, they possess the two kinds of powerful virtues—the power of patience and the power of wisdom—which enable them to protect the essence of the precepts;
it is for this reason that they are able to uphold such a Dharma. Such a person will certainly attain Buddhahood in the future.
Furthermore, even before attaining the Buddha-way, one will first securely obtain five kinds of extraordinary benefits. What are these five benefits?

First, those who possess patience, wisdom, and uphold the precepts will be moved by the compassionate mindfulness and protective guardianship of the Buddhas of the ten directions, ensuring that they advance on the path without demonic interference and succeed in perpetuating the lineage of the Buddhas. Second, those who possess patience and wisdom...
1. A person who maintains the precepts attains right knowledge and vision at the time of death and gives rise to joy in their heart because they have remained far removed from evil objects.

2. Third, a person who maintains the precepts with patience and wisdom will, in birth after birth and life after life, practice together and dwell together as a constant and beneficial friend to bodhisattvas, because they have remained far removed from evil factions.
3. Fourth, a person who maintains the precepts with patience and wisdom [is endowed with] immeasurable...

This is the collection of the merit of the qualities. One is able to fully accomplish all the perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), for there is not a single dharma that is not fulfilled.

Fifth, the person who possesses patience, wisdom, and maintains ethical discipline—from this point forward—will have the essence of their natural ethical discipline and their merit and wisdom become perfect, being called the "Honored One with Two Feet.
Of these, the first four are causes and the last one is the fruit; these five kinds of benefits constitute the maintenance of ethical discipline.
O sons of the Buddha, those who possess the power of patience and wisdom, and who are wise, should contemplate, deliberate, and realize this through diligent practice.
Those who calculate in terms of a self and cling to signs cannot believe in this Dharma; nor can those who seek realization by extinguishing their lifespan.

Nor is it a place for sowing seeds; yet, if one wishes to grow the sprout of Bodhi, one should contemplate with serene stillness that the light illuminates the world. One should observe the true nature of all phenomena:
they are neither born nor extinguished, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither identical nor different, and neither coming nor going.
Thus, within this single mind, one should diligently adorn it through skillful means;

that which a bodhisattva ought to do should be studied in its proper sequence. Regarding those in training and those beyond training, do not give rise to conceptual discrimination—this is called the foremost path, and it is also called the Mahāyāna, free from all conceptual proliferation and evil.
All [defilements] are extinguished from this source; the *sarvajñā* of all Buddhas likewise emerges entirely from this source.

Those who harbor notions of a self—referring to non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) who cling to signs and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)—are unable to believe in this pure dharma of the precepts, which is held without grasping and received without receiving. It is not only ordinary people [who fail to do so].

Those who are externally incapable—namely, the śrāvakas and followers of the two vehicles who are addicted to emptiness, extinguish their life-span, guard silence, and grasp at realization—are likewise not places where the seeds of bodhi can take root;
