they are what are called "scorched sprouts and ruined seeds. Because they do not engage in skillful reflection, they have no share [in this].
Even if they should desire to nurture the roots and shoots of bodhi so that the light of knowledge and the clarity of wisdom may illuminate them, [they remain incapable].

One who observes the world should, within this precept of the mind-ground, calmly contemplate and minutely examine the principle of the true nature of phenomena—the essence of the precepts—which is authentic and without falsehood.
This essence of the precepts of true reality does not belong to arising through conditions, nor does it belong to ceasing through conditions;
it is not like the arising and ceasing of ordinary beings, nor does it belong to permanence. Nor is it...
It belongs to cessation. It is not like the heterodox views of annihilationism or eternalism; its categories are so distinct that they cannot be combined, yet it is not manifold.
Its essence is so unified that it cannot be divided, yet it is not singular. When one moves toward it, one knows not whence it comes, for it fundamentally does not arrive.

When one pursues it, one knows not whither it goes, for it fundamentally does not depart. It is not like the dharmas of cultivation and realization of the two vehicles. Such is the precept of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Within the essence of the one mind, one should give rise to various skillful wisdoms and expedient means, and diligently cultivate the adornments of merit through myriad practices.
Such dual adornment of merit and wisdom is not something that can be achieved by ordinary people, externalists, or those of the two vehicles.
This is indeed the arousal of the Mahāyāna mind and the reception of the Mahāyāna precepts, which is what all bodhisattvas ought to do.

Furthermore, one should study and practice in successive stages according to the Dharma, investigating and severing delusions. When there are dharmas to be studied, one should not give rise to thoughts of discrimination;
when investigation has exhausted all delusions and there are no further dharmas to be studied, one likewise does not give rise to thoughts of discrimination.
The mind is neither divided into existence nor distinguished as non-existence; this is called the Way of the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

It is also called the Mahāyāna, the Great Vehicle. In this manner, all the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and unwholesome dharmas of ordinary beings, outsiders, and those of the Hīnayāna enter into this single path of the great governance of the Mahāyāna, yet they are not melted away.

They are thus transformed, all of them extinguished without remainder. The wondrous fruits of the Buddhas' wisdom, supernormal powers, samādhis, and sarvajñā (all-knowledge) all manifest clearly from within this single path of the Mahāyāna Great Dharma, without the slightest deficiency.
This dharma of the mind-ground precepts can skillfully deliberate; it immediately extinguishes transgressions and gives rise to goodness.
One attains great benefit; such is the case.

Therefore, all you sons of the Buddha, you should rouse great valor and maintain the pure precepts of the Buddhas as if they were bright jewels. The bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in this.
Those of the future shall study; those of the present are studying now.
This is the sphere of the Buddha's conduct, praised by the Holy Lord. I have explained it in accordance with that truth.
May this immeasurable mass of merit be dedicated to all sentient beings, so that together we may proceed toward omniscience. May all who hear this Dharma [attain it].
"Because one quickly attains the path of Buddhahood,
those who are equal [to the Buddhas]... This means that since there is such benefit in extinguishing evil and generating goodness,
all the sons of the Buddha should accordingly resolve upon the Great Mind and exert heroic vigor toward the pure precepts and teachings of the Buddhas, skillfully practicing them.
Protect and maintain it as if it were a bright pearl; do not allow it to be damaged or defiled.
Only then is one a true child of the Buddha, upholding the Vajra Jewel Precepts of the Radiance within the Mind-Ground.
Regarding the phrase "the past," etc., it means that this Great Precept Sūtra is that which the Bodhisattvas of the past who have already realized the fruit studied. And...
Future bodhisattvas who have not yet realized the fruit shall study herein; the present bodhisattvas are now studying herein.

This is truly the sphere of practice for all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and it is that which the Honored Master Śākyamuni praises and extols. As for the phrase "I and others," it means that I, too, [have studied herein].
In accordance with what all Buddhas have taught, one should praise the immeasurable accumulation of vast merit and the immeasurable accumulation of vast virtue within the precepts of the mind-ground.

One should dedicate these toward all sentient beings of the three periods of time, causing them to turn toward the wondrous wisdom of suchness throughout the entire dharma-realm. Furthermore, may all who hear such sublime goodness of the Great Vehicle...
Regarding the precepts: all shall swiftly realize the Truth and early on attain the Buddha-way, perfecting the ocean of fruition.
These three [verses] collectively praise the circulation [of the teaching].
Among the thirty-seven minor [offenses], there are the eight difficulties.
Regarding "if there are national calamities" and so forth: this refers to if within a kingdom these eight difficulties exist.
First, an evil king who does not believe in the Triple Gem. Second, the terrain of the land is uneven and subject to constant change.

Third, the difficulty of dense vegetation inhabited by lions, tigers, wolves, and other predatory beasts. Fourth, the danger of being swept away by floods. Fifth, the danger of being consumed by fire.

The difficulty of [being born as] a hungry ghost is the fifth. The difficulty of being buffeted by winds is the sixth. The difficulty of bandits plotting to seize one's wealth and take one's life is the seventh.
The difficulty of venomous snakes and malevolent insects on the road is the eighth. Regarding the phrase "all difficulties" (*sarvavighna*):
this merely mentions the aforementioned eight difficulties in brief; were they expanded upon, they would be many. In all such places of difficulty, none are permissible.
[The text] enters [the next section].
The Buddha-spoken Brahmajāla Sūtra, Scroll Lower (End). Following the Vermilion Edition.
